en: Now begins the first chapter of the seventh book,
in the dialogue between Yudhiṣṭhira and Nārada.
The King said:
O Brahmana, the Blessed Lord himself is equal toward all beings, dear to them, and their well-wisher;
how is it that for the sake of Indra, he slew the Daityas like one who is partial?
Śrīdhara:
I bow to the wondrous Nṛsiṃha, whose form is supreme bliss, who tears asunder the enemies of his devotees through his partiality for his own followers.
Now, *ūti* (impulse) is described in the seventh chapter across fifteen sections.
*Ūti* is said to be *vāsanā* (latent impression), which follows various actions;
it is twofold—unwholesome and wholesome—due to the distinction in its causes.
Impurity arises from the anger of the great, while purity arises from their favor;
this is just as it was for the two who dwell in Vaikuṇṭha at the gateway of Hari.
The impure latent impressions, such as hatred toward Viṣṇu born from anger at being cast from the four seats,
remained steadfast even while Prahlāda was within the womb of a demoness.
Through the grace of Nārada, a latent disposition toward true devotion for Viṣṇu arose within him;
and Viṣṇu always protects his own devotee, even if that devotee is hostile.
Then, in his third birth, he made the two gatekeepers his own;
therefore, a wise person should exert effort in favoring the great.
For this purpose, the definition of the *ūtis* is stated here;
first, among those, there are ten according to the distinctions in the minds of the Daityas and their sons.
The distinction between the latent impressions arising from great anger and those arising from compassion is now explained;
and for one whose mind is purified, virtuous latent impressions are joined with their actions.
Therefore, the determination of Dharma is made by five outsiders;
therein, in the first chapter, [concerning] the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu.
However, hostility toward a devotee of Viṣṇu is said to arise from the curse of a Brahmin.
As it was stated at the end of the previous section: "Diti, whose sons had been slain by Viṣṇu while he acted as Śakra’s rear-guard,
burning with a fire of grief and fury, reflected thus."

Having heard that, Parīkṣit, filled with wonder, asks in three verses beginning with "sama" (equal). For there can be no partiality in one who is truly equal and a friend; nor is it fitting for one who is dear to show partiality toward those who bestow affection—this is the meaning. ||1||
The Seventh Sandarbha: Śrī Kṛṣṇa is victorious!
In this seventh Sandarbha, a compendium of the various Sandarbhas is being composed; by whose instruction this is done, He is my sole refuge, for I have no other resort.

The Blessed Lord is equal by virtue of being the Supreme Self; He is a friend who acts for the welfare [of others] and is beloved, being the object of affection. This being so, since everyone is equally entitled to His assistance and equally the object of His love, how is it that He acted as if with partiality by slaying the Daityas? This was not a perception of partiality, nor was He like one who is unfriendly or unloving.
And thus it is said. ||1||
Viśvanātha: Salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa!
Having bowed again to my venerable guru and to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the ocean of compassion, I take refuge in that Śrī Śuka, the protector of the world and the eye of the universe.
To the one who is dearer than life to Gopā and Rāmājanā, the exceedingly powerful Lord,
I offer myself and my own self for the sake of being His beloved servant.
In this context, *vāsanā* is here called *ūti*; it is said to be twofold in the seventh [chapter]:
both inauspicious and auspicious, according to the degree of favor toward the virtuous.

The peaceful are also of three kinds: those who possess pure devotion, those who maintain devotion mixed with knowledge and other qualities, and those who are said to possess knowledge mixed with that [devotion].
The auspicious latent impression (vāsanā) that belonged to Hiraṇyakaśipu was innate;
the cause for that was indeed his former anger toward Sananda and the others.
His son was that most excellent Prahrāda,
whose latent impression for pure devotion arose from the abundance of the grace of Śrī Nārada’s feet.
Having protected that offense against the virtuous arising from the elephant through the favor of the good,
he constructed a great enclosure with the stones of dejection, pride, and the like.
The creeper of devotion should be nurtured by men through the watering of the water from the lotus-feet and other such offerings;
thus, in this tenth chapter, one should perceive the absolute perfection of devotion.
In this work of five chapters, I shall demonstrate how devotion is primary while other qualities are subordinate,
and how such devotion is attainable from a guru who possesses it, within a setting suited for it.
In the three [chapters], love, tranquility, and devotion are respectively declared;
thus the fifteenth chapter, the seventh [section], is well-served.
In that regard, however, at the outset, the sage, warding off any notion of partiality on Viṣṇu’s part,
briefly related the story of his two attendants, who were born from the three qualities.
At the end of the previous section:
Diti, whose son had been slain by Viṣṇu acting as Śakra’s rear-guard,
burned with the fire of her grief and reflected in her fury.

Thus, as if unable to endure Viṣṇu’s partiality characterized by favoritism toward Indra, he spoke with three verses beginning with "sama" (equal), in order to taste from the very mouth of that great sage—who had himself realized the established truth—the nectar of the resolution: "How can there be partiality for one who is equal? and "How can there be partiality for one who is dear? etc.
How is it that there is an absence of affection among the asuras, and how is it that they lack friendliness toward their friends? (1)
For the purpose of this [teaching], whose essence is the supreme good, is not directly for the hosts of gods;
nor is there any hatred toward the asuras, for it is free from all defects and thus devoid of agitation.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, one becomes a partisan of those from whom one's purpose is accomplished, and one slays with hatred those from whom one fears; however, none of this applies here, as he says: "For not...
He whose self (ātman) is his very nature (svarūpa), which is supreme bliss alone—that is, liberation (niḥśreyasa)—and who has no agitation toward the Asuras.
There is no fear; therefore, there is also certainly no hatred. The reason for this is: "of one who is devoid of qualities.
The meaning is that affection and aversion are dependent upon qualities. ||2||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Nor should it be said that he favors that [path] because happiness cannot be achieved for him by Indra and the other gods;
thus he says "no. That whose nature (*ātman*) is supreme bliss (*niḥśreyasa*) itself.

The sense is that someone else might bring about his happiness; nor would there be suffering for him caused by the Asuras and others who cause agitation, because of which he would feel hatred toward them. Thus he says: "Not at all. There is no agitation from the Asuras, and therefore no hatred. The reason for this is: "Because he is devoid of qualities" (aguṇasya). ||2||
"—O highly fortunate one! Thus, regarding the qualities of Nārāyaṇa, a very great doubt has arisen within us; therefore, you ought to dispel it."
Śrīdhara: Regarding the qualities of Śrī Nārāyaṇa, such as grace, restraint, and so forth—[resolve] that very doubt. ||3||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: With respect to qualities such as favor (anugraha), restraint (nigraha), and so forth. ||3||
The venerable sage said: "Well asked, O Great King, regarding the wonderful life of Hari."
That which is the majesty of the Bhāgavata, which increases devotion to the Blessed One.
It is sung as supremely meritorious by sages such as Nārada and others;
having bowed to the sage Kṛṣṇa, I shall relate the story of Hari.
Śrīdhara: The connection is that the greatness of Prahlāda, the devotee of the Bhāgavata, is being sung.
"To Kṛṣṇa Vyāsa" means having bowed to the sage Kṛṣṇa. ||4-5||
The sequence of the composition: "Well asked," thus it is connected together. O Great King!

That which has been asked is indeed well-considered; however, the pastimes of Hari are wonderful and unprecedented, appearing as if inconsistent even though they are not, because they transcend rational inquiry—whatever [is manifested] wherever.

The account of Hari increases devotion to the Lord; it contains the majesty of the *Bhāgavata* and the majesty of the multitude of devotees headed by the illustrious Prahlāda. By this, it is shown that the Lord performs everything solely for the sake of the *Bhāgavata*, and not for any other purpose.

It is indicated that the culmination of this very subject matter will occur [in the following]. And the commentary [states] by the words "through partiality toward His own devotees," and so forth. Therefore, regarding the phrase "it is sung": the connection is made by supplying the relative pronoun *yā* and the demonstrative pronoun *tām*, such that it refers to "that story which is sung in such a way as to be supremely meritorious."

And here, by the fact that it is being sung by them, it is indicated that its sole purpose is the happiness of the devotees alone; [this is expressed in] the half-verse beginning with "not however" (na tv iti). ||4-5||
Viśvanātha: Since the deeds of Hari must necessarily be recounted as the answer to whatever question is asked, [this work] is sung for Kṛṣṇa and Vyāsa. ||4-5||
For although the Blessed One is devoid of qualities, unborn, unmanifest, and beyond primordial nature (prakṛti),
he enters into the qualities of his own māyā and assumes the state of the oppressor and the oppressed.
"Madhva: Salutations to the venerable Gurus.

It is proclaimed in the *Bhaviṣyat-parvan* that Hari, though eternally situated in the state of being subject to sublation and so forth, is nevertheless not subject to sublation because He is endowed with freedom from defects."

Śrīdhara: Because He is beyond primordial nature (*prakṛti*), He is therefore devoid of the *guṇas*. For that very reason, He is unborn (*aja*). For that very reason, He is unmanifest (*avyakta*), being free from the body, senses, and so forth, which serve as the causes for passion, hatred, and the like.
Even He, having entered and presided over His own *māyā*—the *guṇas* such as *sattva* and the rest—for the sake of those who are bound; or else, [He does so]...
He has gone to—that is, attained—the state of mutual oppression and being oppressed between the gods and the asuras; the meaning is that the cause for this has arisen. ||6||

The sequence of the composition: therein, he first provides a question and answer that correspond precisely to the implied meaning—beginning with "though devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇo’pi*). "Devoid of qualities" means free from the material qualities (*prākṛta-guṇa*). For this very reason, he is "unborn" (*aja*), eternally established.
And for this same reason, he is "unmanifest" (*avyakta*); because he is devoid of a material body, senses, and so forth, he is not manifested by anything else.

The meaning is that his body and so forth are self-luminous. Consequently, the implication is that he is free from attachment, aversion, and the like toward the qualities of *prakṛti*. Even though he is of such a nature, there exists within him a quality appropriate for the *māyā*—that is, compassion—which consists of grace toward his own devotees; this quality is pure, consisting of the delight of divine play (*līlā-kautuka*), and is known as the attained *sattva*.

Having entered and taken hold [of them] by her, the Blessed One— though eternally manifesting the sixfold sovereign powers (*ṣaḍguṇaiśvarya*)— is also indicated here as having, at times, been born, and though manifest within the senses of the world, having fallen into the state of being the oppressor and the oppressed; that is, at times being oppressed and defeated by the *asuras*, and at other times...
The meaning is that He has attained victory over their obstructiveness.

Here, even though there is another sense [to the word], because the work was commenced solely for the purpose of bestowing grace upon the Bhāgavatas, and because it will be concluded in that same way, and because of the commonality of the underlying intent (*gati-sāmānya*), this is so despite its being produced by *māyā* consisting of deception.
Furthermore, because it would entail the occurrence of excessive defects, that [objection] is not taken into account.

Therefore, since there is an absence of attachment and aversion toward anything other than His own spontaneous play—which has as its sole purpose the diversion of His devotees—there is no partiality here; this is the intended meaning. For this very reason, even that which is subject to sublation is treated as a sublater.

It was stated simultaneously that, by manifesting the play characterized as the expansion of His own essential nature and power (*nija-svarūpa-śakti-vilāsa*), the welfare of all beings is ultimately achieved, and thus His qualities such as friendliness (*suhṛttva*) and so forth do not diminish; this is what Viśvanātha has suggested: having entered and presided over His own *māyā*-quality of goodness (*sattva*) and the rest, [He remains] subject to bondage.

The meaning is that "having become an obstructer" (bādhakatvaṃ gataḥ) means that the state characterized by mutual obstruction and being obstructed among the qualities has been superimposed upon the Blessed Lord, who is the presiding deity of the qualities. ||6||
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the qualities of primordial nature (prakṛti), not of the self (ātman);
nor, O King, do they ever diminish or increase simultaneously.

Śrīdhara: If the qualities were His own, He would be subject to partiality and inequality, like an ordinary person; however, that is not the case, as he says: "The mode of goodness... Now, one might object: even if He governs the qualities by His own will, there would still be partiality and inequality. This is not so; because such [partiality] is caused by time, he says: "not of them..."
Thus, with the half-verse [ending], there is an "exaltation" (*ullāsa*) due to increase. ||7||

The Sequence of Exposition: Now, one might raise the following doubts: How is it that even this quality called *viśuddha-sattva* (pure goodness) is not material (*prākṛta*)? When and where does it transmit its excellence of potency (*vīryātiśaya*)? And how is it that the fallacy of the loss of what has been done (*kṛtahāni*) or the acquisition of what has not been done (*akṛtābhyāgama*) does not arise? Having raised such questions regarding it...

He establishes the relationship of the sublated and the sublator by means of two [verses]. As for those three qualities—sattva and the rest—they do not possess that nature (tadīyatva), nor do they have an entry into it (tad-āveśa), nor are they eternally in a single state;
because, in the preceding verse, the word "his" (tasya) and "entering" (āviśya) were used specifically to show that among those qualities, one or another [is predominant].

It was stated that "having entered his own *māyā*-quality," but it was not said that he does so by means of the qualities of *māyā* as an external adjunct; this is what is expressed by the half-verse beginning with "sattva. The meaning is that while qualities such as *sattva* belong only to *prakṛti* and not to the Self—the Supreme Lord—those qualities of His which are eternally manifest are not of that nature. That...
It has been said:
"O Lord, He in whom the primal qualities such as *sattva* and the rest do not exist—that primordial Person, pure beyond all that is pure, may He be gracious. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.9.44)
Bliss, existence, and consciousness—these three are unified in You, who abide as the foundation of all;
yet in You, who are devoid of the material qualities (guṇas), there is no mixture of pleasure and pain.
Statements such as these have been shown in the works of the Blessed One.

"Not theirs" refers to the [senses] and so forth; because those do not belong to the Self, for that very reason there is neither simultaneous contraction nor expansion. Rather, because they are subject to modification, they mutually suppress one another.
The meaning is that for some there is decline at some time, and for others there is exaltation at some time.
Consequently, he demonstrates the fitness of the gods and others for assisting Him, and of the asuras and others for fighting against Him. ||7||

Viśvanātha: But the Blessed Lord is indeed equal everywhere in His essential nature; thus he says: "Sattva," etc. These are the qualities of *prakṛti* alone, and not of the Self, the Blessed Lord. The sense is that although *prakṛti* is His own power (*sva-śakti*), it does not constitute His essential nature (*svarūpa*). ||7||
At the time of a being’s victory, he resorts to the celestial sages when it is characterized by *sattva*, the asuras when by *rajas*,
and the yakṣas and rakṣasas when by *tamas*, according to the conditions of that particular time.

Śrīdhara: During the period of the predominance of *sattva*, he worshipped the gods and the sages; the meaning is that, having entered their respective bodies, he causes them to prosper. During the period of the predominance of *rajas*, [he worshipped] the asuras. During the period of the predominance of *tamas*, [he worshipped] the yakṣas and rākṣasas. Thus, he acted in accordance with that particular time. (8)

The sequence of the composition: likewise, at the time of the manifestation of *sattva* and the other qualities, that which is perceived as the dependence of His pastimes upon those [qualities] is not avoided by merely restating it; for when *sattva* triumphs, the Lord worships and does worship the gods and the sages, manifesting His own self through the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of *sattva* within their respective bodies.

The meaning is that he transfers his splendor (*tejas*), by which he makes them his allies. In this way, it should be applied as follows: at the time of conquering *rajas*, [he transfers it] to the Asuras, characterized by *rajas*; at the time of conquering *tamas*, [he transfers it] to the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, characterized by *tamas*. And thus, by means of that [splendor], he causes those Yakṣas and others to fight back.
The meaning is that the Blessed One, while performing [this], defeats the gods and others, yet He also manifests Himself in that same way.

Thus, it has been shown that for the sake of the variety of pastimes (*līlā*) which nourish the mellows of devotion (*bhakti-rasa*), He enters into the relationship of the oppressor and the oppressed. And as it is heard regarding the churning of the Ocean of Milk:
Likewise, Viṣṇu entered the Asuras in an asura-form, rousing their strength and heroism,
while simultaneously inflaming the hosts of the gods.
"By fate, he who was of an ignorant nature [attained] the state of the Lord of Serpents" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 8.7.12).
Even here, for the sake of that very variety, it would follow that his respective absorption into those states occurs in such a way;
however, would this not result in a loss of His sovereign play due to His dependence on time, which awakens those various qualities?

Furthermore, suspecting that there might be an obvious inequality and so forth due to the excessive connection with the qualities (*guṇas*), he says: "conforming to their respective times" (*tat-kālānuguṇa*).

This means that His [the Lord's] nature conforms to the very time of those [qualities], such as *sattva* and the rest; He is "equal" (*samasaḥ*) in the same way that one speaks of "the feet of the Blessed One."

While He plays at His own will, there is Time itself, which is eternally subservient to Him; by that Māyā, following His lead, the aggregate of worldly activities— which has flowed in a stream established from beginningless time— is impelled and set in motion as the specific manifestations of His own functions, consisting of the qualities of *sattva* and the rest.

The meaning is that he becomes dependent upon that. It has been illustrated that time is a function of *māyā* in such passages as "Time is destiny" (*kālo daivam*) [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.63.26], wherein it is said, "This is Your *māyā*.
Alternatively, even their time is always followed by [Your power].

The meaning is: he is one whose characteristic power (*prabhāva*) consists of spontaneous activity solely for the purpose of bestowing grace upon his devotees. Furthermore, the implication is that even beyond that, He brings about various manifestations through *māyā* in accordance with those very activities.
As it has been said: "O Lord who has manifested bonds, they say that this which is time is Your own activity."

"By which the universe acts" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.3.26). Thus, in both ways, it follows that there is no dependence on another. In this very manner, the venerable Kapiladeva also said: "That which is the twenty-fifth is time" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.26.15); some call this power the prowess of the Person (puruṣa), while others call it time.

And regarding the statement, "From whom fear [arises]" (Bhāgavatapurāṇa 3.26.16), he has presented two views therein: that [the world] is manifested by Māyā, and that it is an attribute of the Puruṣa.
And in this regard, His activity, which is the primary function of His power, exists solely for the delight of His devotees.
However, since the effects such as the awakening of qualities (*guṇa*) occur therein by themselves alone, there is merely an appearance of activity (*pravṛtty-ābhāsa*).

Consequently, the former part [of time] is itself [the Self], and is thus the play (*vilāsa*) of the power of essential nature (*svarūpa-śakti*). The latter part, however, consists precisely of that appearance and is therefore contained within *māyā*, the power of manifestation (*ābhāsa-śakti*). This is what is called "time" (*kāla*).

In passages such as Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.3.26, it should be understood that the statement "the twinkling of an eye, etc. is intended precisely to express the non-difference between the two. Therefore, it should be explained as follows: just as a servant who follows another servant is called an *anubhṛtya* (a subordinate servant), so too in that case, the quality characterized by its power (*tat-prabhāva-lakṣaṇa*) follows [the primary quality].
The quality (guṇa) is of the nature of a manifestation and is thus subordinate; likewise, time is also subordinate to them, and not a direct quality of that which possesses them. ||7||

Viśvanātha: Therefore, the apparent partiality observed in the Lord everywhere is rooted solely in the partiality of the *guṇas*. And that [partiality] consists in the decrease or increase of the *guṇas*; furthermore, that decrease or increase does not occur simultaneously, but rather sequentially. Thus he says: "Not of them... and so forth.

Diminution is the cause of being sublated, while intensification is the cause of being the sublator. These two—diminution and intensification—are to be inferred from the diminution and intensification of the gods, asuras, and rākṣasas, who arise from [the predominance of] sattva and the other qualities respectively. In that regard, even though there is diminution and intensification of the qualities, they occur solely due to their inherent dullness (*jāḍya*).
Because it is ineffective [otherwise], he speaks of the Lord’s entry there as the presiding authority with the word "Victory" (*jaya*).

At the time of the victory of *sattva*—that is, at the moment of its predominance—he worshipped the gods and the sages. Just as *sattva* was then predominant, so too was his presiding authority there predominant; thus, he [the Lord] presided over that.

The meaning is that, having entered those respective bodies and increasing their particular power, He afflicts the asuras, rākṣasas, and others. Thus, at the time of the predominance of rajas, He afflicts the asuras; at the time of the predominance of tamas, He afflicts the yakṣas and rākṣasas—being in accordance with and conforming to that specific time. Therefore, even though a particular guṇa may be predominant, time alone is the cause.
But it is not that [person], such is the meaning. ||8||
Like light and so forth, it appears as if inseparable from the aggregate; yet,
having churned [the self], the sages finally know the Self abiding within themselves.
"Janārdana is like honey, curd, ghee, and fire within the stomach; yet he is not known by being separated from the body, the senses, the vital breaths, and the individual soul. Thus it is said. (9)
Śrīdhara: Even though [the Lord] is uniform, there is an illustration for the observed diversity caused by differences in limiting conditions (*nimitta*): like light and so forth.

Just as fire (*jyotis*) appears in wood and the like; just as water appears in vessels; just as space (*ākāśa*) appears in jars and the like; in that same way, the Blessed Lord manifests in various forms.

[Objection: "In that case, why is it not perceived through discrimination in the same way as those [other things]? To this he says: "It is not distinguished from the composite body of wine and so forth; it is not perceived separately. [Question: "If that is so, how is it known that [the self] resorts to them?
To this he says: "The wise perceive..."—that is, the learned ones perceive the Supreme Self abiding within themselves.

Having churned [the intellect] by means of the inferential mark (*liṅga*) consisting in the observation of effects, and having investigated, they know [the truth]. Ultimately, this occurs through the refutation of doctrines such as inherent nature (*svabhāva*), time (*kāla*), and action (*karman*). In the reading "they find" (*vindanti*), "attainment" (*lābha*) is likewise nothing but knowledge.
Here too, it should be understood as being like light and so forth; just as in the case of the sun-gem (*sūryakānta*) and similar objects.

Fire is known from the observation of burning, and wind from the observation of fragrance, and so forth; such is the sequence of the composition. Now, one might ask: why is that fire which pervades those various things not perceived there? To this he says: "Fire. Although it enters into those various things with a portion of its own light, [it remains unperceived].
Because it is a composite and a mixture, it is not distinguished by ordinary people; it cannot be separated [by them].

Nevertheless, those skilled in discernment, having finally churned [the mind],—even while negating impossible meanings such as "assistance" or "fighting with that"—discern it, and through that portion, [they perceive] what resides within the self.
They know—that is, they realize—the Self as the Lord who has entered into each respective self.

In this regard, there is an illustrative example containing a reason: because that [Self] shines forth like objects such as light among the perceivers; the word "among the perceivers" is to be supplied. The meaning is this: just as this is not the light of the jewel, since it was not seen previously.
But rather, it is solar heat alone that has entered here through contact with its rays;

thus, in sun-crystals and the like, that [heat] appears in the experiences of burning cotton and so forth. And just as in the previous case, this odor in the air appears in those [experiences] as being nothing other than earth-element [odor] having entered therein, so it is here as well.
Alternatively, one might ask: "Does He not simply sport by means of His own splendors which enter into various objects here and there?
How then is it observed that He sports with those [objects] as well? To this he says: "Light" (*jyotiḥ*).
Just as when the light of the eyes and other senses illuminates only form (*rūpa*) within its own sphere, the five qualities such as smell (*gandha*) and so forth remain as clay.

Thus it is perceived that "this very thing is manifesting," just as when the auditory faculty and other senses perceive even a mere sound within their own domain through the medium of space (ākāśa), it is perceived as "this is indeed a drum.
And that occurs precisely because of the intermingling of its qualities, not in reality. In the same way, poets [perceive] themselves...

The meaning is that others do not recognize the Lord as being present within each respective aggregate; yet [the yogis] know Him, though He is distinct, as abiding in the self and sporting by means of the splendors of His own parts. ||9||

Viśvanātha: Since the predominance or deficiency of the substratum itself follows from the predominance or deficiency of the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest, he provides an illustration for this: "Just as light [appears] in pieces of wood, water in vessels, and space in jars—in a greater form when they are greater, and in a lesser form when they are lesser."

Even while remaining [in that state], he is not said to be unequal. Likewise, when a being is predominantly established in the divine, he too possesses a superior form among the gods; and at that very time, when the *rajas* is diminished and established in the demonic, he possesses an inferior form there—thus, while the demons are subject to oppression by the gods and the gods are the oppressors of the demons, he too [is so].

He is said to be "one who sides with the gods and oppresses the asuras. Likewise, when rajas is predominant in one who is devoted to the asuras, he too sides with the asuras and oppresses the gods; thus, by worldly convention, even though there is an inequality, the meaning is that it is as if there were no inequality. However, at the time of victory, he resorts excessively to the gods through the predominance of sattva.

Thus, that alone is intended there; that very point is what reveals his partiality for the side of the gods. It should be understood, however, that this does not mean a mere lack of devotion at a time when he was not victorious.

Now, one might object: just as fire and other elements exist within wood and such, yet they are perceived through discrimination as "this is fire in this wood," [so too should devotion be understood].

Is it perceived? To this he says: "From the aggregate"—that is, from the bodies of gods and others—it is not distinguished; the meaning is that it does not appear as something separate, as if it were other than them. If so, how is it known that "he partakes of them"?
To this he says: "The wise," meaning the skillful ones, having churned [the self], perceive the Supreme Self abiding within themselves.

They know through inference based on the sign (*liṅga*) of observing effects; even in the reading "they find" (*vindanti*), which means they discover by ultimately negating doctrines such as those concerning intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and action (*karman*), the meaning is simply that they know.

But surely, the Blessed One, being partial toward Indra and the others, is sometimes perceived by all as slaying the asuras; likewise, when rajas and tamas increase, he might become partial even toward the asuras and others and destroy the gods and so forth— only then would his impartiality be established according to the reasoning stated.

Therefore, he says: "like light and so forth. He explains that very same verse by means of a double entendre (*tantra*) to express another meaning: "just as form, taste, smell, and touch—which belong to light and so forth—manifest clearly within their aggregate, that is, within the substance possessing them."
Something shines forth in such a way that it does not appear clearly as something distinct or separate from its aggregate,
but rather appears only as being inherent within it.
In the very same manner, within this world among gods, asuras, and others, the Blessed One manifests clearly in some places, yet in others he does not.

The meaning is that in some cases it remains contained within that. In that regard, because light is predominantly composed of *sattva* and is non-obstructive, the form residing therein is perceived even at some distance—as in "this milk is white"—or even at a very great distance, such as two hundred thousand leagues, as in "that is the white moon. In that case:

In that regard, what is grasped by the sense of sight appears clearly. Likewise, because beings such as the gods have a predominance of *sattva* and are thus unobscured by it, the Blessed One residing within them—being partial toward that *sattva*—appears very clearly in forms such as Upendra. And just as [in the case] of water and so forth, due to a predominance of *tamas* and *rajas*,...

Due to that obscuration, the sound, taste, smell, and touch residing therein do not appear clearly; however, because there is a slight presence of *sattva* even within *tamas* and *rajas* in the sensory organs (*indriya-golaka*), there is no total absence of obscuration for the contact with the object possessing those qualities. Thus, in the case of the tongue, [the taste] of the object possessing taste...

Yoga itself is the essence (*rasa*). Just as sound exists in the ear only when there is contact with space (*ākāśa*), so too touch is merely the contact of an object possessing coldness and so forth with the skin; and smell is merely the contact of wind possessing fragrance with the nose. In the same way, because the *asuras*, *rākṣasas*, and others are dominated by *rajas* and *tamas*, they are obscured by that [quality].

Therefore, it does not appear clearly that the Blessed One is partial toward that [darkness]. In this regard, just as the sun is obscured or unobscured by clouds or sunlight, so too is the Blessed One’s knowledge [obscured or unobscured] by darkness or sattva.
If that is so, then in the absence of clear manifestation, how can we perceive his partiality toward the side of the asuras and others?
To this he replies: "They know" means they understand by means of the inferential mark (*liṅga*) of not observing effects such as the defeat of the gods;
when the Supreme [Lord], desiring to emit, [creates] the cities from Himself...
By his own māyā, this Lord creates *rajas* separately; desiring to sport in various ways, he impels *sattva*;
and when about to sleep, he impels *tamas*.

Śrīdhara: Thus, it has been stated that this inequality is due to the influence of the qualities of *māyā* and is not inherent; if so, one might suspect a lack of sovereignty because of dependence on the qualities. To address this, he says: when the Supreme Lord (*paraḥ parameśvaraḥ*), desiring to create bodies (*puraḥ śarīrāṇi*) for the experience of the individual soul (*ātmano jīvasya*), then [He creates] through equilibrium (*sāmyena*).

Remaining [in equilibrium], he emits *rajas* separately; when he desires to sport—that is, wishes to play—within those various cities (*pura*), he then emits *sattva* separately. When he is about to lie down—that is, wishing to withdraw [the world]—he then impels *tamas* separately; the meaning is that he urges it forth, bringing it to a state of predominance. ||10||

The Sequence of the Composition: Having thus stated that the purpose [of the Lord] is solely the diversion of His devotees through His own pastimes such as battle, and that the protection of the universe is accomplished from Him spontaneously,

He now extends this principle to the creation and dissolution [of the world], including the Lord's glance toward primordial nature (prakṛti), in order to dispel all doubts regarding these three states.

He also states this without distinction: "When... When, at that time characterized by His own activity, this Supreme Lord (paraḥ parameśvaraḥ), desiring to emanate His own abodes in the form of sādhaka-devotees belonging to previous creations before Himself, through His own māyā and out of compassion for His devotees—
It comes to pass that, once those [guṇas] have merged with Prakṛti, He performs an act of observation (īkṣā) for the purpose of their manifestation. Then,

through hundreds of distinct essential natures, that other power called Jīva-Māyā— previously ignited by the appearance of His influence consisting of activity— projects Rajas from its own constituent parts.
From the unmanifest, due to the equilibrium of the three qualities (*guṇa-sāmya*), it causes that [universe] to be dispersed or awakened.

Or alternatively, just as this very Time (*kāla*), accompanied by *māyā*, creates separately, so too by the word "that" (*asau*) it is Time itself that is expressed. Furthermore, in various cities (*pura*) characterized by the diversity of manifold qualities.

When he desires to sport, then he creates *sattva*; when, moreover, having united with those very qualities, he desires to lie down—that is, wishes to sleep—then he creates *tamas*. This is the meaning.
The sense is that all activities, beginning with creation, proceed solely for the sake of food.

As was accepted by the author of the commentary (*ṭīkā*) on the third chapter of the eleventh book at this point: "The Primeval One created high and low beings for the sake of establishing His own nature as the Self of food" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 11.3.3). Thus it was stated even by the commentator there.

For what purpose did He create? For the sake of the supreme accomplishment of His own self as the Mātrā. He who worships Him is the "Mātrā" (the measurer), for he measures and fully evaluates Himself. This is for the sake of the excellent attainment (*prakṛṣṭāyai siddhaye*) of that Self, which is the individual soul (*jīva*). Thus it is said.
Regarding "reclining" (*śayana*): here, the descent of the Supreme Person is sometimes [characterized by] yogic sleep in the ocean of dissolution, and sometimes...

Or [it refers to] the entrance of the Blessed One. Although the Supreme Lord dwells within all living beings as their inner controller (*antaryāmin*), nevertheless, because he is unattached therein, he is as if not present at all;
yet, because he is fully attached to his own devotees, it is not so for them. Furthermore, he has no desire for attachment to them or the like.
The explanation as stated above is indeed the authoritative one. And so it is said in the Śrī Gītā:
"All beings abide in Me, yet I do not abide in them;
nor do beings abide in Me—behold My divine yoga" (Gītā 9.4–5).
"But those who worship Me with devotion, they are in Me, and I am also in them" (Gītā 9.29).
And it is said in the *Haribhaktisudhodaya*:
"The peaceful heart of devotees, along with its splendor, is My dear home."

"I dwell there as Beauty alone; this is the description of [the realm] called Vaikuṇṭha and so forth"—thus says Viśvanātha. Nor should it be suspected that, by means of a mechanism characterized by a gradation in His presiding authority according to the relative superiority of the *guṇas*, He is dependent upon the *guṇas*.

However, he states that even for the Creator of the qualities (guṇas), all of that is merely His own spontaneous play: when the Supreme Lord, desiring to create bodies as cities for the enjoyment of the individual soul (ātman/jīva), then creates the quality of passion (rajas) separately from its state of equilibrium. Within those diverse bodies...
Desiring to sport—that is, wishing to perform the sport characterized by the protection of the disciplined—he emits *sattva* separately;
intending to sleep—that is, wishing to withdraw [the world]—he impels and stirs up *tamas* separately. ||10||
O King, the Lord, the maker of truth, creates Time as the substratum for Pradhāna and Puruṣa as they move about.
O King, since this very Time is the lord who,
like a host of gods, impels the quality of goodness (sattva), therefore he,
the beloved of the gods, [destroys] the asuras who are its adversaries.
He of wide renown overcomes those characterized by passion and darkness.
Madhva: [He is] with Pradhāna and Puruṣa. ||11|| Even regarding time, because he is the Lord (Īśitṛ) and the cause of the body and so forth, his being (sattva) stands like an army of gods;
yet, because he is beloved by nature, Hari is always dear to the gods.
He is disliked by the asuras, but for humans, he possesses both qualities by his very nature.
Place and time, as well as qualities such as devotion, even in the case of the imperishable;
likewise, the fitness for action—this is called "equality."
Although he is dear to the gods by his very nature, the Unborn One bestows these qualities upon them, as well as the faults, pleasures, and pains of others, only after having first produced them.
But for human beings, both [virtue and vice] exist; therefore, they are said to be equal.
Furthermore, among the gods and others, virtues and defects are beginningless and fixed.
"Furthermore, they were increased by Viṣṇu himself according to their respective order and with strict regulation; therefore, Janārdana is eternally unequal. Thus it is said in the Brahma-tarka.
However, Viṣṇu’s inequality is never due to a lack of fitness, but rather in consideration of [the recipients'] suitability.
"According to you, there would be inequality due to the necessity of that capacity," as stated in the Skanda Purāṇa.
"But inequality leads to fault in the reversal of good and evil;
therefore, such inequality was refuted in the Brahma Sūtras."

"His being the controller of the auspicious and the inauspicious is not a defect; rather, it is a merit. Therefore, this is accepted by the all-pervading Kṛṣṇa, the author of the Brahma-sūtras. Thus says Śrīdhara in the *Tantra-nirṇaya*. From the instruction beginning with "When he desired to create," the dependence on time is understood.

By refuting [the doctrine of] dependence on *pradhāna* and *puruṣa*, he also refutes [the doctrine of] time— saying "time" (*kālam*). O King, the Lord (*īśa*), who makes things real and acts unfailingly,
himself [governs] time— which exists as a concurrent cause for those two (*pradhāna* and *puruṣa*) and serves as their substratum— as it moves along.
He creates; the meaning is that because time consists of His own activity, there is no dependence on anything else. ||11||

Even so, what relevance does this have to the present subject? To that he says: because this Time nourishes—that is, increases—*sattva*, for that reason the Lord (*īśitā*), though He is the Supreme Controller (*īśvara*), seems to nourish the host of gods (*surānīka*), which is dominated by *sattva*; [and He likewise diminishes] the Asuras, who are the adversaries of the gods.
The grammatical connection is: "He measures and He destroys. He is one whose *śravaḥ*—that is, fame—is *uru*, meaning abundant.

The meaning of the context here is that the inequality residing in the *guṇas*, which has been agitated by the power of Time (*kāla*), manifests within the Controller (the Lord) merely through His presence. ||12||

The Sequence of Composition: Having thus explained both creation and dissolution as an incidental digression, the author concludes the section with one and a half verses while again explaining maintenance alone, beginning with the word "Time.
[He is] the maker of reality—by His own manifestation of essential power (svarūpa-śakti).

Being the very manifestation of the activity of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), He creates—that is, manifests—time in the form of His own movement. What is He doing? It is solely for the sake of providing assistance to the *pradhāna* and the *puruṣa*, to the various relationships between them, to the devotees who are the means of accomplishment, and to the portions of His own splendor that have entered into the gods and other beings.

He moves by means of the very process of being created and originating from the unmanifest (avyakta) and the aggregate of individual souls (jīva); for this very reason, through their mere proximity, He is the substratum of their respective states and the cause of their manifestation.
By the address "O Nara-deva," it is implied that just as you perform your primary duty through your own effort, [so does He].
Just as by that very [means] other things even more minute are accomplished of their own accord, so it is understood here as well.

Therefore, this time which consists of activity is *sattva*. It seems to nourish the host of gods, who are dominated by *sattva*, and from that very source, the asuras—who are the adversaries of those [gods] and are dominated by *rajas* and *tamas*—[are diminished].

It seems to measure and it seems to destroy. As for those who are devoted to the gods and hostile toward those devoted to the asuras, it has already been stated previously that He Himself protects them and destroys them respectively.
Therefore, such is the nature of Time, which is characterized by their activities; thus, even as the Ruler, He seems to cause growth.
"And he measures [them] as it were. The address "O King" refers precisely to the previous intention.

Now, one might ask: "If there is no purpose for the Lord, then why would He not at some time even make the Asuras His own faction and fight with the gods? To that, he says: "He is dear to the gods (sura-priya) among the gods."

He is one whose beloved devotees exist in the present. Since he generally follows all those among the gods who are dominated by *sattva*, his own following occurs precisely through theirs. Occasionally, even when great offenses are committed against Bṛhaspati and others, because their divinity (*suratva*) conceals such impurity, he [remains] among them.
The intention is that there would be no following [of the deceased], whereas it has been stated [in the Bhagavad-gītā]: "But at the time of victory, the quality of goodness (sattva)... and so forth.
Now, one might ask: "How is it that they too do not follow them? To this he replies: "Those possessed of passion and darkness (rajas-tamaskān)."
The sense is that this is because of a lack of relish for those two qualities which cause one to be utterly turned away from the Lord.

Then, fearing that it might still be inconsistent to say that He always performs only the suppression of the Asuras, he says: "He of great fame (uruśravāḥ), whom the kings [by enmity... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa).
"[He is] like this," and so forth; "O, the son of Bakī! (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.2.23), and so on.
He is one whose *śravaḥ*—meaning fame or renown—is *uru*, that is, spread everywhere or most great. The sense is that he bestows grace even upon them. ||11-12||

Viśvanātha: By the instruction beginning with "when desiring to create," he also precludes the dependence on time that might otherwise be understood—[expressed by the word] "time" (*kālam*). O King, He Himself creates Time as it moves, serving as the substratum for His own activity, because Time is of the nature of His own movement. This...
The meaning is as follows: indeed, the creation of the universe and so forth is merely His pastime (līlā), and that pastime is dependent solely upon His own will.

In this regard, when there arises the desire to create (sisṛkṣā), then the time for creation occurs, characterized by the increase of the quality of passion (rajas). When there arises the desire to protect (pipālayiṣā), then the time for preservation occurs, characterized by the increase of the quality of goodness (sattva). When there arises the desire to withdraw (saṃjihīrṣā), then...

The "time of the increase and destruction of darkness" (*tamo-vṛddhi-nāśa-kāla*) refers to a specific time (*kāla-viśeṣa*), and it is by that very [time] that [the world] is created. In this regard, when it is the time for creation and so forth, then at that very moment there must be the desire to create (*sisṛkṣā*) and so on. Since that which is denoted by the word "time" is itself a specific time, it is indeed something to be created. This is also [implied] by the passage beginning with "at the time of the victory of *sattva*," and so forth.

The well-known dependence on time has been refuted; thus, [the Lord] exists together with primordial matter (pradhāna), the power of illusion (māyā-śakti), the person (puruṣa), and his own portion. In this way, because He is the cause of all, His sovereignty belongs to Him alone, and because the world is His effect, it is dependent upon Him.

Now, some say: "Is it not the case that this world, which is His effect, is indeed non-existent? What is the use of investigating whether a non-existent thing is dependent or independent? To this he replies: [The Lord] is the maker of reality, because the universe—which is the effect of the Lord's power—is incapable of being false; for this applies to every effect whatsoever.
The sense is that, if falsity were inferred [of the Veda], it would follow that there is an absence of authority even in the Blessed One.
Indeed, this very truth—that he created this entire universe—is established by the Śruti cited in the Mādhva-bhāṣya.
Therefore, since time is an effect of him, the properties of the effect are figuratively attributed to the cause; thus he says: "ya..."
Regarding the word "eṣa" (this one): for this very reason, even the Lord, the Supreme Ishvara, seems to nourish *sattva*—that is, the host of gods which has *sattva* as its predominant quality;
and he seems to crush—that is, he destroys—their adversaries, the enemies of the gods. Thus, such partiality belongs to the *guṇa* alone and not to anything else; in that regard, time...

This is the illustration: just as houses possess height, coolness, and so forth—which depend on being created, sustained, and governed by a person—yet these qualities belong to the houses alone and not to the person; likewise, [the Lord's partiality] is explained. Furthermore, the term "beloved of the gods" (sura-priya) implies that even partiality is indeed an ornament rather than a defect, precisely because He is the devotee of the gods.
Thus, this is indeed a distinct established conclusion (*siddhānta*). As it has been said: "I am equal toward all beings.
It should be understood that, at times, the defeat of the gods by the asuras is brought about by the Blessed One himself, who desires their welfare, for the purpose of removing their arrogance.
Now, one might ask: "How is it that He is dear to all and a friend to all? To this, he says:
"Of wide renown" (*uru-śravāḥ*). This refers to those qualities revealed by such statements as: "O Bakī, this breast of yours is a deadly poison" (*bhā.pu.
3.2.23*), and so forth.

The meaning is that his very reputations—characterized by bestowing the destinies of Pūtanas and others who have committed great misdeeds—proclaim his being beloved by all and his being a friend to all. ||12||
O King, this very history was previously recounted here by the celestial sage out of affection, when the great sacrifice was being performed for the sake of the inquiring Janamejaya."

Śrīdhara: At that time, their slaughter was not due to partiality toward the side of the gods, but rather for the sake of bestowing grace upon those who had attained an asuric birth because of a Brahmin’s curse; to state this, he introduces a historical account with the words "In this very [context]..."—here, even though [Viṣṇu] was free from hatred and the like, regarding the slaying of the Daityas...
An ancient history was introduced by Nārada. ||13||

The Structural Arrangement (*krama-sandarbha*): Having thus demonstrated the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), [the author now provides] an illustration of the promised point— that the Supreme Lord performs various actions therein solely for the purpose of bestowing grace upon His devotees— by way of indicating His compassion toward Prahlāda, Jaya, Vijaya, and others.

He states a specific historical account with the words "in this very [context]": here, because there is an absence of hatred and the like, for the sake of delighting the devotees, His activities are merely spontaneous pastimes (*svaira-līlā-mātra*), and even the asuras possess a nature that ultimately results in their supreme welfare. By the use of the particle *eva* (only/very), other doctrines are excluded.
It is excluded. ||13||
Viśvanātha: To clarify the very meaning already stated, he introduces a historical narrative (itihāsa) regarding these matters of equality, friendship, and affection. ||13||
Having witnessed this great marvel at the great Rājasūya sacrifice— that the Lord Vāsudeva had attained union with the King of Cedi— King Yudhiṣṭhira was struck with wonder.
There, at the sacrifice, the son of Pāṇḍu, his mind filled with wonder, questioned the celestial Ṛṣi as he sat there while the sages listened.
Śrīdhara: [This refers to] Śiśupāla, the king of Cedi. ||14-15||

*Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā*: Regarding the passage beginning with "Vāsudeva, the supreme reality," and the statement, "The knowers of reality declare that reality to be that which is knowledge" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 1.2.11), that which is called the supreme reality is indeed Vāsudeva, the son of Śrī Vasudeva. By this, [the meaning of] the word *vāsudeva*...
Another interpretation is both incorrect and incoherent. ||15||
The sequence of composition: "Having seen," etc., is a pair of verses (yugmaka). ||14||
Viśvanātha: Not explained.
—o)0(o— Śrī Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Oh, how truly marvelous is this! Even for those who are single-mindedly devoted, it is difficult to attain;
yet the enemy of the Caidya has attained Vāsudeva, the supreme reality.
Śrīdhara: That the attainment [of Him] has occurred even for an enemy—though such attainment is difficult even for those who are exclusively devoted—is indeed most wonderful. (15)
The Sequence of Composition: Now, devotion to the Blessed One is twofold—*vaidhī* (following scriptural injunction) and *rāgānugā* (following spontaneous attachment).
Among these, *rāgānugā* is the more authentic and even superior to *vaidhī*. In this context, "attachment" (*rāga*) is indeed a state of spiritual absorption (*āveśa*).
Furthermore, that absorption occurs through a mental disposition characterized by a specific inclination (*ruci-viśeṣa*), and not otherwise.

This is because it is a natural property of the mind impelled by ritual injunction; and in that regard, let alone a favorable disposition, even if there were an entry into a state of aversion through something strictly forbidden, then by the power of that very entry, the defect of aversion would be instantly eliminated.

Furthermore, it is observed that there is even an illustrative example for the strength of the path of devotion (bhāva-mārga), namely that all misfortunes would cease. In that regard, if there were a favorable disposition, then this [cessation] would indeed be a supreme and exclusive goal.
Now, the section concerning the superior strength of the general path of devotion (*bhāva-mārga*) is introduced with the word "Aho!

(Oh!). "Of the single-minded" (*ekāntinām*) means "of those possessing supreme knowledge," as in the verse: "The single-minded, whose intellect is wide awake, though hidden, is regarded like one who is deluded" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 1.4.4). This is because even for them, that attainment is not possible.
Viśvanātha: [This applies] even to those who are single-mindedly devoted and free from possessions. ||16||
O Sage, we all desire to know this:
Blessed One, by what censure of the twice-born was Vena cast into darkness?"
Śrīdhara: However, for him [the reviler], a fall into hell is indeed appropriate; thus he says, "by blaspheming the Blessed One. Into that hell. ||17||
The sequence of composition; Viśvanātha: not explained.
—o)0(o— Starting from the wicked son of Damaghoṣa, because of his sweet speech...
Now the evil-minded Dantavakra is also filled with resentment toward Govinda.

Śrīdhara: Śiśupāla is the son of Damaghoṣa. From his childhood, beginning with his sweet and tender speech, he has remained impatient, wrathful, or arrogant even now; this sequence [of events] has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: From sweet speech, beginning with the soft speech of childhood. ||18||
Because they repeatedly cursed Viṣṇu— the supreme, imperishable Brahman—
the two were not born with leprosy upon their tongues, nor did they enter the blinding darkness.
Śrīdhara: *śvitra* is white leprosy (*śveta-kuṣṭha*). ||19||
*The Casket of Caitanya’s Teachings*: Regarding the passage beginning with "of the two who were cursing," etc. Is Viṣṇu the protector of the world?

No, he says—he is the Supreme Brahman. That which is even beyond Brahman, the imperishable (*avyaya*), meaning that which does not pass away from its state of eternal youth, and thus is the most excellent; this is the connection [of the words] "of the two who were repeatedly cursing. Or alternatively:
One who produces *rasa* (flavor) is a *rasakṛt*; he who is both that and Viṣṇu is "he thus" (*sa tathā*).
This is a specific designation by virtue of being a *rasakṛt*. Therefore, by the word "Viṣṇu," it is the *śreṣṭhaka* alone that is to be understood here. ||19||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not commented upon.
*Viśvanātha*: That which is the Supreme Brahman—him, Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa. ||19||
How did they both swiftly undergo dissolution in that Blessed One, whose nature is difficult to grasp, while all the worlds were looking on?

Śrīdhara: They attained—that is, they went to—*laya*, which is *sāyujya* (union), in Him whose *dhāman* (abode) or essential nature is difficult to grasp and difficult to reach. Although the dissolution of Dantavakra was not yet an actual fact, it is described as if it were established, based on the authority of the *Jātaka* [Purāṇa]. (20)
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: On the contrary, *laya* (dissolution) refers to union (*sāyujya*) according to the common worldly perception of the time; it is a state of conjunction for a certain period of time.
It is called *sayuk* because one is joined together (*saha yujyate*), and the state of that is *sāyujya*. Beyond that—

The two attained a state of conformity [with their vision]. Although the future dissolution of Dantavakra had been heard from the mouth of Nārada himself, the use of the past tense (*bhūta-nirdeśa*) is due to the thought that his end was already as good as accomplished. The phrase "of those who were looking" is intended to establish the authority [of the vision] even regarding an impossible matter. ||20||
My mind wanders like the flame of a lamp in the wind;
tell me this most wonderful thing, for you, O Blessed One, must surely know the cause here.
Śrīdhara: This is most wonderful; therefore, my mind reels at this. O Blessed One, you are all-knowing; please explain it. (21)

*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: This [result] causes one to wander; therefore, speak of this most wonderful thing, since the Blessed One is omniscient. [Objection: Is this not merely the literal meaning of these words? To that he says: "In that regard..."
Take up the cause. ||21||
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
Having heard those words of the king, the blessed sage Nārada—
Being pleased, he addressed him and spoke, while the assembly listened to his words.

Śrīdhara: "Ābhāṣya" means having addressed or awakened [the assembly]. "Sīdanti niṣīdanty asyām iti sat" means that which they sit upon is the *sat* (the assembly); "sadaḥ" is derived from "sadasaḥ. The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: he spoke the true words while the assembly was listening. ||22||
The sequence of composition:
Viśvanātha explains that *sat* refers to an assembly (*sabhā*) because people sit (*sīdanti*), despond (*viṣīdanti*), and take their seats (*apaviśanti*) in it;
thus, "of her who is listening" means while she is listening to the stories in that assembly. Having addressed him: "O King."
Having addressed him with the words, "Pay heed! ||22||
Śrī Nārada said:
This body exists for the purpose of censure and praise, honor and insult.
O King, this is imagined through the non-discrimination between the primary cause (pradhāna) and the Supreme (para).

"The fruit of dharma and adharma is experienced by men after death according to their destiny; however, some may experience it even here [in this life]. Therefore, one should not practice unrighteousness. Thus it is said in the *Mahābhārata*. (23)

Śrīdhara: Aho! What is your intention in saying that one who reviles the Blessed One must inevitably fall into hell? Is it because such a person causes pain to the Blessed One, or even in the absence of that, because they perform prohibited and censurable acts like drinking liquor and so forth?
In that regard, [the fall into hell occurs] because the censure and other such acts are caused by the identification with the body.

Since that [suffering] does not exist for the Blessed One, there is no fear of suffering; thus he says with three and a half verses beginning with "Nindan" (censuring). "Nindana" is the proclaiming of faults. "Nyakkāraḥ" is contempt.
For the sake of knowing censure, praise, and so forth, the body is imagined through the non-discrimination of *pradhāna* and *puruṣa*.
Composed. ||23||

The sequence of the composition: Regarding that, the venerable Nārada spoke the reply, beginning with "nindan" (blaming). In that regard, blame and the like are directed by deluded people solely toward material qualities such as *tamas* and so forth.
Therefore, [the Lord is not affected] by the blame and such committed by them, even though He is the ultimate refuge of all down to material nature (*prakṛti*).

There is no engagement whatsoever with Him regarding His extraordinary qualities, form, and so forth; nor does the Lord possess the sense of ego (abhimāna) toward the entire range of material objects as the individual soul (jīva) does. Consequently, He suffers no affliction from them; thus, it is established—as before—that the Lord remains untouched by their censure or the like.

Viśvanātha: To show that the noise caused by Śiśupāla does not cause pain to the Blessed Lord, [the author] first states that praise, blame, and so forth do not bestow suffering or happiness upon the wise, but only upon those who identify with the body: "Praise and blame are verbal; faults and virtues [are likewise]."
Honor and insult, as well as respect and disrespect, are both physical and mental.

For that purpose—that is, for the sake of accomplishing those [reactions]—they are fashioned and constructed through the non-discrimination between nature (prakṛti) and spirit (puruṣa), which is the absence of discrimination between the self and the not-self. ||23||
O King, through pride in that [violence], there arises here among living beings inequality, as well as harshness of punishment, and the sense of "mine" and "I."

Śrīdhara: The connection with what follows is as follows: just as for living beings there arises, through identification (*abhimāna*), the inequality of "mine" and "I," and consequently violence and so forth occur; such is not the case for one [who possesses this knowledge]. Punishment (*daṇḍa*) is beating, and harshness (*pāruṣya*) is censure; from these two, which serve as causes, violence (*hiṃsā*) and affliction (*pīḍā*) arise.

The sequence of the composition: thereafter follows the half-yugma beginning with "hiṃsā. Here, it is not as it is in the material world through identification with that physical body; rather, because of their attainment of purity through liberation—as stated in *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 7.1.34: "of those residing in the city of Vaikuṇṭha, who are devoid of body, senses, and life-force due to their isolation (*kaivalya*)..."—they possess such purity.
The meaning is: from that pure embodiment of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*), which is inaccessible to such censure and the like.
And its inaccessibility is established by such texts as the *Śrī Bhagavad Gītā*, for instance: "I am not manifest to everyone, being veiled by my own *yoga-māyā*" (Gītā 7.25). ||24||

Viśvanātha: Through identification with that—that is, through identification with the body—just as suffering and pleasure arise from thoughts such as "this person is censuring me" or "this person is praising me," so too does injury occur when one thinks, "this person is harming me. When what [is present] does this happen? It occurs when there is punishment, beating, or harshness, such as [the thought], "I shall have you killed."
While those two exist, there is intimidation; and thus, for living beings here in this saṃsāra, inequality is established in the form of:
"These are my enemies, these are my kinsmen; I kill these, and I protect these. (24)
Since this egoism is bound to that [body], the killing of living beings results from its destruction;
likewise, for the Self of all, there is no egoism apart from absolute liberation (kaivalya).
For how can violence be attributed to one who brings about the restraint of another?
"Madhvaḥ": because of absolute isolation (*kaivalya*), that is, precisely due to the absence of a body and so forth. For that non-agent, no other agent exists.
This is based on the rule (*sūtra*) stating: "The root *hiṃs* [is used] in the senses of reversal, excess, censure, and division. ||25||

Śrīdhara: Just as there is death from the destruction of that body to which this sense of ego (abhimāna) is attached, so too [there is no death] for one who has no such ego. Therefore, for what reason could injury be attributed to this Supreme Lord? For none at all. The reason for the absence of ego is his absolute isolation (kaivalya).

Because there is nothing to be conceived as a second [to Him], there is an absence of inequality; the reason for this is stated as "of the Self of all" (*akhilātmanaḥ*), meaning the Self of everything. If so, why does He slay the Daityas? To that he says: it means He inflicts punishment for the sake of the welfare of the Supreme One who brings about self-restraint. ||25||

The sequence of the composition: the cause for such a distinction; being the self of all—therein the cause is that He is the Supreme, free from attachment to the power of material nature. Another reason for [His] violence:
because He is the performer of supreme, wondrous, and infinite power, and thus the instructor of all, including those who practice self-restraint.

Viśvanātha: Just as for the ignorant there is death through the destruction of that body upon which this sense of egoism (*abhimāna*) is fixed, so it is not for Him— Kṛṣṇa— for whom no material egoism exists.

The meaning is that by no one whatsoever can violence against the Supreme Lord be imagined. The reason for the absence of such conceit is "due to isolation" (*kaivalyāt*), that is, because He is the absolute Supreme Self. This is the intended sense: just as for all living beings there exist both the non-self body and the self which is the individual soul (*jīva*), so too, if it were the case for Kṛṣṇa...
In that case, even for Kṛṣṇa, there would certainly have been an illusory (avidyaka) conceit, just as there is for individual souls.

However, Kṛṣṇa’s body is none other than the Supreme Self; therefore, even the conceit "I am Kṛṣṇa" regarding that which constitutes His very nature is composed of that [Supreme Reality] alone. This applies even to the Inner Controller (antaryāmin), who is a portion (aṃśa) of Him, the Soul of all.

The sense is that there is no false identification (*abhimāna*) with the individual soul (*jīva*) or the body of the soul, which are not one's true nature (*asvarūpa-bhūta*). For this very reason, since He is distinct from the Supreme Lord, from illusory things, and from the individual souls—which are all not His true nature—and because He lacks false identification with them, who could be an object of His hatred, or who could be His hater? [This applies] to that which is the body of the Supreme Self.

His conceit consists in the realization "I am indeed the Supreme Self. Knowing him to be the Supreme Self, whom would he hate? Or who could hate Him? If so, why does He slay His own enemies such as Śiśupāla and others? To this He says: [He inflicts] punishment upon them for their own benefit, acting as their subduer.
The sense is that this occurs for one who acts [in this way], because of being a friend to all. ||25||
Therefore, one should engage [the mind] through the persistence of enmity, or through freedom from enmity, or through fear,
or through affection, or through desire; in no way should one view it as separate.
Just as one who is intoxicated by honey does not perceive anything else separately, so too, due to the mind's intense attachment (*abhiniveśa*),

one does not perceive anything other than that. The statement "he who would apply himself even to a single one among enmity and the rest does not perceive" is a description of the natural state (*svabhāva-kathana*), not an injunction (*vidhi*).
The ancestors of one who hates the imperishable Viṣṇu through action, mind, or speech sink into hell for eternal years.
Those hateful, cruel, and most base of men, who are inauspicious, I cast perpetually into demonic wombs within the cycles of worldly existence.
Having entered the womb of an asura, deluded from birth to birth,
they do not reach Me at all, O son of Kuntī, but from there go to the lowest state.
Fools disregard me when I have assumed a human form,
being ignorant of my supreme nature as the Great Lord of all beings.
Futile their hopes, futile their actions, futile their knowledge, and devoid of discernment,
they have taken refuge in a delusive nature that is both demonic and asuric.
Since my father, being ignorant, reviled you who possess divine splendor,
may my father be purified from that wretched and insurmountable sin.
And Hiraṇyakaśipu, who was about to enter the darkness due to his blasphemy of the Blessed One,
passed beyond it through the power of his son Prahlāda.
Even by virtue of a boon, those who harbor hatred are not released from it; yet even by a curse, the devoted are never cast down. Likewise, the higher dharmas are not sublated by lower ones.
"That which is caused by the possession of another [spirit] is removed by means of mantras and the like;

otherwise, for those things whose nature is contrary to that [remedy], there is no way at all. From such statements as these, since there is no affliction whatsoever for the Blessed One, his mind is likewise not affected even by hatred and the like.

It can be established by their own impulsion; such people think only of that [impulsion]. Otherwise, how could there be hatred and so forth, which are causes of suffering for themselves? Śrīdhara [says]: Hari is the controller of all;
since there is no partiality on the part of the Blessed One caused by insults and the like, therefore—by whom...

With the intention that liberation through union (*sāyujya*) is appropriate because even the sin committed through censure and the like is destroyed by that very meditation through some means, he says "Therefore" in seven verses. "Without enmity" (*nirvairaṇa*) means by one toward whom there is no enmity toward anyone; the sense is: "by that yoga of devotion. The word "should join" (*yuñjyāt*) is to be supplied as the object, namely, the mind.

"Because by these means one does not perceive [the Lord] individually," etc. Now, if the attainment of the Blessed One occurs through even one of these [means] such as enmity, then why is there such great effort in the practice of devotion and so forth? True.
Through the persistence of enmity, fear arises; through fear, there is constant agitation;
and in that agitation, one finds fulfillment through the majesty of the object. Therefore, it is from this very agitation that fulfillment results. ||26||

The sequence of the argument: Thus, since there is no partiality on the part of the Blessed One toward those who commit offenses such as blasphemy, therefore, by whatever means— just as in the cases of "even once" (Bhāgavatapurāṇa 7.1.32) and "that which is devoid of even a single limb or image" (Bhāgavatapurāṇa 10.12.39)— for one who meditates even upon a semblance of Him, through that absorption (āveśa), [the goal is attained].
With the intention that even for one who meditates with enmity, because the sins committed through censure and so forth are destroyed by that very absorption (*āveśa*),
union with Him (*sāyujya*) and other states are appropriate, he says "therefore" (*tasmāt*) and so on. Regarding the word "should practice" (*yuñjyāt*),
since it is impossible to enjoin affection, desire, and the like, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is used here in the sense of possibility (*sambhāvanā*).

If one should apply oneself to, or meditate upon, even any one of these—such as the persistence of enmity (*vairānubandha*) and so forth—then one does not perceive the Blessed One as distinct; the meaning is that one becomes possessed by that [state]. "Persistence of enmity" (*vairānubandha*) is the non-interruption of the state of enmity.
"Freedom from enmity" (*nirvaira*) is said to be mere absence of enmity, which is equanimity (*audāsīnya*). By that, the absence of desire and the like is also implied.

It approaches; the meaning is the absence of states such as enmity (*vaira*). Or, by means of that absence of states such as enmity, one should apply oneself. One should meditate with the mere thought that [the practice] is prescribed.
The meaning is that one should perform the yoga of devotion (*bhakti-yoga*) characterized by meditation. Affection (*sneha*) is that which exceeds desire (*kāma*).

It is a special, non-artificial love between one another. Indeed, for the practitioner, that very devotion to Him is Viśvanātha Himself. Now, it may be granted that slandering and the like do not cause pain to the Blessed Lord;
however, they certainly produce bad karma (duradṛṣṭa) for the slanderer. As it has been said by way of a fortiori (kaimutya): [text follows]
"He who, hearing the censure of the Blessed One or of those devoted to Him, does not turn away from it—he too goes downward, fallen from his merit. This is true. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.76.26)
Indeed, censure is of two kinds: that consisting of conformity and that consisting of opposition. Of these, the first is merely a manifestation of love.
Like a hunter following the ways of a deer-stalker, he pierced the Lord of Monkeys.
"Having eaten Bali, though he was himself a devourer of offerings, he bound him like a crow; he made his wife ugly and conquered her who was devoted to him and driven by desire.
Therefore, enough with friendship with the Dark One (Kṛṣṇa); the subject of his stories is difficult to abandon. [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.47.17] Thus it is said.

That [devotion], which is like a cluster of rays from the crest-jewel of the goals of human life, cannot be attained by anyone except for the queens of Vraja. It is of two kinds: that arising from absorption in the Lord, and that arising from non-absorption in the Lord. Regarding the first, [it is illustrated] by the censure uttered by Śiśupāla and others.

Even as it is being produced, that misfortune is instantly destroyed by the very cause of it—namely, by one's intense attachment to the Blessed Lord—and having attained equality with the yoga of devotion, one also attains fitness for the performance of ritual injunctions;
thus he says in seven verses beginning with "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). For since there is [no other way] from censure...

There is no infliction of pain upon the Blessed One by one who reviles Him, and the destruction of the reviler's own sins may indeed occur; therefore, through intense attachment or the persistence of enmity, one should fix the mind on the Blessed One—this is the sense of the remaining words. "With freedom from enmity" means that state in which there is no enmity toward anyone; the meaning is "by means of the yoga of devotion. That...

Alternatively, "enmity" (*vaira*) is the state of being an adversary; its opposite is "the absence of enmity," which is the state of being one's own side, such as the status of being a son and so forth, which will indeed become clear in the subsequent verse as that which is denoted by the word "relationship" (*sambandha*).
Therefore, it should be explained as "desire" (*kāmanā*) arising from affection (*sneha*), which is produced by love (*prīti*). But not—
Affection (*sneha*) cannot be treated as a separate means, for that would result in a violation of the grammatical sequence established by the use of the instrumental case. He states the result:

"In no way does he perceive that Blessed Lord as separate; rather, he perceives Him directly in accordance with his own disposition. This refers to two types of qualified practitioners (*adhikārin*): those characterized by fear and those characterized by enmity.

However, the meaning is that he does not perceive [the Lord] as separate, but rather perceives Him as non-different from himself through the attainment of *sāyujya*. This is because, according to the maxim of "the white horse runs," even a single sentence may have different meanings depending on the subject (*pātra*).
Here, by the use of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) in the word *yuñjyāt*, [it is indicated that one should unite with the Lord] through the abandonment of enmity and so forth.

The injunction "one should fix the mind [on Him]" is understood; however, that is not possible in the case of Śiśupāla and others, because they have already attained passion (rāga). Nor can it be explained that this injunction applies only to others from the perspective of Śiśupāla and the like, for it is impossible to enjoin anything that is contrary to the Blessed One.

As it has been said: "Accepting what is favorable and avoiding what is unfavorable. Furthermore, even if a persistent enmity toward others such as Śiśupāla were enjoined, it does not produce devotion to the Blessed Lord.
Those hateful and cruel ones, the lowest of men, who are inauspicious— I cast them perpetually into demonic wombs alone within the cycles of worldly existence.

This is because it contradicts thousands of such statements. Nor should it be argued that only enmity arising from passion (*rāga*) produces hell, and not that which is prescribed by rule (*vihita*), for this would lead to inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*) in the cases of Śiśupāla and others. Nor can it be said that this restriction applies only to those other than Śiśupāla and his ilk, for [the rule] is seen as a prescription (*vidhi*).

Because the persistence of enmity is not observed among those who follow the conduct of the cultured (śiṣṭas). It is only for one by whom the Blessed One has been recognized as his slayer— whether through being heard of, seen, or inferred— that the persistence of enmity generates an intense fixation (abhiniveśa) upon the Blessed One, just as in the world [intense attachment arises] only toward those determined to be one's own slayers.
The mind of one who is afraid of enemies, tigers, snakes, and so forth is fixed upon them and not on others.

Therefore, some explain this verse as follows: since he brings benefit even to those who harbor enmity, because of the impropriety of enmity in that regard, [he acts] by means other than the state of enmity itself.

He says "therefore" to indicate that one should direct the mind toward a state of being. Since the negative particle *nañ* has the sense of "absence," one should apply the mind through non-enmity—that is, by means of a disposition toward kin, friends, sons, and so forth, which is distinct from the state of enmity.
Of what kind is this persistence of enmity? It is where there is a mental attachment similar to enmity.

Therefore, by the statement that "whoever is attached to something is necessarily fixed upon it," any state of neutrality is precluded. Likewise, regarding the passion born of affection—that passion whose sole cause is affection—by what kind [of passion]?
