By one accompanied by fear, such as the fear arising from abandoning one's kin and the path of the noble ones, and which follows after the young women of Vraja.

The meaning is "by desire. By the word "or" (*vā*) in the phrase "or by fear," it is meant that there is also [validity] when one is free from fear, as well as by desire following after [the longing for] Rukmiṇī and others; thus, there is authoritative proof for both the paramour relationship (*aupapatya*) and the marital relationship (*dāmpatya*). For instance: [love] characterized by the state of a paramour is very affectionate, very firm, and superior in every respect.
The Great Dwarf: "The high-souled sons of Agni attained womanhood through austerity, as well as a husband who is the source of the world, the unborn and all-pervading Vāsudeva. (26)
Just as a mortal may attain absorption in that [object] through the persistence of enmity,
my settled conviction is that he does not do so even through the yoga of devotion.

Regarding *madhvaḥ*: the reason for this is stated as "just as through the persistence of enmity. The sense is that there are none who are so intent upon devotion as those intent upon enmity; otherwise, how could Hari have made so many of his devotees? ||27||
Śrīdhara: Among those as well, the persistence of enmity is superior; thus he says, "Just as... [and] "not so even by the yoga of devotion. (27)
Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā: Now, [the author] says that through enmity, an abundance of manifestation arises—"Just as by the persistence of enmity," and so forth. ||27||
The sequence of the argument: Thus, since it is established that for all [practitioners] immersion (*āveśa*) into That alone is the fruit,

[the author] says "just as" (*yathā*) to show that for the sake of attaining that immersion quickly, even among those paths consisting of emotional states (*bhāva*), there is no equality with devotion consisting of ritual injunctions (*vidhi-bhakti*), such as through even a censured persistent enmity (*vairānubandha*).

The phrase "by a continuity of enmity" is also an elliptical expression for fear. Just as [the mind] attains absorption (*tan-mayatā*) or possession (*tad-āviṣṭatā*) through speed, it does not do so when [an action] is performed by means of *bhakti-yoga*—that is, by a cognition consisting merely of the thought that it is prescribed or impelled by an injunction. ||27||

Viśvanātha: Even for enmity, which is most censurable, its greatness is indeed boundless by virtue of its being a portion of the mind's persistent attachment; thus he says, "Just as... Enmity (*vaira*) refers to the state of hostility; through the persistence (*anubandha*), that is, the continuity thereof, a mortal [is affected] according to the previously mentioned reasoning regarding himself.

Only one characterized by the knowledge that he is to be slain by the Blessed One—and no other—possesses "tan-mayatā" (identification with Him), meaning a state of exclusive absorption in Him, as in the expression "a lustful man absorbed in a woman. The phrase "not so" implies "immediately. Since her mind is certain, this is my own settled conviction; therefore, no further proof need be sought here.

If even enmity (*vaira-bhāva*) is superior to *bhakti-yoga* by virtue of its power to fix the mind [on the Lord], then what need is there to say that such *bhakti-yoga*, characterized by such intense devotion, is so? Therefore, as it was said by you: "No leprosy arose on his skin, nor did darkness enter his tongue" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 7.1.18).

The persistence of enmity on the part of Śiśupāla and others is censured because they perceive [Kṛṣṇa] as a means to undesirable ends; however, I praise Him, who is the crest-jewel of all means to the desired, even through the yoga of devotion (*bhakti-yoga*). Why?

Because there is even the possibility of a miserable rebirth for Śiśupāla and others—this is the implied meaning (*dhvani*). Therefore, among the paths of spiritual disposition (*bhāva-mārga*), [devotion is supreme].

If even a state of enmity, though highly censurable, is praised as being superior to pure bhakti-yoga by virtue of its capacity to swiftly bring about absorption in the Blessed Lord, then how much more so should the parental affection, friendship, and other such sentiments of Vasudeva and others— let alone those of Nanda and the rest— be honored within the paths of devotional emotion?

The term "anudhvani" refers to that which brings about the ultimate perfection of those respective states by awaiting their persistent attachment to them. Therefore, even for contemporary practitioners who desire states such as *vātsalya* (parental affection) in accordance with the moods of Śrī Nanda and others, *rāgānugā* devotion is [superior] to *vaidha* (scriptural) devotion.
"Excellence" is the implied resonance (*paryanudhvani*). ||27||
A worm confined within a wall by a spider, while remembering it,
assumes the very form of that spider through the conjunction of agitation and fear.
Thus, through their enmity toward the Lord Kṛṣṇa, who had appeared as a human by His own Māyā, they purified their sins and attained Him by constant meditation.
The passage beginning with "madhvaḥ kīṭaḥ peśaskṛtā" and so forth establishes that even Caidya and others were endowed with devotion.
By stating "without enmity" (*nirvaira*) and so on, it is shown that for him there is no affliction even from the destruction of the abodes of affection and the like.
Consequently, the Śruti states: "The gods are indeed the younger, while the Asuras are the elder. [This refers to] the state of the mind being absorbed in that.
"In that regard, there is intense attachment: 'The inhabitants of Magadha and other regions always grasp at [the faults of] Hari due to hatred and so forth;
but devotees do not grasp [at such things], with the exception of the imperishable Brahmā'—thus it is said in the *Harivaṃśa*."

"Yoga is affection; [it is] affection joined with agitation and fear. "Affection is love, and likewise yoga is called the bond of love. Thus, according to the *Śabdanirṇaya*, they attained Him even through contemplation joined with enmity. And it is said: "They call that 'contemplation' which is a remembrance preceded by devotion. (28–29)

Śrīdhara: Here is an illustration—a worm [placed] by a *peśaskṛt* (a "cloth-maker" or spider-like creature). Through that very agitation (*saṃrambha*), which is hatred and fear, and through that very yoga; through enmity (*vaira*), by means of that constant brooding (*anucintā*) and reflection, those whose sins were purified attained Him. (28–29)
*The Casket of Caitanya’s Teachings*: Regarding this, there is an illustration beginning with "A worm by the silk-worm maker," and so forth.
Now, one might ask: even so, would everyone not simply engage in enmity, setting aside the yoga of devotion? Not so;
for there is no injunction regarding enmity, nor is enmity to be practiced. [This applies] toward the Lord, the Self of all.

Since enmity is impossible without love for one who is a supreme beloved among all friends, it might be argued: "But because they are by nature asuras, even toward the Blessed One—who is not such [a beloved]—love does not arise without enmity. Let it not arise; what difference is there between those who possess love and those who harbor hatred? Do not say so; there is a difference.

This is the distinction: indeed, those possessed of attachment (rati) attain merely the status of beloved attendants, whereas those who harbor hatred attain liberation itself by virtue of its manifestation; for the Blessed Lord also grants liberation even to enemies because of his enmity toward them, thinking, "I must never again look upon their faces."
"Thus," and so forth. "Illusion" refers to deceit even toward a younger brother; "non-human state" refers to a non-human being. ||29||

The Sequence of Composition: Let alone the matter of the manifestation of the Lord’s form, which possesses the power of such a reality and appears within those [devotees]; even in the case of an ordinary being, the great fruit of immersion in that state (*bhāvāveśa*) is seen from the mere presence of that feeling. He demonstrates this very point with an illustration—the worm.
Thus: *saṃrambha* is hatred and *bhaya* is fear; their conjunction is their possession (*āveśa*).

By that [possession], there is "the state of having that as its essential nature" (*tat-svarūpatā*), meaning that in which its own—its belonging to itself—nature (*rūpa*) or form (*ākṛti*) resides; the sense is that it has similarity with that (*tatsārūpya*).

"Thus" (*evam*) has the sense of "even so. Because he is the Supreme Brahman in human form, he is perceived as an ordinary man through *māyā* alone, and indeed through compassion alone. Now, one might object: "Is there not sin in a worm's hatred toward the silkworm-maker?
In that case, such [sin] would exist [here too]. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The constant contemplation [of Him] with enmity is an absorption in Him."
The sense is that their sins are purified by that very [devotion], because the absorption in meditation upon Him possesses such power. ||28-29||

Viśvanātha: Among those who harbored enmity toward Him, some such as Śiśupāla attained a form identical to His; he states this with an illustration in two verses beginning with "A worm. By the combination of *saṃrambha* (hostility) and *bhaya* (fear)—the former being hatred—the Creator of forms (*peśaskṛt*), a specific type of bee, [bestows grace]. His illusory power (*māyā*) is compassion that leads one to the supreme goal.

In that [Lord], even toward those among men who are His own haters; or rather, among men by means of Māyā, for there is a scriptural statement that He is joined with the eternal power called Māyā, which is His very own nature (*svarūpa*). Purified by the absorption of meditation born of enmity, his sins destroyed—[those sins] consisting of the slandering and insulting of Him by others.
They [are as follows]. ||28–29||
Many have attained that goal, having cast off their sins by fixing their minds upon the Lord through desire, hatred, fear, affection, or even through devotion.
Out of affection, one gives food even when there is fear of being drawn toward oneself;
likewise, even when a slight anger exists, association occurs through affection.
Just as a worm attains the form of a silk-worm,
even so did the Caidyas and others, though filled with hatred for Hari due to the possession of demons, [attain his nature].
Through devotion characterized by their own true nature, they are led to the very form of Hari;
for even Viṣṇu is compassionate, [yet] if he were to become an enemy through the possession of another.
What can be lost by one who is equal [to all] and whose nature is eternal bliss?
For what could be done by those who possess the bondage of a body and are full of hatred?
Who could offend me, who am by nature faultless and blissful? Therefore, any offense against me would in fact be an offense against oneself, not against me.
"Therefore, whatever evil has been committed by him through the possession of an asura,
I shall release him from that because he is my devotee from time immemorial"—
thinking thus, Keśava releases even Caitanya and others. Thus it is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*.

Having likewise directed the mind with devotion—even if that devotion is characterized by desire and so forth—one should abandon whatever sin has been committed through hatred and the like by means of such devotion as it truly is. ||30||
Śrīdhara: Having abandoned that evil—namely, the sin caused by desire and the like. ||30||

*The Casket of Caitanya’s Teachings*: By the words "from desire," and so forth; just as by devotion they fix their minds upon the Supreme Lord and attain His state, so too many have attained that same state through even one among desire and the rest. The "sin" refers to the fault committed through hatred and the like—that sin within those [states] such as desire.

The meaning is that "that evil" refers to the sin committed through hatred, anger, and so forth; however, there is no fault whatsoever in the case of desire (*kāma*). The reasoning here is as follows: desire is not produced without pleasure (*rati*); and pleasure is the experience of happiness in objects that are agreeable to the mind (*mano'nukūleṣv artheṣu sukha-saṃvedanaṃ ratiḥ*). [Sarasvatī-kaṇṭhābharaṇa]

5.138] When there is the experience of pleasure due to something being agreeable to the mind, and there is the possibility of obtaining that object, that is desire (*kāma*). Desire is longing; as the Blessed One has said: "The virtuous person who gradually abandons desire for me leaves behind all latent tendencies of the heart" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.6.23), and so forth. Let the wicked man be satisfied!
Nevertheless, desire, even as it perishes, generates love, just as a substance such as water-perfume, having itself been consumed by fire, produces fragrance in the water.
Therefore, because lightness is possible here as well, he cites those very examples, beginning with "the gopīs," [stating] that the gopīs [fell in love] out of desire.
The connection [of the words] such as these is to be understood according to what is appropriate.
This is the intended meaning: for all [desires] beginning with *kāma*, there is only one supreme object; other incarnations (*avatāra*) are not so.
In that regard, fulfillment is achieved through devotion (*bhakti*) alone. For instance, in another [incarnation], there is only desire (*kāma*).

It does not exist [for them], because cows and others lack recourse to that [refuge]. Fear and hatred existed for Hiraṇyākṣa and others; even though they were killed by the Boar and other incarnations, there was no liberation for them, as they subsequently obtained births such as Kumbhakarṇa. The same applies to Kālanemi, despite his being killed by Viṣṇu.

The connection [of this verse] is as follows: the affection of the gods toward Vāmana and others, and likewise that of Kaśyapa and others, is found in those very instances. By this it is shown that desire and the like, when directed toward the most excellent objects, are indeed the causes of the fulfillment of one's purpose (*kṛtārthatā*). This is because they possess more flavor than fear and the like, and because they generate delight (*rati*). The mention of "desire" (*kāma*) first is for that reason; by this verse [the author]...

It has been established that the state of being higher than the highest in every respect, as well as the preeminence of fixing the mind upon the Supreme Lord, belongs specifically to the gopīs; yet, in reality, what the gopīs feel for the Blessed Lord is not *kāma* (lust).
The world says that *kāma* is merely the feeling of a woman directed toward a man. It is not so.
But that very Kṛṣṇa is Kāma; for he himself will say: "Indeed, by his mere being, the gopīs, the cows, the trees, and the deer... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.12.8). ||30-31||

The Sequence of Arrangement [Bhakti-sandarbha 320]: Nor should it be said that perfection is attained only through the dharma of the Lord as prescribed by the scriptures, and not through desire and so forth as prescribed therein;
for, by means of prescribed devotion, having entered the mind in the Lord, they attain His state.

The meaning is that many have likewise gone [to ruin] even by means of desire and so forth when they are not [properly] regulated. Among those—desire and the rest—one should abandon that evil which constitutes the evil of hatred and fear; for since fear is also permeated by hatred, it should be understood as a producer of evil.

In this regard, some consider even desire (*kāma*) to be a sin (*agha*). Concerning this, it is investigated whether, in the case of the Blessed One, desire alone brings about absolute sin; or whether it is so when joined with the state of being a husband, or perhaps when joined with the state of being a paramour. If it is argued that it is [sinful] only in that [latter] case, then what—?

Whether because he is the lord of the host of hatred and the like, or because of his very nature being such, or by transgressing through acts such as drinking from the lower lip of the supremely pure Blessed One, or by superimposing qualities such as those of a lustful man upon Him,
or by hearing of His sinfulness— it is not the first [of these reasons].

This was stated previously: "And that Caidya attained perfection, O Hṛṣīkeśa, even though he was an enemy; how much more so those who are dear to Adhokṣaja? (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.13). In this passage, because enmity and the like are disparaged while his devotion is praised, he is therefore called "dear."

Just as with oil, since desire (*kāma*) also consists of joy (*prīti*), there is no fault in its being exactly like that; for such [desire] is indeed of the singular form of love (*prema*). As in [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.31.19]: "O Beloved, fearing [the hardness], we shall gently place your well-formed lotus-feet upon our breasts," and so forth—even when transgressing [the bounds of propriety].

For her own happiness, her intent is seen to consist precisely in being favorable toward Him. As for the disposition of Sairindhrī, however, because it is characterized primarily by a desire for sexual pleasure (*riraṃsā*), she lacks that exclusive intent found in the Śrī Gopīs;
therefore, she is censured only in comparison to them, but not in terms of her essential nature. [Bhāgavata Purāṇa, 10.47.58] "Of her two breasts, scorched by the god of love..."

In passages such as this, beginning with "By the infinite feet they wipe away all pains," and "Embracing the beloved who is the embodiment of bliss," there is praise of Him by way of His effects; and therein, in the verse "May He dwell here with us, O dearest one" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.48.8), there is the manifestation of love.
Therefore it is said:
"Having thus attained that Lord, the Master of Liberation who is so difficult to reach,
alas, that unfortunate woman requested this by offering the unguent for her limbs" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.48.8).

"He who, having propitiated Viṣṇu—the Lord of all lords—who is difficult to propitiate, chooses that which is graspable by the mind [rather than Him], is a person of evil intellect due to his lack of being. Thus they interpret it. Kaivalya is the state of single-minded devotion; he who is the Lord to be served by means of that [devotion], him [one should serve].

"O dear one, although she was formerly possessed of such misfortune characterized by her three-fold crookedness and other defects, oh wonder! By means of a portion of the Lord's dharma in the form of the application of body-unguents as a cause, let her now dwell here with me; sport with me for some days in this place. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.48.8)
"He requested the primary characteristic of good fortune. Therefore:
"What merit has been performed by this Avadhūta mendicant, who is destitute of prosperity, despised in this world, and most base? (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.80.25)

Thus, this statement was made just like the words of the city-dwellers addressed to the brahmin Śrīdāman. Now, one might ask: why is that lustful woman praised? To this he replies: "difficult to propitiate. He who chooses—that is, desires—only an ordinary object perceivable by the mind is indeed a person of base intellect; she, however, [desires] the Blessed Lord alone.

The sense is that "he desires" implies she is indeed supremely wise. Thus, having refuted the inclusion of that desire within the category of hatred and the like, its capacity to bring about sin has been refuted.
Now, even the worldly conduct therein—consisting of the attribution of lustfulness and so forth, as well as the drinking of her lower lip and the rest—[is likewise justified].

There is no reason for it to be surpassed; for, according to the maxim "But like the world, His pastimes are absolute," His pastime is established there by His very nature. And here, through Śrī, Bhū, Līlā, and others, such pastimes of His are eternally established in Śrī-Vaikuntha and other realms, constituting His independent diversion of pastimes.

This is understood precisely through His own inclination (*abhiruci*). Likewise, because His beloved consorts also possess a nature that is supremely pure by virtue of their essential form, power, and body, and because they lack any state of being separate from Him, even acts such as drinking from His lower lip are not inconsistent with Him; rather, by the logic previously established, they are indeed what He inclines toward.

Nor should a fault be imputed by ordinary women; for only after attaining that corresponding disposition and such a nature as the embodiment of one's own essential power (svarūpa-śakti-vigraha) does one attain that [state] through His will alone.
Furthermore, this desire does not bring about sin merely because of the hearing of [reports of] sin, precisely because of the non-hearing of it. Therefore:
Moreover, there is certainly no fault in that state of being a wife; on the contrary, praise is heard:

"What can be said of the austerity of those women who, with love and the thought of him as their husband, served the Teacher of the World by massaging his feet and other such acts? (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.9.27).
Thus it is said;
even among sages of great spiritual power, that same disposition is heard of, as in the words of the *Kūrma Purāṇa* held by the venerable Mādhvācārya:
"The high-souled daughters of Agni attained womanhood through austerity,
and [chose] as their husband Vāsudeva, the unborn, all-pervading source of the world.
For this very reason, He is saluted with the words "husband, son, friend, brother," and so forth.

Furthermore, this does not bring about sin by way of being a paramour, because it has been answered by those very women with the words, "O dear one, service to one’s husband, children, and friends... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.29.19), and also by the words of Śrī Śuka, "Of the gopīs and their husbands... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.33.35).
"I am not able to repay the debt of those who are joined with the faultless,

even in a lifespan as long as that of the gods, for your own virtuous deeds"— in this passage, by the phrase "those who are joined with the faultless," the Blessed Lord Himself refers to such persons.
The same state is observed in others as well; for example, a statement from the *Pādmottara-khaṇḍa*:
"In former times, all the great sages dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest, having seen Rāma, who is Hari, there with his beautiful form, desired to eat him."
"All of them, having attained womanhood, were born in Gokula;
having obtained Hari through desire, they were thereafter liberated from the ocean of worldly existence" (Padma Purāṇa 6.245.164).
Therefore, even among men, because they have arisen in the form of women and because their object is the Blessed Lord, [there is no fault].

Although this desire was manifested by the ordinary god of love (Kāmadeva), it should be understood that it is indeed non-material (aprākṛta) desire manifested by the Lord Himself, based on the scriptural statement: "This is not that ordinary desire produced by the material god of love, but rather the destroyer of Manmatha himself" (Bhāgavatapurāṇa 10.32.2), and because in the Āgamas and other texts He is worshipped as the very embodiment of desire.

Furthermore, the praise of Him is heard even from supreme devotees such as Śrī Uddhava, beginning with the verse: "These gopīs on earth are the foremost among embodied beings" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.47.51). What more need be said?
His nature is well known even to the Vedas in the Bṛhad-vāmana; for therein, even the Śrutis [speak of Him].
It is well known that those who desired the eternal state of being gopīs became members of His retinue in that very form. This very fact is indicated by what was said by them themselves:
"That which [is perceived] in the heart by those joined in firm yoga of the breath, mind, and senses..."
"The sages worship Him, and even His enemies attained Him through remembrance; women fix their minds upon His staff-like arms which are like the coils of the king of serpents;
we too are equal to them, for we are equal-seers of the nectar of Your lotus feet. [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.87.23] Thus it is said.

And this meaning is perfectly clear: that reality called Brahman, which the sages worship through the vision of the scriptures with great effort, [the enemies] went to that very same reality simply by remembering You, even without performing such worship. Likewise, those women—the beautiful-browed gopīs of Śrī—are Yours.

O Śrī Nandanandana, those whose minds are fixed upon Your two staff-like arms— which resemble the body of the king of elephants— and who have attained the sweetness of the special love born from the touch of the nectar of Your own lotus feet, have reached that state; so too have we, the Vedas.

The meaning is as follows: *samadṛśaḥ* means those who have attained a state equal to Her; *satyaḥ* means truthful; *samāḥ* means those who have attained equality with Her by attaining the state of being a gopī just like Her; they alone are the ones who have gone to the nectar of the dust of Her feet.
The change in grammatical case is due to the force of the sense (*artha-vaśāt*). The word *aṅghri* (feet) is used out of reverence. In this context, even Her enemies [are included].

By the phrase "they went by means of remembrance," it is shown that the path of devotion (*bhāva-mārga*) accomplishes the goal instantaneously. By the phrase "those of equal vision" (*sama-dṛśaḥ*), it is indicated that only those following the path of passion (*rāgānugā*) are the most effective means in this regard;
otherwise, the Vedic scriptures—which know all means and goals—would have directed them toward something else entirely.

Thus, in this pair of pairs consisting of Smaraṇa and Para, it is shown that within each respective pair, the first is primary and the second is secondary. This is because, in both cases, the inclusion of the word "api" (also/even) along with their subsequent placement indicates they share a single meaning. Therefore, by the term "women" (striyaḥ), those who are eternally Śrī-Gopikās alone are to be understood.

In the same way, it is well known from the *Bṛhad-vāmana* that "they were seen by the Vedas" in the eternal abode of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Thus, the verse beginning with "from lust or from hatred" has been correctly explained up to the point "having abandoned that sin," where it means: "among those [afflictions], the sin consisting of hatred, fear, and so forth. (30)

Viśvanātha says: All those who possess both auspicious and inauspicious dispositions attain Him according to the gradation of their spiritual practice (*sādhana*); however, the gradation of the results (*phala*) must be discerned by oneself through reasoning.
Thus he says, "Out of desire" (*kāmāt*). Therefore, having abandoned the sin (*agha*) born of hatred, [one attains Him] through the very same possession (*āveśa*) that was born of hatred.

The meaning is "rendered destroyed. Furthermore, in this context, the word *agha* (sin) should not be explained as referring to desire (*kāma*), because [the text] states that even one who hates Hṛṣīkeśa [attains his state], let alone those who are dear to Adhokṣaja; thus, they are described as being equally beloved.
*Tad-gatim* means his state—his love and liberation. ||30||
The Gopīs [served] out of desire; Kaṃsa, out of fear; the kings headed by Śiśupāla, out of hatred;
the Vṛṣṇis, out of kinship; you, out of affection; and we, O Lord, out of devotion.

The gopīs are the devotees endowed with desire; Kaṃsa is the personification of Bhṛgu himself, to be known as the devotee possessed of fear; and Jayā and the others residing in Caidya and so forth are the goddesses of victory.
The Vṛṣṇis, along with their kinsmen, are devotees characterized by aversion;
the gods are proclaimed to be devotees through a state of equanimity born of great honor and affection.
"O lords of sages, great respect arises precisely from the subordination of affection;

even among the gods, great respect is considered greater toward the ṛṣis than toward others, such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Kāma, according to their respective order. Thus it is stated in the *Brahmatarka*. (31)
Śrīdhara says: He addresses them as "O gopīs. (31)

The sequential arrangement (*krama-sandarbha*): Now, in order to provide an illustration for the statement "many have attained that state," he says: "the gopīs. By the word "gopīs," it is meant that this is spoken by relying specifically upon the previous condition of those particular gopīs who follow the path of practitioners (*sādhaka*). As for the word "we" (*vayam*), it refers to how, when [the Lord] was engaged with me, as in the case of Śrī Nārada... [she] felt that toward me.

Since the status of being an attendant (*pārṣada*) has been established according to the method stated in passages such as *śuddhāṃ bhāgavatīṃ tanum* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.6.28), he speaks by assuming his former state, saying, "By that very [attendant-body], we ourselves [are present].
In that state alone lies ritualistic devotion (*vaidhī bhakti*). Now, for him who has attained spontaneous attachment (*rāga*), [there is no longer a need for it] toward me.

According to the principle stated in *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 11.20.36, "The qualities arising from the virtues and defects of those who are exclusively devoted [shine forth]," their devotion shines as being essentially characterized by passion (*rāga-ātmikā*) and not dependent on scriptural injunctions (*vidhi-anadhīnā*). For this very reason, there is the description of them as having already transcended even the attainment of results, using the expression "those who have gone to that state" (*tad-gatiṃ gatāḥ*). In this regard, both the ancient Gopīs and contemporary women are included.
Simply by hearing of His qualities and so forth, they would become absorbed in Him. As it is said:
"He who, merely being heard of, forcibly attracts the minds of women—even he who is far away and whose glories are sung afar; how much more so for those who behold Him? (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.90.17).

Alternatively, even for Caidya, who was acting as an attendant, his status as a *sādhaka* (accomplisher) is indicated precisely by the observation of the destruction of the appearance of adventitious afflictions. From the affection (*sneha*) that arises from a connection, there is passion (*rāga*); because of that, "you Vṛṣṇis" and "you"—this constitutes one [point].
Therefore, in passages such as "by the persistence of enmity" and so forth, and "from desire" and so forth...

Because the meaning already stated is made manifest as being identical with that very point in this illustrative sentence; because it conforms to what will be said regarding "the five"; and because both [attachment and affection] exist in both cases, the mention of "relationship" (*sambandha*) is for the purpose of indicating that it is a specific form of passion (*rāga*).

Just as with the gopīs, here too the specific Vṛṣṇis and the specific relatives of the Pāṇḍavas are designated as "accomplishers" (sādhakas) by relying upon their former state; therefore, even in the case of affection born of relationship, it should be understood as consisting merely of a longing for Him. [This is] by means of devotion that has been cultivated, because it is precisely this [devotion] that has been attained.
Because he has begun to explain the path of *bhāva* (emotional transformation).

Viśvanātha says: He names the abodes of the *bhāvas* by mentioning their names—the *gopīs* out of desire, as previously explained; this is due solely to the intensity of their affection, and not in a general sense.

When such an intention is present, the term "the hunchbacked woman and others" (*kubjādyāḥ*) is employed. This arises from the fear born of knowing that they themselves would be killed by Kṛṣṇa; [it is said] "you Vṛṣṇis, the Yādavas, and the Pāṇḍavas," because of your relationship as sons, brothers, and so forth, and because of your relationship as nephews, brothers-in-law, grandsons, and so forth.
"From what kind of affection?

From that which consists of affection"—by this, Satrājit, Prasena, Śatadhanvan, Karṇa, Duryodhana, and others are excluded. Furthermore, one should not explain the attainment of that [affection] as being a separate means here; for it is stated in the subsequent sentence:

Because all entities are defined as being comprised of exactly five categories, the phrase "we, Nārada and others, have attained that state through devotion" is to be understood as a continuation from the preceding verse. In this regard, the gopīs attained the state of beloved consorts (*preyasī*) characterized by love; Kaṃsa attained *sāyujya* (union); and Caitra, Dantavakra, and Pauṇḍraka attained *sārūpya* (similarity in form).

Other devotees attain, as is appropriate, union (*sāyujya*), residence in the same world (*sālokya*), and so forth; the Vṛṣṇis and Pāṇḍavas attain the status of attendants (*pārṣadatva*) characterized by friendship and other such bonds; and Nārada and others attain the status of attendants characterized by lordly power and knowledge. Their respective destinies are determined according to their specific means of practice, as observed in the relevant scriptural passages.

They have departed. Regarding this point: because of the statement in the *Harivaṃśa*, "This excellent mountain was held by me for the sake of the welfare of the Yādavas," and because even the cowherds such as Nanda and others belong to the Vṛṣṇi lineage, they possess an excessive degree of affection due to their lack of knowledge regarding His divine majesty; therefore, the bond of kinship, such as that of sons and so forth, is strongest precisely among them.
It should be understood as indicating predominance. ||31||
No one at all would be a friend to these five with respect to a man;
therefore, by whatever means possible, one should fix the mind upon Kṛṣṇa.

Madhva: Any form of *bhakti-yoga* is superior to that of the flute-player; therefore, one should fix the mind by some means or other, and not without a means. For it is stated in the *Śabdanirṇaya*: "Devotion is declared to be the means, while hatred and the like are non-means. (32)

Śrīdhara: If that is so, why was Vena cast into hell? He explains that because of the absence of intense meditation (*tīvra-dhyāna*), only his sin bore fruit—by the words "not even one" (*katamo’pi*). Regarding the Supreme Person, Śrī Hari: since desire for a person is impossible in the Supreme Person, among the five types of those who meditate out of fear and so forth, Vena was not [among them].
It has been stated: "Which one? (32)
*The Casket of Caitanya’s Teachings*: "Which one? and so forth. Among the five who cause fear and the like, he possesses none of them, such as hatred; rather, he has only the conceit, "I am the Lord.
He has no hatred or the like toward the Blessed One; therefore, he is distinct from those such as Caitya who cause hatred and the like.

Even though they did not attain good fortune, because they attained it through hatred and the like toward Him, [the author] shows that one should fix the mind upon Hari by saying "therefore," etc. Regarding the phrase "by whatever means," etc.—the meaning of the word "whatever" (kiṃ) is: by whichever means the mind enters into Him, by that very same means [one should do so]. ||32||

The sequence of the argument: If perfection can be attained even through hatred, then why was Vena cast into hell? Anticipating this objection, he says: "Which one?"—meaning that among the five types of enmity, such as persistent hostility (*vairānubandha*) and so forth, directed toward the Blessed Lord as the object, Vena would not be even the slightest [degree of such enmity]. For him, toward Him...

The enmity was merely incidental and consisted of simple censure, not a persistent state of hostility. Therefore, the sense is that because there was no intense meditation [on malice], only the evil [of their own actions] bore fruit there.
Consequently, even by those whose natures were like asuras, for the sake of their own liberation from him—

The intended meaning is that one must not commit the rash act of practicing enmity; for this very reason, the over-extension of the rule regarding those "who were indeed spoken of by the Blessed One" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.2.32) and so forth is also precluded, because such acts are neither intended nor spoken of [by the Lord].

"Because it is thus, therefore..."—here too, "one should apply [the practice] as before" is merely a conventional assertion (*sammati-mātra*), not an injunction; the meaning is that among those very means, one should proceed by whichever single one is most appropriate. Oh!
That which is accomplished after a long time through the path of devotion (*bhakti-mārga*) achievable only with such great effort—that very same thing is accomplished [by this means].

Since even hatred and other such emotions arise there through a mere particularity of disposition after a long time, how much more so when that state of supreme, genuine virtue is present? As for the talk of hostility—which is the province of base people—let it remain far away.
For what inferior person, adopting indifference, would not even feel affection? Thus it is said regarding *rāgānugā*.
And thus, that state of being most appropriate is accepted.

[Bhakti-sandarbha 322] Viśvanātha: Now, if that is so, why was Veṇa—who committed blasphemy against the Lord and insults such as those found in the *Śiśupālavadha*—cast into hell? To this he says: regarding the five [qualities] toward the Supreme Person, the Blessed One...
Because he is not the locus of any of the states mentioned in the preceding verse, he is none of them:

he is not, first of all, full of desire like the gopīs out of affection; nor is he afraid like Kaṃsa; nor is he a hater like Śiśupāla, who hated the Lord with the thought, "He will kill me," due to being completely possessed by Him; nor is he...

The meaning is that he does not maintain any relationship there like Vṛṣṇi and others, nor is he a devotee like Nārada and others. Therefore, the implication is that one who, being distinct from Śiśupāla and others, desires to foster an antagonistic disposition, goes to Naraka just like Veṇa. Since this is so, [one should act] by some means whatsoever that is not antagonistic.

Therefore, it should be understood that the injunction "one should fix the mind on Kṛṣṇa" has the same meaning as the method stated in the verse beginning with "by means of a continuous attachment born of enmity. ||32||
O son of Pāṇḍu,
Vaśa the Caidya and Dantavakra were the foremost attendants of Viṣṇu, yet they fell from their station due to the curse of a brahmin.

Regarding the statement that even the King of Cedi and others were haters due to the entry of another [power], despite being naturally devoted to Madhu, the reason is given as "the son of one's mother’s sister" (mātṛṣvasreya) and so forth. ||33||

Śrīdhara: Having thus related this narrative as an introduction to the history, in response to the inquiry as to what the cause was for Śiśupāla’s persistent enmity toward Śrī Kṛṣṇa, he speaks that very history, beginning with the words "mātṛ-ṣvasreya" (the maternal cousin). [They] fell from their position in Vaikuṇṭha. (33)

The sequence of the composition: The intention is to demonstrate, through a question and answer, that Caidya and Dantavaktra were not actually asuras, but rather acted in imitation of them out of Hari’s own desire for spontaneous play, characterized by His graciousness toward the community of brāhmaṇas who promote devotion to Him.

He said: "The daughter of my mother's sister. The meaning of the question is that, in that case, a change of state for those two is in no way possible; for this is so because of the Śruti text, "And he does not return" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.15.1), and because of the principle, "Non-return is from the Word" (Brahma Sūtra 4.4.22); and because of the statement: "But having come to Me, O son of Kuntī, one does not return... (Gītā 8.16).

"Rebirth does not exist" (Gītā 8.16), according to the Śrī-Gītā; and that is indeed consistent with logic. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) in that regard is merely an *itihāsa* (traditional narrative), and its intention is that it is possible only through the aforementioned reasoning. And he himself will state: "Those whose sins have been destroyed by the discus of Viṣṇu... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa).

And they will explain [the verse] *Pā. 7.1.43* as follows: "Of those two, only the sin was destroyed, not the two themselves"—this is Viśvanātha's view. Thus, having concluded this discussion on Śiśupāla, which establishes the doctrine of the path of emotion (*bhāva-mārga*), there arises the inquiry: what is the cause for Śiśupāla’s persistent enmity toward Śrī Kṛṣṇa?
He said: "From the word 'mātṛ-ṣvasreya' [it is understood that they] fell from Vaikuṇṭha. (33)
Śrī Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Of what kind was the curse, and whose was it, that resulted from the assault on the servant of Hari?
The worldly existence of those who are single-mindedly devoted to Hari appears as if it were not worth believing.

Śrīdhara: [The term] *haridāsau* refers to one who touches upon or overcomes [them]; thus it is so called. Whose curse is it, or of what nature? It is as if untrustworthy and unworthy of respect because of its impossibility. *Bhava* means birth. ||34||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: He also touches upon Haridāsa; the sense is that no trust arises in the words of the curse because they are unbelievable, due to their impossibility. ||34||
O Lord,
you ought to explain this which pertains to the connection with a body for those inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha-pura who are devoid of bodies, senses, and vital breaths.

Śrīdhara: He states that this is indeed impossible—for those who are devoid of the material body, senses, and life-breaths which constitute the causes of birth; that is to say, for those whose bodies consist of pure *sattva*. You ought to narrate this account as it relates to their connection with a material body. (35)
The *Krama-sandarbha*: not explained.

The *Bhagavat-sandarbha* (64): Thus, since it has been established that Śrī Vaikuṇṭha is of the nature of the essential form (*svarūpa*), it is all the more established that His attendant associates (*pārṣadas*), who constitute its limbs, are likewise of that same nature.

And this is indeed appropriate for His servants: "One should not worship a god who is not a god," because one lacks the qualification even for worship directed toward Him without the cultivation of the realization of being like Him; whereas directly, there is direct likeness to Him.
Thus, by implication, the same applies to the eternal associates (nitya-pārṣadas). Therefore...

Thus he says: "Of those devoid of body, senses, and life-force," and so forth. The meaning is: of those whose bodies consist of pure *sattva*, being devoid of the material (*prākṛta*) bodies, senses, and life-forces that serve as the causes of [repeated] birth. ||35||

Viśvanātha says: He states the very impossibility [of this] in the words "the body" (*deha*). The meaning is: for those who are devoid of the material bodies, senses, and vital breaths that are the causes of birth—that is, for those whose bodies consist of pure *sattva*—it is impossible for this narrative to be fit to describe a connection [with them] through a connection with a material body.
The commentary of Śrī Svāmī Caranānām. ||35||
Śrī Nārada said:
Once, the sons of Brahmā went to the world of Viṣṇu by chance.
Sanandana and the others departed, wandering through the three worlds.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
Krama-sandarbha: "Ekadā" (once) forms a couplet [with the following verse]. By chance—that is, through some rise of fortune—they went to the world of Viṣṇu. ||36||

"Thinking those children— who were the ancestors even of the ancients, possessing the luster of five- or six-year-old infants, and clad in the directions as their only garment— to be mere infants, the two gatekeepers barred them."
By the words "The two door-keepers of the honey," the state of being established in authority is expressed;
for people are of two kinds: those established in authority and those who are liberated.
Those who reside in the world of Viṣṇu, though they may be subject to boons, curses, and the like,
certainly attain liberation while remaining in their office.
Immediately after their liberation, did not excellent boons, curses, and so forth indeed [occur]?

"Endowed with body, senses, and vital breaths at first, they are later no longer joined with them, even though they were joined with those [elements] by the gods who possessed self-conceit and had absorbed them into their own selves"—thus Śrīdhara says in the *Tantrasāra*. Of what nature are they? They are those whose years—five or six—have passed.

Those whose appearance is like that of children (arbhāḥ) are so called; they were born even before the former ones, such as Marīci and others, and thus were the first-born among them. Since they were naked, with the directions for their only clothing, he regarded them as infants. ||37||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Those who have five or six years are "infants" (*arbhāḥ*);

those who possess an appearance like that of such infants—even the ancient ones such as Marīci and others—he regarded as naked children (*dig-vāsasaḥ śiśūn*), [using] the masculine form [as in the compound].
The word "bhāva" is an archaic usage. ||37||

[In this regard, concerning the passage beginning with "Once, the sons of Brahmā," one should consult the series of verses Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.15.12, 16, 30, 31, and 34, which provide a corresponding description. —
Thus they cursed in their anger: "You two do not deserve to dwell at the feet of the Slayer of Madhu, which are free from the qualities of passion and ignorance."
"O fools, go quickly from here to the most wicked womb of the asuras!
Thus cursed, the two were falling from their own abode, when they were [caught] by those who were compassionate.
Śrīdhara: "You do not even deserve to dwell here—how much less to serve it? This is the meaning of the word *ca* (and).
O fools! For this reason, depart quickly. (38–39)

The sequence of the composition: "He cursed," etc., consists of one and a half verses. Although [the Lord] is devoid of passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas), and thus lacks the ordinary modes of goodness (sattva) and the rest, the intention here is to speak of His lack even of those [subtle elements] consisting of them;
for such a fault is possible only through ordinary sattvic nature. ||38-39||
Viśvanātha: By three births for you two, may the curse be capable—that is, it shall become effective—for the sake of leading you both to Vaikuṇṭha, the world [of Viṣṇu]. (38–39)
[Regarding the phrase "thus cursed" and so forth, one should consult the series of verses from Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.16.34–36, which provide the corresponding meaning.
"May these two, who have been described by you as having three births, be capable of accomplishing the world's purpose.
Thus they were born as the two sons of Diti, honored by the Daityas and Dānavas;
Hiraṇyakaśipu was the elder, and Hiraṇyākṣa was the younger brother after him.

Śrīdhara: "By three births for you two, let this curse be brought to an end; that is to say, let it be completed so that it may suffice for the sake of the world, for the attainment of your own place. This is the meaning of what was said again. ||40||
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain by Hari in the form of a lion.
Hiraṇyākṣa [was slain] by Him who, for the sake of upholding the earth, assumed the form of a boar.
Śrīdhara: For the purpose of upholding the earth, he who would have obstructed that [task] has been slain. ||41||
The *krama-sandarbha*: not explained.
Viśvanātha: when the lifting of the earth (the world) was to be performed. ||41||
Hiraṇyakaśipu, desiring to kill his son Prahlāda— who was dear to Keśava—
inflicted various tortures upon him for the sake of his death.
Śrīdhara: He indicates the cause for the slaying of Hiraṇyakaśipu with the words, "Hiraṇyakaśipu [slew] his son. (42)
The *Krama-sandarbha* by Viśvanātha states: "It has not been explained.
—o)0(o— [He who is] the self of all beings, serene, and possessed of equal vision.
Touched by the splendor of the Blessed One, he was unable to destroy it despite his efforts.
Madhva: Within the Self of all beings, he was born as a being. Hiraṇyakaśipu considered Hari to be a mere being at the time of his death;
therefore, he became terrifying both there and toward the king.
Thinking that he had indeed become a king because of the marks such as the discus on Kṛṣṇa,
and at the time of death, thinking only of Hari with exclusive devotion;
"Even a human being, having entered into and attained the state of being a gatekeeper for Hari... thus it is said in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*.

Furthermore, there are statements declaring liberation from devotion to Viṣṇu and knowledge of Him through other means, as well as statements regarding the diminution of Viṣṇu’s qualities and those of Śrī, Brahmā, and others, in their respective order.

"Furthermore, all pleasant words [addressed] out of hatred for Viṣṇu and others are declared to be intended for delusion, even though they appear to reveal the truth. Thus says Śrīdhara in the *Prakāśasaṃhitā*: "[He sees] the Self-nature of all beings. Why? Because he sees everything as the equal Brahman alone."

Likewise him; therefore, he was tranquil, being free from hatred and other such passions. For this very reason, he was touched—that is, pervaded—by the splendor of the Blessed One. By means of exertions, such as the striking with weapons and missiles. ||43||

The sequence of the composition: "That" (tam) means that because it is touched by the splendor of the Blessed One due to being eternally permeated by Him, it is therefore the self-nature of all beings and the object of supreme love; for that very reason, it is tranquil and free from distraction elsewhere.
It possesses equal vision and is free from attachment and aversion; for that very reason, it was unable [to act]. ||43||

Viśvanātha: [The Lord] has become the Self of all beings; He is as dear as one's own self, and because there is no hatred even toward a father who hates Him, He is serene; and because He views the happiness and suffering of Himself and others with equality, He possesses equal vision. ||43||
Then those two Rākṣasas were born from Keśinī as the sons of Viśravas:
Rāvaṇa and Kumbhakarṇa, who caused affliction to all the worlds.
Śrīdhara: The two sons of Viśravas. ||44||
The *Krama-sandarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon. —o)0(o— Therein it is also said:
"Having become Rāghava, he slew [him] for the sake of liberation from the curse."
O Lord, you shall hear of Rāma’s prowess from the mouth of Mārkaṇḍeya.
Śrīdhara: "Nyahanat" means he killed. To the one who is eager, asking why that very point should be stated, he replies: "The prowess of Rāma. (45)
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha states: "It has not been explained."—
"In this matter, two Kṣatriyas have been born as the sons of your maternal aunt."
Now, freed from the curse and with their sins destroyed by Kṛṣṇa’s discus, they [attained liberation].
Śrīdhara: Those two whose sin (*aṃhas*) was destroyed by Kṛṣṇa’s discus; the meaning is that their sin alone was destroyed, but not they themselves. ||46||

*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: The meaning is that their sin was struck down by the discus of Viṣṇu; it was their very offense that externally transformed into the forms of Śiśupāla and Dantavakra, and not those two [beings] themselves. Thus.

The Master’s feet [comment]: Just as fire destroys only the impurity of gold and not the gold itself, so too the meaning is that the two masses of splendor belonging to Jaya and Vijaya alone entered the Lord and were seen by people. ||46||
Through meditation characterized by intense persistence in their enmity, the two attendants of Viṣṇu attained the nature of Acyuta and went once again to the side of Hari.

Regarding *madhvaḥ*: "Enmity (*vaira*) is the connection (*anubandha*); devotion (*bhakti*) has been described as enmity. But the connection (*anubandha*) may also be devotion; attachment (*bandha*) is declared to be affection (*sneha*)"—thus it is stated in the *Prakāśasaṃhitā*. (47)
Śrīdhara: Not explained.

Krama-sandarbha: Regarding the phrase "vairānubandha" (the persistence of enmity): thus, by describing the curse of the Brahmins, [the author] repeatedly emphasizes the Brahmins' courtesy, and by repeatedly describing the battle, he emphasizes the desire for combat.

He has presented this as the cause; however, the primary factor should be understood as the very desire for war, by which the minds of even the sages toward the two Pārṣadas became perverted. As it was said by the Śrī-Bhagavān himself in the Third Canto: "But my opinion... (Bhāgavatam 3.16.29). Nevertheless, because a literal curse and so forth were absolutely impossible, it was merely a semblance of such.
Thus he is shown to be his effect; by the statement, "His sins were destroyed by Viṣṇu’s discus" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.1.46), the previously stated established doctrine itself must be discerned. ||47||

Viśvanātha: Those two whose forms (ākārau) remained identical to the Self (ātmanau) along with Acyuta—the state of being such (tattā)—were brought [to that state] by meditation alone; they subsequently went to the side of Hari Nārāyaṇa at the conclusion of the *mauṣala-līlā*. Thus, prior to the *mauṣala-līlā*, they were indeed in their superior bodies (*śreṣṭha-śarīra*).

The reality is that because Nārāyaṇa himself has entered [the body], his two attendants, Jaya and Vijaya, have also entered and remain right there. However, the common worldly perception is that Śiśupāla and Dantavakra attained *sāyujya* (union) with Kṛṣṇa. ||47||
Śrī Yudhiṣṭhira said:
How could there have been hatred toward his beloved son, that great-souled one?
Tell me, O Blessed One, by what means Prahlāda attained the nature of Acyuta.
Śrīdhara: The remaining sense is: "Tell me also that reason by which Prahlāda’s state of being the self of Acyuta—that is, his one-pointedness of mind toward Acyuta alone [was attained]. (48)
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: "The state of being Acyuta" (acyutātmatā) means that by which one possesses a mind fixed solely on Acyuta; "tell me that as well," is the ellipsis. ||48||

Thus ends the first chapter of the seventh [section] in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted to the Lord; it is well-composed and truly agreeable to the virtuous.
Thus, in the glorious Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the commentary on the Brahma-sūtras,
in the Vaiyāsikī collection pertaining to the state of the Paramahaṃsas, in the seventh book,
in the dialogue between Yudhiṣṭhira and Nārada.
The First Chapter.
Now begins the second chapter.
Śrī Nārada said:
When his brother had thus been slain by Hari in the form of a boar, [the demon Hiraṇyākṣa...]
O King, Hiraṇyakaśipu burned with rage and grief.
Śrīdhara:
In the second [chapter], having flooded the world with Dānavas through the wrath of Viṣṇu,
he consoled those whose brothers, sons, and others had been slain by them through historical narratives.
With the intention that hatred toward the Lord alone is the cause even for hatred toward Him [the devotee], he says "O brother," and so forth. Thus, by taking the side of the gods... ||1||
The connection of the sequence is as follows: "Thus he was tormented. In the phrase *mūrtinā*, some read *rūpiṇā*. (1)
Viśvanātha:
In the second [chapter], having appointed the Dānavas to the destruction of Dharma out of grief for his brother,
he indeed consoled Mitra and the others with knowledge and historical accounts.

To state that hatred toward the Lord was indeed the cause for Prahlāda’s hatred as well, he first describes that very hatred toward the Lord along with its cause, beginning with the words "O brother, thus... (verse 1).
And he spoke thus, filled with rage, biting his lips,
gazing at the smoky sky with eyes blazing with anger.
Śrīdhara: Gazing at the sky, which had become smoky as if by the very smoke of the fire of his anger, as it blazed up excessively with fury. ||2||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "Looking at the sky" implies the intention: "With my own hand, I shall destroy both Hari’s abode, Vaikuṇṭha, and Hari himself. "Smoky-colored" refers to the fire of the eyes.
The meaning is: "because it is pervaded by smoke. ||2||
With his fierce gaze and formidable fangs, and with a face made terrifying by a frown,
he raised his trident in the assembly and spoke thus to the Dānavas:
Śrīdhara: He whose face is joined with a frown and is difficult to behold by means of a gaze endowed with yoga and terrible fangs. ||3||
The structural arrangement (*krama-sandarbha*): He specifies that very thing which was stated as "and he said this"—namely, "terrible" (*karālā*) and so forth.
"O, O! constitutes a couplet (*yugmaka*). ||3||
Viśvanātha: Not explained.
—o)0(o)— O Dānavas and Daityas! O Two-headed one! O Three-eyed one! O Śambara!
Śatabāhu, Hayagrīva, Namuci, Pāka, and Ilvala.
O Vipracitti, Puloman, Śakuni, and the others, listen all of you to my words immediately; let it be done quickly, do not delay.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
My beloved brother and friend was slain by mean rivals.
Even by pursuing him with an equal force led by Hari acting as the rear-guard.
Śrīdhara: Even by means of equal approaches, such as worship and services that serve as external causes, while being held back by the rear-guard [of obstacles]. ||6||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "Even by one who is equal. Although that Lord Hari is equal toward all, nevertheless, due to the influence of greed, [He may act] as a rear-guard attacker (*pārṣṇi-grāha*) by means of the inducements of approaching Him for worship (*upadhāvana*).
The meaning is that his conduct is one that sides with the gods. ||6||
Of that compassionate one who had abandoned his own nature, who was like a forest-dweller of illusion,
who was devoted to one who was devoted to him, yet whose mind was as unstable as that of a child;

Śrīdhara: Thus, for one by whom the nature of equanimity has been abandoned—[referring to] Him who, though consisting of pure light, assumed the form of a wild boar through *māyā*, and whose self was unstable, his mind being unsettled—from where [could such equanimity come]? For he [the Lord] bestows [favor] upon whomever worships him.
For one who worships and follows [the path]. ||7||
The sequence of composition: the pair beginning with "tasya" [is as follows]. The actual meaning, however, has been set aside;
for he has bestowed his own nature, such as *sārūpya* (conformity in form) and so forth, upon his devotees. This is derived from the root *ghṛṇi* in the sense of "taking" (*grahaṇe*), hence *ghṛṇeḥ*.

He is the one who accepts [the world] out of compassion (*kṛpayā*). In the phrase *māyā kṛpā mayi*, the instrumental case-ending is elided according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa-tṛtīyā-luk*). From that...
He whose lineage is everywhere through compassion alone, who expands His pastimes by His very compassion, and who,

like a child of unsteady mind, expands various states of being according to the disposition of His devotees; He whose neck is distinct from my spear and beyond its reach, and whose form is characterized by that [neck].

"By means of my blood, when I manifest in the form of Śrī Nṛsiṃha, I shall satisfy my brother who is fond of blood with that blood of mine which has become a living being," according to the passage beginning with [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 4.31.14]: "Just as by watering the root of a tree... and so forth. ||7||

Viśvanātha says: If you say, "We too shall follow [him]," do not speak thus; rather, remain engaged in the task assigned by me, and I alone shall slay him. He says this in two verses beginning with "tasya" (of him).
But surely Hari is called the Supreme Self (paramātman) by the scriptures; therefore, how will you kill him?

To this he replies: It is well known that the nature of the Supreme Self consists in universal indifference resulting from the abandonment of all personal inclinations. If He has abandoned that [nature], then how can He still possess the status of the Supreme Self at present?
Such is the sense. On the contrary, he says that he abandoned his state as the Supreme Self and became a beast:
"Formerly, though consisting of pure light, he has now become a forest-dweller subject to *māyā*, and even one taking the form of fish, tortoises, and so forth."

Furthermore, the meaning is that for one who worships Him, even a mere person who worships is like a child captivated by a single piece of sweetmeat (*khaṇḍa-laḍḍuka*). In reality, however, it is precisely because of His affection for His devotees (*bhakta-vātsalya*) that the five attributes beginning with "having abandoned" (*tyakta*) and so forth come to be; and these are indeed His ornaments, not [defects].
The sense is that this is a refutation. Although [the Lord] consists of pure light, [the terms] "by Māyā," "by grace" (kṛpā), and so forth, should be applied to the term "ghṛṇi. ||7||
With the abundant blood from my neck, severed by the fish-spear,
I, freed from pain, shall satisfy my brother who is fond of blood.
Śrīdhara: The connection with the third [verse] is as follows: "While I shall satiate [the ancestors] with his blood, you all go to the earth. ||8||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: The meaning is that since the neck is "separated" (*bhinnā*)—that is, distinct—from my trident (*mac-chūla*), it is impossible even for the ordinary trident to enter there; [here] *kuṅkuma* means blood.
Because it is stated [in the scripture] "it is proclaimed," [the Lord is] "fond of blood" (rudhirapriyam), meaning He is fond of the saffron used for coloring His limbs;
the sense is that this is because my brother is devoted to Him and thus fond of the saffron from His flower-offerings (nirmālya). ||8||
When that enemy peak was destroyed, its root severed like a forest tree,
the gods whose life-breath is Viṣṇu withered away like branches.

Śrīdhara: [Objection: But surely the gods have caused his slaughter; why then are they not killed? To this he replies: "In that Hari," meaning in that deceptive one, the adversary. Or, it means "one whose intended purpose (*īhita*) is fraudulent (*kūṭa*). When he has perished—that is, when he is no longer seen—the gods will wither away and go to their destruction of their own accord. Why?
Those for whom Viṣṇu alone is the vital breath (prāṇa)—just as the branches of a tree with its roots cut dry up of their own accord, so it is with them. ||9||
Krama-sandarbha: Not commented upon.

Viśvanātha: "In him whose efforts (īhitam) consist of deceitful actions (kūṭa-īhite)—that is, in one who, though actually among those who are deceitful (kūṭeṣu kapaṭiṣu), such as myself, exerts himself in the endeavor of battle—oh, what great fortune is mine! Thus he says.
This is the state of affairs. But how much can be described of the good fortune of the gods? They indeed have him as their sole life-breath;

thus he says: when he has perished by fate—even though he was once seen—their branches wither just as the branches of a tree wither when its root is severed; for the word *naśera* has the sense of "not being seen," they likewise wither away. Viṣṇu alone [is their support].
The meaning is that those for whom He is their very life, or rather, those who are equal to Viṣṇu’s own life-breath, are indeed supremely blessed. ||9||
Go now to the earth, which is nourished by the Brahmins and Kshatriyas;
destroy those who perform austerities, sacrifices, Vedic study, vows, and acts of charity."
Śrīdhara: "Sūdayadhvam" means "destroy," that is, cause to be killed, those who are engaged in asceticism, sacrifice, and so forth. ||10||
The sequence of the composition: "Because in that [state]" (yatas tasmin). Or rather, one might object:
"Surely, since he died by his own hand, a divine state has already been attained; what is the use of offering libations to him?
To this, he says: "In this" (asmin)—that is, in the *kūṭastha*, which is immutable, of a single nature, pervading all time, and beneficial.

When the devotee-friend has perished—that is, when he has gone out of sight—all the gods, both material and spiritual, wither away because their very life-breath is centered in him; even though they possess various sources of happiness and prosperity, they reach a state of desiccation.
Therefore, the sense is that one must perform his worship alone. And so, if it is your desire—
Therefore, one should go only as far as that vision [of the goal] extends. ||10||

Viśvanātha: Go to the earth that has been properly nourished and increased by the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas through their asceticism, strength, and power. For what purpose? To slaughter—that is, to destroy it. ||10||
Viṣṇu is the source of the rites of the twice-born; he is the sacrifice, the personification of dharma,
and the supreme refuge of the gods, sages, ancestors, living beings, and dharma itself.
"The view that Hari is the root of the sacrifice of the learned and so forth is the opinion of the Asuras;
for Hari alone is rightly considered the root of everything, O King"—thus it is said in the *Brahma-purāṇa*. (11)

Śrīdhara: But what offense have they committed? To this he says: "Viṣṇu... He is one whose root is the ritual performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) of the twice-born, since that sacrifice consists of dharma and is the supreme refuge (*parāyaṇa*) of the gods and others. Therefore, because Viṣṇu, in the form of sacrifice, is their root, [they have acted] by disregarding me.
And because they rely upon that [view], they are to be slain; such is the meaning. ||11||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Since Viṣṇu himself would perish upon their destruction, he says "Viṣṇu" [in the verse]. When the twice-born are destroyed, because of the cessation of their ritual activities, Viṣṇu’s very root is uprooted.

There will be the destruction of sacrifice and dharma, as well as the destruction of their very essence. Furthermore, since he is the supreme refuge and ultimate support for the celestial sages and others, the implication is that he will die out of grief upon their slaughter. ||11||
Wherever there are twice-born men, cows, the Vedas, and the duties of the castes and stages of life,
go to that very region, set it ablaze, and tear it asunder!"

Śrīdhara: Therefore, he says, "Listen to that supreme mantra," beginning with "Wherever... [The words] "sandīpayata" mean "burn. "Vṛścata" means "cut down"—perform the felling of the trees that provide livelihood. ||12||
Kramasandarbha: This has not been explained.

Viśvanātha: [The phrase] "sandīpayata dahata" (set fire to it, burn it) implies that when a region is burned, those residing there are naturally burnt as well. [The phrase] "vṛścata" (cut it down) means perform the felling of the trees upon which they depend for their livelihood.
Thus, having received their master’s command upon their heads with reverence,
those who delight in slaughter carried out the destruction of the people accordingly."
Śrīdhara: [The commentary on] *Krama-sandarbha* has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: "Kadana" means suffering (*kaṣṭa*). ||13||
They burned cities, villages, cow-pens, gardens, fields, groves, hermitages, mines, market towns, hamlets, settlements,
and ports.
Śrīdhara: A city (*pura*) is one possessing marketplaces and the like; a village (*grāma*) is devoid of those. A cow-pen (*vraja*) is the dwelling place of cattle.
A garden (*udyāna*) is an artificial grove. A field (*kṣetra*) is for rice and other crops. A pleasure-grove (*ārāma*) is a natural grove.
A hermitage (*āśrama*) is the abode of sages. A mine (*ākara*) is for gems and the like. A hamlet (*kheṭa*) is the dwelling place of farmers.

A *kharvaṭa* is a village situated in mountain valleys; a *ghoṣa* is the dwelling of cowherds (*ābhīra*s); a *pattana* is a royal capital. The arrangement of these [terms] in sequence has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: A city (*pura*) possesses marketplaces and the like; a village (*grāma*) is devoid of those. A cow-pen (*vraja*) is the dwelling place of cattle.

A grove (*udyāna*) is a forest where flowers predominate. A field (*kṣetra*) is for rice and other crops. An orchard (*ārāma*) is a forest where fruit predominates. A hermitage (*āśrama*) is the abode of sages. A mine (*ākara*) is for gems and the like. A hamlet (*kheṭa*)...
The dwelling of farmers is a *vāsa*; a village situated in a mountain valley is a *kharvaṭa*; the dwelling of cowherds is a *ghoṣa*; and a royal capital is a *pattana*. ||14||
Some broke down the embankments, walls, and gate-towers with spades;
others, axes in hand, cut down the trees that provided their livelihood.
Some set fire to the dwellings of the people with blazing torches.

Śrīdhara: With *khanitraiḥ*, meaning instruments for digging; *ājīvyān*, meaning things to be subsisted upon, such as rose-apple (*jambu*), mango (*āmra*), wood-apple (*kapittha*), and so forth; and *śaraṇāni*, meaning houses. ||15||
The sequence of composition: "They struck down" constitutes one half-verse (ardhaka). ||15||
Viśvanātha: Not explained.
—o)0(o— Thus, while the world was being repeatedly oppressed by the followers of the lords of the Daityas,
Having abandoned heaven, the gods wandered upon the earth unobserved.
Śrīdhara: Being deprived and afflicted, they wandered upon the earth, characterized by exhaustion due to the absence of their sacrificial portions. ||16||
The sequence of events: because Hiraṇyakaśipu had previously said, "Go to heaven, to the celestial chariot-world, or to the earth," he attained residence upon Mount Sumeru. ||16||
Viśvanātha: "Viprakṛte" means afflicted or distressed; [this occurs] because of the absence of sacrificial portions, having completely abandoned heaven. ||16||
Hiraṇyakaśipu, grieving for his deceased brother,
performed the funeral rites such as the offering of water and the spreading of the grass mat, and then consoled his brother’s sons.

Śrīdhara: Thus, while the demons were thus carrying out the slaughter of the subjects, he describes what Hiraṇyakaśipu first did when he himself desired to perform austerities to attain the sovereignty of heaven and other goals, beginning with the words "Hiraṇyakaśipu... Kaṭodaka is the water to be offered for a deceased person.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the śrāddha for the deceased (preta-śrāddha) and so forth are included. ||17||
Kramasandarbha: This has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: "Kaṭodaka" refers to the water that should be offered to the deceased; by the word "etcetera," the śrāddha for the deceased is also included. (17)
Śakuni, Śambara, Dhṛṣṭi, Bhūtasantāpana, Vṛka,
Kālanābha, Mahānābha, Hariśmaśru, and Utkaca.
Knowing the proper place and time, the lord of men spoke these words with gentle speech to his mother Aditi and to Diti, the mother of Bāṇa, out of anger.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
Śrī Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"O mother, O mother! O daughter-in-law, O sons! You should not grieve for the hero;
for heroes, death facing the enemy is praiseworthy and desired."
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha: He addresses his brother’s wife as "O bride" (vadhū). ||20||
The sequence of composition has not been explained. —
O you of virtuous vows, the dwelling together of beings here is like that at a water-station.
Of those who have been brought together in one place by destiny and raised up by their own past actions.

Śrīdhara: Let it be granted that his slaughter is indeed praiseworthy; nevertheless, if one asks, "Has our kinsman not nonetheless departed? he says in response: "Of beings" (*bhūtānām*). [This refers to] those who were brought together and united in one place by destiny—that is, by past karma—and who have been led away again by their respective individual karmas.
Of those who have been separated. ||21||
The sequence of composition: "If even against an enemy [one should not flee], how much more so against Śrī Viṣṇu? (21)

Viśvanātha says: "And let the sorrow of separation from kinsmen be extinguished by such contemplation"—thus he speaks with the words "of beings" (*bhūtānām*). This refers to those who have been brought together at a *prapā* (a water-station) and then separated once again.
Eternal, immutable, pure, all-pervading, omniscient, and supreme,
he assumes his own subtle body by emitting the qualities through his creative power (māyā).
This [Brahman] assumes for itself its own mark (liṅga), namely the individual soul (jīva) consisting of mind and so forth, which is the substratum of names; it is Brahman. ||22||

Śrīdhara: Having thus dispelled grief from the perspective of worldly experience, he now dispels it from the perspective of ultimate reality, saying "eternal" (nitya). The Self is eternal, devoid of death; immutable, devoid of decay; pure, stainless;
omnipresent, all-knowing, and omniscient; the cause of everything, the Supreme.

[The Self] is distinct from the body and so forth; therefore, the meaning is that one should not grieve, thinking "it is dead," "it is emaciated," "it is impure," "it is separated," or "it is ignorant. How then does its transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) occur?
To this he says: "It assumes"—by means of *māyā*, which is its own ignorance (*avidyā*), the Self assumes a subtle body (*liṅga*) and forms (*mūrti*); [it assumes] the qualities (*guṇas*).

The meaning is that "saṃsāra" refers to the adjunct of the subtle body (liṅga-śarīra), which specifically creates or assumes various high and low bodies, or experiences such as pleasure and pain. ||22||
The sequence of the composition: Regarding the word "eternal" (*nitya*) here, the attribution of the attributes of the Lord to the individual soul (*jīva*) is due to the suitability for Asuras;

furthermore, that [ascription] is contrary to reason, such as claiming that the omniscient one possesses ignorance. However, in its true sense, he is "all-pervading" (*sarvaga*) because he goes to the entire world; he is "all-knowing" (*sarvavit*) because he perceives every body. ||22||

Viśvanātha: This was spoken from the perspective of worldly perception for the sake of awakening you; however, from that [transcendental] perspective, Hiraṇyākṣa was indeed the Self itself and not the body. And regarding the nature of that Self, He says: "Eternal," meaning free from death; "unchanging," meaning devoid of decay; "pure," meaning stainless.

"Omnipresent" (sarvagata) is a description of the nature of the Lord; yet, due to the nature of the *asura*, this term is applied even to the individual soul (*jīva*). In reality, however, he is so called because he goes to all worlds, and because he experiences everything, such as pleasure, pain, and so forth. "The Supreme" (*para*) means distinct from the body and other such things. This Self, by means of *māyā*, [perceives] its own body as a sign (*liṅga*).

It sustains [the world] through its own ignorance. For what purpose? Specifically by creating and accepting various high and low gross bodies, and likewise by repeatedly emitting them—that is, for the purpose of accepting and discarding gross bodies. ||22||
Just as trees appear to move when the water is moving,
so the earth appears to move when the eye is being whirled around.

Śrīdhara: He elaborates upon this with examples through four verses beginning with "yathā" (just as). Trees are reflected [in water]. Having stated the example that the attributes of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) reside in the limited substrate (*upahita*), he states the example that the attributes of the grasper reside in the grasped: "by the eye," etc. (23).
*Kramasandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Thus, by means of two examples, he states that the Self is indeed distinct even from that subtle body which bears the various marks: "Just as [the reflection of the moon] in the waters [is affected] by the movement of the boat..."

Even though they are reflected within [the water], they appear as if moving, yet they do not actually move because they are distinct from the waters. In the very same way, the attributes of the subtle body (*liṅga*), such as grief and delusion, are perceived in the Self as conditioned by that [body], but the Self is not [identical with] grief, delusion, and so forth; for it is distinct from that subtle body—this is the meaning.

Having thus stated the example that the attributes of an adjunct (upādhi) appear in the object so adjucted, he states the example that the attributes of the grasper appear in the grasped, using the word "by the eye": just as a person possessed by a spirit moves or appears to move when being affected by the defect of whirling— that is, being made to spin.
It is said that [the object] is grasped as a real entity. ||23||

"O auspicious lady, when the mind is thus being led astray by these qualities, the unimpaired person attains a state of identity with them, just as one who is without gender appears to possess gender."
"Like a bee, like a living being possessing [limited] characteristics;

it attains equality with the Unequalled solely through the vision of delusion. In reality, the living being is in no way equal to Brahman from the perspective of the ultimate truth. Thus, in the *Ṣāḍguṇya*.
Just as from the movement of water and the shifting of a tree's reflection,
an ignorant person might imagine the movement of the tree standing on the bank.
Likewise, when the reflection is defiled by the defects born of the mind,
the ignorant person imputes that defect to the Brahman which is the reflector.

"Just as one might perceive the illusion of the earth's rotation due to a delusion of one's own eyes, so too does this [individual] perceive Brahman as if it were defective because of the defects of his own self. Thus, in the *Brahma-tarka*. (24)
Śrīdhara: "Avikala" means entirely complete. Therefore, "sāmyatām" means the state of equanimity of the mind.
"Krama-sandarbha": not explained.

Viśvanātha: Thus, the meaning is that the Self, when entered into the body, is said to be graspable by the body and overcome by the attributes of the body. In this way, the Self remains entirely unimpaired and pure; [the verse describes] its similarity with that [body], namely the mind’s state of equality and its capacity to assume the attributes of the mind. ||24||
This is indeed the perversion regarding the self: the conception of signs where there are no signs.
This is union with the pleasant and the unpleasant, as well as separation; it is the cycle of karmic existence.

Śrīdhara: The notion of the *liṅga* (the subtle body) is the identification with the body. This is the self’s perversion, its state of being otherwise. He explains that very thing: separation from the beloved, union with the unpleasant, karma, and the cycle of rebirth consisting of entry into various wombs. (25)
The sequence of composition: "This" refers to the pair [of verses]. "In the bodiless" means in the Self that is distinct from the body. ||25||

Viśvanātha: Even though the Self is without marks (aliṅga), the conception of it as having marks (liṅga-bhāvanā) is the identification with the body.
