This very thing is the perversion (viparyāsa), that is, the inversion (viparyaya) of the Self; and from this very perversion comes this union with and separation from the pleasant and unpleasant for the Self. By the word "and" (ca), [it is implied] the opposite as well: union with the unpleasant and separation from the pleasant.
Karma and cyclic existence, and entry into various wombs. ||24||
Arising and destruction, sorrow of various kinds, lack of discernment, anxiety, and indeed the failure to remember discernment are recorded [as its effects].
Madhva: Non-discrimination itself is the delusion that non-discrimination is discrimination.

"The demons indeed possess devotion to Keśava regarding internal gold and other such things; yet, due to demonic possession, they hate others through the praise of Hari. Thus it is said in the *Pādma*. (26)

Śrīdhara: And from that, *saṃbhava* means origination. [The phrase] "non-recollection of discrimination" (*vivekasyāsmṛtiḥ*)—that is, its non-remembrance—is not explained [by the author]. Viśvanātha: It is the non-appearance (*asphūrtiḥ*) of discrimination, even though it exists. ||26||
In this regard, they also cite this ancient history;
learn that dialogue between Yama and the kinsmen of the deceased.
Śrīdhara: Here too, the meaning is that this grief is in vain, occurring even without a cause for sorrow;
listen to the conversation between certain relatives of a deceased person who has passed away. (27)

Kramasandarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: Here too, there is the sorrow for one who should not be mourned; even the historical account [is relevant]. And for those who are the kinsmen of the deceased, of the one who has died. (27)
Among the Uśīnaras there was a king renowned as Suyajña;
though slain by his rivals in battle, his kinsmen attended upon him.
Śrīdhara: "Upāsata" means they remained surrounding him in his presence. ||28||
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— [He saw him] with his jeweled armor shattered and his ornaments and garlands fallen away.
His heart pierced by arrows, he lay there, stained with blood.
Śrīdhara: He whose jeweled armor was shattered; he whose ornaments and garlands had fallen away; he whose heart was pierced by an arrow; and who was smeared and stained with blood. (29)
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
[He saw him] with disheveled hair, ruined eyes, and having violently bitten his lip.
His lotus-like face was obscured by dust, and his arms were severed of their weapons in the fray.

Śrīdhara: One whose hair is disheveled; one whose eyes are destroyed; one by whom the lower lip has been bitten in impetuous fury; one whose lotus-face is dull and covered with dust; and one whose weapon and arm are severed. ||30||
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Him by whom the lower lip was bitten with impetuosity—that is, with anger. (30)
Seeing their husband, the lord of the Uśīnaras, treated in such a manner by fate, the queens were filled with grief.
Crying out, "We are lost, O Lord!", they repeatedly struck their breasts with their hands and fell at his feet.
Śrīdhara: They fell all around, near his two feet. ||31||
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: The meaning is that at that very moment, having been struck by weapons by his rivals, he remained in that state even though he had died. ||31||
Weeping aloud, she drenched the lotus-feet of her beloved with tears reddened by the saffron from her breasts.
With their hair and ornaments disheveled, they lamented with wailing cries, giving rise to grief among men.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
Alas, O Lord, how merciless the Creator is toward us!
You, who were once highly esteemed and formerly the provider of sustenance for the Uśīnaras, have now been reduced to a state beyond the range of sight,
by which you have become an increaser of their grief.

Śrīdhara: He expresses his lamentation with two verses beginning with "Aho. They speak of the very lack of compassion [of the Creator]: the connection of the words is that by that Creator who led you—that is, brought you—to a state beyond the range of sight, by that same Creator you have now been made an increaser of sorrows. ||33||
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: He utters a lamentation, beginning with "Alas! By that Creator who brought you forth, you have now been made the increaser of the sorrows of the Uśīnaras. (33)
O lord of the earth, how could we exist without you, our most excellent friend, who are so grateful?
Therefore, O hero, grant us permission to follow at your feet as we serve you wherever you shall go.

Śrīdhara: O Lord of the Earth! Without you, our dearest friend, how shall we exist? That is to say, how shall we live? Therefore, O Hero! Grant us permission to follow you—to accompany you and serve at your feet—whithersoever you go.
Kramasandarbha: Not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: Grant us the command to follow you wherever you go—to accompany you for the sake of serving your feet; the meaning is that we too shall die [there]. ||34||
While they were thus lamenting, holding their deceased husband and unwilling to let him be carried out,
the sun set.
Śrīdhara: For those who did not wish for the removal—that is, the carrying away—for the purpose of cremation; "to the setting," meaning toward the mountain of sunset (astācala). ||35||

*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: "Carrying away" means leading for the purpose of cremation. "Having reached the setting-mountain (*asta*)", he turned back; that is to say, he desisted from his movement and took rest. ||35||
There, having heard the lamentation of the kinsmen of the deceased,
Yama himself, appearing in the form of a young boy, approached them and said:

Śrīdhara: Having heard the lamentation—the weeping—while remaining right in his own city, Yama himself approached that place and, having become a young boy, spoke to them with the words beginning "Aho! (verse 36).
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Regarding the phrase "having come of her own accord": some maintain that for meritorious living beings, entry into the city of Yama generally occurs only at the time of their final departure (death). Among those very women, of one in particular...

Others say that because the Vaiṣṇava women could not be led away from his presence by the messengers of Yama, Yama himself came there to remove them from his vicinity; others say he appeared as a child because no one else was able to enter there, and because the speech of a child is sweet.
Because explaining the reality as having that [Lord] as its agent is extremely wonderful, and because it is capable of generating the desire to grasp that reality. ||36||
Śrī-Yama said:
"Oh, how great is the age of these people!"
For those who perceive the way of the world, there is no delusion;
yet even those who share the same nature as others grieve pointlessly over a human being who has gone to where he came from.
"Wherever the origin of honey is, there it has gone; it has become invisible.
Having come here from invisibility, it has again gone to invisibility"—thus it is said in the *Mahābhārata* (12.168.17).

Śrīdhara: Oh, what a marvel! Even those who are older than we in years, who perceive the world’s course—the manner of birth, death, and so forth—are utterly deluded. He describes this very delusion: they grieve over that which has come from the Unmanifest and has returned to that very same place, deeming it a loss. As it is said in the Gītā:
"Beings are unmanifest in their origin, manifest in their middle state, O Bhārata, and unmanifest again in their dissolution; what cause for lamentation is there in this? (Gītā 2.28).
Furthermore, you yourself possess the same nature as the deceased, for death is a condition common to both.
For those for whom [the objects] are likewise [unreal]. ||37||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not commented upon.
*Viśvanātha*: From which unmanifest source; as it is said in the *Gītā*:
"O Bhārata, all beings have the unmanifest as their beginning and the manifest as their middle."
"Indeed, they have their end in the unmanifest; what cause for lamentation is there in that? [Gītā 2.28]. ||37||
Oh, how most fortunate we are, that having been abandoned here by our parents, we do not feel any anxiety!
While she is weak and unable to protect herself from wolves and other predators, he who protects her in the womb indeed protects her.

Śrīdhara: Even though we are weak and frail, we do not worry about being devoured by wolves and other predators. The reason for this is that he who protects us in the womb is the protector everywhere. [The sequence of the composition] has not been explained.
Viśvanātha says: "It is truly astonishing that even this discrimination which we possess, though our age is very young, is not found in them"—thus he says, "Aho! (38).
He who is the immutable Lord creates this world,
and he alone protects it and withdraws it.
They say that the play of that Lord consists of the moving and unmoving world; He is the master in its restraint and its gathering.
Śrīdhara: Now, what is the purpose of protecting that [world]? None at all;

rather, it is solely for sport (krīḍā). Thus he says: "He who... He who is the Lord creates this universe, protects it, and seizes it—that is, destroys it. O women! For that Lord, the moving and unmoving world is the instrument of his sport.
They said: "Therefore, he alone is the lord over restraint, dissolution, gathering, and protection. (39)

Krama-sandarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: Now, one might ask: "What is the reason that You protected him while in the womb, yet did not protect this husband of ours in battle? To this, He says: "He who... [by] *icchayā*, meaning by His own will alone, and not due to anyone else's.
The intended meaning is "precisely by way of compliance.
Now, one might ask: what is the cause of such a desire? To this he replies: [He is] "Īśa," meaning one who possesses supreme sovereignty that is not dependent on anything else.
The point is that if one were to postulate another cause for that [desire], the very nature of His sovereignty would fail to be established as such.

Now, for what purpose does He perform creation and so forth? To this he says: "The weak"; they say that the moving and the unmoving are His mere play. In restraint (destruction) and in gathering (preservation), He alone is the one whose nature is sovereign power. (39)
That which has fallen on the road remains, protected by destiny;
that which stays at home perishes, struck down by it.
Even one who is helpless lives if watched over by him in the forest;
yet one protected at home does not live if struck down by him.

Śrīdhara: He demonstrates sovereignty itself through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) with the words "on the path," etc. Protected by destiny—that is, by God (Īśvara)—[one succeeds]; thwarted by that same God—that is, neglected by Him—one fails. "Of this [person], he was struck down" means he was neglected by Him. ||40||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: He demonstrates sovereignty itself through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—starting with "on the path.
"By destiny" (*diṣṭena*) means by fate, that is, by the Lord (*īśvara*). [The one] obstructed by that Lord, [the one] looked upon by that [Lord].

The meaning is that even when watched over by one person, he is protected; the meaning is that when he is struck down by one person while being neglected by him, he is also struck down by another. ||40||
Beings come into existence through their respective innate natures and karmas at the proper time, and they cease to exist entirely at the same time.
The Self does not abide even in that primordial nature; for it is one of the qualities of that nature which is bound.

Regarding *madhvaḥ*: according to the *Vāmana Purāṇa*, Hari is distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*) because His nature is utterly opposed to it; He is the Supreme Self (*paramātmā*), distinct from any other. Since everything is under His control due to the description of the Lord’s majesty, He alone is the one to be worshipped; there is no need for grief—this is the conclusion of these verses. ||41||

Śrīdhara: Thus, having accepted that the self’s birth, death, and so forth are subject to the Lord, it was stated that one should not grieve; now, however, he says—in three verses beginning with "The beings"—that birth and so forth belong only to the bodies, and not to the self. "Beings" refers to the bodies; "their own source" means their own causal material.

The subtle body (liṅga-śarīra) comes into being and is born through those causal karmas; it ceases to be and perishes—this applies to all bodies, including those of the gods and others. In that state, although the Self remains within the body which is [composed of] primordial nature (prakṛti), it is not affected by the qualities of that nature—the attributes of the body such as birth and so forth.
It is neither bound nor joined, because it is in every respect distinct from the body. ||41||
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: Now, if that is so, then partiality (vaiṣamya) would necessarily follow in that Lord, because of His favoring some and neglecting others; to this He says: "Beings" refers to bodies such as those of humans, animals, and so forth.

By those various karmas which serve as the causes for their respective wombs, through this karma one becomes a cow, and through that karma one becomes a pig; thus they come into being and are born according to what is established in the scriptures, and they cease to exist and perish in due time. Indeed, all of them without exception are subject to this therein.

It is clear that although the Self, which is none other than the Supreme Self, resides within the body as its constituent nature, it remains distinct; therefore, it is not bound by the qualities of the body—birth and so forth—which are the attributes of Prakṛti.
It merely sustains life through its mere proximity, [causing] the fruits of the various auspicious and inauspicious karmas performed by that [body].
The meaning is that this very [state] is both his regard and his equanimity. ||41||
This body of a person, born of delusion, is perceived as distinct from the elements, just like a house.
Just as a person born of water, earth, or fire perishes over time when subject to transformation.
Śrīdhara: But in such cases as "I am thin" or "I am fat," no distinction [between the self and the body] is perceived?
To this he says: "This... This body is born of delusion (*moha*), having arisen through non-discrimination (*aviveka*) as being the self;
in reality, however, it is entirely separate. For it is observed—that is, seen—as material (*bhautika*), just like a house.

The logical sequence (*anvaya*) is as follows: here the formal argument (*prayoga*) is this—the body is distinct from the seer and from the non-material *puruṣa*, because it is an object of sight and because it is material. It is just like a house, which, although regarded as the self by those who are utterly undiscriminating, is nevertheless separate from that [self]. This is the inference based on its being material.
Explaining the non-existence of his own birth and so forth, he concludes: "Just as bubbles and the like produced by watery atoms perish, just as jars and the like produced by earthy [atoms] perish,
and just as earrings and the like produced by fiery [atoms] perish, so too do these [beings] perish through those same three kinds [of elements]."
The meaning is that the person, having been produced from atoms, perishes only when the body itself is transformed and undergoes change; but the self does not. ||42||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He establishes its status as one of the alternatives with the words "this" (*idam*). It is "born of delusion" (*mohaja*), meaning it has arisen solely from the delusion of the person (*puruṣa*), that is, the individual soul (*jīva*); it is indeed distinct from the Supreme Self residing therein, just like a material object.
A house, consisting of walls, doors, and so forth, is understood to be distinct from the person who dwells in it.

He demonstrates that very distinction: just as bubbles and the like are produced and destroyed by watery atoms, jars and the like by earthen ones, and earrings and the like by fiery ones, so too [is the body] produced and destroyed by those same three kinds [of atoms].
The meaning is that a person, having been produced from atoms, perishes only when the body itself has become transformed and evolved, but not the self. ||42||
Just as fire is perceived as distinct within pieces of wood,
and just as wind exists separately though present within the body;
Just as the sky, though all-pervading, is not attached,
so too is the Supreme Person, the support of all qualities.

As Madhva says: "The vital air and the fire residing in the wood of the body, and the all-pervading ether—just as these are distinct from the body and so forth and are not tainted by its qualities, so too Viṣṇu, who resides in the individual soul (jīva), is distinct from the soul and is not tainted by its qualities. Thus it is said. ||43||
Śrīdhara: Even though there is no separate existence [of the two], he provides two examples for their distinctness, beginning with "just as" (yathā).
Just as fire, although situated within wood, is perceived as entirely distinct by virtue of its burning and illuminating nature;
and just as air, although present in the body, exists separately in the mouth, nose, and so forth.
It is understood. Even though the Self resides within the body, there is an absence of association with its attributes; regarding this, he provides an illustration:

just as the sky does not cling—that is, it does not incur attachment anywhere—so too the Person (puruṣa), although the support of all qualities such as the body and senses, or even though resting within them, remains supreme and distinct.
The meaning. ||43||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: Although there is no separate existence [of the qualities], he provides an illustration for their distinctness: just as fire, even while residing within wood, is perceived as distinct by virtue of its burning and illuminating capacities.
And just as the vital air (anila) residing within the body is perceived as distinct even when located in the nose and other parts,

[the author] provides an illustration for the absence of connection with the attributes of the body despite the Self's presence therein: just as space (nabhas) does not cling to anything— that is, it does not incur attachment— so too the Person (pumān) [is unattached] to all the qualities (guṇas).
The meaning is that the Supreme Lord is either the support of the body, senses, and so forth, or He is supported by them, yet He is entirely distinct from them.
Therefore, the sense is: "Why do you not look upon this husband of yours, who has died under the power of his own karma, as one desired by that Supreme Lord? ||43||
"—O you fools! Is this Suyajña not lying here, whom you are grieving for?
He who was the listener and he who recited here would never be seen again."

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, O fools! This Suyajña, your husband for whom you lament, lies here. Why do you grieve? Indeed, until this very moment he used to hear you and respond immediately. If you say, "We grieve because he is dead since we no longer see him now," then [he replies]: "He..."
But he is not to be pitied; for he was not to be pitied even before that vision. Thus he says: "He who hears... (44).

Kramasandarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: Now, this king has recently fallen in battle and lies here; how can we remain indifferent toward him and be devoid of affection? To this, he says: "Suyajña."
"Surely he heard our lamentation for all this time and responded to it? To this he says:
"He who... The meaning is that even previously there was no one visible at all; the point is that whatever is visible is seen even now, namely, the body. ||44||
neither this hearer nor this speaker is the primary great life-breath (*asu*) here;
rather, that self (*ātman*) which possesses the senses in this world is distinct from both the vital breath and the body."
The "intoxicated one" (*madhvaḥ*) is the individual soul (*jīva*), which possesses the senses.
For it is the other, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who enjoys and emits; He alone is the hearer and the speaker.
As stated in such passages as: "There is no other seer than He; there is no other hearer than He—He who is heard from this [Self]."

"Even the chief vital breath (mukhya-prāṇa) is not a hearer by its own nature, much less the individual soul (jīva). This is an objection, namely: "Is this not Suyajña? And whoever is Suyajña, he too is not capable of hearing or speaking by his own nature. Therefore, the meaning is: what is the use of grieving for him?
The living being is distinct from the body, yet the body is said to be under its control;
it possesses the conceit "I see," as well as the conceits associated with the eyes and other senses.
The eye and the other [senses] are not under his control, nor is he the lord over seeing and the rest;
for the eye and the others, the mind, the living soul, and even seeing and the rest are under his control.
He is to be known as Prāṇa; he is the knower, the thinker, and the Lord. Yet, even for him, the state of being a knower and a thinker can never be established by himself alone.
He who is the giver of that [power] of knowing and thinking is the Blessed Lord Hari;
Keśava himself is the knower, the thinker, the seer, and the hearer.
For him, there is no other giver of knowledge and so forth; Hari is the giver of all knowledge.
He worships Viṣṇu with his own body and abandons it at his own will.

As long as Viṣṇu remains situated within the body, so long does the individual soul (jīva) persist without its true nature being realized; for that long, his afflictions and the like endure, and the activities of his senses are in vain.
When that all-pervading Lord Hari abandons the body with his entire being,
then the individual soul (jīva) who identifies with it is liberated from the cycle of transmigration.

"Though their essential natures are utterly distinct, those two—the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa)—reside within a single body. Yet, in this context, one is characterized by identification with the body, while the other is not identified [with it] and is the bestower of honor. Thus it is said in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*.
Through identification with the senses and so forth, the individual soul is described as possessing them.
Because he is beyond that [limited] measurement, Hari is called "adeha" (bodiless) and likewise "anindriya" (without senses).

"Viṣṇu does not reside as the living soul (jīva) within the body that is cherished; therefore, the eternal Supreme Self (paramātman) is designated as being without a body. Thus it is stated in the *Prakāśasaṃhitā*.
And the word "ca" (and) implies that He is distinct from both the hearer and the speaker. [He is distinct] from those whose forms are the elements, the senses, and the mind. The subtle body (liṅga).
"The essential nature has been indicated, as well as the indicative mark and the means of cognition. Thus [ends] the Determination of Words (Śabdanirṇaya), verses 45–46.
Śrīdhara: [Objection: But surely the *prāṇa* that moves through the mouth and nose is indeed seen to be both the hearer and the speaker.

[Response: That is not the hearer or the speaker because it is insentient; thus he says, "not the hearer. It is called "great" (*mahān*) because it is the cause of the activity of all the senses, and for that very reason it is "principal" (*mukhya*). This is according to the Vedic scripture: "The *prāṇa* is indeed the principal one."

Who, then, is the hearer and the speaker? To this he says: "The Self (ātman) here, which perceives various objects by means of the body and the senses, is indeed distinct from the insentient body and vital breath; it is possessed of consciousness. (45)

The sequence of the composition: regarding the phrase "bhūtendriya" and so forth—since the individual soul (*puruṣa*), who is joined with beginningless ignorance, cannot by itself attain self-knowledge, there must be another who knows reality and bestows knowledge, for the Lord—who is "vibhu" (all-pervading) because He manifests in various ways through His own splendor—is worshipped as being the very nature of all things. Thus, through the splendor of the Lord, [knowledge arises].
Thus, from the words of the Blessed Lord in Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam 11.22.10. ||45||

Viśvanātha: Now, it is observed that as long as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) remains, so long do hearing and speaking exist, but not when the breath has departed; therefore, the vital breath alone is the hearer and the speaker. To this, he says: "No. For even the primary vital breath is [not the agent], according to the scripture: "The primary one indeed" (*vai mukhyaḥ*). It is "great" (*mahān*), being the cause of the activity of all the sense organs.
The point is that neither the hearer nor the speaker exists [in the body], because it is insentient. Who, then, is the hearer and the speaker?

To this he says: "But here, the Self—the individual soul (jīva)—who is perceived as possessing senses by virtue of having a body, senses, and so forth, is indeed distinct from the vital breaths, the body, and the sense organs; he is the sentient one. (45)
The omnipresent Lord assumes and indeed casts off various bodies composed of the elements, the senses, the mind, and the subtle body;
and he does so by his own power.

Śrīdhara: [Objection: But if it is conscious and distinct [from the body], how is it that the attributes of the body—such as "I am thin," "I am fat," "I am one-eyed," or "I am deaf"—are perceived? To this he says: those bodies are so called because they are "liṅgyante," meaning they are characterized or indicated by the elements, the senses, and the mind; the Self, being truly other than them, "enjoys" (bhajati) them, thinking "I am [this]."

[The opponent] thinks: "In that case, how is there liberation? To this he replies: "And that devotion, by its own power—that is, by the strength of discrimination—also casts it off. He employs the particle *hi* to provide experiential proof [of this]. ||46||
The *Kramasandarbha* does not provide an explanation.
Viśvanātha says: "In that case, where has he gone now, and what is he doing?
To this, he replies: "Those in whom the subtle body (*liṅga*), consisting of the senses and mind, has arrived (*bhūta*)."
The meaning is that he assumes, attains, and abandons gross bodies, just as he assumed this present body and cast it off;
furthermore, by his own splendor—that is, by the power of knowledge obtained through fortune—he sometimes casts off even that subtle body (liṅga-deha). ||46||
As long as the self is endowed with the *liṅga*, so long is there bondage through karma;
from that, the reverse occurs: affliction and the connection with *māyā* persist.
Madhva: The Self is the Supreme Self; the individual soul (jīva) is bound by karma. Therefore, it is the opposite of the Supreme Self. ||47||
Śrīdhara: [Objection: But surely, even after discernment (*viveka*), since one continues to engage in activities such as eating and so forth, bondage must still occur;

therefore, he says: "As long as... As long as the self remains associated with the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*) and possesses identification with it, only then does that activity become its "bondage," meaning the cause of bondage. Beyond that, however...

The reversal [of the intellect] consists in its participation in the nature of the body and its attributes; from that, affliction continues to follow, but not when the conceit of the *liṅga* has ceased. For this connection with *māyā*, beginning with error and so forth, is such because it is joined with *māyā*; the meaning is that it is not the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). ||47||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: He says "as long as" (yāvat) [in verse 47] to show that one is liberated from the bondage of karma only when the subtle body (*liṅga-deha*) is abandoned, and not otherwise.
This attachment to what is unreal— that which perceives and speaks of objects as possessing qualities— is false;
like a wishful thought or a dream, everything perceived by the senses is deceptive.

"Madhva" means false or in vain, like wealth seen in a dream; however, the individual soul (jīva) possesses the conceit of [identifying with] the body and does not experience its true nature. Before liberation, he is called "mānī" (one who has pride), but Viṣṇu is not said to be "mānī."

"Even while perceiving 'everything is mine,' one has the conviction of being untainted because of the experience of one's own true nature, because of independence, and because of the absence of defects. Thus it is stated in the *Brahma-tarka* (48).

Śrīdhara: Now, since pleasure, pain, and so forth, as well as their means, are perceived as real, how can they be of the nature of *māyā*? Furthermore, many disputants assert that they are indeed real; to this he says: "vitatha... This intense attachment (*abhiniveśa*) is false (*vitatha*), that is, illusory (*mithyā*). Of what [is it false]? Of the qualities (*guṇeṣu*).

Regarding that, as for the view and the word that "in the case of effects such as pleasure and pain, the object is the ultimate reality" (paramārtha), [the author] asks "Whence is that? and therefore says: "Just as... (yathā). ||48||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Now, "eternal" (*nityam*) is according to the view of the Mīmāṃsakas; "non-eternal" (*anityam*), meaning perishable, is "the truth" (*satyam*) according to the view of the Sāṅkhyas. [Objection]: But even that we do not understand through our awakened intellect.
To this he replies: "Not otherwise. (48)
Now, those who know that [reality] do not grieve here, whether it be permanent or impermanent;
for it is not possible to act otherwise, since this is the inherent nature of those who grieve.

Śrīdhara concludes: "Now" (*atha*) means "therefore. Those who know that [the Self] are those who know the Self as eternal and the body as non-eternal; such people do not grieve. But are not even teachers seen grieving in this way? To this he replies: "Not otherwise. This is because of the lack of firmness in their knowledge.
The meaning is that intrinsic nature does not cease. ||49||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Now, "eternal" (*nityam*) is according to the view of the Mīmāṃsakas; "impermanent" (*anityam*), meaning perishable, is "the truth" (*satyam*) according to the view of the Sāṅkhyas. [Objection]: But even that we do not understand through our awakening.
To this he replies: "Not otherwise. (49)
A certain hunter, appointed as the bringer of death to birds in the forest,
spread out his net here and there, luring them with bait.
Śrīdhara: Regarding what was stated—that even those who follow their own duties [attain liberation]—he relates an ancient narrative (itihāsa) beginning with the words "A hunter...
and so forth. Being created by the Lord as the ender of birds, wherever they were, he would entice them there with grains and the like, spread his net, and hold it fast.
In an alternative reading, the meaning is that he enticed them with meat and other such things. ||50||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Regarding the statement that "misfortune arises from the very nature of grief," he tells a traditional narrative (itihāsa) beginning with the words "A hunter...
and so forth. "Created" means by the Lord (*īśvara*). "Vidadhe" means he specifically sustained the birds.
In the reading *pralobhanam*, the meaning is that he practiced enticement by means of meat and other such things. ||50||
A pair of kuliṅga birds was seen wandering there;
of those two, the female kuliṅga was suddenly enticed by a hunter.
Śrīdhara: *Kuliṅga* is a specific kind of bird that feeds on tubers (*kanda*). "Of the two *kuliṅgas*" refers to a pair; the sequence of the construction is "of those two. O queens! ||51||
Viśvanātha: Not explained.
—o)0(o— Bound by the thread of fate, the queens were ensnared.
Seeing her fallen into such a state, the kuliṅga bird was deeply distressed;
out of affection, helpless and miserable, he lamented for his wretched mate.

Śrīdhara: He became entangled—caught in the binding—on the string of the net. Seeing her fallen into such calamity, the kuliṅga bird, being unable to release her, lamented; that is, taking refuge on a tree branch, he wailed aloud. ||52||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: The root *sic* means "in a net" or "in a cord. O queens! ||52||
—o)0(o— Alas! The all-powerful Lord is merciless toward this pitiable woman who mourns for me so piteously; what will he do with her in her distress?
Śrīdhara: What will he do with a woman who is entirely devoid of compassion and lacking in mercy? ||53||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: The Lord, the Creator, out of compassion for me who am full of mercy... ||53||
"Let the Lord take me as he wishes; for what use have I for half of myself,
living in misery with this wretched and distressed life?"

Śrīdhara: [The meaning is: "What purpose is there for me in living in such a way that I experience suffering through this life devoid of a wife, with a lifespan separated from her? Therefore, let him take me as well, according to his will.
This is the syntactical connection (anvaya). ||54||
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— How indeed shall I support them, who are motherless and whose wings have not yet grown?
My offspring, unfortunate as they are, await their mother in my nest.
Śrīdhara: How shall I support—that is, nourish—these children whose wings have grown?
My unfortunate offspring await their mother. (55)
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— Thus, [he saw] Kuliṅga lamenting nearby.
While he was distressed by separation from his beloved and choked with tears,
that very fowler, hidden and impelled by Fate, pierced him with an arrow.
Śrīdhara: A fowler is one who kills birds; [he is] dissolved. ||56||
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— Thus, you, being of little intelligence, do not perceive the ruin of your own selves.
Grieving, you shall not find this husband of yours even in hundreds of years.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha: "The destruction of the self" means one's own death. ||57||
The sequence of the composition has not been explained. —
Śrī Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
As the boy spoke thus, everyone’s minds were filled with wonder;
his kinsmen realized that everything is impermanent and arises in a manner that is not as it seems.
Madhva: From the ego-sense of "I" and "mine," the impermanent [world] arises as it is;
and from that which arises as it is, the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest arise, while the eternal also arises as it is.
"Prakṛti is indeed not independent; Janārdana alone is independent, eternal, and the ultimate reality. Thus [it is said]. (58)
Śrīdhara: "Ayathotthitam" means manifested falsely, as if it had arisen without a real basis. ||58||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: The meaning is that the entire world is impermanent because it does not remain in the same manner as it arose—that is, in whatever way it originated. ||58||
Having related this narrative, Yama vanished right there; meanwhile,
the kinsmen of Suyajña performed the funeral rites for him.
Śrīdhara: *Sāmparāyika* refers to that which pertains to the next world (*para-loka*). ||59||
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
Therefore, do not grieve for others or even for yourselves.
Who here is the self and who is the other? Who is one's own and who belongs to another? For embodied beings, apart from ignorance, there is no obsession with "self" and "other."
Regarding the question "Who is the self? Who is the other?", this is said in relation to the body and so forth;
for neither the body and such can be the self, nor is an enemy said to be it.
Therefore, what purpose is there in the increase or the decay of the physical body?
But that living soul which has entered the body indeed does not undergo destruction.
Therefore, when the enemy prospers and one’s own destruction is imminent, why should there be grief?
But for one who recognizes the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa) as distinct from the body and other such things,
there follows the expansion of the self through firm devotion to Vāsudeva.

"The destruction of the enemy as well as the destruction of ignorance [occur]; there is no other way whatsoever. Thus says Śrīdhara in the *Brahmavaivarta*. Regarding the reading "aśocata," the addition of the augment *aṭ* is an archaic (Vedic) usage. Ignorance is precisely the dogmatic attachment to "self" and "other"; without that [attachment], [ignorance does not exist]. (60)
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: "One's own" and "the other"—this very attachment is ignorance; without that [attachment], [there is no such distinction]. (60)
Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard these words of the lord of the Daityas, Diti, together with her daughter-in-law, [listened].
Having abandoned grief for his son in an instant, he fixed his mind upon reality.
Śrīdhara: "Together with her daughter-in-law" means accompanied by her daughter-in-law. ||61||
The *Krama-sandarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Sārārtha-darśinī*, the *Harṣiṇī*, for those whose hearts are devoted.
The first chapter of the seventh [section] is concluded, well-connected for the virtuous.
Thus, in the glorious Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the commentary on the Brahma-sūtras,
in the Vaiyāsikī collection pertaining to the state of the Paramahaṃsas, in the seventh book.
The second chapter in the dialogue between Yudhiṣṭhira and Nārada.
Now begins the third chapter,
in the dialogue between Yudhiṣṭhira and Nārada,
the venerable Nārada said:
O King, Hiraṇyakaśipu sought to make himself invincible, ageless, immortal, without rival, and the sole sovereign.
Śrīdhara:
In the third [birth], having seen the world tormented by his ascetic penance, the Creator (Brahmā) arrived;
filled with wonder, he was praised by him and granted him boons.

Thus, having commanded the Dānavas to slaughter the virtuous and having dispelled the grief of his kinsmen by means of an investigation into the truth, he describes what he did next with the words beginning "Hiraṇyakaśipu":
he intended to establish an unrivaled, sole monarch— one who was without a rival or opponent.
He desired to act. ||1||
Caitanya-mata-mañjūṣā: No commentary whatsoever on this chapter.
Krama-sandarbha: Not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: [No commentary].
In the third [birth], having performed austerities and having rendered the gods well-disposed or ill-disposed,
he obtained excellent boons from the Creator, who was praised by him.

The meaning is that he was a "sole ruler" (*ekarāj*), one who shines as the sovereign alone; by means of the intention to be described, he desired his own sole lordship extending even unto the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*).
He performed most rigorous penance in the valley of Mount Mandara,
with his arms raised, his gaze fixed upon the sky, and his body supported by the earth on his big toes.
Śrīdhara: He whose arms are raised upward; he whose gaze is fixed upon the sky; he by whom the earth is touched with the tip of his big toe. (2)
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: For this very reason, "he [is] theirs. (2)
He shone with the radiance of his matted locks like the sun at the end of an aeon with its rays;
while he was performing austerities, the gods occupied their respective abodes.

Śrīdhara: With the splendors, the glows, the rays, and the beams of his matted locks, he shone like the sun that brings about the dissolution of the world. Those gods who had previously wandered upon the earth unobserved now returned once more to their own abodes. (3)
Kramasandarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: "Places" means their respective homes; the meaning is that he did not perceive the enmity of that enemy. ||3||
From his head arose a smokeless fire consisting of ascetic power, which, being fanned in every direction, scorched the worlds above, below, and across.
Śrīdhara: "Viṣvag-īritaḥ" means having spread forth in all directions. ||4||
The sequence of composition by Viśvanātha has not been explained.
The rivers and oceans were agitated, and the earth, together with its continents and mountains, trembled.
The stars, along with the planets, fell down, and the ten directions blazed.
Śrīdhara: The earth, together with its islands and mountains, has shaken. ||5||
The *Krama-sandarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon. —
By that [heat], the gods, scorched, abandoned heaven and went to the world of Brahmā (*brahma-loka*).
They made this request to Dhātṛ: "O God of gods, Lord of the world!"
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
O Lord of the Daityas, scorched by our ascetic penance, we are unable to remain in heaven.
And if you think it right, O Lord, bring about his pacification,
before the worlds perish and [the world] ceases to offer tribute to you, O Overlord.

Śrīdhara: [They are] those who bring offerings to you, those who pay tribute, or those who perform worship. "Abhibhū" means one who prevails over all; O Abhibhū! O Lord of All! (In another reading, "bho" is the vocative). The connection is: "as long as they do not perish on all sides. ||7||
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: "Abhibho" means "O Abhibhu!"—O Lord of all! In the reading with the *visarga*, "bho" is the vocative. "Abhi" means "on all sides. (7)
This is indeed his resolve as he practices austerities so difficult to perform; listen, for even though you already know it, I shall nevertheless inform you."
Mādhva: Even for those who possess knowledge, action must always be performed in accordance with one's own nature;
in this regard, some are deluded by ignorance regarding their own nature, or by passion and other such afflictions.

"For even those who know would perform an unworthy act, were it not for the Lord; but the four-faced one (Brahmā) would never, under any circumstances, perform an improper act. Thus it is said in the Nāradīya Purāṇa. 8.

Śrīdhara: With the four verses beginning with "tasya," they describe his resolve in order to produce hatred for Brahmā in Him; [the verse says]: "Is His resolve not known to you? Nevertheless, it has been reported by us; let it be heard from you. (8)
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Nevertheless, listen as we set it forth. ||8||
Having created this world of moving and non-moving beings through austerity, yoga, and meditative absorption,
the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin) occupies his own throne, which is superior to all other abodes.
Therefore, by means of increasing asceticism, yoga, and meditative absorption, I shall accomplish that for myself,
because both time and the self are eternal.

For those who exert supreme effort through austerity, or through knowledge, or through wisdom, meditation, and so forth— whether by these means individually or collectively— there is the attainment of honey-sweet nectar.
Even by means of hundreds or many millions of contractions and expansions,
those steps that are unsuitable for one's own self cannot be ascended.

"Nevertheless, the leaders of the gods would create obstacles for the Daityas who practice such things as austerity, so that their futility may not arise. Thus says Śrīdhara in the *Prakāśasaṃhitā*: "Through meditative absorption and steadfastness in austerity and yoga, [this state] is superior to all celestial abodes."

"Just as he occupies and presides over his own seat, Satyaloka, so shall I likewise accomplish that for myself. [The opponent asks: "Surely that was accomplished by Brahmā through long life and the performance of austerity; how could another accomplish it? To this they reply: "Of time and the self... Even though the body [is subject to decay] due to the brevity of life...
Even if one were to die again and again, nevertheless, because both time and the self are eternal, I shall surely attain that state after performing austerities over many births. ||10||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "From all the abodes. Regarding the phrase "by Vardhamāna":
the sense is that my power shall become even greater than that of the current Parameṣṭhin (Brahmā). [Objection: But surely by Brahmā...

To the objection—"Having performed penance with an exceedingly long lifespan, that was accomplished; how will you accomplish it with such a short lifespan?"—he replies with the word "time" (kāla): even though my gross body may perish again and again due to the brevity of life, nevertheless, because time and the Self are eternal, [the goal is achieved] through many [successive lives].

"Having performed austerities through successive births, I shall surely achieve that supreme seat of the Parameṣṭhin; otherwise, I shall ordain this by my own power in a manner different from what was before."
What is the use of other [doctrines] such as those of the Vaiṣṇavas and others, which have been swept away by time at the end of the aeon?

Śrīdhara: He states the intended meaning of what was said [by the Lord], "by means of Vardhamāna," with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*). "Otherwise" means by the reversal of gods, asuras, and so forth; "not as before" means by the reversal of merit, demerit, and so forth. "I shall create this world"—[the question is: "What is the use of other Vaiṣṇava and other such eternal abodes?"
Therefore, I shall establish that very purpose. ||11||
The sequence of the composition: "What need is there for others?"—this is from the perspective of the asuras. ||11||

Viśvanātha: Furthermore, those who, thinking "I shall create this world otherwise," are miserable in this world due to their celibacy, austerities, vows, and so forth, must be made miserable in the next world as well, destined for hell; whereas those who [are not so] in this world...
Those who are solely devoted to the enjoyment of sensual pleasures will themselves become inhabitants of heaven in the next world; therefore,

one should encourage them with such teachings as that the inclination toward the enjoyment of sensual pleasures alone is merit (*puṇya*) and the means to achieve what is desired, while its restriction is demerit (*pāpa*) and the means to achieve what is undesired.
"Surely, if this were so, it would not have occurred in previous great kalpas"; to this he says: "Even as before, I shall ordain it by my own power and splendor.
Now, why is it that the very throne of Parameṣṭhin, which he desired to attain, [is superior] to all other stations?

Do you consider [this] to be the best? To this he says: "What need is there for others?"—meaning what purpose is served by the Vaiṣṇavas and those who speak of the state of Dhruva and others, since they have been swept away by time?
This is because reflecting on the impermanence of even the state of Dhruva is characteristic of the nature of an asura. ||11||
Thus have we heard: you, having undertaken supreme asceticism with great persistence,
yourself ordain what is appropriate for the next step, O Lord of the Three Worlds."

Śrīdhara said: "We have heard that he is intent on seizing your feet; for this very reason, he remains engaged in supreme austerity. Therefore, do whatever is appropriate in this matter immediately. (12)
Kramasandarbha: This has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: Thus we have heard of his persistence in seizing your feet; for this very reason, he has undertaken this supreme austerity. (12)
O Lord of the World, this supreme seat of yours, belonging to the twice-born and the cows,
is for the sake of existence, spiritual welfare, prosperity, security, and victory.
No one considers that [destruction] as honey for prosperity and ultimate welfare,
nor indeed [the destruction] of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, and likewise of Hiraṇyākṣa and others.

"Nowhere does anyone desire the state of Brahman except for those who are upright and fit; therefore, people desire various blessings, but not for the sake of attaining that state. Thus it is said in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*.
"Prosperity (*bhava*) is declared to be growth, while the highest good (*śreyaḥ*) is exemplified as liberation (*mokṣa*)."

"For one who has grown old, there is no further decline; this alone is called prosperity. Thus says Śrīdhara in the *Śabdanirṇaya*. Otherwise, fearing that if you were to fall from your position, it would bring misfortune upon the virtuous, they say in their grief: "This is your seat of supreme sovereignty (*pārameṣṭhya*), [which belongs] to the twice-born and to the cows."

For existence and for emergence; for the highest good and for happiness; for prosperity and for sovereignty; for security and for the preservation of what has been gained; for victory and for excellence. ||13||
Kramasandarbha: Not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: [The word] "yayau" (she went) implies the intention: "In that case, I shall now turn her away from those austerities by means of granting boons. (13)
O King, having been thus petitioned by the gods, the Blessed Lord, the Self-born,
surrounded by Bhṛgu, Dakṣa, and others, went to the hermitage of the lord of the Daityas.
He did not see the concealed fat, skin, flesh, and blood, which was covered by anthills, grass, and reeds, and infested by ants.

Śrīdhara: First he did not see [the body] because it was covered over by anthills and the like; later, having somehow discerned it, he spoke to him—this is the connection between the two verses. [He saw one] whose fat, skin, flesh, and blood had been devoured on all sides and consumed by ants. (15)
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: First he did not see him because he was concealed by anthills and the like; then, having somehow discerned him, he spoke—this is the connection between the two [verses]. *Ācīrṇam* means "surrounded on all sides."
Eaten. ||15||

Seeing him heating the worlds with his ascetic power like the sun veiled by clouds, he whose vehicle is a swan, filled with wonder, spoke to him while smiling: — o)0(o— Having observed him heating the worlds with his asceticism like the sun covered by clouds, he whose vehicle is a swan, struck with amazement, spoke to him while laughing.
"But if one performs the *madhva* [offering] with desire, it will thereafter become cruel and cause fear to the worlds;
otherwise, it certainly leads to the peace of all the worlds. Thus it is stated in the *Prakāśikā*. (16)
Śrīdhara: Having perceived [him] as if he were the sun obscured and covered by clouds, he was struck with wonder and spoke; this is the composition of the sequence. [This] has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: Like the sun covered by a cloud. ||16||
Śrī Brahmā said:
"Arise, arise! May it be well with you, O Kāśyapa; you have attained perfection through your austerities."
I have arrived as the granter of boons; let the desired boon be chosen.
Madhva: "He [Hiraṇyaka] assigned the status of Brahmā to the one who is the object of the word 'Brahman'"; thus says Śrīdhara in the Skanda Purāṇa. Viśvanātha: this has not been explained.
Krama-sandarbha: by the word "arise" (uttiṣṭha), [it refers to] him who was previously standing upright, and afterwards...
The seating has been indicated. ||17||
I have seen this great wonder within your heart: though your body has been devoured by the gadfly, your life-breaths indeed remain within your bones."
Śrīdhara: *Hṛtsāram* means fortitude. One whose body has been bitten by *daṃśas*, which are specific types of gadflies and the like. (18)
The sequence of events is as follows: it should be understood that being bitten by a snake occurs first, and being eaten by ants occurs afterwards. ||18||
Viśvanātha: The essence of the heart is fortitude. ||18||
Neither the sages of old have done this, nor will others do so in the future:
who indeed could sustain his life-breaths for a hundred divine years without water?
Śrīdhara: "Nirambu" means that by whom water has been prohibited; the sense is "one who has renounced water.
This is the sequence of the composition. Viśvanātha: [This] was not explained.
O son of Diti, by this resolve of yours— difficult for the high-minded to achieve and rooted in asceticism— I have been conquered.
"Madhvaḥ" means conquered or brought under control. According to the *Śabdanirṇaya*: "That which is defeated and remains under one's power is called 'conquered' (*jita*) by the wise. (20)
Śrīdhara: By this very resolve of yours, I have already been conquered by you; but by you, who are devoted to austerity, I am all the more completely conquered. (20)
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha: not explained.
—o)0(o— Therefore, O bull among the Asuras, I bestow upon you all those blessings.
For the sight of you, who are immortal, is not without fruit for me, even though I am mortal.
Śrīdhara: For you, a mortal, and for me, an immortal, this meeting is not fruitless or in vain. ||21||
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Although belonging to the class of asuras, because he is subject to death, he is a mortal; therefore, [he was killed] by you, who are also a mortal. ||21||
Śrī Nārada said:
Having spoken thus, the Lord Ādibhava [beheld] his body being devoured by ants.
He sprinkled [him] with the water from his water-pot, which was divine and possessed unfailing power.
Śrīdhara: Brahmā is "ādibhava" because he exists at the beginning; he "aukṣat," meaning he sprinkled. ||22||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "By ants" (*pipīlikaiḥ*) means by ants, moths (*aṃśu*), and so forth. *Ādi-bhava* is Brahmā; *amogha-rādhas* means that from whom the attainment of success (*saṃsiddhi*) is unfailing (*avyartha*); by him [Brahmā], he (*aukṣat*) sprinkled (*prokṣitavān*).
Endowed with vigor and strength, that youth, possessing all limbs and a body as firm as a thunderbolt, emerged from that Kīcaka-ant-hill.
He rose up, glowing like molten gold, like a fire from its fuel.
Śrīdhara: He whose bodily firmness has a compactness like that of a diamond; he whose bodily luster has a radiance like that of refined gold. (23)
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: He whose bodily frame possesses a firmness like that of a diamond (*vajra*). (23)
Beholding the god arrived in the sky upon his swan-vehicle, he,
for whom the sight of him was a great festival, bowed his head to the ground.

In the Madhva [tradition], words of praise generally refer to Hari alone; however, some words are mixed, referring to the qualities of the individual soul (jīva), while others refer to Hari as the controller of those qualities.

"Because they occupy the same place, perform the same function, and because Viṣṇu is preeminent as well as the individual soul being dependent upon him, the scriptural statements do not refer to two distinct authorities. Thus it is stated in the Brahma-tarka (24).
Śrīdhara: He for whom there is a great festival upon seeing him. ||24||
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— Having risen, with palms joined in reverence and bowing low, he gazed at the Lord with his eyes.
With tears of joy and the bristling of his hair, he spoke with a faltering voice.
Śrīdhara: He whose [body] has tears and the emergence of horripilation due to joy. ||25||
The structural arrangement [of the commentary] by Viśvanātha has not been explained.
Śrī Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
At the end of the kalpa, he who is self-luminous revealed this world, which was enveloped by the blind darkness created by Time, by means of his own radiance.
By means of his own threefold nature, he creates, preserves, and dissolves this universe;
homage to the Supreme, the Great One, whose abode is passion, goodness, and darkness.
The *madhu* [graha] is by nature threefold. ||27||

Śrīdhara: [It is] by dense darkness; the reason for this is that it is not by ordinary gloom (*dhvānta*), but by that which was emitted by Time in the form of the qualities of *prakṛti*. He who made manifest this world enveloped by darkness, and he who creates, maintains, protects, and withdraws this world through his self consisting of the three qualities.
And he withdraws [all things] into that Great Refuge, the abode of Rajas, Sattva, and Tamas, the Supreme Lord; "Salutation" is the connection with these two verses. ||26||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: By that Self which is *trivṛt*—meaning that which manifests (*abhivyanak*), that which made manifest (*abhivyaktam akarot*), and that which chooses (*vṛṇoti*) or takes possession of the three qualities (*guṇas*). ||26-27||
Homage to the Primordial Seed, whose form is knowledge and realization,
who has attained manifestation through the transformations of the vital breaths, the senses, the mind, and the intellect.
Śrīdhara: Here, sixfold nature is stated: self-luminosity, the luminosity of the world, being the cause thereof, being the agent of its creation and so forth, greatness, and supreme lordship.
Elaborating upon that very point, he offers salutation with the four verses beginning with "namaḥ."

"To the seed," that is, to the cause. The reason for this is: "to the primordial. To him whose form is knowledge—that is, cognition, consciousness, and knowledge taking the form of objects. By this, his self-luminosity and his status as the illuminator of the universe are shown;
by "to the seed," his nature as the efficient cause (nimitta) is stated. He states his nature as the material cause (upādāna): "those modifications which are the vital breaths and so forth."
To him who has attained manifestation through those forms, that is, who has reached a manifest state of activity. ||28||
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: To Him who has attained manifestation—that is, the form of an effect—by means of those modifications such as *prāṇa* and the rest. ||28||
"You rule over the moving and the stationary world as the Lord of all creatures by means of the primary vital breath."
He is the Lord of the mind by means of minds, the great Master of the sense-faculties, and the Sovereign of the abode of the elements and qualities.

Śrīdhara: Thus, by the phrase "by the threefold self," the causality mentioned has been shown in two ways; he now states its greatness and lordship with the word "thou": "Thou alone art the ruler—the controller—of the moving (jaṅgama) world and the stationary (tasthuṣaḥ), that is, the unmoving. By what? By the chief vital breath (mukhyena prāṇena)."

In the form of the *sūtrātman* (the thread-self), you are therefore the Lord of all creatures. You are the Lord of their consciousness (*citta*), of their mental states (*cittaiḥ*), of volition (*cetanā*) which is a transformation thereof, of the mind (*manas*), and of the sense organs (*indriya*) which are governed by them.
Therefore, you alone are the Great One (*mahān*). [You are also the Lord] of the elements (*bhūta*), such as space (*ākāśa*) and so forth, and of their qualities (*guṇa*).

And he is the lord of the objects such as sound, of the latent dispositions (*āśaya*), and of their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). By this very [statement], his status as the creator is demonstrated. (29)
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: You rule; you are the controller. By what? By the principal breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*), in the form of the *sūtrātman*. Therefore, you are the Lord of creatures (*prajāpati*), [ruling] over their minds and by means of their minds.

He is the Lord of consciousness—which is a transformation of that [Prakṛti]—of the mind, and of the senses which are governed by them; and He is the Master of the great elements, their qualities, the internal dispositions, and their latent impressions. ||29||
You extend the seven threads by means of the body, the triple Veda, and the knowledge of the four officiating priests.
You alone are the Self of those who possess self-knowledge, beginningless,
boundless, the seer, and the inner soul.
The sweet [soma] together with the vital breath [pervades] the seven threads and the seven rites. ||30||
Śrīdhara: Now, he describes His role as the protector of the world by way of being the instigator of sacrifice and the inner controller (*antaryāmin*).

You alone expand the seven-threaded sacrifices, such as the *agniṣṭoma* and others. How? By means of Your threefold body, in the form of the three Vedas. Of what nature is that [body]? That wherein there are four *hotṛ* priests.

The ritual of the four officiating priests (*cāturhotraka*) is [performed] by means of the knowledge pertaining to its subject matter. You alone are the inner self (*antarātman*) and the inner controller (*antaryāmī*) for living beings who possess a self, having become their very self. Why? Because you are the seer (*kavi*), the omniscient.
Why is that? Because you are one (*eka*), indivisible. The reason for this is that you are without beginning (*anādi*) and without end or limit (*ananta-pāra*). There is no...
He whose end is reached through time and whose limit is reached through space. ||30||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: You alone are the seven-threaded [sacrifices], the Agniṣṭoma and other rites; and the three Vedas (*trayī*).
With a body consisting of those, you are the Hotṛ, Udgātṛ, Adhvaryu, and Brahman—wherein lies that which is characterized by the four officiating priests (*caturhotraka*).

[It is attained] through action and the knowledge concerning that [object]. For embodied beings who possess a self, the "self" (ātman) is the individual soul (jīva), the inner self (antarātman), the inner controller (antaryāmī). ||30||
You alone are Time, the unblinking one, who diminishes the lifespan of living beings through its constituent parts, such as the *lava* and others.
You are the immutable Self, the supreme, unborn, and great;
you are the life-force and the inner Self of the world of living beings.
Madhvaḥ: the sustainer of the life-breath of living beings. ||31||

Śrīdhara: He describes his nature as the destroyer in the form of Time with the words "Thou alone. Thou wastest away—that is, thou causest to perish—by means of the divisions of time such as *lava*s and so forth. Thus, even while being the agent of creation and other cosmic functions, he declares his very state of changelessness with the word "immovable" (*kūṭastha*). The reasons for this are: [Thou art] the Self, whose nature is knowledge.

He is the Supreme Abider (Parameṣṭhī), the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara). He is Unborn (Aja), devoid of birth; Great (Mahān), meaning unlimited. Furthermore, while the world of living beings alone undergoes transformations such as birth and so forth due to the power of karma, You are its very life-force (jīva), the cause of its vitality, since You are its Self (Ātman) and Controller. ||31||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: *Kūṭastha* means pervading time by virtue of being changeless. *Ātmā* means the inner controller (*antaryāmī*).
In the previous verse, the one called the *ātman* of the world of individual souls—that is, of the body which is like a living being—[was described].
While the selfhood of the performers of action was stated by way of their being impelled by and impelling karma, here [it is stated] for all others as well. ||31||
There is nothing other than you, nor even anything else that is unmoving or moving, distinct from you.
The sciences, the arts, and all your bodies—
you are Hiraṇyagarbha, the Great One with three backs.

"Because you, as the eternal Viṣṇu, pervade both the higher and the lower realms, those who know the Vedas declare that there is no distinction [between you and them]. Thus it is said in the Padma Purāṇa.
"Vidyās and Kalās" refers to the branches of knowledge and the arts.

"Since the great sciences (*mahā-vidyā*) and the arts (*kalā*) are supported by you as their boat, those who know the reality call you 'the Embodiment of Knowledge' (*vidyā-tanu*). Thus [ends the hymn].
Tripṛṣṭha is the fourth. (32)

Śrīdhara: To the question "Whence is that so?", he says: "From you" (*tvattaḥ*). If anything were distinct from you, then from that [distinction] there would arise for you modifications such as birth and so forth, or states such as being subject to control;
however, since that does not exist, he says: "The supreme cause and the non-supreme effect. And therein, *ejat* means the moving, and *anejat* the non-moving.
And that which is stationary does not exist apart from You.

If it is argued that the scripture which makes Me known exists as something separate, it is not so; for the sciences—including the Vedas, the Upavedas, and other branches of knowledge—as well as the arts, are Your very limbs, Your own bodies, and not [entities] distinct from You.
[They are] distinct. Why so? Because you are indeed the Great Brahman. Why is that?
To this he says: He whose womb is the golden-formed cosmic egg;
he who stands beyond the "three-backs," that is, beyond the Pradhāna which consists of the three qualities (guṇas); he who is beyond the Imperishable (Akṣara).
Because of scriptural passages such as "the other," etc. ||32||

Regarding the sequence of composition: in the commentary on the verse beginning with "tvattaḥ" (from you), because of the explanation starting with "vidyā refers to the Vedas, Upavedas, and so forth," the term *vidyā-kalāḥ* is a *dvandva* compound; therefore, the reading "vidyāḥ kalāś ca" (the sciences and the arts) is not appropriate. ||32||
Viśvanātha: The Supreme Cause and the subordinate effect; the unmoving (the stationary) and the moving (the animate);
the sciences—namely the Vedas, Upavedas, and other branches of knowledge—and the arts, which are its limbs—all these are Your very bodies.
He whose womb contains the golden-formed cosmic egg is the dweller within the vast Brahman of the three worlds.
He is Tripṛṣṭha because he stands at the back (parataḥ) upon the backs (pṛṣṭhe) of the qualities (guṇānām). ||32||
O All-pervading Lord, it is evident that this gross body is that by which You [perceive] the senses, the vital breaths, the mind, and the qualities.
Abiding in the supreme abode of Brahmā,
you enjoy [the world] as the unmanifest Self, the ancient Puruṣa.

Śrīdhara: [Objection: "But how can I, a living being whose body is the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), possess the nature of Brahman? Or how can I have such things as being the interior of the cosmic egg? To this he says: "This manifest world is Your body. Or, "The manifest is the Truth. By means of which body You [perceive] the objects that are the qualities of the senses, the vital breaths, and the mind.

You enjoy [all things]. Moreover, you enjoy while remaining established in the abode of the supreme lordship, which is your own essential nature (*svarūpa*), and not by means of the concealment of your essential nature as we do. Therefore, the meaning is that you are the unmanifest Self, the ancient Person who is Brahman itself, free from all limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*). ||33||
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: This manifest form of Vairāja is Your gross body, by means of which body You enjoy the objects that are the qualities of the senses, the vital breaths, and the mind; however—

He experiences [the world] while remaining established in His own nature—the abode of supreme sovereignty and the state of the Supreme Lord—and not by concealing His true nature; therefore, You are the unmanifest, Brahman, the Self, the Inner Controller, the Ancient Person, and the Blessed Lord. ||33||
Salutation to that Blessed One, who, by means of his infinite and unmanifest form, has pervaded this entire universe, and who is endowed with the powers of consciousness and matter.
And as it is said: "Even Hiraṇyaka, though knowing Viṣṇu to be superior even to Brahmā, praises Brahmā with his [Brahmā's] qualities with the intention of speaking of that Viṣṇu. (34)
Śrīdhara: [Objection: But how can the state of being Brahman and the state of being the Ancient Puruṣa belong to one and the same?

To this, he says: "O Infinite One. O Ananta, to You, the Blessed Lord of inconceivable sovereignty, by whom—in Your unmanifest form that transcends the reach of mind and speech—this entire universe is pervaded and encompassed.
Salutation! The reason for [His] being the Blessed Lord (bhagavat) is: "to Him who is endowed with the powers of consciousness and non-consciousness";
*cic-śakti* is *vidyā*, and *acic-śakti* is *māyā*; [He is so called] because He is joined with these two. ||34||
The structural arrangement (*krama-sandarbha*): the commentary on the verse beginning with "Ananta" follows the Vaiṣṇava tenets.
In that system, it should be understood that the conscious power (*cic-chakti*) is the essential nature (*svarūpa-bhūtā*), while the unconscious power (*acic-chakti*) is *māyā*. (34)
The Bhagavat-sandarbha (14): One conscious entity resting upon another conscious entity, just as the light of rays and the like rests upon the orb of light. ||34||
Viśvanātha: The conscious power (*cit-śakti*) is internal and constitutes His very nature; the unconscious power (*acit-śakti*), which is *māyā* composed of the *guṇas*, is external.
He is joined with these two for the sake of pastimes that transcend the *guṇas* as well as those consisting of the *guṇas*. ||34||
“O best of givers of boons, if you will grant me the desired boons,
O Lord, let there be no death for me from any beings created by you.”
Śrīdhara: This has not been explained.
Krama-sandarbha: He chooses that [boon] under the pretext that the boon of immortality cannot be obtained—[expressed by the words] "yadi" (if).
"From those created by you" means from those directly created by you yourself. ||35||

Viśvanātha: "But enough with this much praise; first, accept your boons. To this he replies with the words "yadi" (if). This is Hiraṇyakaśipu’s intention here: "If I were to ask for the boon that I might become immortal, then this boon would be impossible, because at the end of the kalpa..."

"Since even we, including Brahmā and the others, must surely die, my boon will certainly become renowned; therefore, by this very reasoning, I choose a boon such that, in effect, immortality itself shall be attained.
As for the phrase 'from those created by you,' since all beings are created by Brahmā, what else remains [to be created]?"
Such is the intended meaning. ||35||
Neither within nor without, by day nor by night, nor even by other weapons;
neither on earth nor in the sky is there death, neither from men nor even from wild beasts.
Śrīdhara: "From another" means even from something other than that which was fashioned by you. "By weapons" means let there be no death [from them].
The sequence of the composition is as follows: "from another" means created by Rudra, Prajāpati, and so forth; because there is no further contemplation beyond Brahman. (36)
Viśvanātha: Death might even occur spontaneously; therefore, he says, "Neither within nor without, neither by day nor by night.
By negating all places and times, natural death is excluded.
Viṣṇu, such as the Varāha and others, is indeed created by Brahmā and possesses form; however, being formless, if [the Lord] were to employ a weapon such as the discus...
Fearing that there might be some calamity if he were to move, he says: "Even by other weapons, there is no death.

Although the words "internal" (*antar*) and "external" (*bahis*) encompass all locations, there is a concern that because these are relative terms, they would bring to mind specific correlates; fearing such a calamity, [he speaks as follows].
Furthermore, he prohibits [residing in] a location. By the words "not on the earth," there is a prohibition of the seven netherworlds (pātālas);
by the words "not in the sky," there is a prohibition of the seven heavens (svargas). Again, fearing danger from beings created by Dakṣa and others, he says: "not by men. (36)
Whether by those devoid of life-force or by those endowed with it, [he grants] invincibility in battle to the gods, asuras, and great serpents,
as well as sovereignty over all embodied beings.

Śrīdhara: "By those without life-breath" means by those who are lifeless; "by those possessing life-breath" means by those who have life. The ellipsis is: "Grant that there be for me, as for yourself, greatness such as being without a rival. (37)
The sequence of the composition: furthermore, he prohibits the group of agents with the three quarters beginning with "not by men" (na naraiḥ).

Because the Blessed One possesses non-material life-breaths (aprākṛta-prāṇatva), the phrase "by those without life-breath or by those possessing life-breath" will be connected right there in that very context, due to the subject matter concerning the agent. Nor is this intended as a prohibition of the action itself—as in "not by non-living beings" (aprāṇibhiḥ).

When it is said "by living beings," since that [killing] is already established for him, even though the killer's life-force and body are identical, he has departed from his vital breaths; furthermore, because the tip of the nail used for cutting has been discarded as its life-force has left,
such [violence] is prohibited by the Blessed Lord.

By Śrī Rukmiṇī-devī, through the statement beginning with "His skin, beard, body hair, nails, and hair are not composed of material elements" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.60.45), the fact that those who are non-material possess the nature of bliss is established by means of the censure of material things. Therefore, it is said in the Vārāha Purāṇa: "He has no material form."
"Arising from fat, marrow, and bone," and so forth. ||37||

Viśvanātha: Since it is impossible to enumerate all the various classes of living beings, he says: "by those without breath" (vāsubhiḥ) and "those with breath" (asumadbhiḥ). Thinking thus, "in reality I have indeed become immortal," he chooses another boon: "without opposition" (apratīti). ||37||
The majesty of all the world-protectors, equal to his own,
through the power of his asceticism and yoga, shall never suffer any impairment.

Śrīdhara: [The meaning is: those whose power consists of austerity and yoga; that which is their sovereignty, beginning with *aṇimā*, does not fail—that is, it does not perish—and they request that very thing. ||38||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Just as it exists for you, O Self, so too the sovereignty consisting of *aṇimā* and the other powers—which possess influence through austerity (*tapas*) and yoga—does not suffer harm and does not perish; and that [sovereignty], he requests. ||38||
Thus ends the third chapter of the seventh [skandha] in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those with devoted hearts; it is perfectly suited to the virtuous.
Thus, in the glorious Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the commentary on the Brahma-sūtras,
in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā pertaining to the state of the Paramahaṃsas, in the seventh book,
in the dialogue between Yudhiṣṭhira and Nārada.
The Third Chapter.
Now begins the fourth chapter,
in the dialogue between Yudhiṣṭhira and Nārada,
the venerable Nārada said:
Thus requested, Śatadhṛti, being pleased by Hiraṇyakaśipu’s ascetic penance, then granted him boons that are very difficult to obtain.
Śrīdhara:
Having obtained boons in the fourth [birth] and having conquered all the world-protectors,
the lord of the Daityas oppressed them all out of hatred for Viṣṇu.
Śatadhṛti is Brahmā. ||1||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha:
Having obtained boons, that enemy [of the gods] cast out all the gods from heaven, which was the specific fruit [of his actions].
The fourth quality of Prahlāda is said to arise from ecstatic devotion (prema-bhakti).
Of Hiraṇyakaśipu, by Hiraṇyakaśipu, his [possession], for him. ||1||
Śrī Brahmā said:
O Father, those boons which you choose from me are difficult for men to obtain.
Nevertheless, my dear, I grant you these boons, even though they are difficult to obtain.
Śrīdhara: From me; that is, from my [perspective]. Even though—even if these are difficult to obtain. ||2||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: Although [the word] "yadyapi" (even though) occurs twice, the distant connection—namely, "Even though these are difficult to obtain, nevertheless I bestow these which are difficult to obtain"—must be accepted if one is to explain it in this way. Of what kind are the boons?
The meaning is: even for those striving to attain them, those things which are difficult to obtain remain unattained despite having reached [the state where they should be attained].
Then the Lord, the omnipresent one whose grace is never in vain, departed.
He was honored by the foremost of the asuras and praised by the lords of creatures.
Śrīdhara: He whose grace is unfailing; [accompanied] by the lords of subjects, such as Marīci and others. ||3||
The *Krama-sandarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon. —
Thus, having obtained the boon, the Daitya assumed a body made of gold.
The Blessed One felt hatred, recollecting the murder of his brother.
And it is said: "The devotees of Madhu, such as Hiraṇyakaśipu and others, were enemies of Hari due to the entry of another [influence]. (4)
Śrīdhara: He states the purpose for which the austerity was performed with the words beginning "In this way" (evam). ||4||
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
Having conquered all the directions and the three worlds, that great Asura...
The lords of gods, asuras, and humans, along with gandharvas, garuḍas, and uragas.
The Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Vidyādharas; the Ṛṣis, the Lords of the Ancestors (Pitṛpatis), and the Manus;
as well as the lords of the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas, and even the lords of the Pretas and Bhūtas.
Having conquered the lords of all beings and brought them under his control,
Viśvajit seized the abodes of the world-protectors along with their splendor.
Śrīdhara: [He refers to] those who are the lords of all beings, of all classes of living creatures. ||7||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Garuḍas are birds belonging to the species of Garuḍa. ||7||
He dwelt in the celestial realm of the three worlds, endowed with the splendor of the gardens of the gods—
a palace of Mahendra built by Viśvakarman himself.
He dwelt in that abode of the Fortune of the three worlds, which possessed every kind of prosperity.
Śrīdhara: He occupied Tripiṣṭapa, that is, heaven; he dwelt there, and even within that heaven, he resided in the abode of Mahendra. ||8||
The *Krama-sandarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— Where the stairs are made of coral and the ground is of great emerald;
Where the walls are made of crystal and there are rows of pillars of lapis lazuli.
There were variegated canopies and seats of ruby,
with couches resembling the foam of milk, adorned with coverings of pearl necklaces.
With their tinkling anklets making noise here and there,
the goddesses with beautiful teeth gaze at their lovely faces upon the jeweled floors.
Śrīdhara: He describes the state of being endowed with all prosperity through three verses beginning with "yatra" (where). ||9||
Those whose ornaments and attendants consist of strings of pearls. (10) Those with beautiful teeth are "sudatyaḥ. (11)
The *Krama-sandarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon. —
In that palace of Mahendra, the one of great strength...
Great-minded, having conquered the worlds as the sole sovereign, he—
