whose fierce commands were powerful and who caused even the gods and others to tremble— delighted while his pair of feet was being worshipped by them.
Śrīdhara: One whose command is exalted, superior, fierce, and intense. ||12||
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
O dear one, him who was intoxicated by the honey of intense fragrance...
The guardians of all the worlds, with palms joined in reverence, worshipped him whose copper-hued eyes were wide open—
the abode of asceticism, yoga, strength, and vitality— without the three [worlds] as offerings in their hands.
The Madhus, Ādityas, Vasus, and Rudras are indeed the threefold gods;
the Maruts, Viśvedevas, and Sādhyas are likewise included therein.
"Therefore, three are declared [as gods], while four are remembered as humans"—thus it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa. And: "Hiraṇyākṣa gave the offerings to all except the gods.
Furthermore, the word *sura* (god) is seen even in reference to those who do not receive sacrificial portions.
"Thus, these three are designated as those who do not partake in the sacrificial portion. So it is said. (12–13)

Śrīdhara: O King, [he was] intoxicated by honey-wine of fierce fragrance and vast scent; therefore, his copper-colored eyes were wide open and rolling. All the guardians of the worlds (*aśeṣa-dhiṣṇya-pāḥ*), with hands bearing offerings, waited upon and served him—by means of three [verses].
Except for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, there is no other state that serves as a refuge. ||13||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: [They] worship with three hands joined in offering, excluding Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra; [they worship] His state which is the locus of refuge, like that of a flute.

Even though he was unrighteous, it was solely out of extreme fear that the earth and other elements possessed qualities such as yielding crops without being ploughed during his reign; otherwise, the destruction of the earth and other elements by him would have occurred immediately. However, Veṇa did not possess such power that even Bhṛgu and the others [could withstand him].
They reduced [the mountain] to ashes; however, it must be discerned that he first abandoned the fiery power of Bhṛgu and the others—
which was said to have remained by its own vigor upon the throne of Mahendra.
Viśvāvasu, Tumburu, ourselves and others—
the Gandharvas, Siddhas, Ṛṣis, Vidyādharas, and Apsarases— praised him repeatedly, O Pāṇḍava.
Śrīdhara says: He describes the manner of worship with the words, "They sang" (verse 14).
The *Krama-sandarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon. —
He alone [is attained] by those belonging to the castes and stages of life through sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
Being worshipped, he accepted his portions of the oblation by means of his own splendor.
The earth, consisting of seven continents, yielded crops without being ploughed for him;
likewise, cows were milk-yielding wish-fulfillers, and the sky was a locus of various wonders.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
And the oceans, with their waves, brought forth floods of jewels and their wives.
Alkaline water, fermented liquor, clarified butter, honey, curd, milk, and nectar-water.
Śrīdhara: His wives are the rivers; they carried [him], that is, they bore him along. He speaks of the oceans themselves as "the salt-ocean" (kṣāra) and so forth. ||17||
Kramasandarbha: This has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: Their wives are the rivers. He speaks of the oceans themselves as "the salt-water [ocean]," etc. (17).
With its mountain valleys serving as pleasure gardens in all seasons, the single mountain alone possessed the various qualities of the trees and the attributes of the world-protectors.

Śrīdhara: *Ākrīḍam* means a place of play. The trees [there] bore qualities such as flowers and fruits during all seasons. And he alone sustained the various distinct qualities of the world-protectors, such as raining, burning, and drying up. (18)
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Ākrīḍam means a place for play. ||18||
Thus, having conquered the quarters and ruling as the sole sovereign, he enjoyed his beloved objects of sense according to his pleasure; yet, with his senses unsubdued, he found no satisfaction.
Śrīdhara: He by whom the quarters have been conquered; "yathopajoṣam" means according to one's pleasure. ||19||
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been explained. —
Thus, for one who is intoxicated by power, arrogant, and acting contrary to the scriptures...
A great length of time passed for him who had incurred the curse of Brahmā.
Śrīdhara: A great period of time consisting of seventy-one yugas and a little more. ||20||
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
All the worlds, together with their guardians, were agitated by his fierce rod of punishment.
Having found no refuge elsewhere, they went for refuge to the Infallible One.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
Homage be to that ultimate limit where the Self is Hari, the Lord.
Having gone there, those peaceful, stainless renunciants do not return.
Thus, those pure ones, with their selves restrained and their intellects concentrated,
remained sleepless and subsisting on air as they waited upon Hṛṣīkeśa.
Śrīdhara: [This is] the *Krama-sandarbha*; it has not been commented upon.

Viśvanātha: "To the direction" (*kāṣṭhāyai diśe*) means: since every region where Hari resides is seized by the splendor of the asuras, we shall go to some sacred pilgrimage site (*puṇya-tīrtha*) in that direction and [seek him].

The sense is: "We praise [him]. Or rather, "Salutation to that excellence," meaning that within this excellence, all other excellences—such as being called "Hari" by others—have been conquered by this Asura. According to Amara, *kāṣṭhā* means "excellence" or "the quarter of the sky. (22–23)
To them there appeared a formless voice, sounding like the roar of clouds,
filling the quarters of the sky and granting fearlessness to the virtuous.
Śrīdhara: "Formless" means devoid of a speaker. ||24||
The *Krama-sandarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
—o)0(o— O best of the wise, do not fear; may it be well with you all!
For my vision leads all beings to the attainment of every highest good.
The wickedness of this lowest of the Daityas is known;
I shall bring about his destruction, but wait for the right time.
Śrīdhara: My sight and hearing lead to the attainment of all spiritual perfections;
for through the sequence of my sight and hearing, there arises the direct experience of Me. (25)
Viśvanātha: "Indeed, my vision..."—the sense is that as long as my vision does not extend even to the pillars, so long will there be suffering for you. ||25||
He who harbors hatred toward the gods, the Vedas, cows, the learned, the virtuous, righteousness, or me— he indeed perishes swiftly.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha have not commented [on this].
Krama-sandarbha: When someone has hatred toward the gods and so forth, then he indeed perishes very quickly, as is well known. ||27||
To Prahlāda,
who is free from enmity, profoundly peaceful, his own high-souled son—
to him I shall grant even a boon of supreme power, should anyone seek to do him harm.

Śrīdhara: Now, one might object that even if there is enmity toward the gods and others, there is no destruction for this [devotee], because he is empowered by the boon of Brahman; to this, he says: "to the one who is without enmity" (nirvairāya). The sense is: "I endure everything, but not the malice toward my devotee. (28)

The sequence of the composition: Nevertheless, because he is immortal and possesses wondrous power, even though he is currently strengthened by boons, I myself shall slay him. However, saying "to one who is without enmity," he indicates that he himself is also waiting for a specific vulnerability that would destroy that power.

Viśvanātha: Now, one might object that this [demon], empowered by a boon from Brahmā, has been hating the gods and others for a very long time and yet does not perish; to this he replies: "To the one free from enmity" (nirvairāya). The sense is: "I endure everything, but I do not tolerate the injury of my devotees. (28)
Śrī Nārada said:
Thus addressed by the Teacher of the World, the denizens of heaven bowed down to Him.
They turned back, their agitation gone, and they considered the Asura to be slain.
"Madhva says: 'Wherever there may be a place of glory for others,' O Keśava;
yet, since [the glory] belongs to the gods everywhere, one should worship others only in certain instances. Thus it is said. ||29||
Śrīdhara: They considered the Asura to have been slain; the implication is that this was because they were then engaged in hostility toward him. ||29||
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— That lord of the Daityas had four most wonderful sons.
Among them, Prahrāda was great, a worshiper of the Great One (Mahat) by virtue of his qualities.
Śrīdhara: In order to explain that very same hatred, he first speaks of the greatness of the son, beginning with "of him" (tasya).
He became great by virtue of his qualities; he specifies those very qualities with the words "a worshiper of Mahat," and so forth. (30)
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
One who is devoted to Brahman, endowed with good character, true to his word, and a master of his senses;
He regards all beings as himself and is their sole dearest friend.

Śrīdhara: He whose resolve (*sandhā*) and promise (*pratijñā*) are true. The sequence of words [is such that] he alone is both the beloved and the best of friends. Viśvanātha: This has not been explained.
Bowing like a servant at the feet of the noble, affectionate toward the wretched like a father,
and as tender toward his equals as a brother; regarding his teachers as lords, he was enriched with learning, wealth, beauty, and noble birth, yet remained free from the arrogance of pride.
Śrīdhara: He by whom the feet of the noble ones are properly bowed to like those of a servant; he who possesses the realization that his gurus are the Lord. (32)
The sequence of the composition: in the commentary on the verse beginning with "tvattaḥ," there is the explanation "the Vedas, Upavedas, and so forth.

The compound *vidyāḥ kalāḥ* is a *dvandva* (copulative) compound; therefore, the reading *vidyāḥ kalāśca* is not appropriate. Viśvanātha [comments]: he by whom the feet of the Āryas have been properly bowed to (*samyak-nata-ārya-aṅghriḥ*). [The locative] *guruṣu*...

The plural number is used out of reverence; the meaning is: toward the guru who has imparted the instruction of the Śrī-Bhagavān-mantra—one whose mind is not agitated by calamities and who is free from worldly desire.
Perceiving the unreal in qualities heard or seen,
with senses, vital breaths, body, and intellect always subdued, his desires eternally stilled, he is a non-asura among asuras.

Śrīdhara: One whose mind is not agitated even when calamities have arisen; who is free from longing for perceived or heard qualities and sense-objects; who perceives them as unsubstantial; whose senses and other faculties are subdued;
and who is devoid of demonic states such as envy—even if he were a demon.
One whose desires are completely stilled. ||33||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: He is one whose demonic disposition—such as envy and the like—is abandoned. ||33||
O King, those great qualities which are repeatedly grasped by poets are not now concealed, as they are in the case of the Blessed Lord.
Śrīdhara: Even now, your virtues are not concealed; they do not remain hidden. ||34||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: The non-material qualities (*guṇas*) of the Great Lord—such as fortitude, profundity, and so forth—exist by their very nature; they are perceived by poets who possess discernment. These qualities reside in the individual soul (*jīva*).

They do not cease to exist; rather, the meaning is that they are perceived by the pure senses, such as the mind and others, as being truly belonging to the Blessed One. He states the eternity of these qualities: "those qualities even now, until this present time, are not concealed"—that is, they are not covered by time, karma, and so forth—for all this duration.
The meaning is that even as time passed, Prahlāda remained distinguished by such very same qualities, shining forth likewise in Sutala, as well as in Vaikuṇṭha and Mahāvaikuṇṭha. ||34||
O King, even the gods, though they are enemies, act as the standard of comparison for one who is present in an assembly of virtuous verses; how much more so others such as yourself?
"Madhva states: 'The equality of others with Hari is declared to be a partial equality;
however, the complete equality belongs to [the incarnations] such as Matsya—this is the conclusion of the scripture. (35)

Śrīdhara: In an assembly where there is discourse on the virtuous—that is, in a gathering characterized by talk concerning saintly persons—[even] the gods, though they are enemies, regard Prahlāda as a model or an example; what then need be said of those like you who are devotees of Viṣṇu? (35)
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: "A comparison" means an illustration, such as "this devotee is equal to Prahlāda"—o)0(o)—.
Enough with his innumerable qualities; his greatness is indicated by the fact that he possesses an innate devotion for the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva.
Śrīdhara: It is merely indicated by me, or illuminated; or rather, it is well-explained. ||36||

The sequence of the composition: the meaning is that it is impossible to say "it is sufficient with his innumerable qualities"; therefore, only a mere indication or illumination of his majesty is provided. Alternatively, by means of those very innumerable [qualities], his majesty is thoroughly indicated to the child; it cannot be fully described.
The meaning is "it is possible. And the reason for both cases is: "Vāsudeva. ||36||

Viśvanātha: The meaning is: "What indeed is his excellence, for he is already fully endowed with such innumerable qualities—that is, qualities impossible to count? The sense is: while other men may indeed be exalted by their virtues, Prahlāda is not [merely] so; rather, there exists in him another distinct factor that is the cause of his excellence.

What is that? To this he says: "The majesty (*māhātmyam*) is indicated," meaning it is well-expressed. What is that? [It is] "Vāsudeva," and so forth. Alternatively, his majesty is indicated; because it cannot be fully described, it is merely manifested through words such as "planets" (*graha*) and so on in the subsequent text concerning those whose souls are seized by the planet Kṛṣṇa.
[The word] *bhāvaḥ* [is used]. In response to the inquiry "Of what kind is he?", [the author] says: "Vāsudeva. Some say [it refers to him] in the form of Nṛsiṃha;

for it is stated by the Vaiṣṇavas that immediately after Prahlāda’s hymn of praise, "the Blessed Lord Hari, wearing yellow garments, appeared," and [he is described as] "one whose soul was seized by the planet Kṛṣṇa" and "embraced by Govinda."

And because of the statement of the *Agrimokti*, others hold that [the devotion] resides only in Vāsudeva in his form as the son of Vasudeva; while others maintain that in the earlier and later stages of Prahlāda’s life, it was respectively fixed upon Vāsudeva and Nṛsiṃha.
It is innate, and not something achieved through spiritual practices performed in previous births like those of others.
The meaning. ||36||
A child who has set aside his playthings remains like one dull-witted due to being absorbed in them;
likewise, one whose self is seized by the planet Kṛṣṇa does not perceive this world in such a manner.
Śrīdhara: He states the signs of natural love (*naisargika-rati*) in six verses beginning with "nyasta-krīḍanaka.
"Tan-manastayā" means by having the mind fixed solely upon Him. (37)
The sequence of events is as follows: with his mind fixed on Him—that is, with his mind absorbed in Kṛṣṇa—he sets aside his playthings.

Immediately thereafter, by that very absorption, he becomes like one insentient and identical to Him. Following that, his self being seized by the "graha" (spirit) of Kṛṣṇa—being possessed by Kṛṣṇa as if by a spirit—he does not perceive this world in such a way.
The meaning is that he saw [her] not as people see her, but rather by means of the very radiance of her manifestation; the sense is that she was as if embraced by the shimmering Govinda. ||37||

Mukunda-dāsa [Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu 3.2.108]: Kṛṣṇa alone is the seizing spirit; his self is seized by Him, meaning his true nature is possessed by Him. Therefore, through being absorbed in His mind, he is like an insentient object and identical to Him.
Even this world, with its manifold variety, did not appear to him. ||37||
Viśvanātha says: He describes the signs of natural love (*naisargika-rati*) in six verses beginning with "nyasta-krīḍanaka.

Even though he is a child, he has abandoned childish play. Because his mind is fixed on Him—meaning his mind is one-pointedly focused on Kṛṣṇa alone—he is perceived by others as if he were dull-witted; yet, unlike other devotees, he does not [need to] direct his own mind toward Kṛṣṇa as an object.

It was done; however, a certain planet has seized his mind just as one seizes a desirable object, namely Kṛṣṇa himself—as he says with the word "Kṛṣṇa. Therefore, the meaning is that the world does not know him as consisting of such worldly dealings, but rather knows him as consisting solely of Kṛṣṇa. ||37||

This verse, numbered 3.2.108 in the *Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu*, which enumerates the various types of verses, is cited as an example of the "invariable emotion" (vyabhicāribhāva) known as the dullness (*jaḍatā*) of non-yoga (*ayoga*).
Whether sitting, wandering, eating, lying down, drinking, or speaking,
he who is embraced by Govinda pays no heed to these activities.
Śrīdhara: These [objects], beginning with the seat, were unified with his own self by Govinda as he embraced them. ||38||
Kramasandarbha: This has not been explained.

Viśvanātha: He does not attend to—that is, he does not know—these matters concerning the seat, the path, the food, the bed, the drink, and what is to be said. Why? Because he is embraced by Govinda, who is exceedingly affectionate.

The sense is that just as a one-year-old child is embraced at every moment and held to the breast by his father or mother, so too was Prahlāda embraced by the Lord even at times of eating, sleeping, and so forth; thus, it is Prahlāda alone who perceives this, and no one else. ||38||
In one place he weeps, his consciousness clouded by thoughts of Vaikuṇṭha;
in another place he laughs, and in yet another place he sings aloud, gladdened by those same thoughts.
Śrīdhara: He weeps, wails, and cries out. His consciousness is variegated—that is, mixed and agitated—by thoughts of Vaikuṇṭha; he whose joy arises from those very thoughts. (39)

The sequence of composition: the first thought flashes forth in separation; the second occurs in union. Thus, in separation she sometimes weeps; in union she laughs. In separation she cries out loudly as if calling; in union and separation, at times there is the contemplation of that [state]. (39–40)

Viśvanātha: And so, just as when a mother has gone elsewhere for household chores and, having placed her child on the ground from the fold of her lap, that child cries because he does not perceive her, in the same way [I think]: "Where has my lord gone now, having abandoned me this very moment?"

He whose consciousness was agitated, variegated, and overwhelmed by thoughts of Him; while he was weeping, at that very moment the Lord, having regained His manifestation, laughed upon saying, "O child Prahlāda, why do you weep thus for even a mere moment without seeing Me? and then laughed again.
The meaning is: like a simple child upon seeing his mother who has returned after a long time and is embracing him;
"with that thought" means he whose joy arises from the thought, "My Lord, out of compassion, gladdens me alone by granting the sight of Himself. (39)
In one place he cried out in longing; in another, he danced without shame; in another, absorbed in meditation upon Him, he became one with Him and imitated His very form.
Śrīdhara: In some places, being filled with longing, he imitated [the Lord] by letting out his voice; that is, he himself performed those gestures and so forth. ||40||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "He cries out" (*nadati*). Having seen Hari, who has become manifest before him, from a great distance, he is filled with longing and raises his neck. "O Prahlāda! My child, without seeing you, I truly cannot..."

"I am liberated, for you alone are my supreme beloved. Having been addressed thus, he dances, utterly distracted by an excess of bliss and devoid of shame. At that very moment, when the [worldly] manifestation is shattered, he—possessed of an intensity of contemplation due to the extreme pain of separation from her—is overcome by the powerful transitory emotion (sañcārībhāva) of madness.
Thinking "I am indeed Hari," being absorbed in Him, he imitated—that is, performed in imitation of—His divine play as it appeared in the incarnations such as Rāma and Kṛṣṇa. ||40||
This verse, numbered 3.2.108 in the *Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu*, which describes the transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*) named "insanity" (*unmāda*) arising from disunion (*ayoga*), is cited here.
In some instances, with his hair standing on end, he remains silent, blissful from physical touch, his eyes closed like lotuses in the waters of the joy of motionless love.
Śrīdhara: "Contact" (saṃsparśa) is the attainment of that state; one who is satisfied by it. "Motionless" (aspanda) refers to a steady affection;
the bliss arising from that, and the water [of tears] produced by that bliss—with his eyes closed, meaning slightly closed, he is one whose eyes are thus joined with that water. ||41||

The sequence of composition: "In some instances of union, there is horripilation. This refers to the sensation of touch, which is the manifestation of being embraced by Him whose nature is compassion. (41)

Viśvanātha: At one time, thinking "Is he Utpalaka? Where shall I go? Where will I find my Lord?", his eyes were sealed with the pain of separation from him; then, suddenly beholding Him within his own heart and being filled with bliss by the touch of His hand, he was so overcome that his hair stood on end and his body became motionless.
And he was that very person whose eyes were slightly closed, with tears of joy flowing from them due to such affection. ||41||
By service rendered to the lotus feet of Him whose fame is supreme,
attained through detachment from all possessions, [he attained his goal].
Extending supreme bliss to himself,
he repeatedly brought peace to the mind of one wretched by evil association.
Śrīdhara, while extending supreme bliss to himself, brought peace—that is, tranquility—to the mind of another who was wretched due to evil association. ||42||

The sequence of composition: In the dental recension, Viśvanātha composed [this work] equal to himself—that is, in accordance with his own internal disposition. Now, one might ask: since Hiraṇyakaśipu and others were wicked associates, how could Prahlāda’s devotion remain steadfast toward him? Furthermore, by association with him, others too became wicked associates.
His companions, the boys, became fulfilled; yet, how could there be even a suspicion of bad association for him?

To this he says: "He"—referring to one who is wretched due to bad association—he brought his mind to tranquility (*śama*). For, according to the words of the Blessed One, "tranquility is the mind's steadfastness in Me," he made [his mind] steadfast in the Blessed One. (42)
O King, Hiraṇyakaśipu committed a great evil against his son, who was a most fortunate, illustrious, and high-souled devotee of the Lord.
Śrīdhara: He committed a sin, an act of malice. ||43||

The sequential arrangement: The characteristics of being a great devotee (*mahā-bhāgavata*) have already been shown; [it refers to one] for whom there is great fortune (*bhāga*), namely the grace of Śrī Nārada, and whose nature is a great, worshipful self endowed with fortitude, profundity, and other such qualities. ||43||
Viśvanātha: Not explained.
—o)0(o— Śrī Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O divine sage of noble vows, we wish to know this from you:
how it was that a father bestowed evil upon his own pure and virtuous son.

Śrīdhara: At the end of the first chapter, he asks again with great astonishment about the very same matter he had already questioned—"O divine sage"—or "from you" (tava), meaning "your word. We wish to know, that is, to understand, how it was that he gave evil to the virtuous, meaning he committed an offense against the saintly. ||44||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: At the end of the first chapter, he asks again with great wonder about the very same matter that was previously asked—"O divine sage," etc. "From you" (*tava*) means from you; "evil" (*agham*) means suffering. ||44||
Fathers who are affectionate toward their sons reprove even their own sons when they act contrary to their will for the sake of instruction, and not out of malice as others might do.
Śrīdhara: They reproach and revile [them], yet they do not actually commit any harm, like another enemy. ||45||
The sequence of composition: "putrān" and so forth, consisting of one and a half verses. ||45||
Viśvanātha: They do not bring about sin; there is no other enemy. ||45||
How much more so those virtuous ones who follow their teachers and deities?
O Brahmin, O Lord, dispel this curiosity of ours.
Whatever hatred was directed by the father against his son for the purpose of causing his death—

Śrīdhara: "Anuvaśān" means compliant; "sādhūn" means those free from passion and anger. The meaning is: what need is there to say that they do not commit sin directed toward those for whom the teacher is a deity, just like a father? There is hatred of the son on the part of the father directed toward the son; the hatred committed by the father leads to the death of the son.
"Employed" means set in motion; dispel this curiosity. Or rather, the meaning is:
since the hatred directed toward the son was employed for the sake of the father's death, therefore dispel this curiosity. ||46||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: *Anuvaśān* means compliant or favorable. *Kautūhalam*—derived from *kutūhala*—means doubt; *vidhama* means dispel it. What is the doubt? It is the father’s hatred toward his son for the purpose of killing that son.
He was intensely engaged for his own death, that is, solely for the purpose of dying. ||46||
Thus ends the fourth chapter of the seventh [section], which is well-composed for the virtuous, in the *Harṣiṇī* commentary that reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted.
Thus ends the Seventh Canto in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā, the Pāramahaṃsyam, which is a commentary on the Brahma-sūtras within the glorious Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa.
The fourth chapter in the Dialogue between Yudhiṣṭhira and Nārada.
Now begins the fifth chapter.
In the *Prahlādānucarita*, Śrī Nārada said:
"The venerable Kāvya was indeed chosen by the asuras for the office of family priest."
His two sons, Ṣaṇḍa and Marka, [lived] near the palace of the king of the Daityas.
Śrīdhara:
In the fifth [chapter], it is told how the Daitya, having abandoned what he had learned from his guru and become devoted to the praise of Viṣṇu,
was unable to kill his son by means of elephants, serpents, and other such creatures.
To state that devotion to the Blessed One alone was the cause of his enmity, he says, beginning with "For the sake of priesthood" (paurohityāya) and so forth.
Kāvya is Śukra; therefore, the ellipsis is that his two sons resided near the palace of the king of the Daityas. ||1||
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha:
The son, having been taught by his guru and questioned by his father, praises Kṛṣṇa.
In the fifth [act], though struck by the elephants of the quarters and others, he shone forth auspiciously.

To state that Prahlāda’s devotion alone was the cause of the enmity, he says, beginning with "paurohityāya" (for the office of priest). Kāvya was the enemy; therefore, the ellipsis is that his two sons resided there. ||1||
The two of them taught Prahlāda, that boy skilled in policy whom the king had brought to them,
as well as other lessons to the other sons of the asuras.

Śrīdhara: [The term] "pāṭhyān" refers to the treatises on statecraft (*daṇḍanīti*) and so forth; alternatively, the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) may be understood as "the sons of the Asuras who were to be taught.
This is the sequence of the composition. Viśvanātha: [This has been] not explained.

Whatever was spoken there by the teacher, he heard and repeated it; yet, because it was based on the dogmatic grasping of his own and others' doctrines, he did not consider it to be sound in his mind.
Śrīdhara: Immediately after hearing [it], he recited it in that very same way; however, he did not consider it to be correct.
The reason for this is: "that which has as its basis the false attachment (mithyābhiniveśa), namely the erroneous notion (asad-graha) that 'this is mine' and 'that is another's. ||3||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He did not consider that [system], such as the science of statecraft (*daṇḍa-nīti*) and so forth, to be correct. Why? Because he thoroughly adheres (*ā-śrayate*) to a false partiality (*asad-anugraha*)—namely, the stubborn insistence (*durabhiniveśa*) on the distinction between "self" and "other. That is what it means.
Once, O Pāṇḍava, the king of the Asuras, having placed his son upon his lap,
asked: "Tell me, my child, what do you consider to be virtuous?"
Śrīdhara: Not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: Thinking that this boy might become paralyzed with fear (*stobha*) when questioned on difficult matters, he said: "That which you have well-practiced, which you know, speak before me."
"And tell me that very thing," such was the intention of Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Śrī Prahlāda said:
O best of asuras, I consider that to be truly beneficial for embodied beings.
For those whose minds are always agitated by grasping at what is unreal, having abandoned their own downfall— the house that is like a blind well—
they go to the forest to take refuge in Hari.

Śrīdhara: O best of Asuras! Because of the false attachment of "I" and "mine" arising from an improper grasp, those whose intellects are properly agitated and settled [in that state] should, having gone to the forest, take refuge in Hari; this is exactly what I consider to be right. Of what nature is the house? One that leads to one's own downfall.
It is the cause for one's own downfall. Why? Because it brings about delusion, like a blind well. ||5||
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: But Prahlāda, although he already knew his intention, reflected with the thought, "Among all things worthy of inquiry in this world, what object do you consider to be the best?"

If you ask me, "How does one make [the world] agreeable to oneself?", listen to this appropriate answer, he said: *tat* (that). O best of Asuras! For those people whose minds are distressed by the false attachment of "I" and "mine" arising from an improper grasp, I consider that alone to be good; what is that? The home, which is the cause of one's own downfall.

I consider that very taking refuge at the feet of Hari to be virtuous—namely, that having abandoned [the world] and gone to the forest, one should take refuge in Hari. Even while staying at home, he alone has truly abandoned the house as a blind well and gone to the forest; otherwise, even though he went to the forest, he merely resorted to the house itself as a blind well.
And they explain it thus. ||5||
Śrī Nārada said:
Having heard the words of his sons, which were directed toward the side of the enemy, the Daitya—
Just as the intellect of children is divided by the intellects of others.
Śrīdhara: [Those who are] "established" (samāhita) in Viṣṇu, the opponent's position, mean those who are firmly settled in him. The reason for the laughter is given as "intellect" (buddhi). ||6||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: "Established" (*samāhitāḥ*) means fixed or settled upon Viṣṇu, who is the "enemy's side" (*para-pakṣe*), that is, the side of the foe.
Regarding the phrase "he laughed": "This boy laughs; whatever he holds, he carries that very thing—what fault is there in this?"*
"From this day forward, Nārada and other Vaiṣṇavas must not be allowed entry here"—such is the instruction; this is the intended meaning.
Let the child be properly cared for in the house of the preceptor by the twice-born.
Just as his intellect would not be divided by the followers of Viṣṇu who were disguised [as his own].
Śrīdhara: [He was] by means of the Vaiṣṇavas, the Bhāgavatas, acting as the cause. [Objection: But how could they have entered your house?
[Reply: True; nevertheless, they were concealed, hidden by another disguise. (7)
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: That too [should be done] only in the house of the Guru. And how they should be addressed, he says: "With the followers of Viṣṇu" (verse 7).
Having brought Prahrāda to their home and summoned him, the priests of the Daityas praised him with gentle words and questioned him with conciliatory means.
Śrīdhara: [He] was brought home by the Daityas. ||8||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: [The word] "ślakṣṇayā" (gently) is used for the question; the intention is that otherwise, being a child, he might not speak to his own teacher, who is a Vaiṣṇava, out of fear. ||8||
"—O child Prahlāda, may it be well with you! Speak the truth, not falsehood.
From where has this perversion of intellect come to you, surpassing even that of children?"
Śrīdhara: Having surpassed all children; "tubhyam" means "to you. ||9||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "But [we shall give] the auspicious" means the sense is that we will give you the sweetmeats and such things you desire;
"passing over the children" means for you alone. ||9||
"O delighter of your lineage, was this change in your intellect caused by another, or did it arise from yourself? Please tell us, for we, your elders, are desirous of hearing."
Śrīdhara: Not commented upon.

Viśvanātha: The intention is that if he utters the name of some Vaiṣṇava, saying "Let it be told," then, recognizing him as a Vaiṣṇava, we shall lead him before the king's assembly and have him executed. ||10||
Śrī Prahlāda said:
The false notion of "stranger" and "one's own" among men is created by His illusory energy (māyā).
Salutations to that Blessed One, who is perceived by those whose intellects are deluded.

Śrīdhara: "Alas! You are deluded by *māyā* that you thus revile me"—with this intention, he first says: "The false attachment that 'this is mine' and 'that is another's' was created by that very *māyā*, and is not real. Therefore, it is seen only by you whose intellects are bewildered by that *māyā*, but not by me."
Salutation to that Lord of inconceivable illusion. ||11||

The sequential arrangement: "For men, the Supreme is the source of fear arising from attachment to a second [entity]" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.2.37), and so forth; thus, for those living beings who are averse to the Lord, [the world] is indeed inferior because their intellects have been deluded by the Māyā of that Lord, who possesses envy.

Salutations to that Blessed One, for the sake of quelling the false insistence of those wicked ones— whose intellects are especially deluded by the notion of the body being the self through the forgetting of their true nature— who, by means of Māyā alone, have claimed another's wealth as their own. Salutations to Him alone.

The meaning is "I pay homage. This word *sva* would be neuter alone when denoting the self; as Amara states: "Sva [is used] for a kinsman and for the self (neuter); *svam* in three genders means 'one's own'; *svaḥ* in the non-feminine means wealth.
Therefore, it has been explained in this way. ||11||

Viśvanātha: "Aha! These fools in this world, being tormented by sin, think, 'He is but a deluded child,'" and reflecting thus in his mind, he said: The false grasping (*asad-grāha*) and the stubborn insistence (*asad-āgraha*) that "this is another's side" and "that is my own side"—by means of a pun (*śleṣa*), this refers to the crocodile (*grāha*) for men who have fallen into the ocean of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*).

The meaning is that the predatory creature—a specific kind of aquatic animal—was previously seen as merely created by *māyā* and inferred [to exist], but now it has been directly perceived (*pratyakṣīkṛta*). Therefore, the implication is that you are being devoured at every moment. ||11||
When that person, though following the path of men, has his animal-like intellect shattered,
the false notion of duality— the idea that "this one is other" and "I am other"— is destroyed.
This scripture, however, independently negates the existence of anything else [apart from the Self], for it says:
"The ignorant one indeed sees, thinking, 'He is one and I am another.'"

"One should meditate upon the Self as the Inner Ruler"—thus [the scripture] declares the distinction [of the self] from its own essential nature. Therefore, the individual souls (jīvas) are always distinct and dependent upon Brahman;
and the state of the liberated one as well—all this is eternally under the control of Viṣṇu. Thus it is stated in the *Brahma-tarka*.
Śrīdhara: "Aha! What is this you are prattling? Tell me the cause from which this delusion of your intellect has arisen. Thus challenged, he replied with three verses beginning with "He":
"When that Blessed One is well-disposed (*anuvrata*) toward one, then the intellect of even those who are like unenlightened cattle (*paśu*) [becomes clear]."

That which has fallen into differentiation is unreal and false; it pertains to the sphere of saṃsāra and is divided, whereas that which is grounded in the undivided self becomes non-differentiated. ||12||

The sequence of the composition: And so, when—by some means or other, through a great opportunity—that [Lord] becomes favorable upon being brought face-to-face, then, by what was previously stated, the "animal-intellect" (*paśu-buddhi*) is split asunder; the meaning is that it perishes. Then, having explained that very point:

He demonstrates this with the words "another" (anya). The meaning is that for those followers of the treatises on wealth and pleasure who have followed the path of devotion, they conceive of the perishable aggregate itself as the self. ||12||

Viśvanātha: To the question, "From where does this difference in your intellect arise? he provides the answer with the word "sa" (he). "Anuvrata" means favorable; [the intellect] is specifically distinguished or torn apart. What indeed is this "animal intellect"?
To that he says: it has fallen into the state of duality, thinking, "This other person is my opponent," and likewise, "I am his slayer."

"Unchaste" means wicked; for it has been said by the Blessed One, "Indeed, there is nothing to be hidden from the virtuous, whether they be enemies, neutrals, or haters. However, the underlying sense is that in reality, because all living beings are of one nature when viewed from the perspective of the Self (*ātman*), and because even from the perspective of the body all bodies consist of the five elements (*pañcabhūta*), there is no difference whatsoever.
This very Self, whose sequence of movement through its own and other states is difficult to traverse, is thus described by those lacking true understanding.
Even the proponents of the Vedas, such as Brahmā and others, are bewildered regarding its path; indeed, this [reality] shatters my mind.

Śrīdhara: Demonstrating the non-existence of difference, he says: "This very Supreme Self is conceptualized by the undiscriminating as 'self' and 'other. And this is logical, because even Brahmā and the other gods are bewildered regarding the path of inquiry into Him. The reason for this is that He is difficult to transcend and difficult to comprehend."
That which has a sequential arrangement, a traditional narrative, or a descriptive account. ||13||

The sequential arrangement: That well-known Supreme Self has, as it were, come within the range of my vision; yet, by those previously mentioned—those lacking the understanding of "self" and "other"—His sequence is difficult to traverse and is determined only through its inscrutable method. Oh, let them be! For on that path...
"Even those who recite the Vedas are deluded; let alone others, even Brahmā and the rest are deluded"—this very statement shatters my understanding and separates me from your doctrine. ||13||
Viśvanātha: He says "He" (saḥ) because [the path] is extremely difficult to understand for those with the intellects of bound souls (*paśu*) as defined above.

This Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is "difficult to traverse" (*duratyaya*), meaning His sequence or following (*anukramaṇa*, *anusaraṇa*) is hard to reach for those whose intellects are debased by such notions as "this is my own side" (*svapakṣa*) and "that is the enemy's side" (*vipakṣa*); yet it is not so for those of pure intellect.
It should be said that following that [path] is indeed easy for those who know the scriptures; thus he says:

even those who speak according to the Vedas (*vedavādinaḥ*), who discern the intended meaning of the Vedas, are bewildered regarding the path of devotion (*bhaktiyoga*)—the very way of following which leads to the attainment of Him. You, however, are merely puffed up by a tiny fragment of knowledge.
The sense is: "How much more so? This Blessed One shatters my mind—that is, he makes it distinct from your minds. ||13||
"O Brahmin, just as iron moves of its own accord in the presence of a magnet,
so too does my mind become agitated by the mere chance of [meeting] the Discus-bearer."
Śrīdhara: Now, one might ask, how can that which is changeless possess the power to differentiate the mind? To this he says: "Just as...

Just as iron, when in the proximity of a magnet, moves of its own accord, so too is my mind in the presence of the Discus-wielder (Viṣṇu). [The opponent asks: From where did you obtain such proximity to Him?
To this he replies: "By chance. The meaning is that it is not known which [act], such as austerity or charity, has this as its fruit. ||14||

The sequence of the argument: Now, [one might ask], "In that case, it is your own understanding that is contradicted by that [scripture], not ours; likewise, it is your own understanding that is contradicted by it, not ours. To this he says: "Just as... (*yathā*).
The meaning is: "by chance" (*yadṛcchayā*), that is, by one's own whim, independently of any other cause. Chance...
"Freedom of will" (*svairitā*)—thus says Amara. The meaning is that just as that is the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of iron and magnet, so too it is for us;
therefore, that [comparison] is indeed appropriate.
[Prīti-sandarbha 93] Viśvanātha: If it is asked what the form of that very distinction of the intellect (*mati*) is, he says in response: "Just as iron..."

Just as iron moves of its own accord in the proximity of a magnet that attracts it, so too my mind moves of its own accord in the presence of the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu); it becomes distinct—that is, separated—from your minds. By the phrase "by chance," there is no role here for virtuous deeds, austerity, charity, or the like.

The meaning is that causality is possible. This is the sense: just as a magnet attracts iron by its own power alone and brings it into contact, and in that process there is no other cause or purpose, so too is the nature of the Discus-wielder (Viṣṇu). His very own nature is such.
The sense is this: what independence do I have in that matter, wherein my own devotee’s mind is drawn toward me by being under the sway of compassion? ||14||
Śrī Nārada said:
Having spoken thus much to the brāhmaṇa, the high-minded one became silent.
Having rebuked him, the king's servant became enraged and deeply dejected.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha [comment]: "The royal servant said"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. ||15||
The sequence of composition: "etāvat" constitutes one half-verse; "tam" constitutes the other half-verse. ||15||
"Bring the cane, you! This disgrace to our family, this evil-minded ember of the lineage— for him, the fourth punishment has now been proclaimed."

Śrīdhara: "Hey! Bring the cane and the whip! Among the four means—conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and punishment—it is the fourth, punishment (*daṇḍa*), that has been proclaimed in the scriptures for this evil-minded one. The reason for his evil-mindedness is that he is a 'brand of the family' (*kulāṅgāra*), one who, like a charcoal, is the cause of the family's destruction. (16)
The sequence of composition is as follows: in the first quarter, "ānīyatām" (let it be brought) is to be supplied with "yuṣmābhiḥ" (by you); in the second, "yasmād ayam" (since this...);

and in the latter half, "yataḥ" (from which) and "yasya" (of whom) are to be supplied. As for what was not explicitly stated, such as "ānayadhvam are vetram" (bring the cane, you there), that was indeed left unsaid because, having observed his delicacy, [the speaker] did not wish to be too blunt.
It is understood [from the context] that this is because [the agent] has the capacity to act. ||16||

Viśvanātha: A *vetra* is a specific type of staff used as a weapon. Since this man brings dishonor, therefore, among the various means [of dealing with him], the fourth—namely, restraint through punishment (*dama-daṇḍa*) alone—is declared in the scriptures for this evil-minded one. ||16||
This thorny tree, born in the sandalwood forest of the Daityas,
has become a mere stalk for Viṣṇu, whose axe is intent upon uprooting its very foundation.

Śrīdhara: To the question "Why is that?", he says: These very Daityas are like sandalwood trees, and in their forest, this one has become like a thorny tree. He explains that very point: for Viṣṇu—who stands in the place of an axe for uprooting the roots of that sandalwood forest of the Daityas—this child alone has acted as the stalk (*nāla*).

He acted like that; the meaning is that just as an axe's capacity to cut is assisted by a handle made of *babbūla* wood or similar trees—since cutting would be impossible without it—so too did this [handle] become the cause for Viṣṇu’s uprooting of the demons. ||17||
The sequence of the argument: furthermore, the idea that he alone serves as the stalk for Viṣṇu, whose nature is likewise supremely pure, is highly inconsistent; such is the intended meaning. ||17||

Viśvanātha: Regarding that forest, Viṣṇu—who stands in the place of an axe for its uprooting—is like its stalk; for in the world, it is well known that the handle of an axe is indeed made of *barbura* wood, and that is a thorny tree. (17)
" Thus, terrifying Prahlāda with various means such as threats and the like,
he caused him to accept the attainment of the three goals of human life.
Śrīdhara said: Thus, while intimidating Prahlāda, he taught him the scripture that expounds upon the categories of dharma, artha, and kāma. ||18||
Kramasandarbha: This has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: "He caused [them] to grasp" means he endeavored to make them grasp it. ||19||
Then the Guru, knowing that the fourfold objects of knowledge had been understood by him,
showed the lord of the Daityas his mother, who was cleansed and adorned.

Śrīdhara: [He spoke] toward that lord of the Daityas, by whom the fourfold means of policy—conciliation, bribery, and so forth—along with the objects of knowledge, had been understood. He was massaged with unguents, rubbed with fragrant pastes, bathed, and adorned with ornaments, forehead marks, and the like. (19)
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: [He is] one by whom the fourfold internal organ—the four means consisting of conciliation (*sāman*), bribery (*dāna*), sowing dissension (*bheda*), and punishment (*daṇḍa*)—which is to be known, that which has been known, and that which is worthy of being known, has been mastered. ||19||
The Asura, having greeted the boy who had fallen at his feet with blessings,
embraced him for a long time with both arms and attained supreme bliss.
Having placed him on his lap and smelled the crown of his head,
Yudhiṣṭhira, drenching his blossoming face with drops of tears, spoke as follows.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"O dear one, let something most excellent that has been studied be recited by you, Prahlāda—
whatever you have learned from your teacher during this length of time, O long-lived one."
Śrīdhara: Not commented upon.

Viśvanātha: "Well-studied" means free from doubt and other such defects; "subsequently" (anu) means favorably following the teacher—either from Hiraṇyakaśipu’s son [Virocana] according to the view of Śukra, or from Nārada according to the view of Prahlāda. ||22||
Śrī Prahlāda said:
Hearing and chanting of Viṣṇu, remembering Him, and serving His feet...
Worship, salutation, service, friendship, and self-surrender.
Thus, if devotion characterized by the nine marks were truly offered to the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu by a person,
I consider that to be the highest study accomplished.

"Madhva" refers to the knowledge of the Self as abiding within oneself; "ātma-vedana" is the knowledge of the Self. As it is said: "Even for one who is liberated, Hari remains forever within me as the Controller"—this knowledge is designated as the perfect surrender of the self (ātma-nivedana). ||23||
Śrīdhara: *Pāda-sevanam* is service; *arcanam* is worship; *dāsyam* is the offering of one’s actions;

*sakhyaṃ* is trust and so forth toward Him; *ātma-nivedanam* is the surrender of one’s own body. Just as no concern for feeding or protecting is felt for a cow, horse, or the like once it has been sold, so too [one regards] the body for Him.
Having surrendered that, the meaning is the avoidance of anxiety. ||23||

Thus, if devotion to the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu is performed with that which possesses these nine characteristics, and if it is offered while still being performed— and not if it is offered only after having been performed— then I consider that study to be supreme; for nothing studied or learned from this teacher is of such a kind.
The meaning is that it exists. ||23||

Sanātana Gosvāmī: *pāda-sevanam* is service at the feet; *arcanam* is worship; *dāsyam* is the offering of one's actions; *sakhyaṃ* is trust and so forth in Him; *ātma-nivedanam* is the surrender of the body. Just as no concern for feeding or protecting is felt for a cow or similar animal once it has been sold, so too [should one regard] the body.
The meaning is that for him, there is the avoidance of such thoughts. ||23||

The sequence of the arrangement: "Hearing" constitutes a pair [of verses]. In that context, hearing (*śravaṇa*) is the contact of the ears with words consisting of names, forms, qualities, retinues, and pastimes. The sequence for chanting (*kīrtana*) and remembering (*smaraṇa*) should be understood in the same way. As for remembering (*smaraṇa*), it is...
A slight mental application; service of the feet, which consists of attending to him in a manner appropriate to the time and place;
worship, which is the ritual adoration of Viṣṇu; salutation, which is prostration; servitude, which is the realization "I am his servant";
friendship, which is wishing for his welfare with the feeling of being a kinsman; and self-surrender.

The offering of everything from the body up to the pure self in every way unto Him alone—this is devotion (bhakti) directed toward the Blessed Lord, characterized by these nine features; it is direct and manifest in form, and not a mutual exchange consisting of the offering of ritual action and so forth. This [devotion] is that wherein even Śrī Viṣṇu himself is offered.
The meaning is this: if one were to cultivate the thought that "this alone is for that purpose," and not fixate upon dharma, wealth,
and so forth— if one were to act in such a manner, then I consider whatever has been studied by that agent to be supreme.

And so says the Śrī-Gopāla-tāpanī Upaniṣad: "Devotion is His worship; that is the fixing of the mind upon Him through detachment from the desire for results here or hereafter; this alone is liberation from karma" (Goṭā.u. 1.14).

The collection of nine characteristics is not strictly necessary, since the non-deviation from the probandum is heard to be established by even a single characteristic. Nevertheless, the occasional inclusion of other characteristics is due to the diversity of faith and inclination. Therefore, by the term "nine characteristics," devotion in its general sense is expressed.
It should be understood that only its performance is prescribed; therefore, it is said to possess nine characteristics because the other ancillaries are included within it.

In this context, the collection of nine characteristics is not strictly necessary, since the non-deviation from the probandum is heard through a single member alone. Nevertheless, there is sometimes a mixing of other members because of the diversity of faith and inclination; therefore, by the general expression "nine characteristics," [the point is made].

It should be understood that the performance of those alone is prescribed, and this [practice] possesses nine characteristics; for it is logical that other ancillaries (aṅgas) are included within them. Furthermore, a portion of this is written here specifically: thus is the sequence of the ancillaries of devotion, beginning with hearing the Name and so forth.

In this regard, although accomplishment indeed occurs through either one [of the two] or even by transposing the order, nevertheless, first of all, hearing the Name must be relied upon for the purpose of purifying the internal organ (*antaḥ-karaṇa*). When the internal organ is purified, through hearing the Form, there arises the capacity for its manifestation. And when it has manifested perfectly—

The manifestation of the qualities occurs within the form; and when the manifestation of the qualities has been accomplished through the excellence of the retinue (parikara), then, once those names, forms, qualities, and retinues have fully manifested, the manifestation of the divine pastimes (līlās) becomes perfectly realized— it is with this intention that the sequence of the means (sādhana-krama) has been written.

The same should be understood regarding chanting (*kīrtana*) and remembrance (*smaraṇa*). Furthermore, if this hearing (*śravaṇa*) is performed while the mouths of the venerable great ones are resonant, it possesses supreme majesty and bestows the highest bliss upon those in whom devotion has arisen. And that [hearing] is of two kinds: that manifested by the Great One and that being glorified by the Great One.
And so it is said [Bhakti-sandarbha 256]: therein, referring specifically to the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, as previously stated:
"This Purāṇa named Bhāgavatam is equal to Brahman."
The venerable sage composed the *Uttama-śloka-carita* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.3.40).
Even therein, among all forms of hearing, the hearing of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam is supremely excellent,
because its nature consists of sound endowed with such power and because it is composed of the supreme aesthetic essence (*rasa*).
[From *Bhakti-sandarbha* 260:

Here, as in the verse "by means of the form desired by oneself," one should repeatedly recite the hearing of one's own preferred name and so forth; and even in that regard, [the hearing] should be from the mouth of a great soul who possesses the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of all [these practices].

Indeed, the hearing of the names and other attributes of Śrī Kṛṣṇa is accomplished only through supreme good fortune, because He is the perfect Supreme Lord. This should be understood in the same way regarding chanting and the other limbs of devotion. Furthermore, that which is being chanted here by oneself at present is also [of such nature].
It should be glorified by reflecting upon it as having its conduct celebrated by great souls such as Śrī Śukadeva;

thus has hearing (*śravaṇa*) been demonstrated. Its priority over glorification (*kīrtana*) and the rest is because, without it, those [other practices] cannot be understood. And especially so, if [the practice] is performed directly by a great soul.
If the fortune of hearing [it] is not attained, then it must be recited by oneself individually;
this is because of its preeminence. For this very reason, it has been stated in such passages as: "The utterance of His speech is the destruction of the sins of the people" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.5.11;
12.12.52). By the authors of the commentaries: "Those names which, when there is a speaker... [and so forth].
They listen when there is another to hear them, and they recite; otherwise, however, they sing it themselves.

Now, therefore, follows the glorification (*kīrtana*). In this regard, the sequence beginning with the name and so forth should be understood as previously described. [In the *Bhakti-sandarbha*, this chanting of the Name is highly praised as being especially exalted: "The names of the Infinite One—casting aside all shame... ]

In passages such as *paṭhan* [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.6.27], and here, regarding the chanting of the Name, it has been taught by the Blessed Lord Himself, who appeared as the purifier of the Kali age: *Bhakti-sandarbha*, p. 265.
"Even lower than a blade of grass, more patient than a tree, free from pride and bestowing honor upon others—by such a person should Hari always be glorified. (Padyāvalī 32).
And this devotion called *kīrtana* [consists of the glorification of the Blessed One] through His substance (*dravya*), genus (*jāti*), qualities (*guṇa*), and actions (*kriyā*).

The renown of the Śrutis, Purāṇas, and other scriptures is that she consists of compassion whose sole object is the miserable person; and in the Kali age, there is misery, as stated in the Brahmavaivarta:
"Therefore, in the Kali age, practices such as austerity, yoga, knowledge, and sacrifice [are ineffective]."

"They remain with their constituent parts unaccomplished even by embodied beings, however skilled they may be. For this very reason, having appeared in the Kali age among people who are by nature exceedingly wretched,
she fulfills them by effortlessly bestowing the entire fruit of all the great spiritual practices (mahāsādhana) belonging to their respective ages.

For this very reason, by that alone, the Blessed One is especially satisfied in the Kali age. [Bhāṣya 270] Here, in connection with the Kali age, the excellence of the virtues of *kīrtana* (chanting) must be stated; even in mere devotion (*bhakti-mātra*).

Because the restriction of time, place, and so forth has been refuted, therefore the power of the glorious *kīrtana* is indeed equal throughout every age. It is established that the praise accorded to it in various contexts is solely due to the expectation that in the Kali age, it should be embraced by the grace of the Blessed Lord. For this very reason, although...

It has been stated that in the Kali age, devotion to another deity may be practiced, provided it is done through association with Him alone—as in the verse: "For the wise indeed worship with sacrifices consisting primarily of congregational chanting" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.5.29). And in this context, the independent chanting of the Name itself is exceedingly praiseworthy.
"Hari’s name, Hari’s name, Hari’s name alone!
In the Kali age, there is indeed no other way, no other way, no other way. Thus it is said in such passages.
Therefore, it is well stated: "The noble ones celebrate the Kali age" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.5.3), and so forth—this triad of verses.
[Here, Bhakti-saṃhitā 273:
In this regard, the ten offenses mentioned in the *Padma Purāṇa* should be abandoned. As stated in the words of Sanat-kumāra:
"Even one who has committed every offense is liberated by taking refuge in Hari."
Even if one were to commit offenses against Hari, they would become as mere dust beneath the feet of the twice-born.
"The basis of the name may sometimes exist, yet one transcends it merely by means of the name;
for even from an offense against the Friend of All, who is the Name itself, one falls downward.
And these are the offenses:
Censure by the virtuous spreads the greatest offense against one's name; for how could one who has attained fame endure such reproach?
This applies to all—the qualities, names, and so forth—of Śiva and Śrī Viṣṇu in this world.
He who perceives [the world] as divided by his own intellect is indeed one who brings harm to the name of Hari.
Disrespect for the guru, reviling the Vedas and the scriptures,
as well as the fabrication of false meanings regarding the name of Hari— indeed, he whose intellect perceives sin through the power of the Name [is liberated].
For him, purification through restraints does not exist.
Even the equanimity toward all auspicious activities, such as the abandonment of religious vows and the offering of oblations,
constitutes negligence when directed toward one who lacks faith, is averse, or does not listen.
And that instruction which is the offense against the name of Śiva.
Even having heard of its greatness, that lowest of men who is devoid of affection and is preoccupied with "I" and "mine," etc., [is truly base].
"He too has committed an offense against the Name.
Regarding these offenses, it is stated in that very same place that there is no other atonement for them:
"For those joined with offenses against the Name, the Names themselves remove the evil."
"Those very [practices], when performed without ceasing, are indeed effective for the goal.

Thus, even when offenses exist, it is appropriate to constantly chant His names and so forth solely for the purpose of pleasing Him, as seen in the story of Ambarīṣa and elsewhere, since He alone is the forgiver; for we observe that there are offenses against the Name.

And it is stated in the *Nāma-kaumudī*: "For one who has committed a great offense, only the experience [of its fruit] or His grace can bring about its cessation. For this very reason, Dakṣa spoke to the venerable Śiva: "He who was [treated thus] by me in the assembly with my perception of reality... (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 4.7.15), and so forth.

Within this kīrtana, one's own humility, the petitioning of one’s desired object, and the recitation of hymns of praise are also included. Furthermore, it should be understood that the kīrtana of the names and so forth found in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam is superior to the kīrtana of the names and so forth of others, as previously described.

Now, if one whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) has been purified by chanting (*kīrtana*) and other such means, then—because it has been stated [in the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 2.1.11]: "For those who are weary of this world and desire [liberation], there is freedom from fear from all quarters"—one should practice remembrance (*smaraṇa*) without abandoning the chanting of the Name. And that consists of mental recollection (*manasānusandhāna*). As for that which...
In this way, it becomes manifold through its connection with names and so forth.

That [manifoldness] is fivefold; whatever slight reflection there is constitutes recollection (*smaraṇa*). Drawing the mind away from everything and fixing the mind upon a general form is concentration (*dhāraṇā*). The specific contemplation of forms and other such qualities is [meditation].
Meditation (*dhyāna*) is the uninterrupted flow like a stream of nectar; that is constant mindfulness (*dhruvānusmṛti*).

Concentration (*samādhi*) is the manifestation of only the object of meditation. Furthermore, when that [meditation] is joined with play and so forth, the non-manifestation of anything else would be concentration. This form [of concentration] belongs to devotees such as the *dāsa*s and others, whereas the former [type of concentration] is generally [the case for others].
For those whose devotion is peaceful, if there is both inclination and capacity, then service to the feet should be performed without abandoning that [peaceful devotion].
This service is performed by some for the sake of achieving remembrance; in this context of service to the feet, the word "feet" (pāda) [is used].
It has been indicated by devotion alone. Therefore, the respectful nature of service is enjoined.

This includes the sight and touch of the Śrī-mūrti, circumambulation, following behind, and going to His holy places such as the temple of the Lord, the Gaṅgā, Puruṣottama, Dvārakā, Mathurā, and so forth;
for these are essentially part of that [service], especially according to the view that the Gaṅgā and others are supreme devotees (parama-bhāgavatas).

However, that service and so forth culminates specifically in service to the great; and the service of Tulasī must be understood as being included within that very [service]. Therefore, like the Ganges and other such [sacred things], the great possess the status of being the primary cause of devotion.
Now, regarding worship: if there is faith in that path, one who has taken refuge in a mantra and a guru should inquire of them in particular.

Although, according to the Śrī-Bhāgavata school, the path of worship (arcana-mārga) is not mandatory as it is in the Pañcarātra and other systems— since it is taught that the goals of human life (puruṣārtha) can be achieved through even one of the practices such as hearing (śravaṇa) and so forth even without it—
the ancient authorities have likewise stated:
Parīkṣit was foremost in hearing the glories of Śrī Viṣṇu, the son of Vyāsa (Śuka) in chanting them,
Prahlāda in remembering Him, Lakṣmī in worshiping His feet, Pṛthu in offering Him honor,
Akrūra in bowing down to Him, the Lord of Monkeys (Hanumān) in servitude, and Arjuna in friendship.
In the offering of one's entire self, Bali attained the supreme attainment of Kṛṣṇa;

nevertheless, those who follow the path of Śrī Nārada and others desire to establish a special relationship with the Śrī Bhagavān through the rite of initiation (dīkṣā) performed by the feet of a Śrī Guru.

Once initiation has been performed, worship must certainly be carried out. For those householders who possess wealth, however, the path of worship is indeed primary. Even if one does not perform it, like a person possessing nothing, by remaining solely devoted to remembrance (*smaraṇa*) and so forth, there would be the realization of a deficiency in wealth through the medium of others.
The performance [of such acts] demonstrates either a commitment to worldly affairs or laziness;

therefore, because it consists of a lack of faith, it is indeed inferior. Consequently, one might fall away from the teaching: "He who, with constant and guileless devotion... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.3.38), and so forth.

Furthermore, although for householders the path of service is obtained as being indistinguishable from the path of worship— since it is accomplished through material means— the path of worship holds primacy for them because it is entirely dependent upon scriptural injunctions. This is likewise true of the duty of the householder stage (*gārhasthya-dharma*), which consists of sacrifices to the deities.
Worship in the form of watering the root is equivalent to watering the branches, leaves, and so forth; thus, there is a great fault in failing to perform it.
It is heard in scripture that for all those who have received initiation, failure to perform it results in falling into hell. This applies even to one who is incapable or unfit.
And in the Āgneya Purāṇa it is said:
"He who, with devotion, beholds Hari when he has been worshipped or is being worshipped,
and he who rejoices with faith— he too shall obtain the fruit of yoga."
In this context, "yoga" refers to the yoga of action (kriyā-yoga) as described in the *Pañcarātra* and other scriptures.

Furthermore, in this path of worship, the prescribed injunctions must necessarily be observed. Prior to that, initiation (*dīkṣā*) must be performed; thereafter, one must be instructed in the scriptural ordinances. In that regard:
The Vaiṣṇava tradition alone is the authority.

Now, it may be asked: are not all mantras essentially composed of the names of the Lord? Among them, those specifically adorned with the word "namaḥ" and others have been endowed with particular powers by the venerable Lord and the great sages.

They also establish a specific relationship between the self and the Śrī Bhagavān. Among them, even the names of the Śrī Bhagavān alone, when used independently, are capable of bestowing the fruit that culminates in the supreme human goal (puruṣārtha). Therefore, within the mantras, even by name—
If superior capacity has been attained, why is there still a dependence on initiation (*dīkṣā*) and the like?

It is said: although it does not exist [as a requirement] from the perspective of one's essential nature (*svarūpa*), nevertheless, for the most part, it is for the sake of removing the various limitations of those people who—due to their connection with the body and so forth—are of miserly character and distracted mind.

The venerable great sages and others have established various specific regulations here in the path of worship at various points; therefore, the scripture prescribes expiation for their transgression. Thus, both [the regulations and the expiation] are entirely consistent.

This worship is of two kinds: pure (*kevala*) and mixed with ritual action (*karma-miśra*). Of these two, the former has been shown for those who possess faith but are independent of [worldly] means. The latter is for those whose faith is characterized by an excellence of worldly activity and the performance of spontaneous devotion (*yādṛcchika-bhakti*), and so forth; likewise, [it is for those]...

This was shown for the sake of householders who are intent on maintaining worldly order (*loka-saṅgraha*), so that even for those established ones whose faith is characterized by the opposite of that [renunciation], there may not be a lapse in the performance of common Vedic rites toward those whose intellects are ignorant of the discourse on devotion.

Its constituent parts are to be understood from the Āgamas and other sources. Likewise, observances such as the Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Janmāṣṭamī and Kārtika, as well as the Ekādaśī-vrata and others, are to be included within this very path.
Furthermore, in this path of service and worship of the feet, the offenses mentioned in the Āgamas must be avoided.
They are written as follows:
traveling to the abode of the Lord by means of vehicles or even on sandals;
failing to attend the festivals of the deity and other such rites; and not prostrating oneself before Him.
Whether one is impure from eating remnants of food or otherwise in a state of ritual impurity, one may perform the salutation of the Blessed One and so forth;
likewise, one may offer a prostration with a single hand and circumambulate before him.
Stretching out one's feet in front [of others], likewise sitting cross-legged [in their presence],
lying down, eating, and even speaking falsely;
Speaking loudly, mutual chatter, weeping, and quarreling;
as well as inflicting punishment and favor upon men, and harsh speech toward them.
Covering oneself with a blanket, disparaging others, praising others,
speaking indecorously, and the emission of downward wind.
Using figurative expressions when one has the capacity [to speak directly], eating what has not been offered,
and failing to offer fruits and other items that arise at their respective seasons.
Giving condiments and other items to one who has been assigned [to serve],
turning one's back on one's seat, and saluting others [while remaining seated]— these are [faults].

Silence toward the guru, praising oneself, and likewise reviling the deity—these, along with [other offenses], are proclaimed as the thirty-two offenses against Viṣṇu [Ha.bha.vi. 8.441–8]. Furthermore, other offenses mentioned in the Vārāha-purāṇa are written here in brief: eating the food of a king.

The touch of Hari in a dark room; approaching Hari without following the prescribed rites; opening His door without making sound; gathering food while being watched by a dog; breaking one's silence during worship;
going to relieve oneself at the time of worship; and burning incense without first offering perfumes, garlands, and other offerings.
Likewise, performing worship with unworthy flowers; not using a tooth-stick and likewise performing the ritual sprinkling [of water] without one;
touching a woman in her menses, a lamp, or even a corpse.
Having seen a corpse wearing a garment that is red, blue, unwashed, belonging to another, or soiled, one should release the downward wind (apāna-māruta).
Having become angry and gone to a cremation ground, even after eating he suffers from indigestion;
having consumed the flesh of a boar, oil-cake, and web-footed birds.

Likewise, having consumed kusumbha-vegetables or applied oil as an ointment, touching Hari or performing service for Hari brings about sin. [Ha.bha.vi. 8.456-9] And likewise elsewhere in that same work: "The practice of that [devotion] through disregard for the scriptures of the Lord..."
Promulgating other scriptures in his presence; chewing betel in front of him;
worshipping with flowers placed upon castor-oil leaves; performing worship at an inauspicious time; worshipping while seated on a seat or on the ground;
touching the deity with the left hand during the time of bathing; and using stale or begged flowers.
Worshiping with flowers during a ritual; spitting upon that [image]; manifesting one's own pride therein;

wearing horizontal sectarian marks (tiryak-puṇḍra); entering its temple even with unwashed feet; placing the foot of a non-Vaiṣṇava [upon it]; worshiping while looking at a non-Vaiṣṇava; and failing to worship Vighneśa [beforehand].

Upon seeing one who carries a skull (kapālin), there is no worship; bathing with one's own water [is prohibited]; and even when smeared with perspiration, worship [must still be performed]—these and others are such rules. Elsewhere, there are many other [prohibitions], such as not treading upon the remains of offerings (nirmālya) and various oaths to the Blessed One.

Nevertheless, even if an offense against the Blessed One has occurred through negligence, one must again perform acts of propitiation toward the Blessed One. As it is stated by Śrī Vyāsa in the *Avantī-khaṇḍa* of the Skanda Purāṇa:
"That mortal who indeed recites a chapter of the Gītā day after day..."
"Keśava forgives thirty-two offenses of his.
In that same [text], in the *Dvārakā-māhātmya*:
"Whoever should recite or even hear the greatness of the Thousand Names (*Sahasranāma-māhātmya*),"
"He shall never be tainted by even a thousand offenses.
In that same *Revākhaṇḍa*:
"Whoever recites the Tulasī-stava during the vigil for Viṣṇu on the twelfth day..."
"Keśava forgives thirty-two offenses for him. And elsewhere in that same work:
"The planting of Tulasī should be performed, especially during the month of Śrāvaṇa."
"The Supreme Person forgives thousands of offenses.
Thus it is said; and elsewhere in the *Kārttika-māhātmya*:
"He who performs the worship of the stone slab with the tips of Tulasī leaves..."
"Keśava forgives thirty-two offenses of such a person.
Thus it is said in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"The man who, marked with the conch and discus of Kṛṣṇa, performs the worship of Hari..."
"Keśava constantly removes thousands of offenses. Thus it is said in the Ādivārāha-purāṇa: "In the middle of the year, at my Śaukaraka-tīrtha..."
Having observed a fast, one may attain purity by bathing in the Gaṅgā.
Likewise, even one who has committed an offense shall become pure in Mathurā;
that virtuous man who serves either of these two holy places [attains this].
"He abandons the offenses committed throughout a thousand births.

Thus [it is said] regarding Śaukaraka, which is called the Field of the Boar (Śūkara-kṣetra). Now, in the path of worship (arcana-mārga), mental worship (mānasa-pūjā) is also prescribed in certain instances; and so it is said:
In the *Pādmottara-khaṇḍa*: "Indeed, mental worship (*mānasa-yajña*) is dear to all [classes] of practitioners.
In the *Gautamīya*: "For renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*) seeking liberation, mental offering (*mānasopahṛti*) is supreme.
Regarding its greatness, as stated in the words of Śrī Nārāyaṇa in the *Śrī Nārada-pañcarātra*: "This which is mental..."

"Yoga removes the fear of old age and disease," and so forth; "O great-minded sage, I am pleased with that person who, with supreme devotion, performs this even once according to the procedure taught in sequence."

This [mental worship] may sometimes be independent as well, because the mind-made form (mano-mayī mūrti) is prescribed as the eighth [form] with independence, according to the statement of Āvirhotra: "In an image or even in the heart, by means of the services as they are obtained," where the word "or" (vā) implies this independence.
In this regard, there is a story in the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa: In the city of Pratiṣṭhāna, there was a certain brāhmaṇa.
Although he was poor, he considered himself to be under the control of Kamalā (Lakṣmī) and remained peaceful.
That man of simple intellect once heard the Vaiṣṇava duties in the assembly of the best of brāhmaṇas. They...

Having heard that even spiritual goals are accomplished through the mind alone, the poor man began to practice accordingly. Then, having performed his daily rites preceded by bathing in the Godāvarī, he became tranquil-minded; sitting in a secluded place, he stabilized himself through practices such as breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
Having mentally established the desired form of Hari, having himself put on silk garments and the like, having firmly girded his loins, and having swept His abode and bowed down to Him,
he brought water from all the holy fords such as the Gaṅgā using silver and golden jars, and likewise...

Having brought various articles for service and completed the royal rites beginning with his bath and ending with the *ārātrika* ceremony, he remained experiencing an abundance of happiness day after day. Thus,
after much time had passed, on one occasion, having mentally prepared *paramānna* mixed with ghee, he said:

Having risen to offer that food with a golden vessel, he stood there; perceiving that his pair of thumbs had been burnt as they entered the vessel which was shimmering from its heat, alas, thinking "this has turned out badly," he abandoned it in distress. Although his meditative absorption (*samādhi*) was thus broken, [he remained] because of his burnt thumbs.

He was also distressed outside. Having perceived this, the Lord of Śrī-Vaikuntha, seated in Vaikuṇṭha, smiled; and when questioned by Śrī and the others as to the cause of it, He had him brought near Him by means of a celestial chariot (vimāna) and showed him to them in His presence in that state.
He established [them] according to their fitness.

Now, regarding *vandanam* (salutation): although it also functions as a constituent part of worship (*arcanā*), it is nevertheless prescribed separately with the intention that it may be performed independently, like *kīrtana* (chanting) and *smaraṇa* (remembrance).
