This should be understood in other cases as well. And the separate prescription of salutation is due to the hearing of [the Lord's] infinite qualities and sovereignty.

This very salutation is extended as a form of worship for the sake of those who maintain a state of humility in practices such as reflecting on his qualities and serving at his feet, and who have resolved upon performing even a mere salutation. Furthermore, there may be transgressions even within that salutation.
And these [objections] must be refuted by the perspective of the Viṣṇu-smṛti and other authorities:

namely, those consisting of the state of being made with one hand, having the body covered by a cloth, standing behind or to the left side of the Blessed One, and being situated near Him within the inner sanctum;
as well as the state of servitude.
He who, throughout thousands of other births, possesses such a mind as this—
"I am the servant of Vāsudeva"— shall uplift all the worlds.
Such is the definition stated in the *Itihāsa-samuccaya*.

Let there be, for now, the effort of worshipping those various [forms]. However, with the intention that accomplishment (*siddhi*) occurs even through the mere conceit of being such [a devotee], he provides a further description of this later on. This is the effect (*kārya*) resulting from that.
If [the practice] were merely service and so forth—meaning it consisted solely of service and the like—there would be no distinction [between the types of service].
Now, as for friendship (*sakhya*): as it is stated in the *Agastya-saṃhitā*:

"Some are intent on service and lie upon palaces; they wish to see him as a human being and to interact with him like kinsmen. For this very reason, regarding the statement "That friend who is supreme bliss" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.14.31):
The placement of the word "mitra" (friend) has been made;

its reading later on is with the intention that it consists of love and confidence, in view of its superiority even to servitude. Furthermore, that which is prescribed in the scriptures as friendship even toward the Supreme Lord—
This is not surprising, for there is scriptural authority for the injunction that even the state of being a deity may involve worshipping a deity—as in "one who is not a god should worship a god.

However, because that state is incompatible with service to Him, it is disregarded by those of pure devotion (*śuddha-bhaktas*). Friendship (*sakhya*), on the other hand, is adopted because it is most conducive to supreme service. This [friendship] consists of direct worship.

Servitude (*dāsya*) and friendship (*sakhya*) are also shown in the commentary (*ṭīkā*) in this passage: "May there be for me, in birth after birth, affection, friendship, loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and servitude toward Him alone" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.81.29).
In the words of the brāhmaṇa Śrīdāmā:
having seen the affection of Śrī Kṛṣṇa for His devotees, he prays for that same devotion— beginning with the words "tasya" (of Him).
Sauhṛda is affection; sakhyam is the desire for one's welfare; maitrī is the quality of being helpful;

and dāsya is the state of service. This is a singular compound denoting the collection of these qualities. May that [state] belong to me, who am connected with it, and not mere worldly prosperity—this is the meaning.

In this context, the surrender of karma and faith would not exist through the roles of maidservant and friend, because there is an absence of direct devotion (*sākṣād-bhakti*). For the fruit of the surrender of karma is devotion, and faith is the cause for the deepening of devotion; as in the passage beginning with "Hearing and chanting [the names] of Viṣṇu," it is stated: "Hearing of Viṣṇu... and so forth.

Regarding "kīrtanam" (proclamation): next is the self-offering (*ātma-nivedanam*). Its effects consist of being devoid of activity for one's own sake, having as one's means and goal that which is entrusted to Him, and being composed entirely of activity for His sake alone. For this indeed—
Just as one who has sold a cow does not perform the labor for the sake of maintaining that cow once it has been sold,
and the one who purchased it would indeed be the one to accomplish its welfare, and that cow would perform work for him alone and not for the one who sold it; so too is the case here.

In this regard, some consider the offering to consist solely of the surrender of the body, as it is said in the *Bhakti-viveka*: "Just as one would not worry about protecting a beast that has been sold,
so too, having surrendered the body to Hari, one should desist from its protection."
Some offer only the pure conscious self (*kṣetrajña*). As it is said in the *Śrīmad-Ālavandāru-stotra*:
"Whether I am of such a nature or otherwise, by virtue of my qualities, whatever I may be within the body and so forth..."
"Therefore, here I am, surrendered this very day by me at your lotus feet" (Stotra-ratna 49).

Here, the phrase "anyone whatsoever" refers to the various types of practitioners according to their essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*). Alternatively, it refers to them "according to their qualities (*guṇataḥ*)."

"May I be of such a kind"—that is, having the form of a god, a human, or the like—in the state of acting according to my will; this is the sense derived from the analysis *sa cāsāv ayam* ("he and he, this one"), which results in *so'yam* ("this very one"). In that regard, the mere offering of oneself is seen in the case of King Bali at the time of giving. This occurs when the dispositions (*bhāva*) are mixed.
The offering of oneself as a servant was shown toward the illustrious Ambarīṣa, and with the sentiment of a beloved wife toward the goddess Śrī Rukmiṇī;
likewise, it should be understood through friendship and other such relationships. (23–24)

Viśvanātha: [Thinking,] "Since these two—the lowest of brahmins and this [other]—possess no status as a guru, I have learned only devotion from my guru, the venerable Nārada; therefore, I shall speak of that alone," he says: "The lotus feet" (*caraṇāravindam*). "Service to the feet" (*pāda-sevana*) means attendance; "worship" (*arcana*) means ritual adoration.

Servitude (*dāsya*) is the cultivation of one's own state as a servant. Friendship (*sakhya*) is the cultivation of one's own state as a friend, characterized by firm confidence. Self-surrender (*ātma-nivedana*) is the offering of oneself and the offering of one's body;
this is accompanied by a specific emotional disposition (*bhāva*), whether it be with or without such an emotion, as was the case for Rukmiṇī and others.

The meaning is that for Vairocanī and the others, the requirement is simply "by a man" (*puṃsā*) or "by a male" (*puṃ-mātreṇa*); thus, there is no restriction regarding caste (*varṇa*), stage of life (*āśrama*), and so forth.

Since the word *pums* denotes the living being (*jīva*) in general, this applies to women as well; the sense is that if any one of these nine characteristics is performed by her, then it constitutes devotion (*bhakti*). *Addhā* means directly (*sākṣāt*).
The meaning is that it is not [offered] through the mediation of knowledge, ritual action, and so forth. And that [offering], being already offered, should be performed;

it should not be performed first and then offered later—so says Śrī-Svāmī-Caraṇa. Or else, if it is to be offered to Viṣṇu, it should be done solely for the purpose of Viṣṇu’s pleasure, and not for the sake of its own fruit.

The sense is that by dedicating [the study] to oneself, one becomes free from desire for anything else; at that time, I consider the study to be "supreme," which is to say, it constitutes supreme devotion. ||23-24||
Having heard these words of his son, Hiraṇyakaśipu then spoke thus to the preceptor’s son, his lips quivering with rage.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
O wretched Brahmin, what is this that you, being wicked, have resorted to as an adversary?
"O evil-minded one, disregarding me, you have caused this fool to grasp at what is essence-less."
Śrīdhara: That in which essence (sāra) is not found is "essence-less" (asāra); or rather, the literal meaning is that from which essence does not exist. ||26||
The *Krama-sandarbha* does not provide an explanation. Viśvanātha says: "O [Goddess], that which is called 'essence' (*sāra*) does not, in reality, exist. (26)
For there are indeed wicked people in the world, ill-disposed and appearing in deceptive guises; in due time, evil arises from them, just as disease arises from sinners.

Śrīdhara: He says, "For there are... [santi hi], to show that even for one like you who proceeds with friendship, hostility as a refuge is not impossible. Those whose friendship is wicked are "durmitras. Regarding the word "roga" (disease): [it refers to the following].
A killer of a Brahmin shall suffer from a wasting disease; a drinker of liquor shall have blackened teeth;
a stealer of gold shall have deformed nails; and one who violates the teacher's bed shall suffer from skin diseases.

The meaning is as follows: just as for those sinners mentioned in the *Smṛti* texts, disease arises at the time immediately following their experience of hell, so too for those wicked people who behave as if they were virtuous, evil such as malice and the like arises. ||27||
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: "Since you, who were on the side of the enemy, have become clearly manifest as auspicious at the end of so many days, I shall give you your appropriate fee this very day."

He says by means of an *arthāntara-nyāsa* (corroboration): "They exist," and so forth. Those whose friendship (*maitra*) is corrupted, for whom enmity (*agha*) such as hatred arises—that is, becomes manifest through fate—it is said:
"A killer of a Brahmin shall suffer from consumption; a drinker of liquor shall have black teeth."
A stealer of gold has deformed nails, and one who violates the teacher's bed has diseased skin.
The remainder of the sense is: "in such a manner as the disease of sinners arises as described in the Smṛti, so [it arises here]. ||27||
The son of the venerable guru said: "It is not composed by me, nor is it composed by another."
"O enemy of Indra, this son of yours speaks thus;
O King, this is his natural disposition.
Restrain your anger; do not ever cause us harm."
O Madhva, where is that self-conceit of mine? ||28||

Śrīdhara: "What has been composed by me" means what has been taught by me. "Do not give us (naḥ) any *kat*—that is, any contemptuous fault"—the augment *aṭ* is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*). The meaning is: "Do not attribute blame to me.
The sense is that anger toward Brāhmaṇas is not appropriate for you, O enemy of Indra. ||28||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "O enemy of Indra"—the sense is that it is not fitting for you to feel anger toward me, a wretched Brahmin. "Do not give us (*naḥ*) *kat*, i.e., contemptible fault. The augment *aṭ* is an archaic (Vedic) usage.
The meaning is: "Do not attribute faults to me. ||28||
Śrī Nārada said: Having been thus addressed by his preceptor, the demon spoke again to his son.
If this [knowledge] did not come from the mouth of a guru, how could such an inauspicious and unchaste thought have arisen in you?
Śrīdhara: [It is] produced from the mouth of the Guru, born of the Guru’s words. O wicked one! ||29||
The sequence of composition: that which has the guru alone as its mouth or door is "guru-mukhī" (one whose mouth is the guru). ||29||
Viśvanātha: O you who are not auspicious! Though she is *asatī* (unvirtuous), she is in reality *bhadrā* (auspicious); she is *satī* (virtuous) and the most excellent of all. ||29||
Śrī Prahlāda said:
My mind is not directed toward Kṛṣṇa through another, nor even by itself.
May those who follow the vows of householders encounter one another;
may they enter the darkness along with their unsubdued cattle,
chewing over and over again what has already been chewed.
Śrīdhara: Let this discussion rest, for those like you who are attached to sense objects have no qualification for this matter;

with this intention, he says: "The mind" (matiḥ). It would not be attained—not reached—from another, from oneself, or mutually from one another. Of whom? Of those whose vow is the home (gṛha-vratānām)—for whom the home itself is the religious observance.

"Saṅkalpa" refers to those whose thoughts are occupied with worldly duties. For this very reason, they enter the darkness of saṃsāra by means of their unrestrained and unquiet senses acting as the cause; therein, they are those for whom there is only the chewing over again of what has already been chewed. (30)
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: This thought directed toward Kṛṣṇa, which exists [in you], would be non-existent according to your own doctrine; furthermore, by means of an indirect expression (*vakrokti*), he implies that such a thought never arises from any source whatsoever for those like you.

Mocking [the opponent], he says: "The intellect" (*matiḥ*). From such a teacher as this, or from another, or from oneself, or mutually from one another, it would not be attained—that is, it would not be accomplished. However, according to the perspective of the subsequent text, the statement here is his own declaration: "for those who are devoid of the desire for the consecration by the dust of the Great One's feet."
This should also be understood from the verse. For whom? For those whose "vow is the home"—that is, those who are attached to the household.

He explains their very state of being "home-vowed": [they fall] into the darkness of hell by means of the senses (gobhiḥ), which are like untrained and unsubdued oxen. But surely, those devoted to the household sometimes even become inhabitants of heaven?
To this he replies: the sense is that for those who repeatedly chew what has already been chewed by themselves or others, a brothel and heaven are exactly the same. ||30||
Those of evil intent, who consider external objects to be real, do not know Viṣṇu, for they do not understand the path to their own true self-interest.
Just as the blind are led by the blind, they too are bound by the wide fetter of the Lord’s governance.

Śrīdhara: [Objection: Since Śrī-Kṛṣṇa is the very nature of supreme bliss, why should they not also be established in Him? [Reply: Because of ignorance; thus he says, "No. Those who are evil-minded, whose internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa) are permeated by sense objects, do not know Viṣṇu. The reason for this is: within themselves...
"Those for whom this very object is the goal of human endeavor (puruṣārtha)—their destination is what is to be reached.

Now, one might ask: "Will they not also come to know Viṣṇu through the instruction of a guru? To this he replies: "Those for whom the object is external things are 'external-objected' (bahir-artha); those whose nature it is to regard only such people as their gurus. Therefore, by the blind...

Just as those being led blindfolded do not know the path and instead fall into a pit, so too they are bound by desirable ritual acts upon the Lord’s loom— the long rope characterized by the Vedas— upon which there are wide bands named after the social classes, such as the Brāhmaṇas and others. Thus, they remain truly bound.
The meaning is as follows. It has been said:
"For those whose minds are absorbed in sense objects, immersion in Viṣṇu is very far away;
can one who is heading toward an object situated in the western direction reach that which belongs to the eastern? (31)

The sequence of the composition: [it is for] those for whom the goal of human life (*puruṣārtha*) consists of love (*prema*), which is the very purpose of Śrī Viṣṇu himself, directed toward Him. ||31||

Viśvanātha: But you fool! Do you even dare to subject me—whose footstool is worshipped by Indra and the other gods—to the mockery of sarcasm? Listen, you of wicked intellect, listen! Are the great scholars who were disciples of Śukrācārya and his teachers not aware of the essential purport of all the scriptures, such that...?
Thinking that you do not consider the meaning learned from them to be beneficial, he says: "No.

The meaning is that they do not know Viṣṇu, who is their own true goal in the form of the ultimate purpose; rather, they know only goals such as heaven, which are in fact non-ultimate (anartha). This is because they possess evil intentions—that is, corrupt internal organs—and seek external sensory pleasure.
Those whose nature it is to consider what is truly meaningless as meaningful—if even they do not know Viṣṇu, how then could his disciples know him?
He states this with an illustration: "Just as blind men, led by others along a path pointed out to them, [fall into a pit]."

The meaning is that they fall into a pit in exactly the same way; for even though they are bound by their actions to that string characterized by the Vedas—a long rope upon which the thighs are the cords bearing the names of the Brāhmaṇas and the other castes—they remain so bound. ||31||
The intellect of these people does not touch the foot of the Wide-Striding One until the removal of that misfortune for which they long.
As long as one does not choose the consecration by the dust of the feet of the Great Ones, being free from all possessions.

Śrīdhara: Now, one might ask: "How is it that they do not know Viṣṇu, who is established by such Vedic texts as 'The one God, hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner Self of all beings' (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.11)? Or from what cause does their entry into darkness arise? To this he says: "Not of these... and so forth.

Until one receives the consecration by the dust of the feet of those great souls who possess nothing and have cast off pride for sense objects, their intellect— though born from the words of the Vedas— does not touch, nor reach, the foot of the Wide-striding Lord (Urukrama). The meaning is that it is obstructed by doubts such as impossibility (*asambhāvanā*) and the like.

The removal of the meaningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) is the purpose and objective of that intellect which touches [Your] feet. The meaning is that, due to the absence of Your great favor, they possess neither certainty regarding reality nor liberation. ||32||

Sanātana [Ha.bha.vi. 10.191]: Until one chooses the sprinkling of the dust from the feet of those who possess nothing, who have cast off pride regarding sense objects, who have renounced all possessions out of love for the Lord, and who are therefore most exalted; until one worships them with love, so long...

Even though [the truth] has been known through the words of the Śruti and other means, the intellect of these evil-minded ones does not touch, nor reach, the feet of the Lord, the Blessed Śrī Kṛṣṇa of wide strides; the meaning is that it is obstructed by doubts regarding the impossibility [of such a thing] and so forth.
[This refers to] the intellect that touches His feet, from which there is the removal of the misfortune of saṃsāra.

The word *artha* means purpose. The meaning is that because they lack great favor, there is neither certainty regarding reality nor liberation for them. Alternatively, it refers to that which appears as a purpose (*artha*) when it is actually a non-purpose (*anartha*), and which is revealed as being of the nature of a non-purpose through inquiry. Or else, it refers to that from which no purpose exists in the Vedānta and other such texts.
The purpose of bathing in the dust of his feet is the departure from liberation itself;

for without the special grace of a devotee of the Blessed One, there is no cessation of the desire for liberation, and without that, there is not even the touching of the lotus-feet of the Blessed One by the mind. ||32||
The sequence of composition: the removal of misfortune and the obstacles that touch upon it. ||32||

Viśvanātha: Now, if it is the case that the scriptures declare Viṣṇu alone to be the goal in His own essential form, then the understanding of those who are your gurus—being knowers of all the scriptures—should necessarily arise as being fixed upon Viṣṇu.
Therefore, precisely because they lack such an understanding fixed upon Viṣṇu, it is inferred that their devotion to Viṣṇu is unscriptural.
Therefore, he says "naiṣām" (not of these). For those who possess nothing, who have renounced ritual actions for my sake,
and who have abandoned their own kinsmen and relatives— based on faith in such words of the Blessed One,
they have renounced worldly wealth, the desire for sons and wife, ritual action, knowledge, and so forth.

Until one chooses the consecration of oneself as a Vaiṣṇava through the dust of the feet of the Great Ones— which is the sole latent impression of pure devotion— one’s mind does not touch the foot of the Wide-Striding Lord (Urukrama).
"For one who has supreme devotion for God, and for the teacher as for God,
these truths thus taught shine forth to that high-souled one" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.23).
"He alone whom He chooses, by him is He attained."
"His very Self reveals His own form" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.23), and so forth, according to such scriptural passages.

The removal of the misfortune of *saṃsāra* is the incidental (*ānuṣaṅgika*) fruit for one whose purpose and aim is the intellect that touches Your feet; however, the primary goal is precisely that touch of the feet of the Lord of the Three Steps.
Having spoken thus, Hiraṇyakaśipu, his mind blinded by rage, cast his son who had ceased speaking from his own lap onto the surface of the earth.
Śrīdhara: "Nirasyata" means he threw. ||33||
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
Overcome with indignation and anger, his eyes became bloodshot.
"Let this one who deserves to be killed be killed immediately; drive him away, O followers of Nirṛti!"

Śrīdhara: "Amarṣa" means intolerance; he was possessed by—that is, pervaded by—anger accompanied by that [intolerance]. His eyes had become "kaṣāyī-bhūte," meaning bloodshot or copper-colored. O Nairṛtas, O Rākṣasas! ||34||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: *Amarṣa* is intolerance. He was possessed by anger accompanied by that [intolerance]. O *nairṛtas*, O Rākṣasas! ||34||
"—O! This is the killer of my brother; this lowest of men has abandoned his own kinsmen and friends, he who worships the feet of Viṣṇu, the slayer of his paternal uncle, like a servant."

Śrīdhara: The reason for his being put to death is that he is the killer of my brother. Why? Because he worships the feet of Viṣṇu like a servant; the meaning is that he is a partisan of Him. Therefore, the syntactical connection is: "This very person is he.
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "This is the slayer of my brother. [Objection: But it is well known that Viṣṇu is the slayer of your brother;
to this he replies—the meaning is that this very person is that Viṣṇu. Why? Because of the words beginning with "having abandoned," etc., and because he acts like a servant.

The meaning is that even though he has become the son of the great Asura king, let him be slain on the grounds that "this one is indeed Viṣṇu," because Viṣṇu bestows his own form upon his servants. ||35||
Or rather, what indeed will this ill-behaved son of Viṣṇu do?
For he was only five years old when he abandoned the affection for his parents that is so difficult to cast off.
Śrīdhara: Aho! He says "Or even Viṣṇu" (viṣṇor vā) to explain why even Viṣṇu accepted that which is not to be accepted by anyone else—he abandoned it on the day [of his birth] (ahāj jahau). ||36||
The sequence of arrangement: "five years old," because of having remained in the womb for a long time. ||36||
Viśvanātha: Even Viṣṇu is untrustworthy; how then, having become wise, could one trust him? To this he says: "Or even from Viṣṇu" (verse 36).
Even a stranger's child is beneficial like medicine,
whereas a son born of one's own body may be harmful like a disease.
One should cut off that limb which is harmful to oneself;
by its removal, the remainder lives happily.

Śrīdhara: [Objection: But how can this child of yours be killed? To this he replies: If even a stranger is beneficial like medicine, then he should be known as one's own child; if one's own son, though born from one's own body, is harmful, he should be known as a disease. Let alone the talk of that which is the object of one's affection, even a limb—if it is harmful, it must be cut off.
The meaning is that even hands, feet, and so forth, if they are harmful to oneself, one should certainly cut them off. ||37||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: Now, one might ask, "How can we kill this child who is your own offspring? To this he says: "Even an enemy, if he acts for one's benefit like medicine, should be regarded as if he were not an enemy; let it be so."
The meaning is that even those limbs such as the hands and feet, which are parts of the object of "mine-ness," should indeed be cut off if they are harmful to oneself. ||37||
By all means, he must be destroyed through shared meals, beds,
and seats; for an enemy wearing the guise of a friend is like the wicked sense-faculty of a sage.
Śrīdhara: Therefore, he must be destroyed by all possible means. "Sambhoja" means eating;
the meaning is by the employment of poison and other such things during meals and similar occasions. Just as a corrupted sense-organ is an enemy to a sage. (38)
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: He says "by all" (sarvaiḥ) [in verse 38], meaning that one should be killed even by the administration of poison and the like to objects such as food.
Those Nairṛtas were indeed commanded by their lord; they held tridents in their hands,
possessed fierce fangs and terrifying mouths, and had copper-colored beards and hair.
Uttering a terrifying roar and crying out, "Cut!
Pierce!", they struck Prahlāda, who was seated, with spears in all his vital parts.
Śrīdhara: Those whose fangs are *tigma*, meaning sharp; and those whose mouths (*karāla*)—that is, faces—are terrifying; and those whose beards and hair are copper-colored. (39)
The sequence of composition: "nairṛtā" constitutes a couplet; "daṃṣṭrā" occurs in some [manuscripts], but it is not approved by the Master (Svāmī). ||39||
Viśvanātha: This has not been explained. —o)0(o— In the supreme Brahman, the indescribable Lord, the self of all;
They were fruitless for one whose mind was disciplined, just as acts of hospitality are for one who lacks merit.

Śrīdhara: In that Prahlāda, whose mind was joined with and concentrated upon the Supreme Lord, the blows of those demons—the Nairṛtas and others—became fruitless. The reasons for this are: because the Blessed One is the Brahman, changeless, indefinable, beyond the reach of the senses, possessed of unsurpassed sovereignty, and the Self of all.

Even weapons and the like act as mere instruments when directed by such a Supreme Being; for one who lacks merit and is devoid of destiny, even good deeds and great efforts are as futile as [the actions of] one without a divine guide. //41//
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "In him whose body (ātman) was joined (*yukta*) with the Blessed Lord Hari," because of what was stated previously, such as [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.4.38]: "embraced by Govinda. By his father, on his own lap...

The sense is: "as if toward a son kept in secret. Now, one might ask: were there not instances where weapons were averted from the limbs of the Blessed One? Indeed, no; for that is impossible. Thus he says: "In the Supreme," and so forth. [This refers to] the Blessed One who is Brahman—the all-pervading, changeless, indefinable, and whose sovereignty is beyond the reach of logic.

The sense is: how could a blow from a weapon possibly occur against the Self of all, who is the controller even of weapons and the like? [It refers to] one who is devoid of merit, i.e., unfortunate. ||41||
When that effort had been frustrated, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the lord of the Daityas became apprehensive and,
with persistence, devised means for his destruction.
It has not been explained by anyone at all—
not even by the world-elephants, the lords of serpents, or those who perform sorcery and cause downfalls.
By means of illusions, suppressions, the administration of poison, and starvation;

Śrīdhara: By *daṇḍaśūkas*—venomous serpents; by *abhicāras*—such as *kṛtyās* and the like; by *avapātanāni*—being cast down from mountain peaks and similar heights; by *māyās*—those created by Śambara—and by confinements in pits and the like. ||43||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: By means of malevolent rites (*abhicāra*) such as *kṛtyā* and the like; by means of precipitations (*avapātana*), that is, causing one to fall from a very high place; and by means of confinements in pits and the like—the plural number indicates the repetition of these malevolent rites and so forth.
They were indicated. The meaning is that he did not succeed, did not attain, and was unable to carry out that killing—
even by means of snow, wind, fire, water, or the assault of mountains.
When the Asura was unable to kill his sinless son,
he fell into deep anxiety and could find no way to accomplish his purpose.

Śrīdhara: By "mountain-attacks" he means the hurling of mountains upon him; by the plural number, he indicates the repetition of such acts as malevolent incantations (*abhicāra*). He was not able—that is, he did not succeed—to effect that destruction;
the meaning is that he was not capable of it. ||44||
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: By means of *abhicāra* (malevolent rites) such as *kṛtyā* and the like; by *avapātana*, which means causing one to fall from a very high place; and by *gartādi-saṃnirōdha*, meaning confinement in pits and so forth—the plural number indicates the repetition of these malevolent rites and other methods.
They were indicated. He did not succeed—that is, he did not attain or was unable—to carry out that killing.
Much that is improper has been said by me, and means for his slaughter have been devised."
He was liberated from those various injuries and unrighteous acts by his own splendor alone.

Śrīdhara says: He expresses his very anxiety with three verses beginning with "eṣa. "By me" (me) means by myself; "asādhu" means harshly, as it happened; [I was addressed] by means of unrighteous acts, injuries, or malevolent spells (abhicāra). ||45||
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: He describes his anxiety with three verses beginning with "eṣa" (this one). [He says it] by means of the practices of the wicked and their malevolent rites.
Even though he is currently not far away and is but a child,
this one of unclouded intellect does not forget my ignoble conduct, just as the lord Śunaḥśepa did not.

Śrīdhara: Even though he is standing nearby, not far away, this boy—though possessed of an unclouded intellect and a fearless mind—does not forget my ignoble, unjust, or hostile conduct. Śunaḥśepa, the middle son of Ajīgarta, having been sold by his parents to Hariścandra...

Just as he, not forgetting the injury done by those two, relied upon Viśvāmitra—their adversary—and thereby entered another lineage; or rather, this is an illustration regarding the non-abandonment of one's own nature: "like Śunaḥśepa’s tail. ||46||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Even though he remains close at hand, he does not forget my ignoble enemy, Viṣṇu.
An illustration for the non-abandonment of one's inherent nature: like the tail of Śunaḥśepha; however, in reality...

Just as Śunaḥśepha, the middle son of Ajīgarta, who was sold by his parents to Hariścandra, did not forget the harm done to them and, having taken refuge with their adversary Viśvāmitra, entered another lineage— so it is here. ||46||
This [being] possesses immeasurable majesty, is fearless, and is immortal;
surely, through conflict with this, my death will come, or perhaps not.

Śrīdhara: He whose power (*anubhāva*) is immeasurable and unfathomable; he who has no fear from any quarter; and he who is immortal, being devoid of death. "Nor shall he come to be otherwise" means that death will never occur for him at all. ||47||
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— Thus, with his mind fixed on that [thought], his splendor somewhat faded and his face cast downwards...
Śaṇḍa and Marka, the sons of Uśanas, said, "It is secluded."
Śrīdhara: The two sons of Uśanas are experts in political ethics (*nīti*). "In a secluded place" means in a private, solitary spot. ||48||
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
By you alone, with a single movement of the eyebrows, the three worlds have been conquered.
O Lord, we do not consider the matter of his [the child's] merit or fault; indeed, for children, there is no footing for either virtue or vice, as all the celestial abodes are terrified by his yawn.

Śrīdhara: We do not perceive—that is, we do not see—anything to be reflected upon in you, by whom all the world-protectors and guardians of the quarters are terrified merely by the expansion of your eyebrows. There is no foothold, that is, no basis [for judgment]. Or rather, the conduct of children is not a matter—that is, it does not fall within the scope—of virtues or faults.
The meaning. ||49||

The Sequence of Events: For children, there exists no locus or basis for virtues and faults; that upon which those two would depend does not exist for them, due to their lack of discrimination between the essential and the non-essential. (49)

Viśvanātha: "There is nothing for us to think upon" means that we see nothing whatsoever to be contemplated because of the failure to obtain the object of your own desire. If [it is argued], "This son of mine possesses a nature contrary to my own," he says "no"—referring to the conduct (pada) or resolve of children.

"Between merits and faults, we do not see anything at all; the sense is that once you have reached maturity of intellect, we shall know their auspiciousness or inauspiciousness. The word "vai" has the sense of "and. The verb "cakṣvahe" (we two look) is to be construed with both [merits and faults]. ||49||
But having bound him with the nooses of Varuṇa, place him here so that, being terrified, he does not flee.
And the intellect of a person [matures] through age and service to the teacher until the Guru Bhārgava arrives.

Śrīdhara: Nevertheless, they said, "Binding him is appropriate," [expressing this with the words] "imaṃ tu" (but him). "Bind him and keep him here until the great Bhārgava arrives. Then what did they say after that?
Because a man's intellect becomes excellent through age as well as through service to noble persons. (50)
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "Let it be; what shall I do now? To this, they both replied: "But this... because the intellect of a mere human being is such [only] when beyond childhood by age, as is the case with a teacher.
And by means of service. Who is the preceptor? Or when is he to be served? To this he says: "As long as" (yāvat) means "at whatever time.
The meaning is that Śakra himself, the descendant of Bhṛgu, is the preceptor. ||50||

" Saying "So be it," and having granted permission to the words spoken by the preceptor's son, he said this: "For that dharma which belongs to kings who are householders must indeed be taught to him."
Śrīdhara: Having granted permission, that is, having accepted by saying "so be it. ||51||
The sequence of application: first for householders, and among them, for kings. ||51||
Viśvanātha: Having granted permission, that is, having accepted [it]. ||51||
O King, he spoke of dharma, artha, and kāma, both thoroughly and in due order, to Prahlāda, who was humble and bowed in reverence.
Śrīdhara: Thereupon, the two of them spoke of dharma and other matters to Prahlāda; and he, being humble and bowing low, [listened] to him.
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
Just as the three aims of life (*trivarga*) were taught to himself by his teachers...
He did not consider that instruction to be good, as it was described as delighting in dualities.

Śrīdhara: He did not consider even that which had been properly taught as the three-fold aim (trivarga) to be truly sound, nor did he value that instruction itself. Why? Because it was described by those for whom there is "duality"—that is, those who take delight in sense objects through passion, aversion, and the like. ||53||
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: He did not consider even that instruction to be good, though it was correctly taught, because it was described solely in terms of worldly life, which delights in pairs of opposites (dvandva), and not [in terms of liberation].
In the ultimate sense, they are one. ||53||
When the teacher had turned away from his domestic duties,
he was invited there by his friends and young companions who were seeking diversion.

Śrīdhara: "Parāvṛttaḥ" means having gone elsewhere. "Sa upahūtaḥ" (he was invited). The *sandhi* (euphonic junction) is for the purpose of filling the meter. Or, it means by those who have made an occasion for play—that is, by those who have celebrated a festival or obtained leisure. ||54||
The sequence of composition: "When" (yadā) [is used], then [the correlative] "then" (tadā) is employed there. ||54||

Viśvanātha: Having turned away from his place of teaching, Viśvanātha returned to his own home and engaged in his worldly duties. At that time, Prahlāda was with those who had made their leisure for play—that is, who were celebrating a festival—or rather, with those who had seized the opportunity under the pretext that this was a time of quietude for the purpose of instruction in devotion. (54)
Then, having summoned them with gentle words, the great sage,
the learned one, spoke to those devoted to that [path] out of compassion, as if smiling.
Śrīdhara: "Knowing their steadfastness"—knowing their steadfastness characterized by birth, death, and so forth.
[This] has not been explained in the *Krama-sandarbha*. Viśvanātha: "Knowing their steadfastness toward himself as their guru"—meaning, being aware of it.
As if laughing, and smiling as he thought, "Ah, even these have been caught in the net of the Blessed One’s compassion"—
they all, out of respect for him, abandoned their playthings and equipment.
The foolish, whose intellects are unrefined, are driven by the impulses of passion stirred up by the pairs of opposites.
Śrīdhara: Those whose intellects are not defiled by the words and deeds of those who delight in dualities—because they are like children. (56)
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Those by whom the heart and the gaze were fixed upon that very [object]. (56)
O King of kings, they waited upon him with their hearts and eyes fixed upon him;
then that compassionate and benevolent Asura, a great devotee of the Lord, spoke to them.
It has not been explained by anyone at all. Thus ends [the section] from the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose minds are devoted.
The fifth chapter of the seventh [book], which is well-connected with the virtuous, is concluded.
Thus, in the glorious Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the commentary on the Brahma-sūtras,
in the Vaiyāsikī collection belonging to the Pāramahaṃsyā Saṃhitā, in the seventh book, in the narrative of Prahlāda.
The Fifth Chapter.
The Sixth Chapter: In the Narrative of Prahlāda,
Śrī Prahlāda said:
In this world, a wise person should practice the Bhāgavata duties from childhood;
for human birth is difficult to obtain, and even that is transient and does not grant its purpose [without effort].
Śrīdhara: When Jupiter was in the sixth house from the ascendant, Prahlāda, out of compassion for the sons of the Daityas, instructed them in the supreme reality as taught by Nārada.
To those who do not perceive the wasting away of their lifespan through meaningless actions and idle talk,
the virtuous Prahlāda always spoke this Bhāgavata Dharma.

By the words "in childhood," and so forth: one should practice the dharmas in this very human birth, because it bestows wealth [of merit]. And therein, one should do so while still in childhood, because even that [human birth] is impermanent. Nor is there another such birth, because it is difficult to obtain. Therefore, one should practice only the dharmas therein, not for the sake of pleasure.
One should perform efforts toward those alone who are devoted to the Lord (bhāgavatas), and not toward those who act out of desire for rewards. ||1||
The sequential arrangement: One should practice the duties of a devotee (*bhāgavata-dharma*), because this birth yields its fruit;
for in births such as those of the gods, there is an immersion in great sense objects, and in births such as those of animals, there is an absence of discrimination.
Furthermore, one should not delay even in that [human birth], as it says: "In childhood" (*kaumāre*), meaning starting from childhood. For even that [childhood]...

Birth is certain, yet it is difficult to obtain again. And so it is said in the Brahma-vaivarta: "Even having attained the human state—which is most difficult to reach and desired even by the gods—those who have not taken refuge in Govinda have long deceived their own selves."
Having wandered through eighty-four hundred thousand births among living beings,
human birth is attained by men only through the turning of the wheel of time;
yet even that has become fruitless for those who are conceited about their own selves.
"Unless the wretched rely upon the two feet of Govinda.

Thus, because this scripture is primarily concerned with and directed toward human beings, it should be understood that this statement is made by referring to them, having superposed the status of "humanity" upon them through the commonality of their intellect and other faculties. ||1||
Viśvanātha:
In the sixth [chapter], Prahlāda caused the child to grasp devotion;
enlightening him, he caused his attachment to the body, home, and so forth to vanish.

Regarding those [people], it was previously stated that he is compassionate and friendly. What, then, does he say? He says: "One should practice the duties in youth. Now, is it not the case that there is no eligibility for the duties of the social classes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*) during youth?
To this he replies: "The *bhāgavata* duties, such as the chanting (*kīrtana*) of the lotus feet [of the Lord], [should be practiced] here on the land of Bhārata."
"Is it not the case that one achieves one's purpose even by performing [the rites] during youth and so forth? To this he says: "The wise man.

If death were to occur at the very end of childhood, what then? The one possessed of superior knowledge indeed has no concern there; however, since another birth will occur, devotion should be practiced precisely for that [future state].
To this he says: Human birth is difficult to obtain; even when obtained through good fortune, it is impermanent, for there is no certainty that it will remain even until tomorrow.
Now, one might ask: how can perfection in devotion be achieved in such a short time? To this he says: "It bestows the goal."
For even those such as Khaṭvāṅga and others, though they possess devotion, are seen to attain accomplishment [only] after it has lasted for a mere moment. ||1||
— for just as a man here approaches the feet of Viṣṇu,
so too does he [approach] this beloved Self, the Lord, and the Friend of all beings.

Śrīdhara: Here, he establishes that one should practice only the duties of a Bhāgavata with the four verses beginning with "yathā hi. The meaning is that, in this world, approaching the feet of Viṣṇu alone is appropriate and fitting for a person; for [it is said], "because He is dear," and so forth. (2)

The Structural Arrangement (*krama-sandarbha*): Therein, he demonstrates the propriety of practicing the *bhāgavata-dharma* alone, beginning with the words "Just as" (*yathā hi*). Since this very nature of beings is dear—that is, the object of love and the agent of love—for that reason, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is [the goal] when approaching at His feet.
And for another reason: because this Lord is capable of acting, not acting, or acting otherwise;
and because He is a friend who desires to bring about the welfare of all. ||2||
Viśvanātha: In response to the inquiry, "In what manner should one practice the duties of a Bhāgavata?
he says: "In whatever way (yathā) the attainment of proximity to the feet of Viṣṇu may occur, in that same manner one should practice"—this is the ellipsis. That very manner is fourfold.

Manifesting Viṣṇu, he distinguishes Him by the words "since He is dear," and so forth. Therefore, by the authority of the Lord's own statement: "For those to whom I am the dear Self, the son, the friend, the teacher, the well-wisher, and the chosen deity" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.25.38).

"Among the states of the beloved (*kāntā*), peace (*śānti*), delight (*rati*), servitude (*dāsya*), and friendship (*sakhya*), by whichever state one desires to approach [the Lord], by that very state one should approach Him and practice the duties of the devotees (*bhāgavata-dharma*).
Thus, even in the case of *rāga-bhakti* (spontaneous devotion), an injunction is implied. Furthermore, because he is equal to oneself, [the Lord] is like a son (*suta*).
Or rather, it may be that the five states mentioned in the Tantra were taught by Prahlāda. ||2||
O Daityas, sensual pleasure for embodied beings is obtained everywhere through the connection with a body by the power of destiny, just as suffering is obtained effortlessly.
Śrīdhara: If it is asked, "How indeed can the effort for enjoyment be abandoned? he says in response: "Happiness," etc.
"Everywhere" means even among animals and the like. "By destiny" means solely by prior unseen karma (adṛṣṭa). ||3||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He says "pleasure" (*sukham*) to show that once one has obtained a human body, effort for the sake of enjoying pleasure should not be undertaken; by the phrase "through connection with the body" (*deha-yogena*), he means that pleasure and pain are indeed attributes of the body alone.
The meaning: everywhere, even in the case of animals and so forth. ||3||
One should not exert effort in that [worldly pursuit], for it results only in the depletion of one's lifespan;
one does not find such security as that found at the lotus feet of Mukunda.

Śrīdhara: Therefore, one should not exert effort for that purpose, because beyond such effort there is merely the waste of one's lifespan; since it is so, one does not attain security (*kṣema*) in that manner—the sequence of the text being that security consists of the lotus-form feet of Mukunda. (4)
Viśvanātha: In that manner, he does not find security (*kṣema*). He explains what security truly is: "Mukunda," etc. (verse 4).
Therefore, relying on existence, the wise person should strive for security as long as his human body remains fully intact and does not perish.

Śrīdhara: Having resorted to fear, one has entered into saṃsāra; as long as this human form of body remains intact—meaning it does not fail, does not become incapacitated, or does not perish—one should strive for one's own welfare with all speed. ||5||

*Krama-sandarbha*: "The form of the Person" (*puruṣa-rūpam*)—thus says Svāmī; "the state of being a person" (*pauruṣam*)—this is the statement regarding the relationship, according to Viśvanātha. "Having resorted to fear"—meaning in the absence of worshiping Hari; "fallen from their station, they fall downward" (*bhā.pu.* 11.5.3)—having heard this fear, there is the injunction regarding scriptural devotion (*vaidha-bhakti*).
It has been stated [that the body is] "abundant" (puṣkala), meaning it is robust due to the absence of old age, disease, and so forth, and capable of exertion, and so on. ||5||
The lifespan of a man is indeed a hundred years; half of that belongs to one who has not conquered himself,
for during that [half] he sleeps at night, fallen into blind darkness.

Śrīdhara: He describes the sequence of the expenditure of lifespan with three verses beginning with "puṃsaḥ" (of the person). As for the phrase "yad yasmāt śete," the sequence of its composition has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: He describes the sequence of the expenditure of lifespan with [the verse] beginning with "puṃsaḥ. ||6||
Twenty years pass for the innocent one playing in childhood and youth;
twenty years pass for the helpless one whose body is seized by old age.
Śrīdhara: Twenty years pass away as his lifespan. ||7||
Regarding the sequence of arrangement: in some places, the term *kaumāra* (childhood) appears as *kaiśora* (youth). (7)
Viśvanātha: "He plays" means with boys and girls. ||7||
Indeed,
for one who is attached to household life and is heedless, life passes away due to insatiable desire and powerful delusion.
Śrīdhara: By those difficult to fill—that is, by sufferings that completely overwhelm one from all sides. ||8||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: "The remainder" refers to the life that remains. ||8||
Who, being a man with uncontrolled senses, could venture to liberate himself when he is bound by the firm fetters of affection and attached to his home?

Śrīdhara: Now, anticipating the objection that even one attached to household life in youth might later become detached and attain security, he demonstrates the impossibility of that and establishes the principle "one should practice while still a youth" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.6.1) with the seven verses beginning with "Who [would remain] in houses? (9).
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Regarding the statement "one should worship Kṛṣṇa here and there," he says "Who? to indicate that even for those possessing discernment (*viveka*), there may be an inability to practice due to various obstacles. Therefore, one should begin the worship from childhood itself.
The sense is that devotion is perfected only when one is attached to the object of worship itself and does not become distracted elsewhere;
it is not otherwise. ||9||
Who indeed would renounce that thirst for wealth which is more desired than life itself— the wealth for which a thief, a servant, or a merchant sells even their most beloved vital breaths?
Śrīdhara: Who indeed would relinquish their thirst for that object which a thief or the like acquires by purchasing it with their life-breaths, even at the cost of sacrificing their own lives? (10)
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: He demonstrates the predominance of attachment to wealth with the words "Who indeed... That object which he says is dearer than even one's life-breaths—that object for which one buys at the cost of one's life-breaths, even to the point of losing those very breaths.
Having accepted [the task], the thief enters the houses of the wealthy at night for the sake of wealth;
the royal servant advances toward the front of battle; and the merchant goes to difficult places such as the ocean. ||10||
How [could one describe] the secret union with a beloved woman who is compassionate, as well as her beautiful incantations?
Attached by affection to his friends, his heart was devoted to the lisping words of children.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, "how? and so forth. The connection with the third verse is: "How could one abandon the company and other associations of his beloved? *Mantrān* refers to beneficial instructions and conversations; *saṅgam* refers to association with friends; *sitaḥ* means bound by their affection; and [the phrase *kalākṣarāṇām*] refers to those whose syllables are beautiful and sweet.
One whose mind is attached to those [objects] is "possessed of attachment. ||11||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He demonstrates the intensity of attachment to wife, children, and so forth—with the words "How? The connection with the third verse is: "How could one abandon [them] while remembering the company and other associations of one's beloved? [He abandons] the mantras.
Beneficial instructions and conversations; white [robes]; bound [to discipline]; and association with children. ||11||
Remembering their sons, their beloved daughters,
their brothers, sisters, and their wretched parents.
He gave them houses with delightful and abundant furnishings,
hereditary livelihoods, and flocks of cattle and groups of servants.

Śrīdhara: They were staying in their father-in-law’s house. "Heart-pleasing" means those that are agreeable to the heart. "Houses" refers to those whose furnishings (paricchada) are vast and pleasing to the mind. "Livelihoods" (vṛtti) means means of subsistence. "Kulyāḥ" means those inherited through the lineage of the family. ||12||

Krama-sandarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: Those [women], staying in their father-in-law’s house, [adopted] heart-stealing (hṛdayāḥ) modes of livelihood (vṛttīḥ)—that is, means of subsistence (jīvikāḥ)—which were hereditary (kulyāḥ), having been obtained through family lineage. ||12||
One who desires [worldly gain] and whose desire remains unsatiated should abandon actions out of greed, just as a weaver abandons his work when seeking profit.
How could one whose delusion is difficult to overcome become dispassionate, while highly esteeming the pleasures of touch and taste?

Śrīdhara: The "treasury-maker" (kośakṛt) is a silkworm. Just as it, while constructing a dwelling for its own benefit, does not leave even an opening for its exit, so too is one who exerts himself in ritual actions. Now, one might object: even if one's desires are unsatisfied, could one not abandon worldly life through detachment born from seeing its defects? To this he says: *aupasthyam*.
One who esteems the pleasure of youth and the tongue, regarding that alone as superior—how could he whose delusion is thus endless become dispassionate? How could he be free from attachment? (13)
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: A "treasury-maker" (*kośa-kṛt*) is a "cocoon-worm" (*kośa-kīṭa*). Just as it dies while building its dwelling without leaving an exit for itself, so too does one who exerts oneself in ritual action [die], [neglecting] the generative organ (*aupasthya*).
Pleasant, delicious, and very sweet. ||13||
The heedless man, bestowing his own life for the sake of maintaining his family, does not perceive that his purpose has been destroyed.
One whose self is afflicted by the three types of suffering everywhere becomes disenchanted,
but not one who delights in his own family.

Śrīdhara: Demonstrating the nature of insurmountable delusion (*duranta-moha*), he says: One does not realize that one's own life is being exhausted while striving to maintain a family, nor that one’s human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) has been thwarted. For this very reason, although the mind is afflicted by the threefold suffering (*tāpa-traya*), one does not become disenchanted; therein, one does not perceive it as suffering.
He acts because Rāma’s delight is centered upon his own family. ||14||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: The meaning is that [the world] does not perceive its own life-span being diminished nor its human purpose being destroyed;
yet it certainly perceives even the loss of a mere pill. That too...
Therefore, it is not found. ||14||
One whose mind is constantly attached to riches,
even if he be a learned man, knows the fault of one who steals the wealth of another.
Whether in this world or after death, the householder whose senses are unsubdued and whose desires are unappeased carries away [the merit].

Śrīdhara: On the contrary, he says that one actually commits theft in the verse beginning with "In wealth" (*vitteṣu*). One whose mind is constantly obsessed with wealth is a stealer of another's property; although he knows the evil consequences—namely, hell after death and punishment in this world—he nevertheless possesses unappeased desire for it.
He indeed seizes the wealth of others. ||15||
Kramasandarbha: Not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: Although he knows the fault—consisting of hell hereafter and the form of royal punishment in this world—he nevertheless seizes those various riches. ||15||
O Danujas, even a learned man who nourishes his family in this manner is certainly not fit for his own world.
He who perceives a distinction between his own self and others falls into darkness, just like one who is utterly deluded.

Śrīdhara: Thus, this has been established by the seven verses beginning with "What man indeed [would remain] in houses? (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.6.9). He concludes that for one who is attached to houses and the like, detachment and so forth are impossible, with the word "vidvān" (the wise one): he is not fit for the self-reflection required for his own world; rather, [he is fit for something else].

Just as one who is deluded, even so the learned man falls into an attachment to darkness. The reason for this is stated: "He who..."—one whose disposition (*bhāva*) or mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is divided by such thoughts as "this is mine" and "this belongs to another. (16)

*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: Even though he is learned (*vidvān*), that is, even though he knows the scriptures, [he acts] "for his own world," meaning to look at himself [with the thought], "Who am I? What shall I do? He is exactly like one who is utterly deluded. O sons of Danu! (16)
for no one, anywhere, or at any time,
is truly able to help their own self when it is distressed.
For those who look with desire, he is a deer for the sport of dwelling; that which binds him is his renunciation.

Śrīdhara: Therefore, he concludes with a supporting reason that one should practice the *bhāgavata* duties while still in the state of youth, beginning with the words "since" (*yataḥ*). Since no one at all is capable of liberating their own self, the connection with the subsequent verse is: "therefore, go for refuge to Nārāyaṇa. This refers to the incapacity [to act independently].

The reason is: he is wretched and lecherous; therefore, he is a "sporting deer" (*krīḍā-mṛga*) for the sake of the sporting or play of those women in whose sight desire resides. In the alternative reading where *vihāra* is read separately, the meaning is that he is the means for their sporting, namely himself; thus the syntactical connection is: "since he is their sporting deer. Furthermore, that which [is found] in them...
The *visarga* (the final letter) is like a chain; it takes the form of sons, grandsons, and so forth, acting as a fetter. ||17||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Because even someone who is capable—possessing the capacity for scriptural knowledge and the like—cannot liberate himself or his own family from any place or at any time whatsoever.

It is not possible; [the word] *vihāram*—in the reading where it stands alone—is an adjective for *ātmānam*, while in the compound reading it is an adjective for the agent (*kartṛ*). May there be such a birth (*sarga*) wherein the very sight of desire is itself a fetter. ||17||
Then, having avoided from afar the association with Daityas who are devoted to sense-objects, the Daityas [departed].
He approaches Nārāyaṇa, the primordial God; impelled by those freed from attachment, he attains liberation.
Śrīdhara: Having avoided association from afar—that is, from a great distance—or rather, having approached Nārāyaṇa quickly from not far away; for He alone is desired as liberation (apavarga). ||18||
The *Krama-sandarbha*: not explained.

The *Prīti-sandarbha* 5: Now, he states that the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of the Blessed Lord is liberation (*mukti*), beginning with the words "Then from afar" (*tato vidūrāt*). And the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says: "Because that alone is desired as liberation"—this is the point here.

The state of liberation (apavarga) belonging to Nārāyaṇa culminates precisely in the direct realization of Him; for that [realization] alone consists in the attainment of supreme bliss preceded by the destruction of saṃsāra, whereas in the mere existence of Him [without such realization], that [state of liberation] is absent. ||18||
Viśvanātha: Apavarga is that which releases one from the bondage of saṃsāra; it is sought after and desired. ||18||
O sons of the asuras, there is indeed no great effort for one who pleases Acyuta,
because he is the self of all beings and is established everywhere here.
Śrīdhara: Now, if it is argued that such worship is impossible for us who are children, he says "no" (na hi) in response. "Great effort" (bahv-āyāsaḥ) means excessive exertion. ||19||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: For one who pleases [the Lord] through service, there is no great exertion required to please Him, just as in the case of one pleasing a family; nor is there any fatigue in seeking Him, for He is within the heart like one's own self.

Because [the Lord] is present, there is no exertion even in pleasing Him; for by every means and in every way, including mental services, the act of pleasing Him is already accomplished. Likewise, even by the mere resolve "May I please Acyuta," His pleasure is achieved.
For perfection is attained by even any one among the acts such as chanting the praises of the lotus-feet. ||19||
Among beings high and low, from Brahmā down to the stationary [plants] and so forth;
among elemental transformations, and likewise among the gross elements themselves.

Śrīdhara explains the two reasons—"because of being the Self" and "because of being established everywhere"—with the four verses beginning with *parāvareṣu*. [The phrase] "in those beings" refers to living entities, from the immobile [plants] up to Brahmā; "in material things" refers to non-living objects such as jars and the like; and also "in the great ones."
In the elements, beginning with space. ||20||
The sequence of composition: with the four verses beginning with "parāvareṣu," he establishes that very nature [of the Lord] as previously described. ||20||

Viśvanātha: Not only is He to be served while residing within one's own heart, but rather, because He resides everywhere, He is to be satisfied with universal respect; to teach this, he describes His pure and eternal existence through two verses beginning with "parāvareṣu."

Among beings and living entities, both superior and inferior—those for whom Brahmā is the highest and stationary objects are the lowest—and among material non-living things such as jars, and among the great elements such as space. ||20||
in the qualities, in the equilibrium of the qualities, and likewise in the transformation of the qualities,
there is indeed only one supreme Self, the Lord, the Blessed One, the Imperishable.

Śrīdhara: [The term "Prakṛti" refers] to Pradhāna when there is equilibrium of the guṇas; and to the Mahat-tattva and so forth when there is a transformation of the guṇas. "Para" (the Supreme) is of the nature of Brahman. ||21||

The sequential arrangement: In each and every one of those [beings], the Supreme Self—the Lord who is the fundamental nature of all, possessing His own inherent and inconceivable respective potencies—is present. For this very reason, He is the Sovereign capable of accomplishing the impossible; for this very reason, He is immutable. (21)
Viśvanātha [explains]: In the state of equilibrium of the *guṇas*, He is the *pradhāna*; in the transformation of the *guṇas* (such as the *mahat-tattva* and so forth), He is the "other" (*para*);
distinct from the elemental principles (*bhūtādi*) derived from *prakṛti* and from *prakṛti* itself, He is the one Supreme Brahman.
Thus, the Lord (*īśvara*)—who is denoted by the three terms *Ātman*, *Paramātman*, and *Bhagavān*—is the object of knowledge (*īyate*).
The connection is with what follows. ||21||
By its own nature as the inner self and by the form of the visible world,
it is indeed both describable as the pervaded and the pervader, yet it is indescribable and free from conceptual construction.
The Supreme Lord, whose essential nature is pure experience and bliss,
appears as one whose sovereignty is concealed by Māyā, which brings forth the creation of the qualities.
"Madhva is the inner controller, the inner self; Hari is remembered as the pervasive Time.
Because He is shrouded by the nature of darkness (tamas), the sovereignty of Hari is not known. Thus [it is said]. (22–23)
Śrīdhara: How then is the distinction between the seer and the seen, the enjoyer and the enjoyed, and so forth, due to *māyā*?
To this he says: The inner self (*pratyag-ātman*) is the seer and the enjoyer; by its own nature, it is to be designated as all-pervasive.
The seen and the enjoyed, such as the body and so forth, are to be designated as that which is pervaded, for they are measured (known) through *māyā*.

The connection [of the sentence] is with what follows. In reality, however, the connection is as follows: although it is itself non-conceptualized and indefinable—or rather, although it is indefinable, being thus made definable—it is apprehended as conceptualized. ||22||

For His essential nature is bliss alone, consisting solely of pure experience. [Objection: If that very nature exists everywhere, then why is omniscience and so forth not perceived everywhere? To this he replies: "He by whom sovereignty is concealed by that Māyā, whose creative manifestation consists of the *guṇas*. (23)

The sequence of the arrangement: although He exists in those various states by His own nature, being the qualified one, He Himself is perceived as the nature of the inner self (*pratyag-ātman*) for some who possess knowledge of that alone;
however, for others whose knowledge is even lower than that, He is perceived in the form of the visible world and in the form of primordial matter (*pradhāna*).

In that regard, He is described as being pervasive by way of the form of the individual soul (*jīva*), whereas by way of the form of primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and so forth, He is described as being the pervaded; such is the meaning. However, for certain non-dualists (*advaita-jñānin*), that very Supreme Lord is indefinable, being free from conceptual construction and devoid of mere differentiation.
He is known as being of the very nature of absolute experiential bliss (*kevalānubhavānanda*), and not as one endowed with sovereignty consisting of the power of His own nature (*svarūpa-śakti*).
How so? To this he says: "by *māyā*. Through His grace, when *māyā* has vanished, He is known as truly real.
The sense is that [in that state] He does not manifest [as an object]. It is precisely His nature to be the veiler of that [reality].
He demonstrates this with the words "by the creation of the guṇas. The meaning is: "by that which causes the agitation of the guṇas such as sattva.
The intention is that even for those who possess knowledge of Brahman, the guṇa of sattva itself acts as an obscuration. ||22-23||

Bhagavat-sandarbha (21): Here, by describing the Lord’s sovereignty as being concealed by *māyā* and by employing *māyā* as a qualifying attribute for the creation of the *guṇas*, [the author] makes known His transcendence of it, just like His own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Therefore, the epithet "Supreme Lord" (*parameśvara*) was already established through that very association.
It should be understood as "given. ||23||
Viśvanātha: Of what nature is he? He is *avyaya*, meaning devoid of decay at all times. [Objection:
If he is known, then let him be specified in this manner; to this he says: *pratyag-ātmā*.
He is the Self of all internal (*pratīcām*) living beings—the Supreme Self (*paramātmā*) who, as the supreme essence, pervades the visible world.

It is designated as the "pervaded" (vyāpya) and the "pervader" (vyāpaka) only by virtue of being pervaded by that form; in reality, it is itself indeed indescribable. Although indescribable, it is conceptualized by various types of practitioners as "Brahman," "Supreme Self," or "Lord"; yet even when made the object of such conceptualization, it remains the one absolute essence of experience, which is bliss alone.
He is one whose very nature is such.

Thus, although He is manifestly shining everywhere by means of His own inherent sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), because He is impossible for individual souls (*jīvas*) to perceive due to the cause of *māyā*— that is, their own ignorance (*avidyā*)— He is regarded as having His sovereignty concealed.

Of what kind? It is that from which there is the *sarga*—the creation—of the *guṇas*, namely sound and the other objects experienced by the senses; thus, it is sound and the rest alone that constitute the manifestations, and not the Lord (*īśvara*) who, though present therein, is not so manifested. This is because, with respect to the Lord, that ignorance (*avidyā*) veils the perception of the individual soul (*jīva*) through its own functioning. Therefore, [it is said:]...
"For this divine illusion of Mine, consisting of the *guṇas*, is difficult to overcome;
but those who take refuge in Me alone cross over this illusion" (Gītā 7.14).
Since, according to the Lord's statement, it is through devotion to Him alone that one crosses over *māyā*, he [does so] as is appropriate.
The intended meaning is that there is also an instruction according to the gradations of devotion. ||24||
Therefore, show compassion and friendship toward all beings;
having abandoned the demoniacal nature, [practice that] by which Adhokṣaja is pleased.
And: "Because Madhva is the abode of Viṣṇu, compassion toward all beings must be practiced by one who possesses true knowledge. (24)
Śrīdhara: Since this is so, therefore show compassion and friendship toward all beings as is appropriate. By means of that compassion—having released, that is, having abandoned [all ill-will]. ||24||

The sequential arrangement: Therefore, show compassion toward all beings indeed—not merely toward those connected to yourself—because the Lord alone is the presiding presence. Cultivate friendliness, that is, the perception of them as your own, O Viśvanātha; for the Lord is accessible only through devotion, and that devotion [is directed] toward all beings.
Through compassion and friendship, [the practice] becomes well-established and free from obstacles; therefore, he ordains these: "Therefore," etc.
Because all these beings consist of the Lord's power, they are indeed the very form of the Lord;
thus, by their very nature, my Lord shines everywhere within them.

The sense is that, through the grace of the illustrious Guru and the Vaiṣṇavas, if the Goddess of Devotion should accept me, then he too must be seen face-to-face; this is the thought, by means of which compassion and friendship [are maintained]. —o)0(o—
When He is satisfied— O Infinite One, O Primordial One— what is there that cannot be obtained?
What is the use of those qualities established here through the transformation of attributes,
or what is the use of dharma and the rest, which are sought after by one devoid of [true] qualities?
May it be for the essence of us who delight in and sing at your feet.
And: "The seeker of honey desires even the happiness of reaching liberation no more than one who does not desire it. (25)
Śrīdhara: What follows from that? To this he says: "When He is satisfied, what is there that cannot be obtained?

Nevertheless, what is the use of those virtues such as *dharma* and the like which are established by their own nature through the transformation of the *guṇas* and achieved by destiny without effort? And what is the use of liberation (*mokṣa*), though it is desired, if it is devoid of the *guṇas*? [This is for] us who sing His praises.

Because that [liberation] is accomplished even for one who does not desire it; or rather, the meaning is: "Let there be no liberation; what is the use of that even for those who resort to the essence of his feet, partaking of the nectar? ||25||

The sequence of the composition: Following the previous [verse], he states that the satisfaction of the Lord is a fruit superior even to the attainment of Brahman—“When He is pleased. He says “Dharma, Artha... (v. 25) to show: "Aha! Even those perishable fruits and their means become capable of yielding an imperishable fruit through connection with Him."

Viśvanātha: Furthermore, when He is pleased, there is no fruit whatsoever to be desired through those [qualities] such as dharma; this is the meaning. What is the use of liberation, which is devoid of qualities (*aguṇa*), for those who, through the transformation (*vyatikara*) or evolution of the *guṇas*, have attained their goals here in this world by themselves? For they partake of the essence of His feet.

By saying "to those who serve [Him], even more than unto liberation" (*upamokṣāt*), the lotus-nature of His feet—characterized by essence, fragrance, sweetness, and so forth—and the bee-nature of those who serve Him are superposed; through this bee-nature, their natural state of being devoid of any other desired object is suggested. ||25||
That which is called the threefold aggregate (*trivarga*) consisting of dharma, artha, and kāma; namely,
the fourfold inquiry (*īkṣā*), the triple Veda (*trayī*), statesmanship (*naya*), self-restraint (*dama*), and the various forms of economic activity (*vārtā*).
I believe that all this is the truth of the Veda:
the surrender of one's own self to the Supreme Person, who is one's own true friend.

Śrīdhara: Now, if dharma and the rest are not ends of human life (puruṣārtha), why did the two teachers state that they are indeed real because they are declared in the Veda? To this he says: "Dharma, artha, and kāma"—this is the *trivarga* (the threefold set); and for the sake of that, those [sciences] beginning with *īkṣā* were taught. *Īkṣā* is the knowledge of the Self (*ātma-vidyā*), while the *trayī* is the triple Veda.
The science of ritual action (*karma-vidyā*), the principles of governance, self-control, logic, and the science of statecraft (*daṇḍa-nīti*), as well as the various means of livelihood (*vārtā*);

all this collection of subjects belonging to the *Nigama* (the Veda) is considered by me to be entirely true, because it is devoted to Truth— provided that it serves as a means for surrendering one’s own self to one's own Friend, the Supreme Person who dwells within.

Otherwise, that would indeed be untrue. Or rather, I consider all this to be the subject matter to be propounded by the Veda, which deals with the realm of the three *guṇas*. Truth, however, is the surrender of one's own self to the Supreme Person, characterized by being beyond the three *guṇas*; this is the meaning. Thus it has been said:
The Blessed One [said]: "The Vedas concern the three qualities; be free from the three qualities, O Arjuna" (*Gītā* 2.45).
This sequence of the text has not been explained [by others].
Viśvanātha [says]: But if dharma and so forth are not ends of human life (*puruṣārtha*), how is it that they alone...?

It was stated by the two sons of the Guru that [these matters] are declared in the Vedas; regarding that, he says: "For the sake of dharma and artha. *Īkṣā* refers to the knowledge of the Self (*ātma-vidyā*) and the knowledge of ritual action (*karma-vidyā*). *Naya* and *dama* refer to reasoning (*tarka*) and the science of governance (*daṇḍa-nīti*), respectively. And *vividhā vārtā* refers to various means of livelihood.
All of this belongs solely to the *nigama* (the Veda); I consider it to be indeed declared in the Veda, and not otherwise.
"I corrupt it," the sense being that such is the consensus of qualified authorities. "Truth" (satyam) refers to that which is beneficial for the virtuous;

however, for the Supreme Person, it is the opposite [of what is generally considered truth]. "Offering one's own self to the Supreme Person" means offering one's own self as belonging to Him. The venerable Svāmīpāda, however, says: "All this belongs to the Veda..."

I consider that which pertains to the realm of the three *guṇas* to be what is to be taught; however, the truth is that the surrender of one's own self to the Supreme Person is characterized by being beyond the three *guṇas*.
This was stated by the Blessed One: "The Vedas have the three *guṇas* as their subject matter; be free from the three *guṇas*, O Arjuna" (Gītā 2.45).
Thus they explained. ||26||
Nārāyaṇa, the friend of Nara, indeed declared this stainless knowledge, so difficult to attain, to Nārada.
May that belong to the single-minded devotees of the Blessed One— those who possess nothing— who have bathed their bodies in the dust of his lotus feet.
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, for the sake of inspiring confidence in them, he describes the lineage of the gurus, beginning with the word "knowledge" (jñāna).

One might wonder: "Where Nārada is the listener, how can there be any qualification for those like me? To prevent such a doubt, he says: "of those who have bathed—that is, been washed—by the dust of the feet of the exclusive devotees of the Blessed Lord."
That knowledge would belong to all embodied beings as well; there is no restriction that it belongs to the highest alone. ||27||

The sequence of the composition: He states the rarity of such knowledge and its obtainability solely through the grace of His devotee in the verse beginning with "jñānam. By the term "nara-sakha" (friend of Nara), the greatness of the grace of the illustrious Nara and His preeminent devotee is demonstrated therein.

The phrase "for those who are exclusively devoted" implies that even direct instruction regarding Him depends upon compassion; how much more so, then, the case of anything else? This is the intended meaning. ||27||

Viśvanātha: To inspire confidence in them, he speaks of the lineage of gurus, beginning with "Knowledge. One should not suspect that those like me, who are lowly, have no qualification where Nārada is the listener; thus he says: "Of those who are bathed—that is, purified—by the dust of the feet of the exclusive devotees of the Blessed Lord."
That knowledge would belong to all embodied beings as well; there is no restriction that it belongs to the superior ones alone. ||27||
This knowledge, conjoined with realized wisdom, was heard by me in the past:
the pure Bhāgavata Dharma from Nārada, who has the vision of the Divine.
Śrīdhara: For this very reason, I too previously heard from Nārada knowledge together with realization up to its culmination in direct experience, as well as dharma. (28)

The sequence of the composition: therein he shows his own [experience] with the words "It was heard. That knowledge—which is the sentence expressing it—and indeed that very fruit which culminates in direct experience, were heard along with the Bhāgavata dharma as its auxiliary; and that [dharma] was purely [devotional], not otherwise.
Mixed with knowledge, action, and so forth. ||28||
Viśvanātha: Not explained.
—o)0(o— The sons of the Daityas said:
O Prahlāda, neither you nor we know any teacher other than these two sons of our preceptor; for even as children, they were indeed our lords.
For a youth dwelling in the inner apartments, association with the great is difficult to achieve;
O gentle one, sever our doubt if there should be a cause for confidence.

Śrīdhara: There, being greatly astonished, they ask, "O Prahlāda... and so forth. "O Prahlāda, we know no other teacher besides these two, Śaṇḍa and Marka. If you say, 'I went to the side of Nārada even before their arrival,' to that they reply: 'Even for children, for those who are very young...'"
These two are our lords and controllers; therefore, it is not possible for you to go elsewhere. ||29||
They say that even the possibility that "he himself has come here" does not exist; this is expressed by the words "of the child. It is difficult to follow and hard to reconcile.
