"The cause of confidence" means the reason for trust. ||30||
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: They ask with astonishment—"O Prahlāda!"—[saying] "We know no teacher other than these two [Amṛta and Amṛtānanda]. You too have liberated yourself from their hands, [regarding them] as the lords of children."
"It is impossible to go to his side; nor is it possible that he himself has come here," they say—referring to "the child. (29–30)

Thus ends the sixth chapter, which is well-connected with the seventh, in the *Harṣiṇī* commentary known as the *Sārārthadarśinī*, for the sake of those whose hearts are devoted to the Lord and who are virtuous.

Thus ends the account of Prahlāda in the seventh book of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, the great Purāṇa, which is a commentary on the Brahma-sūtras, contained within the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā dedicated to the state of the Paramahaṃsas.
The Sixth Chapter.
Now begins the seventh chapter, titled "Instruction for Children.
Śrī Nārada said:
Thus questioned by the sons of the Daityas, the great devotee of the Lord, the Asura,
smiling and recollecting my words, spoke to them.
Śrīdhara:
While he was still in his mother’s womb during the seventh month, Prahlāda described what was spoken by Nārada for the sake of establishing conviction in his disciple.
"I heard this from Nārada that [the child] was in the womb";
thus the wise one spoke the story concerning that introduction in sixteen verses. (1)
Krama-sandarbha: This has not been explained.
Viśvanātha:
In the seventh [canto], he obtained that knowledge from Nārada while still within his mother’s womb.
He taught that very thing to the simple-minded: devotion and love, which are its fruit. ||1||
Śrī Prahlāda said: When our father had departed for Mount Mandara to practice austerities, [the demons seized the kingdom].
The gods made a supreme effort for battle against the Dānavas.
Śrīdhara: While our father Hiraṇyakaśipu was being devoured—meaning he was eaten—the wicked ones, shouting with joy, "He has been devoured! He has been devoured!", made preparations for battle. (2)
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
By good fortune, like a snake by ants, the tormentor of the world [is destroyed].
Saying, "He who eats [the flesh] becomes sinful through sin," Vāsava and the other gods [spoke].
Hearing of their exceedingly powerful exertion, the leaders of the asura hosts,
being struck by the gods and filled with fear, fled in every direction.
Without looking back at their wives, sons, wealth, kin, homes, cattle, or belongings, they all hurried away, desiring only to save their lives.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
Desiring victory, the immortals plundered King Śibi’s camp.
Indra, however, seized my mother, the queen-consort of the king.
Śrīdhara: They plundered the king’s camp—that is, his residence—by seizing all his possessions;
the sequence of words has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: They plundered the camp, the residence, of King Hiraṇyakaśipu.
They destroyed [him] by seizing all his possessions. ||6||
As she was being led away, agitated by fear and weeping like a female osprey,
the divine seer, who had arrived there by chance, beheld her on the path.
It has not been explained by anyone at all. [The Lord said:
"O Lord of the Gods, you ought not to take her away, for she is innocent."
Release her, release her, O noble one; she is a virtuous wife, the consort of another.
Śrīdhara said: "You ought not to take her away, for she is innocent and without fault. (8)
The sequence of composition; Viśvanātha: not explained.
—o)0(o— Śrī-Indra said:
"The invincible seed of the enemy of the gods dwells within her womb;
remain here until her delivery, for I shall depart on the path of my purpose."

Śrīdhara: "Inviṣahyam" means unbearable or difficult to endure. Therefore, let her remain here until the birth. Then, having reached the path or way of the goal—meaning, having arrived at the point where he can kill the born son—he will release [her]. ||9||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: "Sit here; let her remain in my prison until her delivery. Having reached the path of wealth—the way to my own interest—I shall release her after killing the born son."
The meaning is: "I shall release this. ||9||
Śrī Nārada said:
This great soul is truly free from all sin; he is a direct and supreme devotee of the Lord.
The powerful Anantānucara shall not meet his end at your hands.

Śrīdhara: He is great by his own qualities alone, and not through connection with his father or others. By you acting as the cause, he shall not go to *saṃsthā*, which is death. The reasons for this are "free from sin" (*niṣkilbiṣa*) and so forth. ||10||
The sequence of composition: "Anantānucara" (the attendant of Ananta). His prior refinement through devotion has already been shown. ||10||
Viśvanātha: By you, acting as the cause, [he attained] his end, that is, death. ||10||
Having been addressed thus, Indra, honoring the words of the celestial sage, left her;
and with devotion dear to Ananta, he circumambulated her and departed for heaven.
Śrīdhara: Having circumambulated this [earth] with devotion toward me—me, who am dear to Ananta, or toward him who is dear to me—[one attains the fruit]. ||11||
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: By means of that devotion which [I possess] for me, the beloved of Ananta, having circumambulated and having prostrated with the words, "Obeisance to the devotee of Hari who dwells within this womb," ||11||
Then the seer, having brought my mother to his own hermitage,
consoled her, saying: "Stay here, child, until the arrival of your husband."
Śrīdhara says: "Let it be stated here," such is the ellipsis to be supplied. ||12||
The *Krama-sandarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been explained. —
Thus, she dwelt near the divine sage, free from all fear.
Until the lord of the Daityas desisted from his terrible asceticism.
Śrīdhara: *anti* means "near" (*samīpe*). ||13||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: "Antike" means in the vicinity. ||13||
There, the virtuous woman attended upon the sage with supreme devotion,
being pregnant for the sake of the safety of her fetus and for a birth according to her desire.
Śrīdhara: "Antarvatnī" means pregnant. For the sake of giving birth after her husband's arrival as desired, and likewise for the safety of her own fetus. (14)
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: [The word *yatheṣṭam* means] for that which is a birth according to one's will immediately after the arrival of the husband. ||14||
The compassionate sage, the Lord, bestowed both the essence of Dharma and pure knowledge upon her, and also directed them toward me.

Śrīdhara: For the sake of pacifying her grief, He bestowed both the reality of dharma characterized by devotion and knowledge, which is the discrimination between the self and the non-self; for the Lord is capable. ||15||

The sequence of the composition: [The Lord said,] "To the seer (Ṛṣi), for the sole purpose of pacifying his grief, He imparted the reality of Dharma, its common nature, and the knowledge concerning the Self; and therein, with reference to me as well, He taught that stainless reality of this Dharma known as the Bhāgavata—[for] mere knowledge does not suffice."

According to the maxim, "Enough of that which is stainless" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.5.12), he also explained that which is called knowledge and its bestower when describing it; however, the sense is that she was unable to grasp it. ||15||

Viśvanātha: "Both" refers to the safety of the womb and birth at one's own will; by the qualifying term "immaculate," he indicates the reality of dharma, the yoga of devotion, and the knowledge approved by the Bhāgavata.
By the word "api" (also) in the phrase "me too," he includes my mother as well. ||15||
But because of the length of time and the female nature of my mother, it vanished from her sight;
yet, favored by the Rishi, the memory of me has not left her even now.
Śrīdhara: This has not been explained.
Krama-sandarbha: "That indeed" (tat tu) means "that also" (tad api). By this, it is implied that Śrī Nārada did not receive full grace from his own mother. ||16||
Viśvanātha: If that is so, why is devotion to your mother not seen? To this he says:
"But that... Why did it not disappear for you as well, given your childhood and the long duration of time?
To this he replies: "By the sage... Because my mother was not favored by him [the sage].
The sense is that they attained [their respective states] there due to their female nature and the long duration of time. ||16||
If you have faith in my words,
may you also possess abundant wisdom born of confidence, just as I do, even among women and children.
Śrīdhara: *bhūyāt* means "may it be. *Vaiśāradī*: the suffix *-taddhita* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*).
The meaning is: "skilled in cutting through the ego-identification with the body and so forth. (17)
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not commented upon.
*Viśvanātha*: With the benediction "May it be so," he hopes that the grace of Śrī Nārada, which resides within himself, may also exist in them as a cause for devotion. If you have faith, then...
The Blessed One is "fearless" because he possesses fearlessness; faith has him as its object.
Thus, through my grace, one should understand from the subsequent text that faith arises from faith, devotion from faith, and love from devotion. ||17||
These six states, beginning with birth, are observed to belong to the body and not to the self,
just as the fruits of a tree appear in due time through the form of the Lord.
"Madhva states: 'The six modifications belong to the body, not to Viṣṇu who resides within it;

knowing that the body is dependent upon Him, one should abandon the sense of "mine-ness" toward it. Thus, because it is the cause [of these modifications], the body's dependence on Viṣṇu is established. (18)

Śrīdhara: In response to the inquiry, "What is this 'wisdom born of discernment' (vaiśāradī dhīḥ)? he states the very method for discriminating the body from the self as taught by Nārada in ten verses, beginning with "birth" (*janma*). These six states of being—namely, "it is born," "it exists," "it grows," "it transforms," "it declines," and "it perishes"—are the modifications (*vikāra*).

The meaning is that just as fruits are seen only when a tree exists, so too are [the bodily states] seen while the Self remains; by Him whose form is the sovereign power capable of transformation. //18//

The Sequence of Composition (*Krama-sandarbha*): Therein, for the sake of abandoning the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the body and so forth, Viśvanātha states, at first glance, that mere knowledge of the Self as realized by his own mother, beginning with the words "Janmādyā" and so on;
for some devotees seeking liberation (*mumukṣu-bhaktas*), however, such knowledge is required. Thus [he speaks].

He said: "By the ten [verses] beginning with 'birth and so forth' [it is shown]: birth, existence, growth, transformation, decay, and destruction—such states are the six modifications. Just as these occur every year only for the fruits of a tree that remains eternally constant, and not for the tree itself, even so [is it with the Self]."

These six are seen as belonging only to the body—which is itself eternally situated within the Self—and not to the Self; for by that [Self], there exists the form of the Lord, which consists of both the aggregate and the individual. ||18||
The Self is eternal, immutable, pure, one, the knower of the field, the substratum,
changeless, self-luminous, the cause, all-pervading, unattached, and unobscured.

Śrīdhara: Thus, by means of the attributes of the body and its contrast with them, the difference of the self from the body has been shown. Now, clarifying that difference through the very attributes of the self, he causes one to abandon that egoism and so forth, beginning with the word "the self": "The self is eternal; for this self is indeed indestructible" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.14).

According to scripture: He is "immutable," meaning devoid of decay, for scripture says, "In the imperishable syllable, in the highest heaven" (Ṛgveda 1.164.21). He is "pure," for scripture says, "Blameless and stainless" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.19).
He is "one," for scripture says, "One only, without a second" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.8). He is the "Knower of the Field" (kṣetrajña).
According to the Śruti: "By what means could one know the Knower? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14). It is the substratum, according to the Śruti:
"In whom the heaven, the earth, and the intermediate space [are woven]" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.5). It is changeless, according to the Śruti:
"Partless, actionless, and tranquil" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.19). It is self-luminous, the light of the Self.

"He is the Sovereign (samrāj)," according to the Śruti; "He is the Cause," according to the Śruti: "He created these worlds" (Ai.U. 1.2); "He is all-pervasive," according to the Śruti: "Truth, Knowledge, Infinite" (Tai.U. 2.1.1);
"He is unattached," according to the Śruti: "For this Puruṣa is indeed unattached" (Bṛ.Ā.U. 4.3.15); "He is unobstructed."
For there is the Vedic scripture: "Taking the fullness from the full, the full alone remains" (Īśopaniṣad 1). ||19||

The sequential arrangement [of the topics]: [the Self] is one, and not of the nature of an aggregate consisting of the body, senses, and so forth. The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) possesses attributes such as being a knower; it is the substratum of the senses and other faculties. Because its knowership is innate, it is changeless (avikriya), self-seeing (svadṛk), and self-luminous to itself. It is the cause—the instrumental cause—of creation and the rest. Thus it has been said:
Śrī Sūta stated: "The cause of this creation and so forth is the individual soul (jīva), the agent of ignorance and karma" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 12.7.18).

Thus, the Lord of the Universe—pervasive, whose nature is to pervade, unattached, and by His very nature unobscured due to being self-luminous—is the one in whom the realization of the absence of the six transformations within the individual soul constitutes the purification of the meaning of the term *tvaṃ* (the "thou").

And since that [realization] can only come through devotion (*bhakti*) consisting of meditation upon the Supreme Self, who is the referent of that word, he describes the nature of the Supreme Self with two verses beginning with "The Self" (*ātman*). The Self is the Supreme Self; He is eternal (*nitya*), for the Śruti says, "Verily, this Self is indestructible" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.5.14). He is immutable (*avyaya*), meaning devoid of decay.

He is the one in whom the *ṛc* verses abide in the supreme firmament, according to the Śruti: "In the syllable of the *ṛc*, in the supreme firmament" (*Ṛgveda* 1.164.21). He is pure, according to the Śruti: "Blameless and stainless" (*Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* 6.19). He is one, according to the Śruti: "One alone, without a second" (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.8.8).
He is the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), according to the Śruti: "O Maitreyī, by what means could one know the Knower? (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.5.15).

[2.4.14] Thus says the Śruti. It is the substratum (āśraya), according to the Śruti: "In whom the heaven, the earth, and the intermediate space [are woven]" (Mu.U. 2.2.5). It is changeless (avikriya), according to the Śruti: "Partless, actionless, and tranquil" (Śve.U. 6.19). It is self-luminous (sva-dṛk), according to the Śruti: "The light of the Self, O Emperor," so he said. It is the cause (hetu); it is that...

He created these worlds, according to the Śruti: *ai.u. 1.2*. He is all-pervasive, according to the Śruti: *satyaṃ jñānam anantaṃ* (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1). He is unattached, according to the Śruti: *asaṅgo hy ayaṃ puruṣaḥ* (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.15). He is unobstructed; having taken from the Full the fullness of the Full...
For it is stated in the Śruti: "Only this remains" (Īśa Upaniṣad 1). ||19||
By means of these twelve supreme characteristics of the self,
the wise man should abandon the unreal notion of "I" and "mine" regarding the body and so forth, which arises from delusion.

Śrīdhara: By means of these twelve supreme and excellent characteristics of the Self, which are capable of discernment, the wise man, knowing his distinction from the body, should abandon the state of unreality—that is, false cognition.
[This is] the sequence of the composition: "he should abandon that which is born of delusion. It refers specifically to that which is born of delusion having the body and so forth as its locus.

It is implied that renunciation applies to the ego-sense (*ahaṃ-artha*) and not to that which constitutes its very nature. Thus, because the individual soul (*jīva*) is a part of Him, some maintain that it is subtle and of the nature of light; for it is indeed manifested as a portion of the Kaustubha gem. And so it is stated in the *Prabhāsa-khaṇḍa* of the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
In the description of the individual soul (jīva), neither its form nor its color or dimension is seen anywhere;
it cannot even be described, for it is subtle and possesses an infinite body.
Divided a hundred times, and then again divided into a hundred parts of the tip of a hair;
subtler than that is the Divine One, and he is fit for infinity.
He has the luster of the sun, a subtle radiance, like a drop of water upon a lotus leaf.
"Yogins behold it like a star with the eye of knowledge. Thus [ends verse 20].

Viśvanātha: [The phrase] "by others" refers to those superior even to the individual souls (jīvātman), namely the eternally meditated-upon [deities]. Regarding the body and its constituents (*deha-daihika*), the notion of unreality—that is, the realization that they are not ultimately real—does not cease;
even when discrimination (*viveka*) exists, delusion (*moha*) persists like a confusion of directions (*dig-bhrama*) unless there is meditation upon the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
Such is the intended meaning. ||20||
Just as a goldsmith, skilled in its nature, may obtain gold from among stones in the fields through specific methods, so too [does one find the Self].
Likewise, through the yoga of the self within the fields of the bodies,
the knower of the inner self shall attain the state of Brahman.

Śrīdhara: Now, one might ask: "Even for one who possesses the knowledge of the Self as distinct [from the body], how can the attainment of Brahman-hood occur through direct experience such that one would abandon the ego (ahaṅkāra) and so forth?
In response to this expectation, he describes the manner of that attainment along with an illustration: "Shining in the gold-mining fields..."

Just as a goldsmith who knows the means obtains gold from specks of gold within stones through methods such as smelting, so too does one who knows the means— through the yoga of the self, which are the means for attaining the self—
attain the state of Brahman, that is, the nature of Brahman, being a knower of the inner self.
The Self is the knower of the aggregate of causes and effects pertaining to itself. ||21||
The sequence of composition: He also states the knowledge of the meaning of that word—“gold,” etc. ||21||
Viśvanātha: If it is asked, "In that case, where would the Supreme Self reside? [the answer is] "Even in one's own body.

He states the manner of perceiving Him along with an illustration, beginning with the words "gold" (svarṇam). [The meaning is: by means of methods (*yogaiḥ*) in mines (*kṣetreṣu*), that is, in gold-mining sites, among rocks (*grāvasu*), that is, among stones in which particles of gold are shimmering.

Just as a goldsmith who knows the means obtains gold through methods such as heating, which have been learned from the mouth of his teacher, so too does one obtain the state of Brahman— the Supreme Self— within the fields of the body-form by means of self-yoga, that is,
the methods for attaining the Self, such as reflection and the like.
The destination and the attainment. ||21||
Eight primary natures have been declared, and indeed only three are their qualities;
the modifications are sixteen according to the teachers, and the Spirit is one because of its inherent connection.
"Viṣṇu is traditionally known as the twenty-fifth in relation to Madhva (the intellect);
Hari is traditionally known as the soul (jīva) who is to be correctly understood in relation to insentient matter and the rest. Thus [it is said]. (22)
Śrīdhara: He explains the discernment of the inner self (*adhyātma-viveka*), which is the means for attaining the Self, in three verses beginning with "eight.

The eight are: primordial nature (*mūla-prakṛti*), the great principle (*mahat*), egoity (*ahaṅkāra*), and the five subtle elements (*tan-mātra*). The three qualities, such as *sattva* and the rest, are merely the attributes of primordial nature and are not distinct from it. [Then there are] the eleven organs.

The five great elements (pañca-mahā-bhūtāni) make sixteen; the Person (pumān), the Self (ātmā), is declared by teachers such as Kapila to be one. The reason for its oneness is that it persists through these [sixteen] as their witness. Thus it has been said:
Root-nature is unevolved; the seven, beginning with the Great One (mahat), are both nature and evolved;
the group of sixteen is the evolved alone; and the Person (puruṣa) is neither nature nor evolved. Thus [ends the verse]. 22.
*Kramasandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Since it was stated [in the previous verse] that he is "a knower of the inner self" (*adhyātmavit*), he speaks regarding the subject of the inner self with the following half-verse and the next: "Eight," etc. These eight are: primordial nature (*mūlaprakṛti*), the great principle (*mahat*), egoity (*ahaṅkāra*), and the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*).
The three—sattva and the others—are the transformations (vikāras). The eleven organs and the five great elements constitute the sixteen [evolutes].

The Puruṣa, the Self, is one, as declared by the teachers Kapila and others. "Samanvayāt" means existing by attaining a correct connection or relationship; or else, it means following (atati) that connection or relationship.
One attains it constantly; therefore, the form *sātatyagamana* contains a *kvip*-suffix. ||22||
The body is a composite of all [elements], while the world is twofold as that which moves and that which stands.
It is precisely here that the Puruṣa is to be sought— one who abandons what is "not-that" by means of "not this, not this."

Śrīdhara: "The world" refers to the moving; "the stationary" refers to the unmoving. Right here, within this very body which consists of all composite aggregates, the Person (puruṣa) is to be sought—that is, investigated. And this is easily accomplished, as he says:
"By the removal of what is other through 'not this, not this' (neti neti), [the Self] itself abandons what is non-Self. From the category of the non-Self.
The meaning is: "being perceived separately. ||23||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: The "entire aggregate" (*sarva-saṅghāta*) consists of the collection of all things possessing the aforementioned characteristics; "the moving" (*jagat*) refers to mobile beings such as humans, and "the stationary" (*tasthuḥ*) refers to immobile beings such as trees. In this very context, the body itself is the person (*puruṣa*).

The Supreme Self (paramātman) is to be sought, that is, it is to be investigated. He states the manner of investigation: "by rejecting"—meaning by those who reject—that reality which is different from It, expressed as "not this, not this" (neti neti). ||23||
By means of positive and negative concomitance, through discernment with a subtle mind,
and by reflecting upon the traditional accounts of the celestial realms, those who are free from haste [attain this].

Śrīdhara: [The term] *anvaya* refers to the state of being pervasively strung through everything, like a thread through jewels; for this very reason, there is also the individual separation of each [jewel] from the thread, as in the case of the thread from the jewels. The two [terms] form a copulative compound (*dvandva*).
By that—either by the aforementioned discrimination (*viveka*) or by that "shining" (*uśatā*), i.e., pure—self, which is to say, the mind (*manasā*).

The meaning is: by means of the traditional accounts of creation and abiding—namely, creation, maintenance, and dissolution—in accordance with the teachings of the Śruti beginning with "from whence indeed these beings are born," and so forth; [He is] to be sought by those who reflect, that is, those who investigate with composure and without agitation. This is to be construed with what precedes. ||24||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Now, one might object: "In that case, the body would not be composed of that [Self] at all; upon the abandonment of that which is not the Self, only a void would remain.
To this he says: "By way of concomitance (*anvaya*)," etc. There is the concomitance of the Supreme Self in the body, and the exclusion of the body from the Supreme Self.
That which is well-known is that even for the insentient—such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth—it is only through its presence (*anvaya*) that activity occurs;

and that which is distinct from the intellect and the rest is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) residing within the body. By means of such discernment (*viveka*), and by means of that same radiant, pure Self—that is, the mind (*manas*)—through the traditional accounts of creation and its locus.

The phrase "by means of creation, maintenance, and dissolution" implies that these have been thoroughly contemplated; the meaning is: by reflecting upon the processes of emanation and so forth as described in such Vedic passages as "from which indeed these beings are born. He is to be sought by those who are not passionate—that is, by those who are undistracted. ||24||
Waking, dreaming, and deep sleep are the functions of the intellect;
that by which these are experienced is the supreme Puruṣa, the witness.

The word *madhvaḥ* refers to the intellect (*buddhi*) and the individual soul (*jīva*). Indeed, the individual soul is also sometimes expressed by such terms as "sattva" and "intellect," while the words "waking" and so forth refer to its activity as well as its pleasure and pain.
The Witness who is beyond the state of wakefulness and so forth is remembered as Hari, established in bliss;
because of His dwelling together with the individual soul (jīva), He appears as having that same form.

"By the ignorant vision—that is, by the vision of one who does not know—just as the wind becomes associated with fragrance, so too, when the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para) is not perceived, one undergoes transmigration;
through the certainty of non-difference, one goes to darkness. There is no doubt about this. Thus it is said. ||25||
Śrīdhara: He states the manner of deliberation with two verses beginning with "of the intellect" (*buddheḥ*). The term *adhyakṣaḥ* means the witness;
the sequence of the composition has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: He states the manner of deliberation with two verses beginning with "of the intellect" (*buddheḥ*). [It refers to] that which is indeed accompanied by...
Three states arise within the intellect; that is the Supreme Person, the Supreme Self. ||25||
By means of these three colors, which are distributed as distinct states of intellect arising from activity,
one should perceive the true nature of the Self through their connection, just as one perceives the wind by its scents.
Madhvaḥ: [He is so called] because of the various states of intellect of living beings, which indicate their relative gradations. ||26||
Śrīdhara: Therefore, by these various states of the intellect (*buddhi*), which are transformations (*pariṇāma*) that have been cast aside— that is,
discarded as not being the properties of the Self (*anātma-dharma*)— and which are of the nature of the three qualities (*tri-varṇa*),
consisting of the three *guṇas*, and arising from activity (*kriyodbhava*), produced by past actions (*karman*), they belong to the intellect alone.

Because they consist of the three *guṇas* and because of [the principle's] being both the object and the agent of action, these are merely its states (*avasthā*). However, the Self (*ātman*), through its association with the intellect (*buddhi*), appears as if possessing those states, though not in reality; thus, "one should know the nature of the Self" means that one should understand it. Here is an illustration: by means of the fragrances, which are the properties of the flower...
Or like the wind, which is the support [of the clouds]. ||26||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He states that he who appears as possessing these three states of the intellect is the individual soul (*jīvātman*): by means of these distinctions of the intellect, namely the transformations such as waking and so forth, which are of three colors.

By means of these very [qualities]— which consist of the three *guṇas*, arise from activity, are produced by karma, and though overturned, are discarded as being non-self-attributes— one should perceive, that is, know, the nature of the impure self (*jīva*);
just as one perceives the wind through its mere connection (*anvaya*) with the fragrances of flowers and the like.

One should know that which possesses fragrance. That accompanied by which the intellect functions is the Supreme Self (paramātman); that which is accompanied by the intellect is the individual self (jīvātman)—such is the distinction. ||26||
This indeed is the gateway to saṃsāra, bound by the qualities (guṇas) and actions;
though rooted in ignorance and devoid of purpose, it is presented to man like a dream.
Even though the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) is of the nature of suffering, it is entered into intentionally,
just as one who voluntarily causes his own decapitation in a dream must endure that suffering even when awake.
"Even though he knows his own suffering, he proceeds against his will. Thus it is said. ||27||

Śrīdhara: Now, one might object: "In that case, just as the fragrance of the wind—which is conditioned by flowers—is removed by discriminative knowledge (*viveka-jñāna*), so too the transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) of the Self would not be removed. Anticipating this, he says: "This door refers to the door of the intellect (*buddhi*) or the door of its states; transmigratory existence is not [inherent] in itself. For (hi) because..."

It is said that one is bound by the qualities and functions of the intellect (*buddhi*). Thus, because it is rooted in ignorance, this [bondage] is considered to be purposeless and illusory, like a dream. However, since the connection between the wind and the substance of fragrance is real, the analogy is dissimilar. (27)
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He whose door is this very intellect; for that very reason, he is one in whom there is complete bondage by means of the qualities (*guṇas*) and actions (*karmans*) belonging to it. Furthermore, he is one who possesses no knowledge (*jñāna*).

He whose root is of such a nature—that is to say, he whose root is not known. Even though the world-process of the individual soul (*jīva*), which consists of the superimposition of the body, is without purpose and devoid of reality, it is nevertheless presented like a dream; the meaning is that it is projected upon that person by the power of the Supreme Lord alone. ||27||
Therefore, you must perform the yoga that extracts the seed of actions consisting of the three qualities, and brings the flow of the intellect to rest.
Madhvaḥ: The flow of wisdom is its [nature]; it is the supreme delight in the Supreme Lord. ||28||

Śrīdhara: Since cessation occurs in this manner, therefore the seed is ignorance (*ajñāna*), and its removal is its burning. What is that? Yoga. Of what nature is it? It is such because it causes the stream of the intellect—consisting of the states of waking and so forth—to cease. (28)
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Therefore, he says "tasmāt" (therefore), implying that one must strive for its cessation. The "seed" (*bīja*) is the intellect (*buddhi*) within primordial nature (*prakṛti*); its "extraction" (*nirharaṇa*) is its burning. What is this burning? That...

He said: Yoga is precisely that cessation of the flow of cognitions—that is, of the states such as waking and so forth—which constitutes the fruit. Regarding the word *yoga*, the *Medinī* lexicon states: "Yoga [is used] in the senses of attaining a previously unattained object, conjunction, meditation, and method. (28)
Among those thousands of means, this one was taught by the Blessed One:
that by which and how devotion may be easily attained toward the Lord, the Blessed One.

Śrīdhara: Having thus described the nature of knowledge, he now states the means for its attainment—the reality of dharma as spoken by Nārada—in five verses beginning with "tatra. By means of those dharmas, when performed exactly as they are, there arises devotion (*rati*) toward the Blessed Lord Śrī Nārāyaṇa; this is the method.
It was said by the Blessed One; and likewise, there is the well-spoken verse of the Gītā:

"Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give, and whatever austerity you practice, O son of Kuntī, perform that as an offering unto Me. [Gītā 9.27] Thus it is said.

"By devotion he comes to know Me in truth, both who I am and what I am" (Gītā 11.55), and so forth; such is the sequence of the connection. Now, he sets forth his own realization through the words beginning with "therein, by means" (*tatra-upāya*).
In that regard, even though the seeds of actions consisting of the three *guṇas* have been removed by thousands of means as previously described...

Among all the means taught by the perfected ones (siddhas), this very method was instructed to me by the venerable Nārada; for through this method, compared to thousands of other methods, one attains directly—without any intervening obstacle—attachment and love for the Lord, the Blessed One, exactly as it is. Therefore:

The sense is that the removal of the seeds of karma is also merely a secondary result of this. Alternatively, regarding the removal of those seeds as the objective, among all the thousands of means taught by the venerable Nārada, this very means has been declared by the Blessed One; by this very means, one's duties are fully accomplished.

The meaning is: "they come to be. What is that? To this he says: by which means, from whatever perfected means, there arises in the Lord, the Blessed One, devotion (*rati*) that is direct (*añjasā*), exactly as it is, and without the intervention of other means. ||29||

Viśvanātha: Regarding the extraction of the seed-syllable (*bīja*), among thousands of methods, this method has been proclaimed by the Blessed One. The implication is that others are indeed inferior to this one, as they have been proclaimed by other sages.
What is this very [method]? To that he says: "by which" (*yad*). By which...
Since devotion (*bhakti*) arises from that *bhakti-yoga* which is produced by its constituent limbs such as service to the guru,
the logical connection (*anvaya*) is that this very *bhakti-yoga* is the means. Here, from the word "from" (*yataḥ*,
ablative case) and the word "directly" (*añjasā*), it follows that *rati* alone is the primary fruit of *bhakti-yoga*, which constitutes the removal of the seed [of worldly existence].

But for those of pure devotion, this may occur as a secondary result quite effortlessly. As it is said: "Just as fire quickly digests what has been swallowed, so does she [devotion] swiftly consume the storehouse [of karma]. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.25.30). ||29||
Through service to the guru with devotion, through the offering of all that is gained,
through association with saintly devotees, and through the worship of the Lord.
Śrīdhara: In that very context, he states the internal factors: "By service to the guru, by devotion, by love, and by offering all that has been obtained. (30)

Sanātana [Ha.bha.vi. 10.495]: Through service to the guru, through devotion and love for him alone, and by offering all the gains one has obtained to him; and through association with the saintly (*sādhu*) Vaiṣṇavas who possess virtuous conduct. ||30||
The sequential arrangement: [the triad consisting of] service to the guru, and so forth. ||30||

Viśvanātha: Regarding the two things—the reality of dharma and knowledge—which were introduced as subjects to be taught, he has already described knowledge. Now, indicating that the reality of dharma is indeed *bhakti-yoga*, he states the previously mentioned limbs of the referent of the word "yat" (that) in three verses beginning with "guru": [of] the guru...
By means of service— such as bathing, massaging, and so forth— as well as by the offering of all things obtained,
and that offering must be done with devotion alone and not for the sake of prestige or other motives;
through association with those devotees who are saintly and of good conduct, those devotees who are of bad conduct are to be served and honored.
The meaning is that they are beautiful to behold, but they should not be grasped for the sake of attachment. ||30-31||
Through faith in Him and in His stories, by chanting of His qualities and deeds,
through meditation on His lotus feet, and by beholding and honoring His emblems and so forth;
Śrīdhara: And by those [practices] beginning with the beholding and worship of his *liṅgas* and *mūrtis*, such as salutation (*vandanā*) and so forth. ||31||
Sanātana [Ha.bha.vi. 10.495]: "And by those [practices] such as salutation, which have as their beginning the beholding and worship of the Śrīmūrtis possessing His [divine] marks. (31)
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon. —
o)0(o— Hari, the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign, dwells within all beings.
Thus, one should properly honor all beings with one's mind through those very desires.

Sanātana [Ha.bha.vi. 10.496] states: "And by means of desires that grant those various desired objects, devotion is thus performed by those who have conquered the six internal enemies"—this applies to all [the verses]. Furthermore, in this context, it should be understood that the worship of the Lord and so forth are the limbs of devotion (*bhakti*), while the service to the guru and so forth are the means (*sādhana*) for achieving them.
It has not been explained by others.
Thus, by those who have conquered the six internal foes, devotion toward the Lord is practiced.
That by which delight is found in the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva.
Śrīdhara: Those by whom the group of six—namely desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy—or the group of the senses, has been conquered. ||33||

Sanātana [Ha.bha.vi. 10.522]: By those who have thus conquered—through the aforementioned methods such as service to the guru—the group of six, namely desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy, or the group of the senses;
by whom devotion (bhakti)—which consists solely of the worship of the Lord—is practiced; and by that devotion, there arises attachment (rati), which is love (prema). ||33||
The Sequence of Composition: Now, having stated the various limbs of that very means, he speaks of others with the words "In this way" (*evam*).

In this very manner—that is, precisely through the previously mentioned methods such as service to the guru and so forth, and not by a separate effort for that purpose—devotion is indeed practiced again by those people whose seeds of karma have been conquered, characterized by the subduing of desire and the like.

Viśvanātha: Thus it is. By means of this very kind of devotion—characterized by the limbs such as service to the guru, by those [practitioners] who have conquered the group of six beginning with desire (kāmādi) or the senses—it is said that devotion is the aforementioned secondary fruit, consisting of the cessation of the flow of discursive thought. Of devotion...
He states the primary fruit with the words "by which": *ratiḥ* means love (*premāṇam*). ||33||
Having heard of the incomparable deeds, qualities,
and heroic exploits performed by his playful incarnations,
When, with hair standing on end from excessive joy, with tears and a faltering voice, one sings aloud, cries out, or dances in intense longing;

Śrīdhara: He describes the symptoms of devotion to the Lord with three verses beginning with "niśamya. [The Lord's] qualities refer to His affection for His devotees and so forth. With hairs standing on end and tears flowing due to excessive joy, he sings aloud with a choked voice, being intensely longing and with unrestrained throat. (34)

Sanātana Gosvāmī: [He sings loudly with longing] such that his voice becomes faltering due to the hairs standing on end and tears flowing from excessive joy, as he sings of the *guṇas*—such as affection for devotees—and the *vīryas*, the heroic deeds such as the slaying of demons. [Ha.bha.vi. 11.637]
The sequence of composition: "Having heard thus" constitutes a triad. (34)
Viśvanātha states the signs of love (*rati*)—beginning with the words "having heard" (*niśamya*). These include his *karmas* (deeds) such as the theft of yogurt and milk;
his *guṇas* (qualities) such as affection for his devotees; and his *vīryas* (heroic powers) such as the lifting of Govardhana and the slaying of Kaṃsa. ||34||
When, as if seized by a planet, he laughs at times, cries out, broods, or pays homage to people;
Sighing repeatedly, his mind fixed on the Self and free from shame, he says: "O Hari, Lord of the World! O Nārāyaṇa!"
Śrīdhara: Not commented upon.
Sanātana Gosvāmī: Being one whose mind is fixed on the Lord, the Supreme Self, and for that very reason being "gata-trapaḥ," that is, devoid of shame. [Ha.bha.vi. 11.638]
Viśvanātha: He whose intellect—meaning his faculty of reflection—is such that he speaks with both his own voice and mind, saying, "O Hari, Lord of the World, Nārāyaṇa! [35]
Then the person, with all bonds released,
has his disposition and form conformed to the state of being that [Supreme Being].
Having met with Adhokṣaja through the practice of supreme devotion, one whose latent tendencies and seeds have been utterly consumed [is liberated].
Madhva: Devotion is the state of being absorbed in that [Lord], which is according to one's own nature.
Some devotees dance and sing as they desire;
some merely chant silently; and some perform both. Thus it is said. (36)

Śrīdhara: His state consists of his disposition, gestures, and so forth; that state is his contemplation (*bhāvanā*). He is one whose mind and body have been conformed to that [contemplation] in their underlying intent and outward form. He is one whose seed—ignorance—or latent tendency (*anuśaya*) and impression (*vāsanā*) has been utterly consumed.
Such a person "attains" (*samyag eti*), meaning he reaches [the goal]. ||36||

Sanātana Gosvāmī: *Tasya bhāva* means his state of being or his activities; *bhāva* here signifies the internal cultivation [of that state], and it is imitated by those two. Alternatively, *bhāva* refers to the love for that Lord Hari; the *bhāva* of those people who possess such love consists of their external and internal activities. The two [the heart and the form] are thus described as having an imitation (*anukṛta*)—that is, a resemblance—to that [divine state]. Such are their disposition (*āśaya*) and form (*ākṛti*).

He whose mind and body [are such]; he whose seed—namely ignorance (*ajñāna*), latent tendency (*anuśaya*), and impression (*vāsanā*)—has been utterly consumed; he "attains" (*samyag eti*) [the state of being] eternally united [with Brahman], is the meaning. Thus, the majesty characterized by the cessation of external and internal modifications has been described. This should be inferred in the same way for what follows as well.
[Ha.bha.vi.
11.639] The *krama-sandarbha* has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: "In that [state], the *bhāvas* are those such as servitude (*dāsya*), friendship (*sakhya*), and so forth; their cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is the thought, 'I am a servant.'"

He is one by whom his own mind and body—the internal disposition (*āśaya*) and physical form—have been made conformable (*anukṛta*), that is, made similar, through the contemplation of the Self beginning with "I am a friend" and so forth. Nor should it be suspected that *saṃsāra* consists merely in the existence of the body;
thus he says: the seed, namely the primordial intellect (*prākṛtī buddhiḥ*) which is the latent tendency (*anuśaya*), has already been burnt and destroyed long ago.
And he whose latent impressions (vāsanā) have become despondent—that intellect, when possessed by the great path of passion, attains union with Adhokṣaja. ||36||
For an embodied being here whose nature is impure, taking refuge in Adhokṣaja is the shattering of the wheel of saṃsāra.
The wise know that to be the bliss of Brahman-nirvāṇa;
therefore, worship the Lord of the Heart within your own hearts.
Madhvaḥ: The bliss of liberation through Brahman, and the bliss of liberation caused by Brahman. ||37||
Śrīdhara: What follows from that? To this he says: "The touching [alambham] of Adhokṣaja"—that is, contact with Him by means of the mind;

in another reading, it is "taking refuge in Him" (tasyāśrayaṇam). Of one whose self is impure—that is, one whose self, meaning the mind, is joined with passion and other such defects—the wise know that [meditation] to be the shatterer of the wheel of transmigration, its bringer to an end. That indeed is...

They know that liberation (mokṣa) is absorption into Brahman, which is Nirvāṇa; it is the bliss whose essence is that [Brahman]. [One should meditate on] the Lord of the Heart as the Inner Controller (antaryāmin). ||37||
The sequence of the composition: Now, one might ask, "When there is the attainment of Adhokṣaja, does saṃsāra still exist or not?

To this he replies with the words beginning "Adhokṣaja. The suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of habitual action (*śīla*), meaning "one who cuts away" (*śātana*). The intended meaning is that by his very nature, he himself proceeds [to liberation] spontaneously. ||37||

Viśvanātha: Now, is it not well known that the bliss of liberation (nirvāṇa) in Brahman alone is the essence of the goals of human life? True; however, even that is included within the bliss of union with Adhokṣaja. Thus he says: "The touching of Adhokṣaja"—meaning a slight contact by means of the mind, or direct attainment.
They know it to be the shatterer and the terminator of the wheel of worldly existence;
and that very thing is the bliss of Brahman-nirvāṇa, because Brahman is indeed Adhokṣaja,
and the experience of the sweetness of His feet is itself the nature of supreme bliss.

Because it has the nature of the bliss of nirvāṇa, the pleasure arising from a particular sense of "mine" through states such as servitude and so forth is merely superior and finite; whereas the natural joy found in the moon— which is beloved by all people and supremely delightful— is surpassed by a joy ten million times greater in one's own son.
Even for one who is crippled, blind, and deaf, or even for one unfortunate among all people, if there should arise the sense of "mine" toward the Blessed One—
regarding her as a servant or the like— then the ultimate limit of supreme bliss arises from her very nature as the Supreme Brahman.
If such bliss occurs even when the sense of "mine" arises [toward her], then what need is there to speak of [the bliss arising] when she is recognized as her true self?

The greatness of the Great One consists in the excellence of His good fortune, being cast into the midst of a crush of more than a thousand people on both banks of the Ānanda river. For this very reason it is said: "That which is the bliss of embodied beings... [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 4.9.10], and so forth;
and elsewhere as well:
"Even if this bliss of Brahman were multiplied by a parārdha, it would not equal even a single atom of the ocean of the bliss of devotion. Thus [it is said].

In the reading *adhokṣajālambam*, "that which has Adhokṣaja as its support" means that whose object of focus (*ālamba*) is Adhokṣaja. By implication, [it refers to that state] where He is the objective support.
The mellows of servitude, friendship, and so forth; by the terms "Lord of the heart" and "Master of the heart," devotion characterized by such states as servitude and the like is indicated. ||37||
O children of the asuras, what great effort is required for the worship of Hari, who resides within one’s own heart like a hole?
Since [the Self] is the friend of oneself and of all embodied beings alike, what is the use of providing objects [of enjoyment] in general?
Madhvaḥ: Because [He] resides in the hearts of all embodied beings in general. ||38||

Śrīdhara: One should not think that devotion is impossible; thus he says, "Who? [referring to verse 36]. For one who dwells in the heart like space—pervasive like the sky—what is the use of the procurement and acquisition of sense objects? The reason for this is that if all embodied beings were generally intent upon sense objects, it would result in their being no different from pigs and other such creatures.
This is the meaning. Nor is there the fault of tautology at the beginning, because this section consists of a restatement of what was spoken by Nārada. ||38||
The sequence of composition: generally, that of a friend (sakhi), as stated in the *Mundaka Upanishad* (3.1.1): "two friends who are united. ||39||
Viśvanātha says: Even though devotion is the most excellent [means], he states its ease of accomplishment with the words "Who... and so forth.

Like a void, like space, it belongs to the *ātman*, the individual soul (*jīva*), who is a friend—according to the Śruti: "The two who are united are friends" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1). The sense is that there is no difficulty whatsoever in the worship of one's own friend. Of the object of worship...

The sense is that because [the object] exists by its own nature and is beloved, and because the act of worship consists of [meditating upon] his lotus feet and so forth, and because the means for that—

such as the ears and other senses— are also inherently present, no collection of materials whatsoever needs to be brought from anywhere. It is better, indeed, to exert oneself even in the means for attaining hell.

Manifesting the engagement in sensual pleasure, he censures it: "What is the use of acquiring objects such as garlands, sandalwood, women, and so forth, through the procurement of wealth and other means? The reason for this is that if all embodied beings were generally intent upon sense-objects, it would result in their being no different from pigs and other such animals.
Such is the intended meaning. ||38||
Wealth, wife, cattle, sons and the like, houses, land, elephants, treasuries, and prosperity— these are all [transient].
All objects of desire, fleeting as a moment and unstable, can bring only how much joy to a mortal?

Śrīdhara says that the acquisition of sense-objects is useless: for one whose wealth consists of objects and whose life is momentary, how much pleasure can these things provide? As it is said in the Itihāsas:
"In this world, a man possesses wealth, or wealth possesses a man."
One must inevitably abandon one [of these]; therefore, what is the use of craving for wealth? (39)

*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: Nor does even sensual pleasure exist as a reality for those possessed by desire; thus he says: "Wealth" (*rāyaḥ*) means riches; and "objects" (*arthāḥ*) and "desires" (*kāmāḥ*). (39)
For thus these worlds, fashioned by sacrificial rites,
are subject to decay, characterized by inequality, and not pure.
Therefore, for the sake of attaining the Self, one should worship the Lord with devotion, setting aside all criticism of what has not been seen or heard.
Śrīdhara: That happiness which is unmixed with suffering, not followed immediately by its destruction, and free from the desire for more— that is the referent of the word "heaven."

He says "for thus" (evam hi) to show that even such enjoyments as those of heaven are not worthy of pursuit. The reason for their perishability is that they are "produced by sacrifices," according to the Vedic scripture: "Just as here the world acquired by action perishes, so there the world acquired by merit perishes" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.6). Therefore...

Thus, by the gradation of merit, they possess excellence but are not stainless, because they are characterized by rivalry and the like. That in which no perceived or heard defect exists [is the ultimate]. (40)
The sequence of the composition: "For the sake of attaining the Self" means for the sake of attaining one's own very self, who is the Lord. Alternatively, the sense is:
"Worship for the sake of attaining the Self; otherwise, you will destroy yourselves. (40)

Viśvanātha: He states that even the enjoyments of heaven and the like are not worthy of pursuit, saying "For thus... They are perishable, according to the Śruti: "Just as here the world acquired through action perishes, so there the world acquired through merit perishes" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.6). They are characterized by degrees of excellence according to the relative degree of merit.

Furthermore, because they consist of rivalry and the like, they are not pure. [They are practiced] for the sake of attaining the self—that is, for the attainment of Hari, whose agent is the self, or for the attainment of the Supreme Self; or else, for the acquisition of the jewel that is the nature of the self. Otherwise, it would be cast into the mire of heaven, hell, and so forth.
The intended meaning is that one should know it as already lost. ||40||
O you who are honored by the wise, whatever purpose a man repeatedly pursues here through his actions,
he obtains from that very effort an unfailing result, even if it turns out otherwise than expected.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, whatever one requests and whatever one resolves, from that resolution one inevitably obtains the opposite result—an unfailing fruit that is contrary to what was intended. ||41||
Kramasandarbha: This has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: Whatever is intended for a particular purpose, from that which was so intended, one inevitably obtains the opposite result—an unfailing fruit contrary to the intention. ||41||
The intention of an agent here for the sake of happiness and liberation from suffering always brings about suffering through striving; one who is free from striving is enveloped in happiness.
And it is said by the wise: "The effortless performance of honeyed [deeds] is called 'lack of striving' (anīhā). ||42||
Śrīdhara: He demonstrates that very point with the words "for the sake of happiness" (*sukhāya*). By "effort" (*īhayā*), he means by desire or by action.

The sequence of the argument is as follows: he who was previously covered—meaning pervaded—by happiness due to the absence of effort, necessarily encounters suffering through effort; this has not been explained [in detail].
Viśvanātha: Due to the absence of desire, one would be enveloped in happiness, that is, filled with bliss. ||42||
That body for the sake of which a person here desires objects of desire by means of desirable things— that indeed is another's property; fragile, it comes and goes.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, "desires" refers to enjoyments; [attained] through objects of desire or through ritual acts. It belongs to others—it is fit to be enjoyed by dogs and the like, not one's own—and it is fragile. ||43||
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: By means of rites performed for the sake of desired objects (*kāmya-karmabhiḥ*), [the impression] departs—that is, it perishes; yet it returns—that is, it arises once more for the purpose of bestowing suffering. ||43||
How much more so, then, those distant offspring, wives, houses, wealth, and the like;
the kingdom, the treasury, elephants, ministers, servants, and kinsmen— all these objects of "mine-ness."
Śrīdhara: Should it not be stated that children and the like—who are focused upon the body and so forth—are objects of possessiveness and belong to others? ||44||
The *Kramasaṃdarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— What is the use of these insignificant things of the self, along with this perishable body?
[He was deluded] by non-objects that appeared as objects, [and thus failed to reach] the ocean of the essence of eternal bliss.
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, since [the Self] is itself the very nature of the human goal (puruṣārtha), what use has it for these extremely insignificant things?
Thus he says: "What use have they? (verse 45).
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Of that person among the devotees whose own eternal ocean of the rasa of bliss consists of the nature of worship. ||45||
"O Asuras, consider here how much self-interest there is for one who bears a body and is tormented by karmas throughout the stages beginning with conception."
Śrīdhara: [Objection: Since there is no opportunity for enjoyment, what is the use of these? He says: "Let it be examined.
The sequence of the composition is: "of one who is being afflicted by past actions," or the connection is: "how much of his own interest is served by those actions? This has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: "Of one who is suffering" means that there is no opportunity for enjoyment at all; this is the sense. ||46||
The embodied being undertakes actions with the body that follows the self;
through those actions it expands the body, yet both [body and self] arise from a lack of discrimination.
Śrīdhara: Now, one might object that there would be an occasion for enjoyment only when the karmas are completed. To this he says: "The karmas...
This action, its fruit, and the body and so forth are not ultimately real; thus he says: "Both—the karma and the body—he expands through non-discrimination, that is, through ignorance alone. (47)
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: By means of the body—that is, the human body which is the instrument for performing action—one [identifies] with the body, namely the celestial body;
through non-discrimination (*aviveka*) regarding both of those two bodies, one thinks, "I am performing this action," and thus identifies with both.

Because the conceit "I am enjoying the fruit of my actions in heaven" is rooted in such conceit, and because that conceit is rooted in non-discrimination (aviveka), and because the Self is distinct from the two bodies. ||47||
Therefore, one should worship with desirelessness the Lord Hari, the effortless one, who is the refuge of wealth, desires, and dharma.
Śrīdhara: Wealth and the other [aims] have him as their refuge; they are dependent upon him. (48)

The sequence of the argument: "By effortless means that are free from limiting conditions, [I worship] the Effortless One who likewise possesses compassion free from limiting conditions; for I am desireless and Your devotee, while You are the Master who has no other refuge" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.10.6)—this is because it will be stated thus. ||48||
Viśvanātha: What, then, is discernment (*viveka*) itself? To this he says: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

The meaning is that the agency, enjoyment, and so forth of bulls (*anuḍuhaḥ*, i.e., oxen) are dependent upon, or subordinate to, their owner. [The Lord acts] "without effort" (*anīhayā*), that is, by being free from desire; He is "effortless" (*anīham*), meaning independent. ||48||
Hari is the Self, the Lord, and the Beloved of all beings;
He is designated as the individual soul (jīva) within those bodies created by the great elements fashioned by Himself.
And it is said: "Madhva is the seed of the world from its manifestation, not by way of measurement. ||49||
Śrīdhara: Of beings—that is, of living creatures—the one known as the *jīva* is the inner controller (*antaryāmī*). ||49||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: Since, in reality, for all beings—the body, the individual soul (*jīva*), the supreme self (*paramātman*), and even what is dear—the substance is indeed Hari alone, he says "worship Him" because He is the essence of all, including gods, animals, and so forth.

Moreover, that very Self is the Supreme Self and He alone is the Lord. Because He is the cause of all things created by His own acts, there arises the milk-like flow [of creation]; thus, He is the one to whom the designation "jīva" (individual soul) has occurred, since the jīva is of the nature of His external (taṭastha) potency. Or rather, because He is dear to all, it is He alone [who is meant].
He says, "Worship [Me]," meaning: [I am] dearer even than that which is called the 'living soul' (jīva)— the name for all beings—
whether one be a god, an asura, a human, a yakṣa, or even a gandharva.
By worshipping the feet of Mukunda, one shall become possessed of well-being, just as we are.
Śrīdhara: Nor should it be said that we Asuras have no entitlement here; thus he says with five verses beginning with "The Lord" (deva). ||50||
Kramasandarbha: This has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: Since this is so, he says "The Lord" (deva) [in verse 50], meaning that therefore everyone should indeed practice devotion.
O sons of the asuras, neither the status of a twice-born, nor divinity, nor the state of a seer is sufficient to please Mukunda; neither conduct nor extensive knowledge [achieves this].
Śrīdhara: Not explained.
Sanātana Gosvāmī: O sons of the Asuras! Devahood and the like are not sufficient—that is, not capable—of pleasing Mukunda. Vṛtta refers to virtuous conduct. [Ha.bha.vi. 11.590]
The sequence of composition: "Not sufficient," this constitutes a pair of verses (yugmaka). ||51||
Viśvanātha: The meaning is that it is not *prīṇana*, i.e., not capable [of satisfying]. ||51||
Neither charity, nor austerity, nor sacrifice, nor purity, nor vows please Hari; He is pleased only by stainless devotion; everything else is a mere mockery.
Śrīdhara: "With the stainless [mind], meaning free from desire; anything else is mere mockery, nothing more than a performance. (52)

Sanātana Gosvāmī: "By means of that which is stainless, desireless, or pure. "Mere imitation" means it is merely a performance, not something real. [Ha.bha.vi. 11.591] Krama-sandarbha: Not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: The meaning is that [this] is, on the contrary, a mockery of man and a cause for his humiliation.
Therefore, O Dānavas, cultivate devotion toward Hari, the Blessed Lord.
By means of the analogy of oneself, one should regard the self of all beings everywhere as the Lord.
Śrīdhara: This has not been explained.

Krama-sandarbha: Regarding the word "tat" (that), in all places and at all times, by means of the analogy of oneself (*ātmaupamya*), perform worship in the form of the activities of body, mind, and speech with favorableness toward the Self.
"Do likewise," [he said]. ||53||
Viśvanātha: Regarding the phrase "by way of comparison with oneself," the ellipsis is "having observed [their] pleasure, pain, and so forth. ||53||
Daityas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, women, Śūdras, the inhabitants of Vraja,
birds, beasts, and those of sinful livelihood— indeed, all have attained the state of Acyuta.
Madhvaḥ: the state of being unshakable, which is the avoidance of falling away. ||54||
Śrīdhara: "Acyutatām" means immortality. ||54||

Regarding the sequence of the text: because the inhabitants of Vraja are mentioned here in conjunction with low-born peoples—as in passages such as "the Kirātas, Hūṇas, Āndhras, Pulindas, Pulkasas, Ābhīras, Kaṅkas, Yavanas, Khasas, and others" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 2.4.18)—it should be understood that the Ābhīras are indeed a specific low-caste group who subsist on worldly existence (*bhava*). It is not otherwise.

"Agriculture, trade, cattle-rearing, and usury are said to be the fourth; this is the fourfold livelihood (vārtā). Among these, we are constantly engaged in the occupation of cowherding. [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.24.21]
In this way, the distinction that there are various types of Vaiśyas is to be understood. ||54||
Viśvanātha: Nor does devotion depend upon noble birth and the like; thus he says, "The sons of Diti," etc.

"Imperishability" (*acyutatām*) means equality with Acyuta by virtue of having a body composed of consciousness (*cinmaya*). Alternatively, "having attained imperishability" (*acyutatām*) means that they do not fall away, unlike those who merely perform ritual actions (*karmiṇaḥ*). As it is said in the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa*:
My devotees do not fall even in the great calamity of universal dissolution;
therefore, they are celebrated by the wise throughout the entire world as "Acyuta" (the Imperishable). 54.
This alone is considered the supreme self-interest for a person in this world:
exclusive devotion to Govinda and seeing Him everywhere.
Śrīdhara: He concludes what was stated in the two preceding chapters with the words "this much" (etāvān). That very act of looking [at Govinda] is an honoring by the vision of Govinda. ||55||

The sequence of composition: his vision and manifestation of that [Lord] occurs only within the Bhāgavata, according to such passages as, "He who sees [the Lord] in all beings" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.2.45). ||55||

Viśvanātha: Exclusive devotion (*ekānta-bhakti*) is non-dual devotion (*ananyā bhakti*), which means that when such devotion exists, there is the vision of Him—that is, the vision of the Lord—in all things, both stationary and moving, through the ripening of contemplation upon the Lord. As it has been said:
"The wise who seek the ultimate truth perceive the world as consisting of Nārāyaṇa; the greedy see it as consisting of wealth, and those full of desire see it as consisting of women.
Just so, this Prahlāda perceived the Blessed One even in a pillar. (55)
Thus ends the seventh chapter of the *Sārārthadarśinī*, the *Harṣiṇī* commentary for those whose hearts are devoted, which has been perfectly composed for the sake of the virtuous.

Thus ends the instruction for Bāla, titled "The Instruction for Bāla," in the seventh book of the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam*, the great Purāṇa, which is a commentary on the *Brahma-sūtras*, in the Vaiyāsiki collection concerning the state of the Paramahaṃsas.
The Seventh Chapter.
Now begins the eighth chapter:
The Slaying of Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Śrī Nārada said:
Then all the sons of the Daityas, having heard that description,
did not at all accept what had been taught by their preceptor, because it was faultless.
Śrīdhara:
In the eighth [chapter], the Daitya, while slaying his son with excessive rage, was himself killed;
having manifested as Nṛsiṃha, he was praised by Brahmā and the other gods.
Filled with the nectar of compassion within, the Man-Lion manifested outward anger; he regarded the lord of the Daityas, who was serving him with enmity, with equanimity.

The structural arrangement of the commentary verse: "Worshipping him as an enemy"—because he acted according to his command, she caused him, who was worshipping her only externally, to perceive himself toward her as one devoid of such [external] intent. ||1||
Viśvanātha:
In the eighth [chapter], the demon Stambha killed his own son out of rage;
Nṛsiṃha, praised by the gods, arose from that pillar and slew him in person. (1)
Then the teacher’s son, perceiving that their minds were fixed on a single point,
became alarmed and quickly reported the matter to the king exactly as it was.
Śrīdhara: [He spoke] regarding the final goal situated in solitude, exactly as it is. ||2||

Kramasandarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: "Ekānta" means that which is both primary (*eka*) and the end (*anta*) of all things; it refers to devotion to Viṣṇu (*viṣṇubhaktiyoga*). [She is] established therein. ||2||
Having heard that unpleasant and unbearable misconduct of his son, the Daitya,
his limbs trembling with a fit of rage, set his mind on killing his son.
Having addressed Prahrāda, who did not deserve such treatment, with harsh words.
Śrīdhara: And he set his mind upon killing his son. Of what nature was he? He was one whose body and limbs were trembling due to the intensity of the onset of anger. (3)

Regarding the sequence of composition: the half-verse beginning with "śrutvā" does not exist in the Gauḍa and Mithilā recensions and is inconsistent with the author's own intent, as the supply of the word "sa" (he) would be redundant. (3)
Viśvanātha: Not explained.
—o)0(o— One who looks with a sinful, sidelong glance...
To him who stood bowed in humility, self-controlled, with palms joined in reverence,
the serpent— naturally cruel— hissed like one struck by a foot.

Śrīdhara: *kṣiptvā* means having cast aside or disregarded; *pāpena* means with anger; *tiraścīnena* means crookedly. This is the sequence of the composition. Viśvanātha has not commented [on this]. —o)0(o—
Śrī Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"O ill-behaved one, O dull-witted one, O lowest of those who cause family dissension!
Today I shall send you, stiff with pride and rebellious against my command, to the abode of Yama."
Śrīdhara: O dull-witted one! O man of small intellect! Today I shall lead you, who have transgressed my command, to the abode of Yama.
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "O Durvinīta! This is the literal meaning of the name: he whose characteristic compassion is directed even toward the wicked; and he in whom the minds of even the dull-witted find rest because of his inability to endure the suffering of others.
Because they attract all minds, they cause divisions among families and create various lineages;

therefore, even the Prajāpatis are inferior, for despite their great power, they are arrogant and lack the realization that [I] am worthy of worship among the Asuras. "One who has turned away from my teaching" means one who transgresses my command. That which...

The meaning is: "I shall lead you—who are the imperishable abode of Yama, yet who, on the other hand, are the dwelling place of the destruction of the eightfold limbs of yoga—to myself as my own protector. ||6||
"—O fool! When I am enraged, the three worlds together with their lords tremble; why, then, with what strength have you transgressed my command as if you were fearless?"
Śrīdhara: Fearlessly. What strength? What power? ||7||
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: As if fearless; he is one whose strength is what? [He is one who possesses such strength. ||7||
Śrī Prahlāda said:
O King, this is not true for me alone, nor even for you.
He is indeed the strength of the strong and of others as well;
he by whom all these— superior and inferior, whether stationary or moving,
from Brahmā downwards— have been brought under his control.
He is the Lord, Time, and He of the wide stride; He is vigor, endurance, and the essence of existence, strength, and the senses.
He alone is the supreme universe through His own powers.
The Lord of the three qualities creates, protects, and devours.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
Abandon this asuric nature of yours!
Set your mind on equanimity; there are no enemies other than the self that has strayed onto the wrong path.
For that indeed is the great worship of the Infinite One.
Regarding "madhvaḥ": from that which is endowed with twelve qualities—
namely, knowledge, truthfulness, self-restraint, tranquility, lack of envy, modesty, forbearance, and freedom from malice.
"Charity, sacrifice, austerity, and sacred learning—these twelve are the great vows of a Brāhmaṇa," so it is said in the *Mahābhārata* (5.43.12). //9//

Śrīdhara: The reason why they were brought under control is stated as "He is the Lord" (sa īśvaraḥ). He is one whose strides or foot-falls (kramāḥ) are vast; or, he is one of great prowess (bahu-parākrama). He consists of forms such as *ojas* and so forth. *Sattvam* means fortitude or intelligence. ||10||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "Abandon" means cast away. Make your own mind equal—make it the same everywhere as if toward yourself. [Objection: But how can I make my mind equal toward enemies?

To this he says: "Enemies" (vidviṣaḥ) means adversaries; they do not exist at all except for the unconquered, uncontrolled mind. When that [control] exists—namely, equanimity (sāmya), characterized by seeing one's own self everywhere—the state of mastery (vaśībhāva) is attained.
Since no adversaries are seen when that is present, the sense is that there are no enemies whatsoever. That very thing is equanimity toward all.
Thus, *samarhaṇa* is *ārādhana*. ||9||
Some believe that in ancient times, after conquering the Dasyus, ten directions were seized by those who plundered them as if they were mere game.
For the self-conquered, wise, equanimous, and virtuous embodied being, how could there be others arising from one's own delusion?
Śrīdhara: [Objection: But how can he who is my enemy be my strength? To this he says: "Abandon. Abandon your own state, your very nature.
For there are no enemies other than the unconquered self—the mind. Furthermore, that indeed is [the means], for it is by means of equanimity (*sāmyena*)...
The very holding of the mind is itself worship and propitiation.

If you should say, "Indeed, all enemies were conquered by me during my conquest of the quarters; therefore, there are currently no foes," that is true. To this, he says: "the bandits. Some dull-witted people like yourself [thought] in the beginning—that is, formerly—that they were destroying them.

Those who have not conquered the enemies characterized by the six senses—which steal away everything—yet consider themselves to have personally conquered the ten directions, are fools; for the virtuous man whose mind is conquered, who is equal toward all embodied beings, and who is wise and learned, how could there be any other enemies imagined through his own ignorance? (10)
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Some—those dull-witted like you—who plunder thieves such as desire and the rest, seize their entire possessions even while they remain within their own grasp;
yet, without having conquered the ten directions, they consider them conquered by themselves.
They think thus: for one who has conquered the mind, by that very conquest of the mind, the six adversaries have already been defeated;
therefore, for what reason could there be further enemies for the wise and learned man? Indeed, the meaning is that there would be none at all.
This is because [all enemies] originate from one's own delusion. (10)
Śrī Hiraṇyakaśipu said:
"It is evident that you desire death, since you boast so excessively."
For indeed, O dull-witted one, the words of those who are about to die must surely be faltering.
Śrīdhara: "Vyaktam" means certainly. The meaning is that they are "viplava," i.e., disconnected. ||11||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: The meaning is that you boast—on account of being a devotee of Hari—you say, "I alone have conquered the six enemies, and not my father," thus engaging in self-praise. [The words] *viklavāḥ* mean "incoherent" or "irrelevant. (11)
"—O you of little fortune! As for that Lord of the World other than me whom you mentioned, where is he?
If he is everywhere, why is he not seen in this pillar?"

Śrīdhara said: "O unfortunate one, if there is a Lord of the Universe other than me, then where is He? Prahlāda replied: "He is everywhere. Hiraṇyakaśipu asked: "Then why is He not in this pillar? Prahlāda, however, while gazing at that pillar and bowing down to it, said:
He said: "It is seen. (12)

*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: "O unfortunate one! The sense is: just as the sovereignty over the world belongs to me, so too does it rightfully belong to you because you are my daughter; yet it is being abandoned by you.
"If he exists, then where does he exist? Prahlāda said, "He is everywhere. Hiraṇyakaśipu asked, "Why is he not in the pillar? Prahlāda, looking at it with a bow, replied, "He is seen. (12)
Therefore, I shall sever from your body the head of you who boast so much.
Let Hari protect you today, he whom you desire as your refuge."
Śrīdhara: But Hiraṇyakaśipu, not seeing him there, said: "So am I!
[The sequence of the argument is: regarding the phrase "vikatthamānasya," it refers to self-praise consisting of various such utterances while speaking falsely.
Because of the finality [of the teaching]. ||13||
Viśvanātha: Thereupon, Hiraṇyakaśipu, not seeing him, said: "That is I. (13)
Thus, repeatedly afflicting his son, the great devotee of the Lord, with harsh words out of anger, the great asura—
Grasping his sword, the exceedingly powerful one leapt from his excellent seat and struck the pillar with his own fist.
Śrīdhara: While Prahlāda was looking on with his palms joined in reverence upon his head, [the Lord] struck the pillar with His fist. ||14||
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— At that very moment, in that [place], there was an exceedingly terrifying roar.
By him the shell of the cosmic egg was shattered; indeed,
O dear one, when Brahmā and the other gods perceived him arrived at his own station,
they realized that their own abodes had come to an end.
Śrīdhara: [Not commented upon].
Viśvanātha: The meaning is "with indistinct cries. *Ninadam* means sound; *atyayam* means destruction. ||15||
Desiring the slaughter of his son, that Vikrama, hearing with his might that unprecedented and wonderful roar, [acted].
Within the assembly hall he did not see that foot by which the leaders of the hosts of the enemies of the gods had been struck with terror.
Śrīdhara: That "pada" is the locus of that sound; by which resonance... ||16||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: That is the locus, the substratum, of that [type of] suggestion (dhvani). ||16||
— to make true the words spoken by his own servant, and to demonstrate the pervasiveness of the Self within all beings.
Bearing an exceedingly wonderful form that was invisible, neither beast nor human, he stood within the pillar in the assembly hall.
Śrīdhara: At that time, the Blessed One, having split the pillar, became visible; he became visible for what purpose?
To make true—that is, to fulfill—what had been spoken by his own servant Prahlāda, namely, "I am seen. Likewise, to make manifest his pervasion of all beings as a reality.

He appeared upon the pillar. For what purpose? To make true that which had been spoken by that very servant—that the Blessed One dwells within elemental beings, as well as within the great elements—while assuming and bearing a most wondrous, exceedingly terrible form that slays the Daityas.

For what purpose was this? It was to make true that which was spoken by his own servants, Sanaka and the others, who were filled with remorse after receiving the curse: "May our release from the curse come about through three births.
Thus, he assumed such a most wonderful form—a form never seen nor heard of before in the creation of Brahmā. That...

And why was he seen in the midst of the assembly bearing neither the form of a deer nor the form of a human? Because Hiraṇyakaśipu, his own servant, had spoken thus to Brahmā: "O Lord, let there be no death for me from any beings created by you" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.3.35).
Thus, [it is said]: "neither within nor without," and "neither by men nor even by wild beasts" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.3.36).
Furthermore, in order to make true the words spoken by both—the Lord Brahmā and his own servant, who had replied, "So be it"—[the Lord acted].
For that being was not created by Brahmā, nor was it a man or a beast;
