it was neither inside the assembly hall nor outside in the courtyard. Thus, in order to make true what had been spoken by those two, and in contradiction to what had been spoken by Hiraṇyakaśipu—
"Death shall come to me," and "I am immortal, having no fear from any quarter" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.5.47);
and that which was spoken by his own servant Nārada to Indra: "This great one shall not meet his end at your hands; he is an attendant of Ananta" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.7.10).

Furthermore, that which was spoken regarding His partiality toward His own devotees was made true by Him appearing in such a manner; He thus fulfilled His own statement. What was that? "O son of Kuntī, know for certain: My devotee perishes not" (Gītā 9.31), and likewise, "I am their deliverer."
"From the ocean of death and saṃsāra" (Gītā 12.7), and so forth. And that truth must be seen as being invisible; enough with excessive detail. ||17||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: The meaning is that [the Lord spoke thus] so that the statement "the speech of His own servant Prahlāda is seen" might be made true, and so that truth itself might be manifested as truth even in that world.

In that very manner, in order to make manifest the pervasion of His own form as Nṛsiṃha and others throughout all things, He was seen appearing within the pillar. Of what nature was He? He was not bearing the form of a deer, nor the form related to a deer, nor even a human form within the assembly; the reason for this is stated: "truly" (satyam). [He appeared] to His own servant...

In order to make true the words spoken by Hiraṇyakaśipu— namely, "O Lord, let there be no death for me from any beings created by You" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.3.35), as well as "Neither within nor without," and "Neither by men nor even by beasts" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.3.36)— He did so because that [promise] was not otherwise possible.

Neither a being created by Brahmā, nor a man, nor a beast, [is present] inside the assembly hall, nor even outside like in the courtyard. And thus, some explain that this was said in order to make the words of his own servants, such as Nārada and others, true. Nevertheless, O son of Kuntī, you must promise: "No..."

"My devotee does not perish" (Gītā 9.31)—this was spoken by Him Himself; "This great one shall not meet his end" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.7.10)—this was spoken by Nārada to Indra; "Surely my death will come about through him" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.5.47)—this was spoken by Hiraṇyakaśipu. By Hiraṇyakaśipu...
And when the bridegroom was being chosen, Brahmā said, "So be it. ||17||
He gazed all around at that being as it was emerging from the middle of the pillar.
This is neither a deer nor a man; oh, what a wondrous thing is this form that is both human and that of the king of beasts!

Śrīdhara: Having heard such a wonderful sound, that Daitya looked in every direction for the creature—the specific living being—to which it belonged; then, seeing a form that was a mixture of man and lion emerging from the middle of the pillar, he reflected, "Aha! What is this?"—this is the implied meaning. ||18||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Enough of this; his form as the Man-Lion is exceedingly terrifying. (18)
As he was thus reflecting, there arose before him the form of Nṛsiṃha, which was exceedingly terrifying.
Śrīdhara: As he was thus contemplating that terrifying form of Nṛsiṃha, Hari appeared before him in the form of Nṛsiṃha.
Krama-sandarbha: Regarding the phrase "mīmāṃsā," there are three and a half verses; therein, "mīmāṃsā" constitutes half a verse. (19)
Viśvanātha: The grammatical construction is that, as he was thus reflecting, the form of Nṛsiṃha arose right before him. ||19||
With eyes fierce like molten gold and a mouth agape with quivering manes and whiskers;
With formidable fangs, a tongue as flickering as a sword with razor-sharp edges, and a face made terrifying by a frown;
Śrīdhara: Demonstrating the very nature of its terror, he describes that form with the passage beginning with "pratapta" and ending with "vidrāvita-daitya-dānavam.
[It is] that in which the fierce eyes are tawny like heated *cāmīkara* (gold); [and] the mane...

Jaṭāḥ means manes; kesaraḥ refers to the hair on the neck. It is that in which the face is expanded with pride by means of quivering manes and tufts of hair (saṭākesaraiḥ). Karālāḥ means prominent fangs, which are present in it. Karavālaḥ means a sword;
like that, the tongue in it is flickering and sharp as the edge of a razor. [The face is] endowed with a frown (bhrukuṭī-yuktena).
With his mouth wide open. ||20||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: Explaining the state of being terrifying (*bhayānakatva*), he qualifies the form with three [epithets]. "Pratapta" refers to *cāmīkara*, which is gold. *Saṭā* means matted hair (*jaṭā*); *kesarāḥ* means the hairs on the neck. *Karavāla* is a sword (*khaḍga*).
With a face knit with a frown, it was formidable. ||20||
with ears stiffly erect, with mouth and nose gaping wide in a manner as wondrous as a mountain cave, and terrifying with the protrusion of his jaw—
His body reaches to the heavens, with a neck, thighs, and chest that are neither too long nor too thick, and a slender waist.
Śrīdhara: That in which the ears are stiff, elevated, and upright like stakes;
that in which the mouth is wide open and gaping like a mountain cave, and the nostrils likewise;
and that which is terrifying due to the separation—that is, the parting—of the jaws (the ends of the cheeks), with the expanse of the mouth reaching as far as the ears.

This is the meaning. "Touching the heavens" refers to the body; this is an *aluk* compound. That which has a neck that is not long, but short and thick (stout); and that which has broad and expansive chest; and that which has a small waist and belly. ||21||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Terrifying due to the separation—that is, the splitting apart—of the jaws (*hana*), meaning the edges of the cheeks;
that in which the neck is neither long nor thick; and that in which the chest is broad and expansive.
It has small joints with the middle sections diminished; it possesses hundreds of arms stationed in all directions like moonbeams, white and fair, and its nails are like weapons. ||21||
His body was covered with body hair as white as the rays of the moon,
and his hundreds of arms on all sides had nails for weapons.
Unassailable, he had routed the Daityas and Dānavas with the excellence of all his own weapons.
Śrīdhara: [The body] is strewn—that is, pervaded—by body hairs that are as white as moonbeams.
It is that in which there are hundreds of multitudes—that is, throngs—of arms extending in all directions;
and in which the very claws are the weapons. It is difficult to approach, meaning it is impossible to attain. And all...

His own [weapons] were the discus and so forth, while the others were the thunderbolt and so forth; these very ones are the "pre-eminent weapons" (āyudha-pravekāḥ), meaning the best of arms. With them, the Daityas and Dānavas were routed. That form, which arose before him as he was scrutinizing it, is to be connected with the preceding verse. ||23||
The sequence of composition: [it occurs] in the moon; the arms themselves are the *anīkas*, the armies. ||22||

Viśvanātha: "All his own [weapons], such as the discus and others, as well as the other [divine weapons] such as the thunderbolt and so forth—those very preeminent armaments; that [place] where the Daityas and Dānavas were routed by those most excellent of missiles. —o)0(o—
"Is this slaughter of mine by the one who deceives with deer-like thighs [the deer] remembered by him as he stands ready?"
Speaking thus, that elephant among the Daityas, armed with a mace, rushed roaring toward the Man-lion.
Śrīdhara: [This describes] the encounter between him and the Daitya, preceded by an investigation into the purpose of his manifestation.

He describes the battle with seven verses: "Generally, this very kind of slaughter by the great illusionist Hari was remembered—that is, considered—by me as the cause of my death; nevertheless, thinking 'What could happen from him even if he were prepared?', he rushed forward. This is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*). ||23||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Having seen that wonder, he describes his mental and verbal conduct with the words "mostly" (*prāyeṇa*). That it was "remembered as a slaughter" (*vadhaḥ smṛtaḥ*) meant it was already intended to be done previously; now...

The meaning is that it has been made the object of his recollection. Even by this Hari, who is prepared—that is, who has exerted effort for that purpose—it is "nothing at all," meaning not even a little; the sense is that because my power is difficult for him to overcome. ||23||
Then that asura fell unobserved into the splendor of Nṛsiṃha, like a moth falling into a fire.
It is indeed not surprising that he, who formerly drank up the darkness by his own splendor within the realm of sentient beings, should now do so once more.

Śrīdhara: Then that asura, having fallen into the blazing splendor of Nṛsiṃha’s majesty, became unperceived—that is, unseen. It is not surprising that one consisting of darkness (tamas) becomes invisible when falling upon Hari, who is the abode of goodness (sattva) and the light of goodness; for this is the reason: Hari, who formerly...
At the beginning of creation, he drank up the darkness belonging to the time of dissolution within that [egg]. ||24||
Krama-sandarbha: This has not been explained.

Viśvanātha: Having fallen into the splendor—that is, the radiance—of Nṛsiṃha’s prowess, he became unobserved, meaning unseen. That invisibility of his, who was composed of darkness (tamas), occurred within Hari, the abode of *sattva*, which is the manifestation of pure *sattva*.

It is not surprising; for in the past, at the beginning of creation, he destroyed the darkness of the dissolution period only by presiding over the *mahat*-tattva. What need is there to mention now, when it is his very own essential nature? Such is the meaning. ||24||
Then, having approached, the great asura struck the Man-Lion in fury with a mace of immense velocity.
As he was thus advancing with his mace, Gadādhara seized him just as the son of Tārkṣya seizes a great serpent.
Śrīdhara: "Moving here and there" means striking [the enemy] from various directions. "Slipped from the hand" means having escaped.
*Krama-sandarbha*: This has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: "From there" means having become separate from that [place], "having approached" means having come forward toward him. (25)
Then that Asura, seized by his hand,
was like a serpent sported with by Garuḍa.
O Bhārata, the immortals who dwell in all the celestial abodes, their own domains having been seized, considered this act unrighteous when they were shrouded by the clouds.

Śrīdhara: Then all the immortals, the gods who protect the celestial abodes (*dhiṣṇya-pā*), considered this to be improper. They were those whose dwellings and places had been taken away. Out of fear of that, being covered by thick clouds—that is, hidden by the clouds—the sequence [of the narrative] was not explained.

Viśvanātha: [The arrow] has slipped from his hand; it has been discharged. "These [clouds], with their thick covering, desire to witness my slaughter"—out of fear of the Daityas' wrath, they have hidden themselves behind the clouds.
Thinking, "He has seized our dwellings," they consider it improper; thus, he has indeed now taken away their abodes. If this is so...
The sense is: "If he lives, he will take away even our remaining life-breaths. ||26||
Thinking that Narahari, released from whose hand he was, was suspicious of his own prowess, that great asura— (o)0(o— taṃ manyamāno nija-vīrya-śaṅkitaṃ yad-dhasta-mukto nṛhariṃ mahāsuraḥ |)
Seizing his sword and shield once more, he rushed forward with speed into the fray, free from fatigue.

Śrīdhara: The syntactical connection and sequence of the words is as follows: "Thinking that Nṛhari, from whose hand he himself had been released, was [still] apprehensive of his own prowess, he seized sword and shield and attacked him again. This has not been explained [in detail].
Viśvanātha, considering himself threatened by his own prowess, released him from his hands—
that one with the speed of a hawk— along paths adorned with a hundred moons.
Hari moves without interruption above and below.
Letting out a loud, harsh, and resonant laugh with eyes closed, he of great speed seized him.

Śrīdhara: [He saw him] whose speed was like that of a hawk; moving above and below in such a way as to leave no gap through the paths of sword and shield—which are like the tracks of a hundred moons—he uttered a loud laugh (*aṭṭahāsa*): harsh and intense, formidable with its great resonance and terrifying sound.
Out of fear of him and because of Hari’s splendor, his eyes were closed, being deprived of their own luster.
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Him whose eyes were closed out of fear arising from the sound of the "attahāsa" laughter [of Śiva], by means of the paths of sword and shield [which resembled] a hundred moons. ||28||
Like a serpent seizing a rat whose skin was unscarred by the thunderbolt, Hari seized him as he was quivering in all directions, seized by the madness of grasping.
Leaping at the door, he playfully tore at her thigh with his claws, just as Garuḍa tears at a highly venomous serpent.

Śrīdhara: The illustration for seizing is as follows—a snake [seizing] a rat or mouse. The illustration for tearing apart is—as Garuḍa [tearing apart] a serpent. "Flashing forth on all sides" means emerging everywhere.
By seizing, he renders the enemy helpless. It was not by the thunderbolt wielded by Indra in battle.

Even he whose skin was wounded, neither inside nor outside the assembly hall at the gate; having thrown him from lap to lap, neither on the ground nor in the air; with his nails, neither while lifeless nor while still possessing life—thus it should be understood that this was done at twilight in order to avoid [the act] by day or by night. ||29||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: "As a cat [seizes] a mouse" is an illustration for seizing; "as Garuḍa [seizes] a snake" is for tearing apart. "Even his skin was unscarred by the thunderbolt"—[this refers to him] with mere ease, that is, with utter nonchalance.

He tore [her], neither at the door nor in the assembly hall, neither inside nor outside; he struck thigh against thigh, neither on the ground nor in the air; with his claws, neither those who were lifeless nor those who were living. Thus, it should be understood that he avoided [these times] by day and by night, [attacking] during the twilight. ||29||
With eyes fierce and difficult to behold due to his fury,
he licked the corners of his wide-gaping mouth with his own tongue.
With his face and mane reddened by drops of blood, he was like a lion after slaying an elephant, adorned with a garland of entrails.
Śrīdhara: Having described the slaughter of the Daityas, he describes the slaughter of their servants with two verses.

He whose eyes were formidable and difficult to behold due to his fury; whose face and limbs were red—because they were sprinkled and moistened with drops (lavas) of blood (asṛj), and for that very reason crimson; who was he like?

By the slaying of the island-dweller—that is, by the killing of the elephant—Hari, like a lion, became such [a being] and killed his followers; this is the connection with the following verse. He is one who has a garland of entrails upon his neck. (30)
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "Smeared" means sprinkled with drops or particles of blood (*asṛj*). For this very reason, his filaments and face are reddish. "Wearing a garland of weapons" means he bears weapons in the form of a garland.
Like a lion accompanied by the slaughter of an elephant—that is, by the killing of a tusker—[so was Hari]. ||30||
Having torn out the lotus of his heart with the sprout of his nail,
he cast aside his followers who stood with raised weapons.
With my multitude of staff-like arms, I slew by the thousands all those who followed me, using my nails as weapons.

Śrīdhara: [He refers to Him] whose heart-lotus was uprooted by the sprouts of [Kṛṣṇa’s] nails; he who possesses multitudes—that is, groups—of staff-like arms. "Those whose path follows that of the lord of the Daityas" means others as well who have joined his side. ||31||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: He whose heart-lotus has been uprooted by the sprouts of [her] nails; he who, once I myself dwelt there in happiness at every moment, is now, alas, this unfortunate one.

The poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*)—as if [the Lord] were desiring to see how he might dwell within the tamasic qualities such as anger and envy—is manifested through the metaphor (*rūpaka*) of the lotus. For this very reason, the metaphor of the "sprout" is understood precisely to prevent the destruction of the lotus. He is the one who possesses multitudes of staff-like arms.
Those who follow along and act in accordance [with them]. ||31||
Shaken by his trident, the clouds fell away,
and the planets lost their luster, eclipsed by the radiance of his gaze.
The oceans were agitated, struck by his breath;
the elephants of the quarters shrieked, terrified by his roar.
Śrīdhara: With two verses, he describes the majestic display of Nṛhari, who was intent on slaying the Daityas.
"The clouds were shaken and struck down by his manes; they fell and were shattered.
(By this, he gave the command: "Let those gods who were hidden by the clouds see clearly.")
[The meaning: By his gaze, the luster of those planets whose light was stolen away became eclipsed; this is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. The *dig-ibhās* are the elephants of the quarters. ||32||
The *Kramasandarbhā*: not explained.
Viśvanātha: He describes his majesty with the words beginning "saṭā" (mane), etc. ||32||
The sky was crowded with celestial chariots tossed upward by his hair,
and the earth, pressed down by his feet, sank away.
The mountains leapt up by his speed,
and by his splendor, neither the sky nor the quarters of the horizon remained still.
Śrīdhara: Being crowded with—that is, pervaded by—the celestial chariots tossed up by its manes, it moved forward from its own place, meaning it surged forth and shifted away. ||33||

Kramasandarbha: This has not been explained. Viśvanātha: The earth was crowded—that is, pervaded—by aerial chariots tossed upward by their manes and set in motion; and "protsarpata" [is used] with the absence of the augment *aṭ* and the substitution of *taṅ* (the middle voice ending), which is Vedic.
He remained in the states of the horizontal, the upward, and the downward. ||33||
Then, the Lord, whose splendor was fully gathered, sat upon an excellent royal throne in the assembly hall.
No one could face him, who was intolerant, with a fierce countenance, and whose duel was unnoticed [by others].
Śrīdhara, regarding his own servants’ power as something wonderful, sat upon his seat out of curiosity;
yet, out of fear, no one approached or served him, nor did anyone notice his opponent in the duel. (34)
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: [He is] seated upon the royal throne, as if demonstrating the maxim of statecraft that whoever overcomes another assumes that person's authority; or else, [as follows].

Even toward his own servant who was seized by a curse, he manifested an absence of abandoning his self-respect; for that very Lord, who indeed would not personally accept even those offerings such as seats— which were presented by the sages themselves, free from other intentions, and purified by mantras— nevertheless accepted them when offered by his own devotee, even though that devotee was possessed by a demonic nature.

The truth is this: that he personally occupied the throne—which had been lost due to a curse, was not rightfully his to give, and had even been enjoyed by another—demonstrated to all the power of his own devotion.
He possessed accumulated splendor and full radiance, such that no rival warrior capable of engaging him in a duel was perceived.
No one, even though devoted, attended upon him with fans and such out of fear; no one served him. ||34||
Having heard that the primordial Daitya, who was a fever to the heads of the three worlds, had been slain in battle by Hari;
With their faces uplifted by the surge of great joy, the celestial women repeatedly rained down showers of flowers.

Śrīdhara: The celestial women, their faces blooming with the intensity of great joy as if it were a headache unbearable like a fever at the crown of the three worlds, showered the Man-Lion with rains of flowers. (35)
Kramasandarbha: Not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: Having perceived—that is, having seen—the fever of the head as it were, unbearable. (35)
Then the surface of the sky became crowded with rows of celestial chariots belonging to the gods who desired to behold him.
Then the drums of the Suras resounded; the chief Gandharvas danced, and the women sang.

Śrīdhara: The expanse of the sky was crowded with rows of celestial chariots belonging to the *nākas*, the gods. The drums (*ānaka*) and kettledrums (*paṭaha*) of the deities were beaten and sounded. The women, the *apsarases*, danced;
the *gandharvas* sang. (36)
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: It was (āsa) / became (babhūva) for the *nākas*, that is, the inhabitants of heaven (*svargiṇaḥ*). ||36||
Then,
having approached that place, the gods led by Brahmā, Indra,
and Śiva, as well as the ṛṣis, the ancestors, the siddhas, the vidyādharas, and the great serpents [gathered].
The Manavas, the Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis), the Gandharvas, Apsaras, and Cāraṇas;
the Yakṣas, Kimpuruṣas, O dear one, and the Vetālas together with the Kinnaras.
All those attendants of Viṣṇu, headed by Sunanda and Kumuda,
standing not too far away with their palms joined in reverence upon their heads, praised individually that tiger among men as he sat there, blazing with intense splendor.
Śrīdhara: The meaning is "the Gandharvas, the Apsarases, and the Cāraṇas. [38] "The tiger among men, the Supreme Person. [39]
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: "Apsarasaś cāraṇaś" is an archaic (ārṣa) form. ||38||
Śrī Brahmā said:
I bow down to the Infinite One, whose power is boundless.
Salutations to the one of manifold vigor and pure deeds,
the imperishable Self who, by means of his own powers, through his divine play, effects the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe.
Śrīdhara:
Brahmā and the others, their minds agitated by fear of Nṛsiṃha,
praised him from afar with seventeen verses, each separately.

I bow to you, the infinite, in order to propitiate you who are beyond all limits. The reason for your infinity is that your powers are boundless. Why is that? Because your heroic exploits and majestic powers are manifold. For what purpose [do I bow]? Because your deeds are purifying, cleansing merely by being heard.

He speaks of the very nature of his manifold heroism with the words "of the universe" (*viśvasya*). "They perform" (*sandadhate*) means they act correctly. Even so, [he acts] for the sake of the Imperishable Self (*avyayātmane*), whose essential nature is never lost. ||40||
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: You provoke Sanaka and the others; you cause them to fall from their own devotion; you cause me to grant boons; and you manifest the King of Devotees in the house of a demon. Having incited the demon, [you favor] the devotee...
He says, "I bow," because no one knows Your intended purpose when You thus manifest Yourself for the sake of protecting Your devotees; [he addresses You] as "Ananta," to whom no end can be known—
that is, to You who are infinite— and as "Duranta-śakti," whose powers have an unfathomable end— that is, whose powers are difficult to comprehend.

To Him who possesses such powers, whose heroic vigor is manifold; to the slayer of all unconquerable Daityas in a mere moment; to Him whose actions are pure because they consist of *sattva*, even though He acts out of anger—to Him [we offer salutations]. Sandadhate means "they perform. ||40||
Śrī Rudra said:
This time of your wrath is like the end of a Yuga; this insignificant Asura has been slain.
Protect that son who has approached you, O lover of your devotees, for he is devoted to you.

Śrīdhara: Rudra, however, knowing that this was not the time for his anger, requested him as follows with the words beginning "kopa" (anger). "The end of a thousand yugas is the time for your anger. And he says that this [present moment] is unfit for anger—"alpakah," meaning extremely slight. Therefore, do not harm Prahlāda by failing to withdraw your anger.

He said: "That [is] the son. Or rather, if it is thought that even at an improper time this anger of his is for the sake of protecting his devotee, then the meaning is: "Now, having abandoned your anger, protect him. ||41||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Perceiving Your terrible form, all are struck with fear due to the apprehension of universal dissolution (*pralaya*), but I am not; thus he says: "By [Your] anger... *Yugānta* refers to the dissolution at the end of an eon. It is the time of Your wrath.
The meaning is that even in the act of dissolution, I alone exist as your own portion.

If it is argued that this anger was for the sake of affection toward His devotees, [the reply is: compared to you, this demon is insignificant; indeed, he is already as good as slain. Therefore, He approached—that is, followed after—his son Prahlāda. ||41||
Śrī-Indra said:
O Supreme One, our own shares have been recovered by You, our protector.
That heart-lotus, which was seized by the Daityas, has awakened toward Your abode.
Alas, how much of this [world] is swallowed by Time! O Lord, for those who desire to serve You, liberation is not highly esteemed; for what is it that is not attained by others besides Nṛsiṃha?

Śrīdhara: But for us, Indra, the attainment of a share of the sacrificial oblation and so forth is not the goal of human endeavor; rather, it is service to You alone. However, by this agitation, you have accomplished Your own purpose; since that has been achieved, conclude this anger—with this intention, He says: "O..."

O Supreme One! By Your protecting and guarding us, our very own shares have been recovered from the Daitya; for it is You alone, as the Inner Controller, who are the enjoyer in the sacrifices. Our heart-lotus is indeed Your abode, yet until now it has been [held] by us as a source of fear.
The Daitya, who had always remained within the path of mindfulness, was overcome—that is, pervaded—by the true awakening, which led him to an expansion through the removal of fear.
If it is argued: "Is this not an effort of yours for the sake of attaining sovereignty over the three worlds?"

To this he says: "Seized by Time. [The word] "te" means "you. O Nārasiṃha! You who have manifested through the forms of both man and lion—for what purpose are other things such as heaven and the like? ||42||

The sequence of the composition: Indra, however, propitiates him by expressing approval for his particular assistance—[as expressed in the verse] "He believes. Our own portions, the groups of servants in our form, have been brought back and restored to their very places;
likewise, that which was seized by the Daityas—these two [things] alone [have been recovered].
He says "Time" [verse 42] to show that even the gift of sovereignty over the three worlds is something quite insignificant compared to these two supreme benefactors.

Viśvanātha: He says, "Until this day, I have remained utterly indifferent to the remembrance of Your feet, O Supreme One!"—by You, our protector and savior, Your own portions were recovered from the demon; [the portions] belonging to us, the servants of Indra and the other gods, among our possessions.
For it is only fitting that ownership belongs to You alone, O Lord. Furthermore, our heart is indeed a lotus;

because we constantly meditate upon You within it, it is Your abode. And just as that lotus becomes devoid of beauty at night—overcome by darkness, soiled, and closed in sleep—so too has it been since the birth of the Daitya.

The meaning is that because [the house] had been meditated upon by the Daitya out of fear for so many days, it became manifest as if seized by the Daitya; or else, "it was awakened toward Vaikuṇṭha" means that it attained the intelligence [to turn] toward service at His feet.
[The Lord says: "O you who take pride in being a devotee, 'Take the position of Indra'—is that true?

I shall accept it only if I am full of desire and devoid of devotion. To this he replies: "But for those whose devotion to You is free from desire, this position of Indra is swallowed by Time, along with other powers such as yoga and lordship. (42)
The venerable sages said: You have told us that supreme austerity is the splendor of the Self.
O primordial protector and refuge, by that very power through which you fashioned this world as it resides within the Self of the First Person, you have now restored what was lost to them,
having assumed a body for the sake of protection.

Śrīdhara: The sages said, "You have indeed bestowed a great favor upon us by initiating this austerity," saying: "That which you have told us is the supreme austerity characterized by meditation. The reason for its supremacy is that it is the splendor and power of your own self. They express this very point when they say: "By means of which austerity [all things] are dissolved into the Self."
"You created this universe, yet it has been plundered and rendered powerless by that Daitya.
O Protector of those who seek refuge, you have authorized him to perform penance once more by means of this body assumed today for the sake of protection; salutations to You."
The fourth quarter of the following verse is to be supplied here. ||43||
Krama-sandarbha: This has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: They say, "Until this day we have not performed penance";
[the Lord replies] that the supreme penance consisting of meditation upon You is Your own, His very splendor, for us.

The sense is that you spoke thus for the purpose of instigating austerity (*tapas*) within us. By that splendor in the form of austerity, you created (*sasarktha*—though *sasarja* is also a reading) this universe which was latent within yourself; for it has been said by you: "I create this very world through austerity alone. That austerity [was overcome] by that Daitya, who [seized] the solar splendor (*sauraṃ tejaḥ*).

Just as if it had been eclipsed by Rāhu, you have now— by assuming this body in the form of a Man-Lion (Nṛsiṃha) for the sake of protection— again performed that which was approved and consented to as our duty. ||43||
The venerable ancestors said: "Our *śrāddha* offerings were forcibly consumed by our sons."

Salutations to that Nṛhari, the protector of all dharma, who drank the water mixed with sesame seeds even at the time of a sacred rite, and who rescued him from his belly after tearing open its body with his claws.

Śrīdhara: The ancestors bow down to Śrī Nṛsiṃha, who has been their supreme benefactor by rescuing them from the śrāddha rites. He himself forcibly took over and consumed the śrāddhas—the offerings of rice balls and so forth—which were given to us by our sons with great faith. Furthermore:

At the time of his ritual bath at a sacred ford, he even drank the water mixed with sesame seeds that had been offered; and today he extracted those very seeds from his belly. From what kind of belly? From one whose omentum (*vapā*) had been torn open by his own claws.
The sense is that the tearing of the omentum was itself the fruit of his having swallowed those pellets. ||44||
The sequence of composition: the reading "even at the appointed time he drank water with sesame seeds" is approved by the Master (Svāmī).
"Māyā Nṛsiṃha" means Nṛsiṃha who is preeminent in compassion. ||44||
Viśvanātha says: "We have remained devoted to fasting for all these days," they said.

*Śrāddhas* refers to the funeral rites, such as the *piṇḍas* and so forth. At the time of bathing at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), there is water with sesame seeds (*tilāmbu*), that is, the water used for the sesame libation (*tila-tarpaṇa*); those [rites] and that [water]. He who extracted (*ārcchat*) it from his belly—that is, he who brought it forth.
Because of his chanting, his skin, fat, and marrow were torn away by his fingernails. The Śrī-Siddhas said:
That wicked one, who by the power of his yogic austerity had stolen our destination attained through yoga—
him he tore apart with his claws, crushing his pride.
To you, O Nṛsiṃha, we bow down.
Śrīdhara: To you, who possess various manifold prides [arising from] the attainment of yoga—the perfection of powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth—it is for your sake, addressing you. ||45||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "We are indeed paupers, devoid of the attainment of yogic powers and lordship; we await this time," they say—[referring to Him] who is our goal, the perfection of *aṇimā* and so forth, the mirror for manifold [realities].
That asura, who possessed manifold pride. ||45||
The Śrī-Vidyādharas said:
"The Vidyā, accomplished through separate dhāraṇās..."
We perpetually bow down to that Māyā-Nṛsiṃha, by whom that ignorant one— who was arrogant because of his strength and heroism— was slain in battle like a beast.
Śrīdhara: [He attained] the science characterized by invisibility and so forth; "anurāddhām" means obtained;
"saṅkhye" means in battle. ||46||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: They say, "We too have remained devoid of knowledge until this very day"—knowledge characterized by such powers as invisibility (*antardhāna*), perfected (*rāddhā*) or accomplished, [attained] in battle (*saṅkhye*).
Nṛsiṃha, who is primarily compassion, the illusory Nṛsiṃha. ||46||
The Śrī-Nāgas said:
"By whatever sin those jewels and the jewel of women were taken from us,"
O you who grant joy by rending their chests, homage be to you!

Śrīdhara: [The name] "Ratnākara" refers to one by whom joy has been bestowed upon these women—the jewels situated upon the hoods [of serpents], as well as the "jewels among women," that is, excellent women. In an alternative reading, it means "one by whom joy has been bestowed upon us. (47)
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "We have been tormented for all these days merely because our wealth was stolen and our wives were taken"—thus they speak with the words beginning "by which. By the rending—that is, the tearing open—of his chest, [the pain of] these women... [is relieved].
O you who bestow bliss! ||47||
the Manavas said:
"We are the Manavas, the executors of your commands."
O Lord, that wicked one by whom the boundaries established by the gods were transgressed has been destroyed by you, O Master; what shall we do for you? Command your servants!
Śrīdhara: Being gazed upon by Nṛsiṃha, the Manus, with palms joined in reverence upon their heads, said:

"We are the Manus, the protectors of dharma; yet we are those whose boundaries—the limits of the duties of the social orders (varṇas) and stages of life (āśramas)—have been transgressed. Please instruct us; teach us. (48)

The sequence of the composition: The meaning is that the Manus here include those of the present who are engaged in austerity, as well as those of the past; and they, having also considered themselves as future [Manus], made their report, which is why it is said, "the Manus spoke" (manava ūcuḥ). ||48||

Viśvanātha: Beheld suddenly by Nṛsiṃha, the Manus, with their palms joined in reverence upon their heads, said, "We shall be Manus who carry out your command"—thus it should be understood that the term "Manus" applies to those who follow hereafter as well. "Setus" refers to the boundaries of the duties of the social classes (varṇas) and stages of life (āśramas). ||48||
The venerable Prajāpatis said: "O Supreme Lord, we are the lords of creatures created by You."
He by whom we were indeed forbidden from creating progeny—
this very incarnation, the auspiciousness of the world and the embodiment of pure being, now lies with his chest pierced by you.

Śrīdhara: Even the Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis), having been looked upon by Him, said: "O Supreme Lord, we, the lords of creatures created by You, have been restrained by whomsoever so that we do not create offspring; he indeed lies there dead with his chest split open. From now on, we shall create progeny."
Rejoicing, they said: "O embodiment of goodness, this incarnation of yours is an auspicious blessing for the world. (49)
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: O Supreme Lord! O Parameśvara! "O you who are forbidden—do not create progeny," thus were you commanded. O embodiment of goodness (sattva)! Your incarnation is the auspiciousness of the world. (49)
The Śrī-Gandharvas said: O All-pervading Lord, we are Your actors, dancers, and singers.
He who, by his own self-reliant vigor, strength, and energy, achieved these [victories],
has been brought to this state by you; for how can one who stands on a wrong path be fit for what is wholesome?

Śrīdhara says that the *gāndharva* [performance] consists of the dancing of the *madhu* [demon], but not the composition of a story, nor the display of dramatic sentiments (*bhāva*) as in a drama (*naṭaka*).
The *gandharvas*, having witnessed it, said: "O Lord! We are your own actors, dancers, and singers in the art of drama and dance, by whom we have been brought under your control."
In what state [was he]? By him whose vigor (*ojas*), that is, prowess, strength, and power, was possessed through both valor (*vīrya*) and might (*bala*).
This very person has been brought by you to this condition, which is death. And they say that this is appropriate—why so? ||50||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: The meaning is that we, having been made his own by that Daitya, became his very actors in his drama and his singers. (50)
The Śrī-Cāraṇas said:
O Hari, we have taken refuge at your lotus feet, which grant liberation from worldly existence.
Since this Asura, who lay as a thorn in the hearts of the virtuous, has been brought to an end by you.

Śrīdhara: [He is] the one who brings about liberation from worldly existence—that which turns one back from *saṃsāra*. He is the cause for taking refuge, because he dwells or remains in the hearts of the virtuous as the generator of fear; such is this Asura who has been brought to his end by you. ||51||

The sequence of composition: "O Hare" is the reason for not having sought refuge previously; "dwelling in the hearts of the virtuous" is the reason for seeking refuge now; and "having brought [the world] to completion" is the reason for this present state. ||51||

Viśvanātha: He [Śeṣa] used to lie even within the shadow of you in the hearts of the virtuous; therefore, as if unable to endure that, he was delivered over by you and brought to his end. Consequently, from this day forward, you alone shall lie within their hearts—this is the intended meaning. ||51||
The Śrī-yakṣas said:
"We are the foremost of your attendants by virtue of our pleasing deeds."
They have been reduced here to the state of beasts of burden by the son of Diti;
yet you, O Nṛsiṃha, knowing the suffering caused to people by him, have brought that twenty-fifth principle to its end.

Śrīdhara: By our agreeable deeds, we—who were once the foremost among Your attendants—have been reduced by the son of Diti to the state of palanquin-bearers. [We have reached] *pañcatā*, that is, death. O Pañcaviṃśa, O Controller of the twenty-four principles! 52.

The structural connection (*krama-sandarbha*): O Narahari! We are those whose primary masters are the attendants of You—such as Śiva, Kubera, and others—who follow You because of Your charming deeds. (52)

Viśvanātha: By your pleasing deeds, we have become the foremost among your attendants; or rather, we ourselves—who possess as our chief followers only those devoted to you—have been reduced to the state of carrying your palanquin.
Knowing the torment inflicted upon people by that son of Diti, you [brought him] to death.
O Death, O Twenty-fifth, you who govern the twenty-four principles! ||52||
The Śrī-Kimpuruṣas said:
"We are Kimpuruṣas, but you are the Great Person (Mahāpuruṣa), the Lord."
When this wicked man was ruined and censured by the virtuous, [he fell].

Śrīdhara: "What are mere *kiṃpuruṣas* [monkeys] to praise you? We are but wretched beings," they say—"we" (*vayam*). We are *kiṃpuruṣas*, insignificant creatures, while you are a great Person (*puruṣa*) of marvelous power. Anticipating the objection, "Why is this great demon not described as having been slain? he says:
"How much is this? they asked—"this very thing. When he was rejected by the saintly devotees of the Lord, at that very moment he perished. (53)
The sequential arrangement [of the commentary] by Viśvanātha has not been explained.
The venerable bards said:
In assemblies and sacrificial sessions, by singing of your stainless glory, we receive great honor;
yet this wicked man has brought that very honor under his control.
O Blessed One, by your grace, my affliction has been destroyed.
Śrīdhara: "In the sacrificial sessions (satra), in the sacrifices (yajña). He was killed by you; this is fortunate, a good deed has been done. [The sequence of words] is not explained.
Viśvanātha: "That worship directed toward us, its subjection—that is, its specific state of being under one's own control—"
He brought; he led. ||54||
The Śrī-kinnaras said: "O Lord, we are the hosts of kinnaras, your followers."
O Hari,
O Lord Narasiṃha, that Daitya— who caused the gods to perform forced labor for him— has been destroyed by you; may you be our source of prosperity.
Śrīdhara: By this son of Diti, we have been made to perform incessant labor for nothing; therefore, from now on, be for our prosperity and well-being. 55.
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: They were made to perform incessantly menial labor (*viṣṭi*) that was without reward; *vṛjina* means causing suffering. ||55||
The attendants of Śrī Viṣṇu said:
"Today this wonderful form of Yours as Hari and Nara— "
O Giver of Refuge, we have seen the source of happiness for all the world; O Lord,
we recognize that this death of the Brahmin who cursed you— this servant of yours— is for the sake of bestowing grace upon him.
Śrīdhara: O Giver of Refuge, O Bestower of Shelter for us, Your devotees—this wondrous form, the auspiciousness and blessing of all the worlds, has been seen this very day, but not before.
[I am] a servant who carries out Your command.

The sequential arrangement: these attendants of Viṣṇu are to be understood as belonging to the one who delights Śrī-Vikuṇṭha, because they descended together with the Lord Śrī-Nṛsiṃha, having become one with Him. ||56||
Viśvanātha: This very Hiraṇyakaśipu was indeed your servant who carried out your commands, yet he was cursed by the Brahmins, Sanaka and the others. ||56||

Thus ends the first chapter of the seventh [section] in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted to the Lord; it is well-composed and truly pleasing to the virtuous.
Thus, in the glorious Bhāgavata Mahāpurāṇa, in the commentary on the Brahma-sūtras,
in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā concerning the state of the Paramahaṃsas, in the seventh book,
in the dialogue between Yudhiṣṭhira and Nārada.
The Slaying of Hiraṇyakaśipu;
the Eighth Chapter.
Now begins the ninth chapter in the narrative of Prahlāda; Śrī Nārada said:
Thus all the gods and others, led by Brahmā and Rudra,
were unable to approach his wrathful fury, which was exceedingly difficult to withstand.
Śrīdhara:
In the ninth [chapter], the demon child, urged by Brahmā out of fear,
pacified his anger and praised the exceedingly terrifying Nṛsiṃha.
Though fierce, this Man-Lion is indeed gracious toward his own devotees, just as a lion is toward its own cubs; yet he possesses a formidable form for others.

He speaks of this compassion for his devotees as described in the scriptures beginning with these words, using seven verses starting with "Thus": "Thus, while standing from afar and offering praise, they were unable to approach him who was possessed by an outburst of fury. (1)
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not commented upon.
*Viśvanātha*:
At that time, everyone was afraid of the arrival of Hari in their vicinity during the ninth month.
Commanded by Brahmā, Prahlāda approached his presence and offered praise.
Where even Ramā had no power, what need is there to speak of others?
Yet Prahlāda experienced that very compassion in its embodied form.

[Objection: "But why did the gods and others, announcing their respective sufferings and praising [the Lord] from afar, not come near to attend upon Him? To this he says: "Thus..."—referring to Him who possessed fury (*manyu*), that is, agitation and intense passion. ||1||
Having witnessed that great marvel, Śrī herself was sent by the gods;
yet, because it was something never before seen or heard, she approached him with hesitation.
Because he was neither seen nor heard of before by other common people,
Śrī, as if apprehensive of Nṛsiṃha, departed for the world of Māyā.
And when Brahmā perceived that even Hari’s mind was inclined toward showing affection for Prahlāda, he then dispatched Prahlāda [to him].

"Hari, who is affectionate by nature, may manifest His special parental love for one person among many; yet, being affectionate, He does so even toward an inferior being, either all at once or gradually. Thus it is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*. (2–3)

Śrīdhara: Although the goddess Lakṣmī was sent by Śrī, she did not approach him upon seeing his form, being struck with apprehension at that great wonder. The reason for its wonderfulness is given as "unseen" (adṛṣṭa) and so forth. ||2||
The sequence of composition: "She is Śrī herself" means that she too is his beloved;
this is because she has never before been seen or heard of. Here, it should be inferred that her state of being unseen and unheard of arose precisely from [his] agitation. ||2||

Viśvanātha: Regarding the phrase "because it has never been seen or heard before," although the form of Nṛsiṃha was seen in a previous kalpa, and although Nṛsiṃha is always seen in Vaikuṇṭha, the fact that He was perceived as unseen and unheard at that time was brought about solely by the power of His divine play (līlā-śakti).
They say [this is] for the purpose of attaining the tasting of the marvelous aesthetic flavor (adbhuta-rasa). ||2||
He sent Prahrāda, who was situated nearby in a state of composure,
saying: "O dear one, go and pacify the Lord, who is angry with your father."
"So be it," O King; slowly the great devotee, though still a child, approached and bowed his body to the ground with palms joined in reverence. ||4||
Śrīdhara: Come hither; approach. ||3-4||
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
That child, having fallen at the base of his own feet...
Beholding this, the Lord, overflowing with compassion,
raised him up and placed his lotus-hand upon his head—
a hand that grants fearlessness to those whose minds are terrified by the serpent of Time.
Śrīdhara: His lotus-hand is that by which fearlessness was granted to those whose intellects were terrified by Time (Kāla), who had been brought under its power. ||5||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: That by which fearlessness has been granted. ||5||
With all his impurities shaken off by the touch of that hand,
he immediately attained the manifestation of the vision of the Supreme Self.
With his body bristling with joy, his heart melting and his eyes filled with tears, he, finding peace, held those lotus feet within his heart.

Śrīdhara: By the touch of the hand of that Śrī-Nṛsiṃha, all inauspiciousness was shaken off and dispelled for him. At that very moment, the vision of the Supreme Self—the realization of Brahman—became manifest and directly perceived. Being thus liberated, he held it within his heart while rejoicing. Hṛṣyantī.

His body was thrilled with horripilation; his heart was moistened, being tender with love; and there were tears in his eyes. He maintained these as the supreme human goal (parama-puruṣārtha), not as a means to an end—this is the meaning. ||6||

The sequential arrangement: Now, following Prahlāda’s realization of Brahman— which was preceded by the shaking off of all sins through the direct vision of the Blessed Lord— there occurs his supreme bliss consisting of a specific direct vision of the Blessed Lord.
He states [this] because it is most desired: "That he... (verse 6).

Viśvanātha: He is one by whom that which was previously impure—characterized by the impossibility of attaining his touch and so forth due to his belonging to the class of *asuras*—has been shaken off and cast away.
By the power of the touch of his hand, that which was already established from before is then manifested.
He whose vision of the Supreme Self and his experience of the Paramātman had become manifest in every respect,
being perfectly composed with a one-pointed mind, praised Hari.
With his heart and eyes fixed upon him, he spoke with a voice faltering with love.
Śrīdhara: He describes *susamādhi* itself: "by whom the heart and the gaze are fixed upon that very [object]"—this is the sequence of the composition; it has not been explained [further].
Viśvanātha: He describes *susamādhi*: "by whom the heart and the gaze are fixed upon that very [object]."
Śrī Prahlāda said:
Brahmā and the other hosts of gods, as well as the sages and the perfected ones (siddhas),...

Even now, those whose minds are solely intent on the Supreme Being have not been able to satisfy Him with floods of words, despite their many virtues; how then could that Hari of fierce birth be pleased with me?
Śrīdhara [comments]:
"Prahlāda praises Hari with forty-two excellent verses so that all may behold the nectar-like glance of His grace as if it were directed toward themselves. Thus.

In this regard, first anticipating that he might lack the qualification for praising the Blessed One and thereby seeking to establish his own qualification, he says [the following] in five verses beginning with "Brahmā and others. The *munayaḥ* are those whose nature is contemplation (*manana*).
The *siddhāḥ* are also those possessed of knowledge (*jñānin*). Of what nature are they? She [the Goddess] is that in whom there is *tānaḥ*, an expansion, within the single principle of *sattva*.

Even those whose intellects are of such a kind— yet who, despite floods of words and even the many qualities that will be described hereafter, were not able to satisfy (pipruḥ), meaning they did not fulfill or please—
that Hari, how can He attain satisfaction with me? In this regard:
The cause: he belongs to a fierce lineage; "fierce" means his birth is fierce, terrible, and demonic. ||8||

The sequence of the composition: therein, he first suggests by way of a *kaimutya* (a fortiori) argument his own unworthiness, beginning with the words "Brahmā and others. [This is achieved] through the streams of words—those expressions primarily concerned with action (*karma-yoga*) and knowledge (*jñāna*)—and through their continuous practice. ||8||

Viśvanātha: "O Lord of wondrous and inscrutable power, relying upon what quality in me do you show such compassion? To this he replies with the words "Brahmā and the others. Even your own goodness (*sāttvikatva*) is not the cause of your compassion, much less your lack of goodness; thus he says that [the gods] are "one-pointedly intent" (*ekatānāḥ*) only upon virtue, knowledge, and austerity among all beings.
Those whose minds do not turn elsewhere—what then of us, whose minds are single-mindedly intent upon the enjoyment of objects that are unrighteous and ignorant? This is the intended meaning.
Amara states: "ekatāna" means having no other function. And it is not only in the case of words of praise...

He says that [the purpose] is to win your favor through streams of words endowed with many virtues, as well as with resonance (*dhvani*), poetic qualities (*guṇa*), and ornaments (*alaṅkāra*). In the case of the "streams" [of water], this refers to qualities such as clarity, coolness, sweetness, and purity. [The purpose is] to propitiate you—that is, to satisfy you—with these [qualities].
This is the meaning. "Na pipruḥ" means they were not able; "me" means in me; "ugra-jāteḥ" means of one born of a fierce lineage, that is, of a lineage characterized by great darkness (tamas). ||8||
— I think that wealth, noble birth, beauty, austerity, learning, vigor, splendor, majesty, strength, manliness, and the application of intelligence [are all in vain].
For these do not lead to the propitiation of the Supreme Person; yet the Blessed One was pleased with the one devoted to the leader of the elephant herd.

Śrīdhara: Thus, having raised the doubt regarding his own unworthiness to please Hari, he considers his worthiness in two verses beginning with "I consider. *Abhijana* is birth in a noble family; *rūpa* is beauty; *śruta* is learning; *ojas* is proficiency of the senses; and *tejas* is splendor.
*Prabhāva* is majesty; *pauruṣa* is manly effort; *buddhi* is wisdom; and *yoga* is the eightfold path. These twelve qualities, beginning with wealth, do not serve to propitiate the Supreme Person.
For indeed, He became pleased with Gajendra through devotion alone. (9)

Sanātana Gosvāmī: *Abhijana* is birth in a noble family; *rūpa* is beauty; *tapas* is the practice of one’s own duty; *śruta* is scholarship; *ojas* is proficiency of the senses; *tejas* is luster; *prabhāva* is majesty; *bala* is physical strength; and *pauruṣa* is exertion.

Intellect is wisdom; yoga is the eightfold path. These twelve qualities, beginning with wealth, do not serve as means for the propitiation, the attainment, or even the equipment for the worship of the Supreme Person—how much less for Your satisfaction? For indeed, He became pleased with Gajendra through devotion alone.
||9|| [Ha.bha.vi.

11.592] The sequence of composition: Having thus determined it because it has been seen in this way, he says with three quarters of a verse, beginning with "I think" (*manye*): those [virtues] such as non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and so forth, which are the fruits of the practice of various scriptures, they too...

"Not for propitiation"—meaning not for the sake of gratification. Then, in response to the expectation of "by what means would there be satisfaction?", he demonstrates that very point by way of an illustration: "by devotion" (*bhaktyā*). Although Brahmā and others are devotees of a few [deities] such as Brahmā, He is not satisfied even with them by virtue of that [mere devotion].
This was stated with the intention of saying "it exists. ||9||
Viśvanātha: And he says that You are not satisfied by the giving of much wealth and so forth with the words "I consider...

*Abhijana* is birth in a noble family. *Ojas* is proficiency of the senses. *Tejas* is luster. *Prabhāva* is majesty. *Pauruṣa* is exertion. *Yoga* is the eightfold [yoga]; [it is] the yoga of action (*karma-yoga*).
Furthermore, neither the yoga of knowledge nor [other means] lead to my propitiation or satisfaction. If so, by what am I satisfied?

To this he says: "by devotion. By the use of the past tense in the word "tutoṣa" (was satisfied), no other reasoning need be sought here; rather, this is simply your own nature, or else some wonderful power of devotion.

Thus it shines forth. And by that, through the impossibility of your satisfaction otherwise, it is implied that even in me there exists a trace of devotion, born from the wonderful grace of Śrī Nārada. ||9||
A dog-eater (outcaste) is superior to a Brahmin who lacks the twelve qualities and who turns his back on the lotus-feet of the Lord whose navel is a lotus.
I believe that one who has dedicated their mind, speech,
actions, wealth, and life to Him purifies their lineage, but not one who possesses great pride.
Regarding "madhvaḥ": from that which is endowed with twelve qualities—
namely, knowledge, truthfulness, self-restraint, tranquility, lack of envy, modesty, forbearance, and freedom from malice.
"Charity, sacrifice, austerity, and sacred learning—these twelve are the great vows of a Brāhmaṇa," so it is said in the Mahābhārata. (10)
Śrīdhara: It has been stated that the gratification of Hari occurs through devotion alone;

now he says that nothing other than devotion is a cause for his gratification—with the words "from a brahmin" (viprāt). Even compared to a brahmin endowed with the twelve qualities previously mentioned, such as wealth and so forth, a dog-eater (śvapaca) is superior.
Or rather, I think that the twelve qualities beginning with *dharma*, as spoken by Sanatsujāta, should be regarded:
"Dharma, truth, self-restraint, austerity, lack of envy, modesty, forbearance, and freedom from malice."
"Sacrifice, charity, fortitude, sacred learning, and the vows— these indeed are the twelve duties of a Brāhmaṇa" (Mahābhārata 5.43.12).
Or else:
"Tranquility, self-control, austerity, purity, forbearance, straightforwardness, detachment, wisdom, realization, contentment, truthfulness, and faith—these are the twelve qualities.
From what kind of brāhmaṇa? From one who has turned his back on the lotus feet of the One whose navel is a lotus (Viṣṇu).
Of what nature was that dog-eater? He was one by whom the mind and senses were offered to that Lord whose navel is a lotus;

this refers to his performed action. The reason for his superiority is as follows: such a dog-eater purifies his entire lineage, whereas a Brahmin possessed of abundant pride and arrogance does not even purify himself. Why is this so?
What is the point of lineage? For these qualities, in one devoid of devotion, lead only to pride and not to purification;
therefore, the sense is that he is "lowly. ||10||
Sanātana [Ha.bha.vi. 10.192] says: "I consider wealth, lineage, beauty, austerity, learning, vigor, splendor, power, strength, manliness, intellect, and yoga" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.9.9);
thus, by those previously mentioned twelve qualities—beginning with wealth—[he is bound].

I consider even a dog-cooker (śvapaca) who is disciplined to be superior to a Brahmin who is not; or rather, one should look to the twelve qualities beginning with Dharma mentioned by Sanatsujāta in the Udyoga Parva. For it is said: "Dharma, truth, self-restraint, and austerity..."
"Indeed, non-miserliness, modesty, forbearance, freedom from envy,
sacrifice, charity, fortitude, and sacred learning—
these are the twelve vows of a Brahmin. (Mahābhārata 5.43.12) Thus it is said.

From what kind of brahmin? From one who has turned his face away from the lotus-feet of the One whose navel is a lotus (Viṣṇu). Of what nature was the dog-eater? He was one by whom the mind had been offered—that is, directed—toward those very lotus-feet of the One whose navel is a lotus. This refers to his performed action. The reason for his superiority is that he was of such a nature.

A dog-cooker (outcaste) purifies his own family; however, a Brahmin who possesses abundant pride and arrogance does not purify even himself, much less his family? For these qualities in one devoid of devotion lead only to further conceit;
thus, the sense is that he is truly base.

Or rather, I consider even a *śvapaca* (outcaste) to be superior to such a brahmin; for, due to being averse to the Blessed One, the brahmin is lower even than a *śvapaca*, since a *śvapaca*— by virtue of his birth and inherent nature—
is incapable of possessing knowledge of the Blessed One and so forth, and thus lacks only the lack of orientation toward the Blessed One, but not [the capacity for devotion].
It means turning away. Therefore, for this reason as well, this alone is right.

"For this very reason, I consider him [the best]"—I consider him who has dedicated his mind, speech, actions, objects of desire, and life-breath to Him to be the most excellent, the supreme among all.
The reason for this is: "He purifies."

Alternatively, from the very beginning, the Brahmin already possesses a natural and constant orientation toward the Lord through his worship of the *sandhyā* and other rites; subsequently, by means of study and so forth, he has acquired such twelve qualities.
Therefore, let alone any further distinction in his orientation at this stage, [he thinks]: "I myself..."

"Truth is the Supreme Brahman, Nārāyaṇa; and everything else that is seen or heard, being other than Me, is fashioned by My Māyā and is merely superimposed upon Me"—with such false pride, he became averse to the lotus feet of the Blessed Lord. The rest is the same. ||10||
The Sequence of Composition: Now, some might object that even certain qualities other than devotion are proclaimed as being superior; not tolerating this, they say: "From a brahmin... (10).

Viśvanātha: What else need be said? He says that this distinction is made solely by the presence or absence of devotion: "I consider even a dog-eater (śvapaca) superior to a Brahmin devoid of devotion—how much more so those belonging to the Kṣatriya and other castes? Furthermore, regarding that [superiority], there are the twelve qualities previously mentioned, beginning with wealth and ending with the six pairs. By these...

How much more so one endowed with seven, eight, three, four, or more qualities, and how much more so one who is even more deficient in those respective qualities? Among them, "most excellent" (*variṣṭha*) means preeminently superior.
The twelve qualities mentioned by Sanatsujāta should be understood here. Thus it has been said:
Knowledge and truth, self-restraint and tranquility, lack of envy, modesty, endurance, and freedom from malice;
generosity, sacrifice, austerity, and sacred learning.

"The twelve great vows belong to the Brāhmaṇa" (Mahābhārata 5.43.12). By this, the view that a Brāhmaṇa who possesses the reality of knowledge-yoga and so forth is not called "one who has turned away from the Blessed One" is refuted. What kind of person is a *śvapaca*? One whose mind is fixed upon that Aravinda-nābha (the Lotus-navelled One).

That by which [the aforementioned] things—namely, desired action (*īhita*), purpose (*artha*), and wealth (*dhana*)—are attained; the reason for his superiority over the Brahmin is that this *śvapaca* purifies his entire lineage. Even though he possesses great honor (*bhūri-māna*) and is respected in the worlds, such a Brahmin does not even purify himself, let alone his lineage—this is the intended meaning.
The venerable teacher’s feet have said: "For one devoid of devotion, these qualities lead only to pride and not to purification. (10)
This compassionate Lord, who is already full of His own attainment, does not seek honor from ignorant people, for He is not the master of Himself.
Whatever honor people may bestow upon the Blessed One,
that is for his own sake, just as the beauty of a face is reflected in a mirror.

Śrīdhara: If that is so, does the Blessed Lord expect honor through the offering of wealth and the like as an ordinary person does? No; he says "not at all. This Lord, the Supreme Controller, does not choose—that is, does not desire—for his own sake worship from an ignorant person of small merit, because he is already fulfilled by his own inherent gain. If so, [then...]

He does not desire worship at all; regarding this, he says: "Being compassionate (*karuṇaḥ*), that is, merciful (*kṛpāluḥ*), he therefore accepts it. The reason for this is: "Whatever... That is, whatever honor (*mānam*) [is offered]; or rather, because (*yad vā yasmād*) by whatever wealth or means one offers honor to the Blessed One, that alone accrues to oneself and nothing else. It is just as in the case of the mouth.
Just as the beauty of the tilaka mark and so forth is produced only in the reflection and cannot be directly applied to the object itself, so it is in this case. ||11||

The sequence of the composition: Since devotees are by their very nature the most beloved forms even to the Blessed Lord, and since devotion itself is the embodiment of happiness for the devotees, [the Lord] was satisfied by devotion.
Thus, extolling this very point, He concludes that devotion alone is His duty, saying: "Not indeed for My own sake... (naivātmanaḥ).
This Lord does not choose—or desire—homage or worship from people who are His own devotees.
The reason for this is that He is already full and supremely satisfied by the mere attainment of His own devotee.
There is another reason: He is compassionate and cannot endure the effort and exertion involved in such worship. From what kind of person?

"From the ignorant person"—that is, from his father who knows nothing at all before him, like a child; this is an expression of wretchedness because she belongs to the same class of people as he. Alternatively, the meaning is that through absorption in him, she knows nothing else whatsoever. In either case, that very fact is the cause of his compassion.
[The author states] the intention.
Then, anticipating the objection, "In that case, why do people not perform worship for him? he says: "yat...
That person, whatever honor (*māna*) they bestow—that is, accomplish—for the Blessed One, all of that...

It is for his own sake alone; the meaning is that, imagining his own honor to be achieved merely by that person's honor, he considers it happiness and thus indeed performs that act of honoring. And since for a person whose very life depends on that one, self-honor through mere honor from them is entirely appropriate, he provides an illustration: "Just as..."
Whatever beauty is produced in the *mukha* (opening), that alone constitutes the beauty of the *pratimukha* (counter-opening); there is nothing else. ||11||

Viśvanātha: [Objection: "In that case, devotion (*bhakti*) is indeed the honoring of Me through hearing, chanting, worship, and so forth; I am pleased by that alone, and not by austerity, learning, and the like. If you say [I am pleased] by qualities residing in the person (*puṃ-niṣṭhair guṇaiḥ*), then it would follow that I am intent on my own self-interest (*svārtha-paratvam*). To this he says, "Not at all" (*naiva*). This...

You, the Lord, the Sovereign, do not seek honor or respect for Yourself from any person whatsoever. From what kind of person? From the ignorant. The meaning is that, in comparison to Him, every single being—from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—is indeed ignorant. For it is not so.

It has been stated that the reason for not accepting honor is the quality characterized by knowledge residing in people—the notion that "some fortunate person accepts the honor bestowed by those ignorant of the sciences such as the scriptures. However, he says that there exists a reason characterized by knowledge residing in you yourself: "He is full through his own gain."

However, being compassionate and merciful, he chooses; and it is observed that he chooses from some source or another. That [choice] is solely for the purpose of favoring him. Thus, even in the acceptance of honor, the cause is indeed the quality residing in you characterized by compassion—this is the sense. And not...

He says that any excellence resulting from the honor bestowed by ordinary people would accrue only to the giver of that honor: "Whatever worship one may offer to the Blessed One—that honor belongs to oneself, for one's own exaltation alone; just as the beauty of the face [belongs to the face itself]."

The beauty of the tilaka and other ornaments would indeed belong to the reflected face itself, but not to the reflection; that is to say, it is not as if the decoration were actually applied to the reflection. ||11||
Therefore, free from all distress, I praise with my whole soul the greatness of the Lord, according to my understanding.
For by what quality, when described, does even a base man, having entered into the abandonment of virtues, become purified?

Śrīdhara: Since the Blessed One is pleased by devotion alone in this way, therefore, although I am lowly, being free from dejection and devoid of fear, I shall describe with every effort the greatness of the Lord’s majesty according to my own understanding. He states the reason for offering praise even though he is ignorant: "by whom indeed..."

The meaning is that by means of His majesty as described, a person who has entered into transmigratory existence through ignorance may be purified—that is, cleansed—for no other [entity] possesses such a capacity for purification. ||12||
The sequence of the composition: He concludes with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt). ||12||
Viśvanātha: Since you are pleased by devotion alone and not by noble birth and the like, and since honoring you indeed results in benefit for oneself,
therefore, though I am lowly, I celebrate— that is, I praise— your greatness, by which [greatness] yours is...
By means of the renunciation of qualities described [in this work], may people who have entered the disease of saṃsāra be purified;
that is to say, they may be liberated from it. ||12||
O Lord, abode of all beings, all these— including Brahmā and the rest— are performers of your ordinances like us; yet they do not tremble.
The playful sport of the Blessed One, through his beautiful incarnations, is for the sake of security, prosperity, and also for the happiness of this world.

Śrīdhara: Thus, having resolved the objection regarding his own lack of authority to offer praise, he now praises Him and prays for the withdrawal of His anger with two verses beginning with "sarve hi. O Lord! All these beings, from Brahmā downwards, trembling and afraid, are the executors of Your commands as You are the embodiment of pure goodness (*sattva*).
Only Your devotees are the performers of Your commands, and no others. Nor are we devoted to You out of a spirit of enmity like the Asuras; rather, it is solely through faith.
Your pleasure in various sports through the incarnations of Airāvata is for the sake of the welfare and other benefits of this universe, not for the purpose of instilling fear.
The sequence of the composition: Now, one might object that in this way Brahmā and the others are not devotees, while you alone are a devotee.

Anticipating this doubt, [the author], describing himself as being of that same nature through his wretchedness due to birth in a demonic lineage, employs a negative example (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*) to cause Brahmā and the others to become objects of His grace. Their...

He further confirms His state as the object of devotion with the words "all": "And they are not like us or like the Asuras, who, upon seeing Your incomparable glory, become agitated and fall into states such as envy; You, however, possess only entirely auspicious conduct," he says with the word "for their welfare" (kṣemāya).

Viśvanātha says: "We are indeed demons in this world, undevoted and unfortunate; but you, on the contrary, are all His devotees and truly highly blessed. He explains: "All are 'doers of His will,' meaning they perform Your commands and are merely servants; we are not like the demons who possess a spirit of enmity."

Being agitated and terrified by their own nature, this play of Yours— such as the slaying of the Asuras and so forth— must be for the sake of the welfare, prosperity, and success of this universe which consists of Your own devotees, and also for the sake of Your own happiness. ||13||
Therefore, restrain your wrath; for even a virtuous man might rejoice today at the slaying of a scorpion or a serpent, O Asura, now that you have been slain by him.
And all the worlds that have attained liberation turn toward you;
O Nṛsiṃha, people remember your form for the sake of fearlessness.

Śrīdhara: Therefore, for the sake of removing their fear, restrain your wrath; withdraw it. He for whose sake this wrath was directed has now been slain for the satisfaction of the virtuous. Since there is no further purpose for anger beyond this, restrain it. But surely, what is gained by the slaughter of others?

Would he rejoice? To this he says: Even a virtuous person would indeed rejoice at the death—that is, the killing—of a scorpion or similar creature that causes harm to others, thinking, "By its being slain by another, a blessing has come to it. If it is argued, "In that case, since it brings happiness to many, I shall not abandon this anger," to this he says: "And the worlds..."

If you think, "Having attained the state of those who have reached extinction (nirvṛti), they turn back and wait for the withdrawal of my anger; therefore, I maintain my wrath so that people may no longer be afraid," to that he says: "The form.
For the sake of being without fear—that is, for the cessation of fear—it is not necessary [to maintain anger], since fear ceases simply from the recollection of this form.
The meaning is that there is a purpose served by the maintenance of indignation. ||14||

The Sequence of Composition: Now, [one might object]: "Since this man is a slayer of you, the supreme saint, even great beings such as Brahmā, Marīci, and others—who are themselves saints yet ignorant of this truth—would not tolerate my killing him; therefore, it is not appropriate to show favor even toward them."

Anticipating this objection, he says: "May [the virtuous] rejoice. The meaning is: who am I, a wretched person? Nevertheless, even a virtuous person would approve of the killing of this [demon], who is as murderous as a scorpion and the like; how much more so, then, those [who are devoted]?
What need is there to say that they themselves will obtain joy? Because of this, and because of the phrase "and the people," therefore...
"Because it bestows universal happiness, it has indeed been well-performed"—this is the sense that this is an occasion for grace, not for anger. Furthermore, "the form" [is as follows]—14.
Viśvanātha: Since from him the welfare (*kṣema*) and so forth of the universe arose, therefore restrain—that is, cast far away—your anger.
[Objection: But since he finds happiness through the suffering of others, how can this universe be considered virtuous?
To that he replies: even a virtuous person [is not blamed] for the killing—that is, the harming—of scorpions, snakes, and the like, which cause distress to others.

The meaning is that there is no ungrammaticality in the injunction "one should rejoice in what is done by another. They perceive—that is, they attain conviction—regarding your agency in the subduing of the wicked and the protection of the righteous. And he says that beyond this, you have no further need for such an incarnation: "O Nṛsiṃha! This very form of yours is for the sake of inspiring fear."
They remember [Thee] for the sake of the absence of fear; the sense is that by the mere remembrance of this form of Yours, the terrified Asuras shall henceforth perish. ||14||
"— O Ajita, I do not fear those [beings] who are so terrifying, with their tongues like suns, eyes like the sun, frowning brows, and fierce, formidable fangs."

From the enemy’s claw-tip, which was like a spike with intestines for its garland and blood for its filaments, and from which the elephants of the quarters fled in terror at the roar, [he was rescued].
Śrīdhara: If you say, "If you are afraid, then I shall abandon it," he says in response: "Not I.

O Ajita! I am not afraid of this form of yours. Of what kind [is it]? It is one whose mouth, tongue, sun-like eyes, the impetuosity and swelling of his knitted brows, and his fierce fangs—[are all formidable].

Because of that [place] in which these things were exceedingly terrifying; because of that [place] which possessed garlands made of entrails (*āntra-srak*); because of that [place] in which the manes were smeared with blood, and in which the ears were stiff and protruding like conch-shells; and because of that [place] from which the elephants of the quarters were terrified by the roar.
I do not fear even such a form of yours as that in which the tips of your nails are "enemy-piercers" because they pierce enemies. (15)
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Even though he belongs to the class of *asuras*, he says "I am not [afraid]" to show that he has no fear of him, unlike other *asuras*—[the verse begins] "I am not... (*nāham*). I do not fear you from your form as it appears to us. Of what kind [of form]? Exceedingly... [text continues].
From that [face] which has a terrifying mouth and tongue, eyes equal to the sun, a violent swelling of the brow, and fierce fangs; from that [head] which has garlands made of entrails (āntra-srak);
and from that [body] whose manes are smeared with blood, and whose ears are elevated and stiff like horns.
Because of that [sound], and because of this and that; because the elephants of the quarters were terrified by the roar;
because the tips of the claws were "enemy-piercers" (ari-bhinditāni), as they pierced the enemies; because of that. ||15||
"—O you who are compassionate toward the wretched! I am terrified; I have been cast into the crushing whirlpool of this unbearable and fierce cycle of existence by those who devour."
O most beloved one, when will You, being pleased, call upon me— who am bound by my own karmas— to come to the root of Your feet, the refuge of liberation?

Śrīdhara says: He speaks of another great fear, saying, "I am terrified. I am terrified of that unbearable and fierce torment—the suffering within the wheel of saṃsāra. And therein, bound by my own karmas, I have been led—that is, cast—into the midst of devouring predators.
O you who are compassionate toward the wretched, O most excellent one, when indeed will you, being pleased, call me to your lotus feet—the refuge that is liberation itself—and summon me? 16.

The sequence of the composition: "Duḥsaha" (unbearable) implies that it consists of being turned away from You. Even there, among the demons who swallow everything—that is, those who devour Your devotion—O most beloved one (*uśattama*), [I seek] Your foot-base, the eternal abode of Your two lotus feet.
When indeed will you call me toward Śrī-Vaikuṇṭha? ||16||

Viśvanātha: However, he says "I am terrified" to express that he is afraid specifically of evil associations and the like which cause aversion toward you; for I am terrified of that very same fierce torment of the wheel of worldly existence which consists of censure, hatred, and so forth regarding you, and not of ordinary worldly existence.
The intention of Prahlāda is to be explained as follows:
"I am not at all afraid of the Vaitaraṇī river, which is so difficult to cross, for my mind is immersed in the great nectar of singing your heroic deeds" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.9.43).
This is because of his subsequent statement:

"For I was led—that is, cast—into the midst of the Asuras who were devouring [others] and who seemed to desire to devour me, your devotee. [The King asks: "But why were you cast by me? [The Sage replies: "Not at all, not so."
He said: "Being bound by my own very actions, when indeed will you, being pleased, call out toward your lotus feet—the refuge that is liberation—and summon me for the purpose of massaging them? (16)
— for one is being burned in all states of existence by the fire of grief born from the separation from the beloved and union with the unloved.
O Infinite One, even that medicine for suffering is itself suffering; yet, perceiving it as not such, I wander in delusion—tell me, therefore, the yoga of service unto You.
