Śrīdhara: If it is argued that "my pleasure lies in servitude," then [Arjuna] prays: "Since I am suffering in various wombs and lack the knowledge of servitude, you yourself must instruct me in it. For he is consumed by the fire of grief born from the separation from those dear to him and the union with those not dear to him, respectively.

I am being scorched within all wombs. If you think that a remedy for suffering must be performed, he says in response: the medicine for suffering is its remedy, yet even that is indeed suffering. Even so, I am deluded by the conceit of identifying with the body and so forth through the notion that it is not [suffering]. Therefore, O Bhūman, O All-pervading One! [Grant] this to me from You.
Tell me of the yoga in the form of service, which is the means for crossing over.

The sequence of the argument: [Objection] "But surely, while I am calling you, enjoy the paternal royal happiness"—if this is said, that is indeed suffering; yet, even so, this very thing must be requested.
Thus he says: "Because... Service (*dāsya*) is the work of a servant, and that...
The service of the image of the Blessed Lord is itself yoga, which consists of union with You; that [is what I desire]. ||17||

Viśvanātha: [The Lord says: "But what will you achieve by serving my feet? Enjoy, for now, the happiness of sovereignty over the three worlds inherited from your father. To this he replies: "By that fire of grief, born of which—through its corresponding conjunctions and disjunctions with the pleasant and the unpleasant—"
The meaning of "in all wombs" is that even in the body of a king, there is no absence of such burning by the fire of grief.
Now, one might object that there are indeed many remedies for the fire of grief; therefore, he says: "the medicine for suffering."

Even that remedy is indeed suffering itself. Yet, through the lack of such understanding—that is, with the very notion that it is not suffering—I wander even in the wombs of swine and other such beings with the thought, "I am happy. Therefore, tell me the yoga, the means, of Your service; by what means may I attain service unto You? Teach me the truth itself.

Even while existing in various wombs, if I possess the state of being Your servant, teach me that very reality; the sense is that even while existing in various wombs, if I possess the state of being Your servant, I shall have no suffering whatsoever.
Thus, O Nṛsiṃha, by chanting these playful stories of You— which were sung by Viriñca concerning Your dear friend and supreme deity—
I am easily liberated from the material modes and cross over [the ocean of existence].
For you, through association with the swans that dwell at the abode of Your pair of feet, all difficulties are overcome.

Śrīdhara: But surely, even for one engaged through the yoga of servitude (dāsya), how can there be the removal of those various previously mentioned sufferings which constitute obstacles to it? To this he says: "Being your servant, O Nṛsiṃha! while chanting your playful stories, I easily [cross] over difficulties—that is, great sufferings."

*Titarmi* means *tarāmi*; the sense is "I shall not take account [of them]. The reason for this is: being completely liberated from the qualities (*guṇas*), namely attachment and the rest. Why is that? Because I am one whose association is with those *haṃsas*—the wise devotees—for whom Your pair of feet alone is the abode.

Of what nature are these discourses? To this he says: "of the Beloved," and so forth. From where were they known? They were sung by Viriñca and have been transmitted through his tradition. Thus says the Atharvaṇa Śruti: "The gods indeed said to Prajāpati," and so on. [This discourse was revealed] to one engaged in service through your grace.

The meaning of the statement is: through association with the virtuous, there arises a description of the Lord’s qualities due to freedom from passion, and consequently, there shall be no overcoming by suffering. ||18||

Sanātana [Ha.bha.vi. 10.533]: "I am that very person, your servant. O Nṛsiṃha! By chanting the stories of Your divine play (līlā), I easily cross over—that is, I overcome—the difficulties of great suffering; the meaning is that I shall not take them into account. The reason for this is: being completely liberated from the qualities (guṇas) such as passion (rāga) and the rest."

Why is that? I am one whose association is with those *haṃsas*—that is, the wise devotees who possess discernment between the essential and the non-essential—and for whom Your pair of feet alone is the abode.
Of what nature are the stories [I tell]? To this he says: by means of these three adjectives beginning with "of the Beloved," [he describes] the nature of the story.

Furthermore, by the intention to express qualities such as being beloved, [qualities] such as consisting of supreme bliss are [implied]. And by that, constant glorification is intended. From where are they known? They were sung by Viriñca and have been transmitted through his tradition. Thus says the Atharvaṇa Śruti: "The gods, indeed, [approached] Prajāpati..."

"Thus they spoke," and so forth. By this, it is shown that the narrative possesses the nature of the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*), for it has been practiced even by the masters of the *paramahaṃsa* order, such as Sanaka and others. The statement "one crosses over difficulties" refers merely to a secondary fruit (*ānuṣaṅgika-phala*); such is the direction [of the argument]. ||18||
The sequence of the composition: The removal of those various afflictions, however, occurs through a specific manifestation of Your presence by way of a self-evident alternative means;
thus he says: "I am He" (so'ham). ||18||

Viśvanātha: [Objection: "Even while you remain in my service, you must surely seek another remedy for the worldly suffering currently presented by you. To this, he replies with pride and bold confidence: "I am his [the Lord's] own, an exclusive devotee of Him, by virtue of being a servant of the venerable Nārada."

The sense is: "I am the well-known Prahlāda; like no other, I do not accept ritual action or knowledge even in my dreams. While merely chanting and glorifying the stories of Your pastimes, I have become liberated from the modes—that is, transcended the qualities.
If I have thus become beyond the modes, then from where could this present suffering come to me?
The sense is that it is the medicine for suffering.

Now, one might object: "Are not sufferings seen even in a devotee who has transcended the gunas? To this he says: "I shall easily, that is, very quickly, cross over the difficulties—the torments of separation from You. I shall cross over them exceedingly.

The sense is this: even though direct service of You has been obtained, there will be no great delay for me due to the grace of chanting Your glories. He is one who possesses association with the swans—the attendants of Your lotus-feet—who have come to lead him away; [this refers to] the stories known as the *Viriñca-gītā*.

[He states that] there is authority [in this], and that no one has exerted effort in proclaiming Your story: "Of the Beloved" for those whose devotion is *ujjvala*; "of the Lover" for those whose devotion is *sakhya*; "of the Friend" for those like me whose devotion is *dāsya*; and "of the Lord, the Supreme Deity. (18)
O Nṛsiṃha, for the child here there is no refuge in his parents; nor is there medicine for the afflicted, nor a boat for one sinking in the ocean.
O All-pervading Lord, for embodied beings who are scorched by suffering and neglected by you, that remedy which is desired here is indeed the most direct one.

Śrīdhara: Now, it may be argued that for one tormented by sufferings, a remedy for them is well-known in the world; what then is the use of service to Me and so forth? To this he says: "Of the child," etc. O Nṛsiṃha, whatever remedy for suffering—that is, the counter-measure against pain—is desired here in this world for one who is tormented, that is indeed [available] for those who are neglected by You.

It is merely momentary and not ultimate. He says this very thing: for a child, his parents are not a refuge or protectors in this world, because even while being protected by them, he is seen to suffer, and because in some cases, such as with Ajīgarta and others, it is seen that they themselves even kill him. Nor [is there refuge] for one who is afflicted.

For a sick person, medicine is the refuge, yet death is seen even when the medicine has been administered. Nor is a boat the refuge for a man drowning in the ocean, since he is seen to drown along with it. Therefore, the meaning is that you alone are the refuge. Or rather, this may be understood through a change in tone (*kāku*).

This must be explained. Regarding the remedy for what is afflicted, that which is well-known here [in this world]—is that accepted by you as being direct (*añjasā*), or rather is it not accepted at all? Or else, one should apply the argument:
"Is that remedy which is accepted here truly direct, or is it not direct? and so forth. [The phrase] "of the child," etc. [is to be understood].
It is exactly as before. ||19||

The sequence of the composition: He says "not from another" with the words "of the child. If that is so, how is it that in other scriptures various remedies are prescribed? To this he replies: "of the one who is tormented," meaning those whom You have neglected, those in whom neglect of You has arisen, and those who are turned away from You; for their sake.

The meaning is that whatever counter-measure is desired in each respective case through direct instruction is intended merely for the sake of immediate fortitude. Therefore, the implication is that even in those instances, protection must come from you alone, who are the supreme power and the refuge of all devotees. ||19||
Viśvanātha: Nor do remedies for suffering bear fruit without you; thus he says:
"In this world, parents are not a refuge—that is, protectors—for a child.
For even when being protected by them, suffering is observed in his case, as in the instances of Ājīgarta and others.

And because of the observation that even the sight of its slaughter [does not save one]. Nor is medicine the refuge for an afflicted patient, since death is seen even when the medicine has been administered. Nor is a boat the refuge for a man drowning in the ocean, since it is observed to drown along with him. Therefore, for one who is tormented by suffering—

The remedy for that—the alleviation of suffering which is desired here—is not [possible] for those people who are neglected by you and have thus become objects outside the scope of your will; this is the connection with what precedes. The word *tāvat* is used as an ornament of the sentence. ||19||
In whom, from whence, at what time, by what means, for whom, from what cause, for what purpose, in what manner, and whatever else that is either other or supreme;
Existence acts and transforms; though its nature appears diverse when impelled, all of that is Your own essential form.

Madhva: "The existence and activity of the agent, the object, the action, and so forth, as well as everything else, are dependent upon Viṣṇu; therefore, He is said to be the form of all. Thus it is stated in the *Brahma-tarka*.
Śrīdhara [objects]: "But surely, in some cases, by someone, from something, at some time, a protector is also seen [to exist independently]."
Anticipating this doubt, and having affirmed that even in those cases You alone are the protector in each respective form,

He declares His very nature as the Self of all with the words "In whom": whatever another— that is, a later being such as a father or the like, or a higher being such as Brahmā and so forth— performs as an agent through various instrumental factors, all that [is Yours].
It is your very own nature and not something separate. In whatever substratum,

from whatever cause, at whatever time, by whatever instrument, impelled by whatever causal agent, belonging to whom, from whatever point of departure, for whatever recipient, that which is most desired, and who [is so impelled]— [all these are you].

The agent—thus are the seven meanings of the case-endings. "In what way" (*yathā*) refers to the meaning of indeclinables functioning as adverbs of manner. "Distinct nature" (*pṛthak-svabhāva*) refers to the primordial matter (*prakṛti*) consisting of *sattva* and the other qualities. [The root *kṛ*] means "to do," "to produce," or "to transform," that is, to lead something into another form. (20)

The sequence of the composition: he demonstrates its very nature with the words "in which" (*yasmin*). In the commentary, one should understand the readings to be "another, more recent" (*yo'paro'rvācīna*) and "whatever [is produced] by the causal factors" (*yad yat kārakaiḥ*). The term "essential nature" (*svarūpam*) means that which has become the effect of its own material cause (*svopādāna-kārya-bhūtam*). ||20||

Viśvanātha: He states that even those who are seen as protectors, such as fathers and others, are likewise Your very form—beginning with "yasmin" (in whom). Whether it be another person who is recent, or one who is ancient such as Brahmā and others; whatever an agent (*bhāva*) performs by means of various causal factors (*kāraka*), all of that belongs to You, who are endowed with the power of *māyā*.

"Svarūpam" means one's own form. In whatever substratum (*adhikaraṇa*), from whatever cause (*nimitta*), at whatever time (*yarhi*), by whatever instrument (*karaṇa*), for whatever reason (*hetu*), or impelled by whatever agent (*kartṛ*); that which belongs to whom, from whatever material cause (*upādāna*), for whatever recipient (*sampradāna*), and that which is most desired (*īpsitatama*)—that is he.

"Agent" (kartā) refers thus to the meaning of the seven case-endings; "in what way" (yathā) and "by which manner" (yena) refer to the meaning of indeclinables functioning as adverbs of action. From you, who are devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), the primordial nature consisting of sattva and the other [guṇas], having a distinct nature, acts—that is, it produces and transforms—into another form.
He leads. ||20||
Māyā creates the mind, which is composed of karma and is most powerful,
impelled by time and in accordance with the qualities (guṇas) of the person.
O Unborn One, who other than You could transcend this wheel of worldly existence, which consists of the Vedic meters and is set in motion by Aja with its sixteen spokes?
The root of the ten faculties, the vital breaths, and the mind is the mind itself; it is the wheel of saṃsāra. ||21||

Śrīdhara: Since there is no other protector and because [the Lord] is beyond saṃsāra, he is eternally liberated; thus, with the two verses beginning with "māyā," he prays: "Protect me, who have come to you for refuge. By the grace of the Person, who is a portion of You, in the form of His glance—consisting of the mind, which is the subtle body (liṅga) dominated by the mind, and characterized by Māyā—[the world is perceived].
She creates. Of what nature is she? She whose *guṇas* (qualities) have been impelled—that is, agitated—by *kāla* (time).
Of what nature is the mind (*manas*)? It consists of action (*karmamaya*), taking the form of that which acts; it is more powerful (*balīyas*), difficult to conquer;
and it consists of *chandas*, meaning it is primarily concerned with the actions prescribed in the Vedas. [She creates] by means of *ajā*, the ignorance (*avidyā*) of the individual soul (*jīva*).

In that [mind], which consists of the wheel of saṃsāra, sixteen spokes—representing the modifications (vikāras) offered for the sake of enjoying those objects—are fixed; who then could cross over such a mind? O Unborn One! "Other than You" means one who stands apart from You and does not worship You. ||21||

The Sequence of Composition: Demonstrating that everything is dependent upon Him, [the author] establishes that He alone is its protector—with the words "Māyā. Māyā first creates the mind in the form of karma, Māyā, and so forth;
therefore, because of its weakness, the wheel of saṃsāra, consisting of the Vedas (chandas) and other forms, does not reach Your mercy.
"Who could cross over? means "no one at all. ||21||
Viśvanātha: Now, if I myself am indeed the form of all, then saṃsāra is also I alone;

why then do you wish to be liberated from this saṃsāra which is my own form? To this, he says in two verses: Māyā is your external power (*bahiraṅga-śakti*), the subtle body (*liṅga-deha*) consisting of the mind, the great principle (*mahat*), and so forth, which serves as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for the individual soul (*jīva*).

She creates actions consisting of worldly and Vedic activities; she is composed of that which is powerful and difficult to conquer. She is one whose qualities (guṇas) are impelled and agitated by the glance in the form of permission granted to the person who is her portion.
She consists of *chandas*—that is, consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—for Amara states: "The word *chandas* refers to meter and to desire. That very [nature]...

Indeed, this wheel of saṃsāra would exist. Of what nature? It is that in which sixteen spokes—the modifications—are fixed by *aja* (the unborn), namely *avidyā* (ignorance). Who could cross over this? One other than you—one who is separate from you and does not worship you; such is the meaning. But one whose devotion is directed to no one other than you may cross over.
The meaning is "so it is. ||21||
For you are eternally one whose self and qualities are ever-conquered; by your own splendor, you are Time itself, having brought under your control the powers of both creation and withdrawal.
O Lord, drawn into the sixteen-spoked wheel released for the sake of conquest, O All-pervading One, draw back this one who has sought refuge and is being crushed.

Śrīdhara: [Objection: "But since I too am connected with *māyā* and possess no distinction from you in terms of agency (*kartṛtva*) and so forth, what is my difference from you? To this he says: "He" (*sa*). You indeed are he by whom the qualities of the self—that is, of the intellect (*buddhi*)—are eternally conquered through his own abode, which is the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*). For time is the impeller of *māyā*; therefore, for that very reason...
He by whom the powers of things to be abandoned, of actions to be performed, and of means to be employed have been brought under control;
therefore, draw me, who am being crushed like a stalk of sugarcane, toward yourself and lead me near. 22.
The sequence of composition: showing that very same point again in particular, he declares his own desired conclusion with the words "You are He" (sa tvam). ||22||

The Bhagavat-sandarbha (17): Here, the "self" refers to the individual soul (jīva), and its qualities are sattva and the others; for it has been stated: "Sattva, rajas, and tamas—these are the qualities of the jīva, and not mine" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.25.12). ||22||

Viśvanātha: Therefore, although this wheel of worldly existence (*saṃsāra-cakra*) consists of that [Māyā] because Māyā is Your power (*śakti*), and thus is of that same nature, You are nonetheless distinct from it by virtue of Your own essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*).
For this reason, He says "You, that one" (*sa tvam*), meaning: "Having liberated these people from that [wheel], lead them to the vicinity of Your own feet. As for what... [the verse continues].

Indeed, Māyā creates the limiting adjunct (upādhi) for the individual soul (jīva), which consists of the material qualities (guṇas). You, however, are one by whom those qualities of the self and the qualities of the intellect have been conquered through Your own abode, Your essential power (svarūpa-śakti). You are also that Time (kāla) which agitates the qualities. Therefore, the limiting adjuncts—which are the effects of Māyā and are subject to being cast off—have been brought under control; in them, there is no further emission (visarga).
He by whom [the world] is characterized as a deposit, a power, and ignorance—therefore, like a stalk of sugarcane being pressed, draw near and lead to your side those who have come for refuge. 22.
O Lord, I have seen in heaven the lifespan, prosperity, and power of all the guardians of the celestial realms, which this world desires.
Those who were shaken by the quivering of the eyebrows in the expansion of our father’s angry smile— he indeed has been cast out by you.

Śrīdhara: [Objection: "Enjoy the pleasures of the world-protectors, or I shall give you this ancestral kingdom; why are you so terrified of worldly existence? To this he replies with three verses beginning with "dṛṣṭāḥ. "Śriyaḥ" means riches or prosperity; "vibhava" means manifestation or power. By the rhetorical question "are life-span and the rest seen? their worthlessness is expressed.
He says that very thing: "Those who were destroyed by the mere knitting of the eyebrows, distorted by the anger and laughter of our father—he too has been rejected by you. (23)

The Sequence of Composition: Once again, moved by compassion upon seeing his own suffering, he prays for his heart’s desire with two verses beginning with "dṛṣṭā. His sole and supreme heart's desire is the direct service of love at the lotus feet, following in the footsteps of those who serve them.
It should be understood that [the Lord] was entreated in many ways by concealing [His true nature] through a display of humility, both previously and later. (23–24)

Viśvanātha says: "I do not see anyone other than you who possesses such sovereignty that I might take refuge in him, and who would deliver me from this cycle of existence. Thus he says: "Beheld" (dṛṣṭāḥ). The lifespans and so forth of all the world-protectors stationed in heaven have been beheld; as have their splendors (*śriyaḥ*), which are riches and material wealth, and their powers (*vibhavaḥ*).
Sovereignty: The sense is that those who guard the sacrificial hearths recognize you alone as the Supreme Lord, even from the power common to both the anger and the laughter of our father. ||23||
Therefore, O wise one, I do not desire those blessings for embodied beings—
longevity, prosperity, power, and sensory enjoyment— reaching even as far as Brahmā.
I do not desire Your disheveled hair, O You of great prowess;
since You are Time itself, lead me instead to the side of Your own servant.

Śrīdhara: Since this is so, therefore, the wise one—knowing that those blessings are enjoyments and understanding their ripening—desires nothing at all, even having pervaded with Brahman the enjoyment of the senses, which is to be experienced by the senses as "I. He regards even the *aṇimā* and other powers as being agitated and destroyed by the prowess of Time, the Self. (24)

Sanātana [Ha.bha.vi. 10.293]: Since the prosperities of those who dwell in heaven—their lifespans and so forth—which are sought after by the world, have been destroyed by the mere knitting of my father’s brows in anger, therefore, whatever there may be—be it blessings, enjoyments, that which is to be experienced by the senses through the senses, or even the enjoyment of Brahmā—[all are included].
I do not desire them; for the wise one knows their ripening—that they are perishable—this is the meaning.
[I do not desire] even the *aṇiman* and other powers when they have been agitated by You, whose nature is Time (*kāla-ātman*) and whose prowess is vast;
or rather, [I desire] those objects which are unagitated and untouched by You as the Self of Time.

"I do not desire even the states characterized by sālokya, sārūpya, sāmīpya, and sāyujya. If so, what do you desire? To this he says: "May [the Lord] lead [me]" (upanaya). The sense is: "May my association with Your devotees, which constitutes the supreme fruit, occur wherever it may; I have no insistence on a particular place or the like. (24)

The sequence of the composition: [The devotees] have transcended time and are in close proximity to the supreme goal of life even for those who are supremely devoted; thus he says, "Therefore," etc. This is clear. ||24||

[Bhagavat-sandarbha 66] Viśvanātha: What follows from that? To this he says: "Therefore" (tasmāt). Since even my father, though possessed of such abundant sovereignty, was cast out, therefore I, being wise, [despise] blessings and enjoyments.

Knowing that ripening, I desire nothing at all— even that which is enjoyed by the senses, extending even to the enjoyments of Brahmā up to the realm of Āviriñci; nor do I desire those powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest, though they are agitated and destroyed by the nature of time— nay, I desire only that [state] which is at the side of my own servant, for that alone is the most excellent of all.
The meaning is: "I know. ||24||
Where are the blessings, pleasant to the ear yet of the nature of a mirage?
And where is this body, the breeding ground for every kind of disease?
Even though he is wise, a person does not become weary of the fire of desire, even while attempting to extinguish it with drops of honey that are difficult to obtain.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, he states that even in the present time they are not fit for enjoyment—with the words "Where? Hearing (śruti) is the act of listening; those [desires] in which that itself is the pleasure are such. And where are these aspirations, which are as false as a mirage? And where is this body, the source and place of origin for all diseases and ailments?

If this were so, why does every person not become dispassionate? To this he says: *yad api*—even though this person is thus wise, *tathāpi* nevertheless, he does not become weary of the world; he does not become detached. Why?
Because he pacifies with drops of pleasure, which are like honey, even that fire which is desire itself, though it is difficult to extinguish.

The meaning is that for one preoccupied with quelling the fire of desire, there is no opportunity for world-weariness (*nirveda*). Alternatively, the sense is that this activity of Your illusory power (*māyā*) is inconceivable. ||25||

The sequence of the composition: Furthermore, in order to demonstrate his own extreme wretchedness, he shows the general wretchedness of living beings, beginning with the word "kutra" (where). [He says: "By that which is like honey, there is instead an increase of the fire. (25)

Viśvanātha: If it is asked, "Then what [is desired]? and if one says, "The entire world desires enjoyment and sovereignty," [the author] replies, "But everyone is indeed ignorant," by asking, "Where? Desires such as kingship and the like are like the form of a mirage (*mṛgatṛṣṇā*); just as a mirage consists of the pleasure of sight, so too these blessings consist merely of the pleasure of hearing.
Since, in reality, there is not even a trace of happiness due to rivalry, envy, passion, hatred, anxiety for one's loss, and so forth;

or, even if there were happiness, because of the inability to enjoy it, there is only great suffering. Thus he says: "Where is this?"—meaning, since even a wise person does not become disillusioned after reflecting on this, how much less so a fool?
This is the intended meaning. Of what nature is he? He is one who attempts to quench the fire of desire with mere drops of honey—that is, with fragments of pleasure;
for indeed, an actual fire is not extinguished by drops of honey, but rather it only blazes all the more.
As for those fragments of pleasure, they are difficult to obtain and are acquired only through sufferings. ||25||
O Lord, where am I, born from passion (rajas) in this world dominated by darkness (tamas), within a family of those other than the gods; and where is Your compassion?
This is not a favor from Brahmā, nor from Bhava, nor indeed from Ramā; it is the grace of one who has placed his lotus-hand upon my head.
The sweetness of Lakṣmī and the others has not yet been offered;
even their superior exaltation arises solely from the excellence of their service.
They are praised by the triads of Śrī, Brahmā, and Brāhmī, as well as by Indra and the other gods, along with their respective wives and male attendants.
Therefore, others as well are always [engaged] in liberation and mindfulness precisely through this sequence.
"In devotion to Hari, in knowledge of Him, and in happiness, there is indeed a constant rule;
it can never be otherwise, whether through another, oneself, or by action. Thus [it is said] in the *Brahma-tarka*.
Śrīdhara [comments]: "In that case, why are you despondent? [This is due to] the [devotion] directed toward me, even though I am unworthy."

With the intention that "it is solely by Your grace," he says: *kva* (where). He whose origin or birth (*prabhava*) is from *rajas* alone—that is, one born in a family characterized by *rajas*, or where *tamas* is predominant; where am I, born in such a family of the *asuras*, and where is Your compassion? He describes that very compassion: [He who is] upon the heads of Brahmā and the others...
It is not that this hand, which like a lotus removes all suffering, has been offered;
rather, it is that this grace, which takes the form of the goals of human life (puruṣārtha), has been placed upon my head—either as such, or out of the compassion she felt for me. ||26||

The sequence of the composition: Now, showing his own wretchedness and, through that [compassion], demonstrating the intensity of His state of being free from limiting conditions (nirupādhitva), he says: "Where am I? And the phrase "not even of Brahman" is said with reference to the circumstances at that time. ||26||

Viśvanātha: Furthermore, although there is no one more wretched than I, you have nonetheless made me the most excellent of all. How can I describe the greatness of your grace? Thus he says: "Where am I?
and so forth, referring to how the lotus-hand of Him who is Brahmā and the rest was placed upon my head. (26)
This lack of discernment between the higher and the lower would surely not belong to you, for you are as a friend to yourself as you are to all beings in the world.
Through service, your grace is like that of the celestial tree;
its manifestation corresponds to the service rendered, not to one's high or low status.

Śrīdhara: Nor is this at all surprising in your case; thus he says, "Not this... This notion of superior and inferior—that these beginning with Brahmā are superior and this asura is inferior—would not exist in you at all, just as it exists in an ordinary person. The reason for this is that you are the Self of the universe and its friend. If so, [then...]

Why should My grace not be of such a nature everywhere? To this He says: "Through service to You, grace arises. And in that regard, in accordance with the service and following their respective desires, there occurs the manifestation of dharma and the other goals of life.
Even while such inequality exists, there is no lack of fairness; the illustration for this is: "just as the celestial wish-fulfilling tree."

Just as [the sun] bestows fruit according to the resolve of the servant alone and is not partial, so it is here; the implication is that superiority or inferiority is not the cause in this case. ||27||

The sequence of the argument: Although it is indeed marvelous that you bestow grace upon your devotees, it is not excessively so because such examples exist. However, your grace toward me is exceedingly marvelous precisely because of the absence of such examples. "Oh, how powerful is your compassion!"—this is the meaning of the preceding verse.
In order to exalt it thus, he says: "Not this," [verse 27].

Viśvanātha: Nor do you distinguish between high and low by way of your own essential nature; thus he says, "Not this. Just as this notion of superior and inferior—that these beings beginning with Brahmā are superior and this demon is base—exists for an ordinary person, such a distinction would not exist for You at all. The reason for this is that You are the Self of the universe.
"And [you are] a friend. "In that case, may your grace be present at all times? To this he replies:

Just as the celestial tree (suratara), by its very service, gives fruit to the one who has taken refuge in it according to that person's resolve yet remains impartial, so too are you; even there, the manifestation [of grace] is in accordance with service, precisely through the gradations of service.
The meaning is that the degree of the arising of compassion is the cause of the degree of its arising, and not its superiority—that is, its being either supreme or inferior. ||27||
Thus, while people have fallen into the well of worldly existence,
longing for sensual pleasures, he who follows after them through attachment likewise falls.
O Blessed One, since he has been taken by the celestial sage and made his own,
how indeed could I, who am his servant, abandon service to you?

Śrīdhara says: "And since I have obtained this through the grace of Your servant, please direct me to go to that very servant of Yours. Thus he speaks with this instruction: "In this way"—meaning, just as I have been shown compassion by You, so too was I previously favored by Nārada, who took me under his care; such am I.

How indeed can I abandon service to Your servant? How am I so favored? For I am like a well situated at the very source of a river; when people, desiring their own pleasures, fall into it, I too fall after them due to that association. Thus, by the grace of Your servant Nārada—
I have been exceedingly compassioned by you; this alone is my supreme favor, and not this most trivial matter such as the preservation of my life. (28)

The Structural Connection (*krama-sandarbha*): Now, even while recollecting the cause of such grace, he prays for that very same desired object—beginning with the word "thus" (*evam*). "Thus"—meaning, one who has been favored in such a way as to be worthy of Your grace;
being such, how could I [not be so]? Because of the extraordinary grace shown by the servants of the Lord whom I have seen.
"Shall I release it? means "Am I able to abandon it?"—the answer being "by no means. ||28||

Viśvanātha: Now, regarding the statement "By my service toward you, I have bestowed full grace upon you," you have here dispelled the charge of partiality on my part by means of the analogy of the celestial wish-fulfilling tree (*suratru*). However, what is the cause for such service? To that, he says: "In this way, [I regard] every person according to their superior or inferior state..."

While I was thus intensely desiring sense-objects, like one who has fallen into a well connected to a serpent, I was about to fall further along that same path; however, the divine sage Śrī Nārada took me under his protection,
asserting "Let this living being be mine," and having superimposed ownership over me, he seized me by force.

The sense is that, having taken him by his own hand from that place and brought him into his presence, he instructed him in that king of mantras and thus made him his own servant. "I am he"—meaning, one who had indeed fallen into the well of saṃsāra;
yet now I am Prahlāda, your devotee, by whose grace this came to pass—of you, [O Lord].
"How can I abandon—that is, give up—the service of my glorious Guru, the servant?
The meaning is: just as those who follow the paths of action (karma), knowledge (jñāna), and yoga abandon their means once they have attained the fruit;
for in the path of devotion (bhakti-mārga), even the means itself becomes the fruit, [and thus] even for those who have attained the Lord..."
The longing for the means such as association with the saintly, beginning with Dhruva, is as follows:
"O Infinite One, may I have constant association with those great souls of pure heart who flow with devotion toward You again and again" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 4.9.11).
"I move about meditating; please favor me so that mindfulness may remain," it is said [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.69.18].
For this very reason, having reflected, I prayed: "Lead me to the side of Your own servant" [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.9.24]. ||28||
O Ananta, I consider the protection of my own life and the slaying of my father to have been intended to make the word of the sage, my own servant, come true.
Having grasped his sword, he said: "Since you wish to do me wrong, whom else but you, O Lord, shall I slay? May he protect me!"

Śrīdhara: He said this to show that he did not act out of favor toward him, but for another purpose: "O Ananta, both this protection of my life and the slaying of my father who was intent on killing me were done in order to make true—that is, to fulfill—the word of the sage who is your own servant. I [did this].
I think so. Why? Because, desiring to perform an improper act, he seized his sword and said:
"What is it? If there is a Lord other than me—distinct from me—then let him protect you now;
I shall take away your head. This is the meaning even in the alternative reading (*pāṭhāntara*). As for what he said:

Alternatively, the construction may be "then, for the sake of protecting my life. And this has been explained in many ways in that very passage: *satyaṃ vidhātuṃ nija-bhṛtya-bhāṣitam* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.8.17), according to the *Krama-sandarbha*: "And the protection of my life and so forth is likewise," he says with the words "my life" (*mat-prāṇa*).

Viśvanātha: Therefore, because You are subject to Your devotees, Your compassion toward the worlds is seen as following after the grace of Your devotees; yet it is not the case that You do not show compassion to anyone who has taken refuge in You, Your own devotee.
Thus, there is no partiality in You anywhere, for even toward me, everything [is done] solely in accordance with Your own devotees.

He says that this is indeed a favor: "Mad" (by me). I believe that he said this in order to make true the words of the sage Nārada, his own servant. By my measure—that is, by Śrī Nārada, who was entreated for my sake—it will come to pass that your son’s welfare shall be secured through the destruction of his enemies and other blessings.
Because of the granting of a boon; as it was said:
"There, the virtuous lady attended upon the sage with supreme devotion, being pregnant for the sake of the safety of her fetus and for a desired delivery."
"The compassionate sage, the Lord, bestowed both the essence of dharma and pure knowledge upon her, with reference even to me. [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.7.14–15] Thus it is said.

Since you, desiring to kill me, asked "Whose head shall I take?", it is because protection from the elephants of the quarters and the like is not possible by their hands; thus, their slaughter was carried out by you. Such is the case even though the Blessed One is equal toward all.
That being subject to the devotee is what is distinguished [in this context], as made known by Prahlāda. ||29||
O you who are one alone, this world is yours; for you abide separately at its beginning, its end, and in its middle.
Having created this world through His own Māyā by the intermingling of the *guṇas*, He entered it and, as it were, became manifold through them.
Śrīdhara: Nor is this protection of one side and the slaying of the Daityas natural to you;
rather, they are conditioned by the qualities (*guṇa*) of *māyā*, because such [actions] are impossible in you who are the Self of all (*sarvātman*) by your own nature.
Thus he says: "The One. And this world is you alone as the One. For this reason, [you are present] at the beginning and at the end of this [world].

"You appear as distinct; you take on a pause [of separation]; the meaning is that You exist as the mere measure, as the cause, and as the limit. Therefore, You alone are also in the middle. If so, from where does the perception of difference arise? To this he says: having created this world, which consists of the transformation of the *guṇas*, by Your own *māyā*."
Having entered into that [body], you are perceived as if manifold through those qualities acting as causes—as a protector and as a slayer.
Thus it is said at the beginning of the *Skandha*:
"For although the Blessed One is devoid of qualities, unborn, unmanifest, and beyond primordial nature (*prakṛti*)."
"Having entered into the qualities of his own māyā, he has become the oppressor and the oppressed," and so forth. ||30||

The sequence of composition: Now, the pacification of that anger by means of another rasa. For instance: "How can this wretched being be the object of your anger, since he is but one," and so forth. Nevertheless, a connection with what precedes is observed. For instance, that very [anger] is directly [connected] through its relation to the grace bestowed upon devotees.

While it is true that You descend in this way and protect those like us, You perform the general protection of the universe as its inner controller (*antaryāmin*). And even though that is performed by You alone, it is not done directly;
rather, You show that it occurs through others as well. Thus, following upon that, He describes the pastimes (*līlā*) of creation and so forth, beginning with the word "eka" (one).
Thus [ends section 30].

Viśvanātha: Thus, the protection by You—who transcend the *guṇas* and are affectionate toward Your devotees—of devotees like me who have transcended the *guṇas*, is itself beyond the *guṇas*. However, as for the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world composed of the *guṇas*, these are performed by You while remaining indifferent; speaking thus of Him...
Since the world has you as its cause, it is indeed composed of you; thus he says: "The One.

Because, at the beginning, the end, and the middle of this world, although you appear distinct from it, you alone remain—you are determined and perceived by those possessed of discernment; such is the meaning. Why, then, is there no such perception?

To this he replies: "Having created this world, which consists of the transformation of the *guṇas*, by Your own *māyā*— the sense being that for You, who are devoid of *guṇas*, *māyā-śakti* lacks the status of being an essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*)— You, having entered into it,
are perceived as if manifold through those *guṇas* acting as causes, appearing as if the destroyer, the protector, and the creator."

In reality, however, it is the quality of *tamas* alone that is the destroyer, the quality of *sattva* alone that is the protector, and the quality of *rajas* alone that is the creator; yet, because You enter into them with equanimity, You receive such designations as "the Destroyer" and so forth.
You alone are this existent and non-existent; you are the Lord, and there is nothing else besides you.
This notion of "self" and "other" is indeed meaningless, for it is merely *māyā*.
Whatever has birth, death, maintenance, and perception—[all that is you].
That very same [procedure] applies to the *aṣṭi* and *taru* meters, just as it does for the *vasukāla*.

Regarding the term *madhvaḥ*: just as a tree and the burning of the tree are both said to be "fate and time" (*daiva-kāla*) because they are dependent upon fate and time, so too, because everything is dependent upon You, everything is said to be "You. Although [the world] is inherently distinct from Him, the erroneous notion that "I and others are the Supreme Lord alone" is meaningless.
The meaning is that they are said to be "together" precisely because of their dependence on that [object], and not because of their own intrinsic nature. ||31||

Śrīdhara: Now, one might object: "If this world is indeed myself, then would I not also possess inequality due to the inequality of the world? To this he says: "You alone are this world, consisting of both the existent and non-existent, the effect and the cause; it is not separate from you. But you—"

It is other than that, because it exists separately at the beginning and the end. Since this is so, therefore the notion that "this is mine" and "this is another's" is meaningless and is merely illusion (*māyā*). He establishes the non-difference between cause and effect by means of an illustration: from which [cause] there is the birth, the perception, and the manifestation of that [effect]. In which...

Dissolution and persistence are indeed that very same thing. Just as non-existence (*aṣṭi*) is the seed and the cause, while the tree is the effect, so too do these two possess the nature of being merely substance (*vasu*) and time (*kāla*).
This is the meaning: by the word "time," earth is intended because of its association with unique qualities such as blueness.

By the word *vasu*, the mere substance—the subtle element (*bhūta-sūkṣma*)—is meant. In this regard, just as a tree consists of nothing but its earthy seed, and that seed consists of nothing but the subtle elements, so too the entire world, consisting of cause and effect, consists of nothing but the supreme cause. And thus:
The aphorism of the Great Sage (Bādarāyaṇa) states: "That [effect] is non-different [from the cause], on account of the words concerning its origin and so forth" (Vedānta-sūtra 2.1.14).
And there is a Śruti passage: "A modification is a verbal handle, a mere name; 'clay' alone is the reality" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.4). ||31||
The sequence of the composition: therein he establishes its distinctiveness with the words "Or you... (31).

Viśvanātha: Now, even if the world is illusory (*māyika*), since *māyā* is Your power (*śakti*), why should You not also possess partiality (*vaiṣamya*) due to the world's inequality? To this he says: "You indeed are this world"—consisting of cause and effect, both real and unreal; because it is fundamentally composed of *pradhāna*, it is truly real, but it does not arise from You [as its inherent nature].

Distinct. Therefore, you are indeed other than this world, precisely because you exist separately from it at its beginning and end. As for whatever notion there is within that very world—such as "this is my self," "this is mine," "this is another," or "this is my enemy"—that is *māyā*, that is ignorance (*avidyā*); it is merely imagined by the ignorance of the individual soul (*jīva*).

The meaning is as follows: that [cause] is indeed false and devoid of purpose; this is the sense. Furthermore, while establishing the non-difference of the effect from its cause, he also refutes the inequality of the Supreme Cause, the Blessed Lord, by means of an illustration:
"That from which something is born, in whom it has its vision and its manifestation, and in whom its dissolution occurs..."
And its persistence is indeed that very same thing. "Support" (*āśraya*) is the seed, the cause; "tree" is the effect.
The meaning is: just as between those two there is the relationship of substance and time, so too is the relationship of substantiality and temporality.
By the word "substance" (*vasu*), the mere entity—the subtle element (*bhūta-sūkṣma*)—is expressed. By the word "time" (*kāla*)...

Earth [is established] through its connection with the uncommon quality of blueness; here, the word "time" (kāla) denotes the quality of blue. Consequently, just as both the root and the tree—which constitute cause and effect—possess the nature of earthness and the nature of odor.

This is the meaning: just as a vessel consists merely of clay, time consists merely of time, the earth consists merely of earth, and a tree consists merely of a tree; even so, primordial matter (pradhāna) consists merely of the Lord (Īśvara), and the world composed of gods, animals, and so forth, consists merely of the Great One (mahat) and the other evolutes. Thus it is.
And you alone are the one who consists of the cause and effect of all things, such as trees and so forth. Thus says the aphorism of the Great Sage:
"That non-difference [of the effect from the cause] is established on account of the words concerning the beginning [of the effect], etc. (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 2.1.14). And the Śruti says:
"The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'clay' alone is the truth" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.4).

Thus, just as there is no disparity in the fragrance— the ultimate cause— of earthly objects such as wood and stone despite their disparity, so too there is no disparity in the Blessed One despite the disparity of the world. ||31||
Having thus dissolved this world within oneself into the midst of the waters of dissolution, one should remain as the Self alone, free from desire, experiencing one's own innate bliss.
With eyes closed through yoga, having drunk up sleep with your very self, you abide in the fourth state (turiya); thus you are joined neither to darkness nor to the qualities (guṇas).
Madhva is situated upon the drum. ||32||
Śrīdhara: In that regard, he first shows the separate state [of the Lord] at the end [of creation] with the words "having deposited this.

Having cast this universe into Himself by means of His own Self, experiencing only His own bliss and being devoid of activity, You lie down in the midst of the waters of dissolution. If so, is it as if I am merely a *jīva*?

Is sleep of the nature of a function of darkness (*tamas*)? No, indeed not; rather, it is said that yoga itself is called "sleep" due to the similarity of the absence of external functions: "by whom the eyes are closed through yoga," "by whom sleep is drunk away by the light of the Self's own nature," and "therefore in the Fourth State (*turya*), which transcends the three states."

You remain established in yourself, yet unlike one who is asleep, you do not associate with darkness; that is, you neither join with nor perceive the qualities (guṇas) or sense-objects, as occurs in the states of waking and dreaming. ||32||

The sequence of the composition: By way of context, through the grace of the great devotees such as Viriñca and others, he specifically describes the pastimes consisting of creation and so forth in seven verses beginning with "Having deposited this... [within] himself, in the form of the one reclining in the waters of the cosmic egg (garbhodaka-śāyin); [he describes] the world, the three realms, and the yoga.
Thus he says: "Abiding in the fourth state, the fourth reality known as Śrī Vāsudeva"—the meaning is that one's manifestation is accepted within the Self as being nothing other than You alone. ||32||

Viśvanātha: He elaborates upon the state of being the cause of the universe, as previously stated through its initial, final, and intermediate conditions, by means of five verses beginning with "nyasya. Having deposited this universe within himself alone, he rests upon Śeṣa in the midst of that causal ocean, whose waters have been dissolved—that is, whose waters have ceased their flow and are imperishable.

"You sleep. [This means: He is one who experiences His own bliss solely by Himself, through the power of His own essential nature (*ātma-svarūpa-śakti*). "Without desire" (*nirīhaḥ*) means not desiring the play (*līlā*) of *māyā*. If so, do I also have sleep in the form of a state of darkness (*tamas*), as the individual soul (*jīva*) does? Certainly not, certainly not. It is called "sleep" because of the similarity in the absence of external mental activity (*bahir-vṛtty-abhāva*).
He said: By whom the eyes are closed through yoga; by whom sleep is swallowed up by the manifestation of the Self's own nature;

and because he remains established in the *turīya* state—which is beyond the three states—he does not "yoke" [himself] like an ordinary living being, nor does he accept the qualities (*guṇas*) as one does in the waking or dreaming states. He merely "joins" [himself] with that state, as if it were darkness in deep sleep.
The sense objects. ||32||
This very body of yours is hidden within yourself, its material nature impelled by your own power of time.
From the navel of Him who was resting upon the infinite waters and whose meditative absorption was ending, there arose a great lotus, like a banyan tree from its own seed-pod.
The lotus, which is the very soul of the world, is also the body [of the Lord] because it belongs to the lineage of the Blessed One. Furthermore,
she who is the presiding deity of all stationary beings is especially established within the banyan seed and the holy fig tree.
The invisible one is named Kaṇikā. ||33||

Śrīdhara: Now, demonstrating that You exist separately even at the beginning as the cause, and elaborating on the fact that "You alone [exist] in the middle," he explains this in four verses. That You lie upon the waters—this entire world is Your very body, Your own essential nature, and not that of anyone else; for You are...

Also from his center. Of what nature was he? One by whom the qualities of *prakṛti*, such as *sattva* and the rest, were impelled by his own power of time (*kāla*). The reason for his being in his essential form (*svarūpa*) is: from your navel, belonging to him who had desisted from his meditative absorption (*samādhi*) after rising from the couch of Śeṣa, where he lay infinitely.

In the waters of the single vast ocean, there arose the world-lotus, a great lotus; of what nature was it? It was hidden within you yourself, just as a great banyan tree [arises] from its own minute seed-kernel. (33)

The sequence of the argument: How can the seed, though existing by way of its own part within the locus of the sprout as soon as it has arisen, be perceived? The meaning is that it is not perceived at all; rather, it is perceived only in that very place [where it was before].
The sense is that, although it was indeed present there, it remained inaccessible to perception. ||33||

Viśvanātha: And then, at the commencement of that very creation of yours once again, by whom the qualities of *prakṛti*—such as *sattva* and the rest—were impelled by his own power of time (*kāla-śakti*), this body in the form of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), which was already hidden within you, His own self, became manifest from *prakṛti*. Thereafter...

From Your navel, a great lotus emerged— just as a massive banyan tree arises from a minute banyan seed— even as You lay upon that egg within the waters, ceasing Your meditation on the Infinite Bed (Ananta-śayana). ||33||
The poet born from that, seeing nothing else, contemplated you as the seed extended within himself and outside.
Even after submerging himself in the waters for a hundred years, he did not find it; how then could he perceive the seed once the sprout has already grown?
That [power] of the honeyed [nectar] also causes the trees to blossom; therefore, it is called the "seed," and it remains present even when the sprout has arisen.
In this way, Hari resides within the causes as the dust that generates the effect.
"Having entered into his duties, he is not seen here at first. And so it is said. (34)
Śrīdhara: Thus, it has been stated that you alone exist even in the midst [of creation], being followed as the cause.

To clarify this very point through the experience of Brahmā, who is composed of pure *sattva*, he describes his former state: "In whom there was birth in that lotus"—[he is] the poet, Brahmā. Therefore...

Not seeing anything other than the lotus as the seed that serves as the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), he did not perceive you, even though you were pervading it. And this is indeed logical, O Sage! For once a sprout has arisen, how could a person perceive the seed—the cause inherent within it—as something separate? ||34||

The sequence of the argument: How could the seed, which exists in its own part within the locus of the sprout as soon as it has arisen, be perceived? The meaning is: "It certainly could not. Rather, it would be perceived right there [in the seed];
however, the sense is that it was indeed inaccessible to it [the sprout] at that time. ||34||
Viśvanātha: The poet Brahmā, born from that lotus—that is, produced from that lotus—perceived nothing other than that lotus;
yet, having reflected that You, the material cause, exist pervasively within his own self (ātman) as if existing outside of himself by Your own power, he searched for You for a hundred years.
He did not find it. And this is indeed appropriate. Oh! Once the sprout has arisen, how could the seed—which exists therein by way of its own part—be perceived within that very locus of the sprout?
Rather, the meaning is that it would be perceived only beneath it. [This applies to] lotuses, heroes, and so forth.

Even though sprouts arise again and again and then perish, this is not seen to result from the destruction of the seed; rather, the meaning is that at that time, its very foundation was inaccessible even to Brahmā. ||34||
He, whose origin is the Self, filled with great wonder and having resorted to the lotus, became purified in his being through intense asceticism over time.
O Lord, he beheld you within himself, like an exceedingly subtle fragrance spread throughout the earth, pervading the body composed of the elements, the senses, and the mind.
Śrīdhara says: "But by means of your worship, he saw [the Lord] within himself," as he states with the words "sa tu" (he, however).
Being seated upon a lotus, having turned back [from the world], through intense austerity and meditation;
by this, his vision is described as being by way of the material cause (*upādāna*) in the form of pure existence (*san-mātra*). ||35||
The sequence of the composition: And then, having first experienced Him in that very state through samādhi as the mere existence called Brahman, he says: "But he... (verse 35).

Viśvanātha: Having desisted from his search and returned to the lotus itself, while remaining there, he beheld you—like the causal fragrance residing within the earth, which is the effect—within his own body through intense austerity and meditation upon you. ||35||
Thus, [he is] richly endowed with a thousand faces, feet, heads, hands, thighs, noses, ears, eyes, ornaments, and weapons.
Having seen the Great Being, whose form was composed of illusion yet possessed a perfectly perceived configuration, Viriñca attained joy.

The "honey" (madhu) is that which consists of illusory power (māyā), whose essential nature is knowledge, whose configuration is characterized by existence, and whose form is a collection of attributes such as bliss.
Just as the deity named "fragrance" (gandha) remains pervading the earth.
Thus he beheld Viṣṇu pervading the world, abiding as the Self within Brahman. And so it is said. ||36||

Śrīdhara: He states that [the sage] became one who has accomplished his purpose by perceiving [the Lord] as the Sovereign (Īśvara): "In this manner," by this method, [he saw the Lord] as "rich" (*āḍhyam*), meaning endowed with a thousand—that is, immeasurable—[features] such as mouths and so forth;
"consisting of *māyā*," meaning having *māyā* as its primary constituent; and "whose configuration is characterized by the existent manifold" (*satā prapañcena upalakṣitaḥ sanniveśaḥ*).
That which has the arrangement of feet and so forth. ||36||

The sequence of the composition: And then, he says "thus" (evam), meaning that he also beheld his form, which consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss (sac-cid-ānanda). Now, one might ask: how can there be a vision of him right there, when he is like a seed situated elsewhere? To this, he replies: "in this way," namely, by the very manner of experiencing his expansion within meditative absorption (samādhi).
The meaning is that although His body is seen to have a medium size, He is experienced as all-pervading (*vibhu*).
"Consisting of *māyā* and abounding in its power" means because He is the presiding controller of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). ||36||

Viśvanātha: In this manner, [he perceives] Viṣṇu as "consisting of Māyā"— that is, the Great Person (mahāpuruṣa) who is enriched by a thousand, that is, immeasurable, faculties such as speech and so forth, whose form is consciousness and bliss, and who, because he is joined with the eternal power called Māyā which constitutes his own essential nature, is therefore "consisting of Māyā."

"The wise declare thus," according to the Śruti. Or alternatively: [He is] that whose disposition—the arrangement of the eyes, neck, and so forth—is characterized by excellence (*upa*), being endowed with the marks of a great man (*sāmudrika-lakṣaṇa-anvita*); who, through *māyā*—that is, through the ignorance (*avidyā*) of the individual soul (*jīva*)—is like a destroyer of disease (*āmaya*) as it were; and who is "good" (*san*), meaning excellent by virtue of being appropriate. That...

Or rather, the connection is as follows: having seen that Vairāja form, which consists of Māyā and whose arrangement—the structural composition of the feet and so forth—is characterized by the manifest world (prapañca) such as Pātāla and the rest, because of the identity between cause and effect. ||36||
To him, you indeed assumed the form of Hayashiras, [in order to slay] the two exceedingly powerful enemies of the Vedas known as Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
Having destroyed the multitude of Vedic scriptures, as well as passion and darkness, they declare that goodness (sattva) is Your most beloved form.
Śrīdhara: And then, he says that you bestowed grace upon him with the words "to him" (tasmai).

Assuming the form of Hayagrīva, you slew the two demons named Madhu and Kaiṭabha, who were of the nature of *rajas* and *tamas*, and delivered the collections of the Vedas (*śruti-gaṇān*) to him. The reason for this is stated as "the quality of goodness" (*sattvam*). ||37||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: He says, "And you protected that devotee of yours by descending again and again"—"to him," etc. Assuming the form of Hayagrīva, you led the hosts of the Vedas to him.
He offered [them]. The meaning is: what are the two named Madhu and Kaiṭabha like? They are of the nature of *rajas* and *tamas*.

The cause for their slaying is *sattva*; although for Hari—who is indifferent even toward the mere category of the *guṇas*—the *sattva-guṇa* is not dear, nevertheless, it is so because of the pure *sattva* that constitutes His very essence (*svarūpa*).

The state of being most beloved is merely imagined based on the observation of the absence of hostility toward the quality of *sattva*; it is not, however, actual supreme affection. Rather, your partiality toward the world of *sattva* is the cause for such an imagination. Therefore, your suppression of the wicked is solely for the sake of protecting the virtuous.
The meaning is that this is indeed the very nature of qualities, and not a factual inequality in You.
Thus, through incarnations as humans, animals, sages, gods, and fish...
You manifest the worlds, You strike down those who oppose the universe,
and You protect the Dharma followed through the ages; since You remain hidden in the Kali age, O Great Being, You are indeed that very Trivikrama.

Śrīdhara: With these eight verses beginning with "But You alone," that which was stated—namely, that protection through partiality and the destruction of adversaries are conditioned by the quality of *sattva* and not inherent [to You]—is now summarized with the word "Thus" (*ittham*). You manifest [ Yourself as a protector], You protect; You slay [directly] and cause [others] to slay.

But in the Kali age you do not do that; for at that time you remain concealed. Therefore, because of your manifestation throughout all three ages, you are thus renowned as "Triyuga" (the one who exists in the three ages). ||38||

With these eight verses beginning with "You alone are one," that which was stated—namely, that protection through partiality and the destruction of adversaries are conditioned by the nature of beings (*sattva*) and not inherent—is here concluded with the word "ittham" (thus).
You protect (*vibhāvayasi*) and you preserve; you slay and cause to be slain. But in the Kali age, that is no longer so.
You act [thus]. Since you were concealed at that time, therefore, because of your manifestation throughout all three ages, you who have become such are renowned as Triyuga (the Three-Aged One).
The sequence of events is as follows: having descended directly in various places, you protect them.
He concludes: "In this way. ||38||

Viśvanātha: Just as there was the incarnation of Hayagrīva for the sake of Viriñca, so too there are other incarnations for the sake of other devotees; thus he says, "In this way. You manifest (vibhāvayasi) means you protect;
you slay (haṃsi) means you cause to be slain. He is one whose conduct (vṛtta)—that is, whose character—is appropriate to each respective age (yuga), because (yad) [of that].

In the Kali age, You are concealed—concealed by being devoid of another's form and disposition. For this very reason, You are renowned as "Triyuga" (the one who appears in three ages). The meaning is that You manifest Yourself only in the three ages beginning with Satya, but not in Kali.
Therefore, there will also be scriptural evidence for this further on.
"He will be described as being concealed by another form; listen likewise to how He appears even during the Kali age through various scriptural injunctions:
'He who is dark-complexioned, yet not dark in His splendor, accompanied by His limbs, secondary limbs, weapons, and attendants. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.5.31)
"For the wise indeed worship with sacrifices consisting primarily of congregational chanting" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.5.32).
Thus: "O Lord of Kuṇṭha, this mind of yours [is not fixed] upon Your stories..."
The wicked man, corrupted by evil,
intensely afflicted by desire and tormented by joy, grief, fear, and longing—
how can I, being wretched, contemplate your path within him?
Śrīdhara: Having thus described the true nature of the Blessed One and declaring his own unfitness for such contemplation, he prays with three verses beginning with "This is not...
[The mind] is unwholesome, being turned outward; it is intense and difficult to restrain; and it is afflicted by joy, sorrow, and fear, as well as by the threefold pursuit.
Even when suffering, one finds no delight in your teachings; while the mind remains in such a state, how can I investigate your reality? ||39||

The Sequence of Composition: Thus, having recounted that story and recalled his state in each preceding birth, and having attributed that [state] to this present life through his wretchedness, he considers himself as if not having served her even with intense longing in that [previous life] as well; thus he censures his own mind, saying, "This is no mind. (39)

Viśvanātha: Thus, although You descend again and again and shower the nectar of Your own form, qualities, and pastimes, our most sinful minds do not take delight therein; they repeatedly fall into the pit of wicked sense-objects. What can we do? To this he says with three verses, beginning with "This is not [so]," regarding You.
Regarding the stories of His form, qualities, pastimes, and so forth:

[the objection is raised]—"But why does one not take pleasure even in these most sweet stories? To this he replies: "Corrupted by evil," meaning that just as a tongue corrupted by bile [does not relish] sweets; [the evil is] intense and difficult to restrain. This is *eṣaṇā* (craving).
With such impressions of wealth and the like in your mind, how can you contemplate the reality of my state?

Even though the mind of Prahlāda, the great devotee, was not of this material nature—as is evident from the subsequent statement: "His heart was submerged in the great nectar of singing His heroic deeds" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.9.43).
Even that [bondage], because it possesses various and diverse waves of affection and arises from extreme wretchedness, does not contradict the liberation of the world of lovers alone. ||39||
O Acyuta, my tongue drags me here from one side, unsatisfied; my genitals, skin, belly, and ears drag me elsewhere from this or that.
The nose is distracted by another [object], the restless eye wanders elsewhere, and the power of action is divided;
like many co-wives, they tear at the master of the house.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, O Acyuta! while the tongue remains unsatisfied, it draws me toward sweet and other flavors; yet the belly, tormented by hunger, immediately seeks any kind of mere food. The eye is fickle, as is the power of action.
The organs of action cut and sever. ||40||

The Structural Connection (*krama-sandarbha*): Thus, having recollected the suffering of people by way of its similarity to his own suffering, being overcome by compassion and disregarding even his own suffering, he offers [himself] for their sake alone in two verses beginning with "jihvaikataḥ. (40)

Viśvanātha: If it is argued that even when the mind is wicked, a person achieves their purpose through the chanting of my names and so forth, he replies to that: O Acyuta, the tongue—the organ of speech and the organ of taste—being unsatisfied, draws me toward vulgar, harsh, false, and other such prattle, as well as toward sweet flavors and the like.

And this is the sense: because of that, elsewhere—whether among amorous women, in the acquisition of merit and wealth, or in the beating of others—one’s power or capacity is cut away or destroyed; therefore, the sense is that one finds no opportunity at all for the glorification of Him. ||40||
[In this regard, the verse from Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.9.27–28 should be consulted.
— Thus, one who has fallen into the Vaitaraṇī river of worldly existence due to their own karma...
Beholding people— frightened by one another’s birth, death, and devouring; engaged in mutual strife, enmity, and friendship—
O Wanderer to the Far Shore, save this deluded world today!
Śrīdhara: It is not only I alone who has fallen into such a miserable state;

rather, even the great multitude suffers in this very same way. Therefore, he prays for the protection of all people, saying "thus": *bhava* is *saṃsāra* itself, the Vaitaraṇī river at the gate of Yama.

In that [world], which is terrified of those births and so forth that arise from one another; and in which there is enmity or friendship, as the case may be, toward the bodies of one's own kin or others—beholding such deluded people, O Pāracara! you who stand on its further shore, eternally liberated! Alas! Oh, what misery!
Thus, out of compassion, rescue us today; having ferried us across, protect us from the Vaitaraṇī river.
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: It is not only I alone, but every person in the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) who suffers; thus, he prays for their deliverance with the words "In this manner" (*evam*). Worldly existence (*bhava*) itself is the Vaitaraṇī river.

O You who dwell on the far shore of that river at the gate of Yama—the Vaitaraṇī—in which there is, as appropriate, enmity toward one's own kin and friendship toward others! O Pāracara! Since You take Your pleasure precisely upon the far shore of such a Vaitaraṇī, alas, out of compassion, please protect us by ferrying us across the Vaitaraṇī.
O Blessed One, teacher of all, what effort is this of yours here, for the sake of delivering him and causing the destruction of the cycle of worldly existence?
O kinsman of the distressed, there is indeed a great favor shown toward the deluded; what need have you for that, while we serve our beloved ones?
Śrīdhara: If it is asked, "How can I alone deliver all people?", he says in response: "Who indeed...
(*ko nv iti*). Who indeed would have any exertion (*prayāsa*) here in this matter of delivering all people? None at all. Why?
Because [He is] the cause (*hetu*) of the origin, maintenance, and destruction—that is, the birth, sustenance, and dissolution—of this entire universe; and for that reason, too...

The sense is: "How can this be difficult? And he says that this is indeed appropriate with the words "among the deluded. If you say, "I shall deliver you and your own people; do not harbor this stubborn persistence," to that he replies: "What is the use of that deliverance for us, who are devotedly following those who are dear to you and are your devotees?"
"O child of the asuras, what great effort is required for Hari?
O Blessed One, teacher of all, what effort indeed is needed for you here?
Having thus addressed one another in private, Prahlāda spoke these words to men.
He formed a friendship with Īśa, having cast aside his illusory power.
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: If it is asked, "How can all people be delivered by me alone? he says in response: "Who indeed...
Even by you alone, who are the teacher of all and who assume the form of the Teacher, [the world is saved], even more than by another [who might be] a hundred billion times greater.

The sense is: "Let all people indeed be delivered by one who is capable of being so. Nor should it be said that such capability does not exist in me; thus he says: "If you were the cause of the birth and so forth of this universe, which is the cause of its creation, maintenance, and destruction, then..."

The sense is that you ought indeed to be the cause of their deliverance as well. To show that this is entirely appropriate, he says: "Among the deluded," and so forth. If you should say, "I shall deliver you and your own people; do not harbor such excessive persistence," he replies to that: "For those who serve your beloved devotees... [and so on].
The meaning is: "What need have we for that rescue performed by you? By the power of our service to Your devotees, we ourselves shall cross over. ||42||
I do not tremble at the Vaitaraṇī river, so difficult to cross, for my mind is immersed in the great nectar of singing your heroic deeds.
Therefore, I grieve for those deluded ones whose minds are turned away [from the truth], who bear the burden of the illusory pleasures of the objects of the senses.
Śrīdhara: "O child Prahlāda, I shall deliver you first; by that alone you will have achieved your purpose.
What is the use of this persistence? To this, he replies: "Not at all" (naiva). O Supreme One, O Best of All!
I am one whose mind is immersed in that great nectar which is the singing of Your heroic deeds.
I am not at all terrified by the Vaitaraṇī river of worldly existence; rather, I grieve for the deluded. He speaks of them:

those whose minds are turned away from that great nectar (mahāmṛta), and who, on the contrary, carry the heavy burden of family and so forth for the sake of that illusory happiness which is caused by sense objects. 43.

The sequence of the composition: Now, one might object that even those who serve my beloved persons, if they have not transcended worldly existence (*bhava*), would surely experience anxiety regarding it; anticipating this, [the author] says "not at all, not at all" and provides himself as an example with the words "never indeed.
Those who sing of Your heroic deeds are the beloved persons; the great nectar (*mahāmṛta*) associated with them—
I am one whose mind is submerged in that very form of His singing; therefore, I do not tremble at all.

As for what was previously stated in passages such as, "In this matter, I was formerly terrified" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 7.9.16), that was indeed due to being turned away from Him and having no relish for the limbs [of devotional service]. Now, however, the statement beginning with "I do not tremble at all" refers to that [state of being turned toward Him].

Because one is permeated by the sweetness of the nectar of the narrative, it should be understood that in the middle [of the text], passages such as *na etan manaḥ* (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.9.39) are intended to express "extreme thirst" (*atitṛṣṇā*), due to the diverse nature of emotional states (*bhāva*). ||43||

Viśvanātha: Furthermore, he says "not at all" (*naiva*) to express that his own purpose is not merely crossing over the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). O Supreme One, O Best of All, I am not afraid of the Vaitaraṇī river.
The reason for this is "by Your power" (*tvad-vīrya*). However, I grieve for the deluded ones, because [their suffering] is caused by the objects of the senses.
O Lord, for one who carries the burden— the burden of maintaining a family and so forth— for the sake of that illusory happiness,
the sages generally desire their own liberation.
They practice silence in solitude, yet they do not strive for the welfare of others;
leaving these wretched ones behind, I, who seek liberation, see no other refuge for this wandering soul than You.

Madhva: Generally, gods and sages [should show compassion]. Compassion toward those who have taken refuge should especially be exercised by the true deities and likewise by certain sages, even in all their activities.
Nevertheless, they have come to be the objects of the grace of the true gods;
for this very reason, they are liberated, whereas by any other means it would not be possible. (44)

Śrīdhara: If it is argued that you should first take liberation for yourself, while those sages who know the truth will instruct them [the others], he says in response: "Generally," etc. "I do not desire liberation" (*na vimumukṣe*) means I do not wish for liberation.
If it is asked, "In that case, request something else; why do you persistently entreat me alone?"—to this [he replies]: "Therefore..."
He said: "I see no refuge for this person other than you. (44)

The sequence of composition: Just as he spoke to the Blessed Lord with the words beginning "Who indeed here... (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.9.42), in that very same manner he speaks also to the sages, beginning with the word "mostly" (prāyeṇa). ||44||

Viśvanātha: If you say, "You take liberation for yourself, while the sages who know the truth will instruct you in the means of liberation," he replies to that with the words "mostly" (*prāyeṇa*). He says "not these" (*naitān*) to show that he does not desire to become like them. "I see no refuge for this person other than You."
— that pleasure of householders such as sexual union is indeed trivial, like the misery resulting from scratching with one's hands.
The miserable, who partake in manifold sufferings, do not find satisfaction here;
a wise man should endure the mind-born [passion] as one endures itching.

Śrīdhara: But surely these [beings] are happy through the enjoyment of women and so forth; they are not miserable. To this he says: "That which... That in which there is suffering after suffering, as if from the scratching and rubbing of the hands. If that is so, then because it is merely suffering, they would become disenchanted with it and be liberated; to this he says: "miserable" (kṛpaṇāḥ).

Even though they experience manifold sufferings, those who lust after sensual pleasures do not find sufficient satisfaction in the happiness of household life; they do not realize this because desire is as difficult to endure as the itch. Now, one might ask: "Do some people not even tolerate the itch and [renounce] desire? To this he says: "But by your grace alone, a certain wise person indeed [subdues] the mind-born [desire]."
One may indeed endure desire, but not all of it; here too, the analogy is "like itching. ||45||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Now, one might object: "Are these not indeed happy through their enjoyment of women and other such pleasures, rather than being miserable?
To this, he says:

Regarding the word *yat*: that in which there is suffering after suffering, as if by the scratching and rubbing of the hands. If it is argued that they would become detached from and liberated from that very state because it is suffering, he says: "The wretched ones," meaning those who lust after desires, even though they partake in much suffering, are not satiated with this happiness of householders—which is in fact of the nature of suffering—but rather cry out, "Enough! (*alam*).
