They do not think so; "like itching" means as if in the midst of itching. [Objection: But surely some person is seen to be free from that [suffering]? [Reply: True; by your grace alone, O Wise One, would one truly endure the mind-born Kāma, which is of the very nature of suffering, but not everyone. ||45||
Silence, vows, sacred learning, austerity, study, the performance of one's own duty, exposition, secret recitation, and meditative absorption lead to liberation.
O Supreme Person, for those who have not conquered their senses, these [teachings] are generally mere talk; and for the hypocritical, they do not even exist here at all.

Śrīdhara: [Objection: But surely, by means of silence (*mauna*) and other such instruments for attaining liberation, is liberation not easily obtained even through those? To this, he says: "Silence," etc. O Puruṣa, O Inner Controller! Those ten well-known factors conducive to liberation (*apavargya*), which are the causes of liberation—namely, silence and so forth; *rahas* means dwelling in solitude; and those indeed...
For those who have not conquered their senses, the means of livelihood (*vārtā*) generally consist of selling goods for the sake of wealth in order to enjoy sense-objects.
But for the hypocrites, even these means of livelihood may or may not exist, because hypocrisy yields uncertain results. (46)

*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: Now, one might object: since for the Brāhmaṇas liberation is already established by itself through means such as silence (*mauna*) which are naturally accomplished, is not liberation also established by itself? To this he says: "By silence," etc. O Puruṣa!

The sense is: "O Inner Controller! What more can I request of you? Those ten practices beginning with silence (*mauna*) are well known as *āpavargya*, meaning they are the causes of liberation (*apavarga*). "Solitude" (*rahas*) means dwelling in a secluded place.
However, for those who have not conquered their senses, these [practices] generally become mere talk for those who sell them off for the sake of sensual enjoyment.
These indeed become the means of livelihood; but for the hypocrites, even their very livelihood may not exist, because the fruit of hypocrisy is uncertain. 46.
O you who created the Vedas, these two forms, existence and non-existence, belong to You alone, like a seed and its sprout; for there is nothing else apart from You, who are formless.
Those disciplined ones perceive you through yoga in both states directly before them, just as fire is perceived within pieces of wood; it could not be otherwise.

Regarding the term *madhvaḥ*: in view of its dependence on that [Lord] in the form of cause and effect, there is no form other than His own essential nature when considered in terms of His direct essential nature. ||47||

Śrīdhara: He says with three verses beginning with "In form" (rūpe) that knowledge of You does not arise for those with desires through mere silence and other such practices without devotion. These two, the existent and the non-existent, which have entered into a continuous flow like a seed and its sprout, are Your very forms as cause and effect; they were created and revealed by the Veda as mere indicators, and not otherwise.

It is something else inherent [in the self], like the whiteness and so forth belonging to Devadatta and others. Why? Because You are formless—that is, devoid of material form and the like; therefore, only those who are self-controlled perceive You through the yoga of devotion as manifest before their eyes, pervading both the effect and the cause, just as one perceives fire within pieces of wood by means of friction.
The ellipsis is: "Your knowledge would not arise from anything else. Alternatively, he states the very manner of that knowledge:

these two [the world and its knowledge] could not exist from anything else, such as *pradhāna* or atoms (*paramāṇu*), because of scriptural passages such as, "He thought" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.2.5). Therefore, you alone, by virtue of being the cause, are the thread running through everything.
Thus [ends the section]. ||47||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He states that the attainment of You does not occur through silence (*mauna*) and other such means without the yoga of devotion (*bhakti-yoga*)—in the verse beginning with "rūpe. These two, the existent and the non-existent, are cause and effect, like a seed and its sprout.
The totality and the individuality existing within the stream of manifestation are indeed Your own forms.

This entire universe, consisting of both the totality and the individual, is not distinct from You; for You are formless, devoid of material form. Therefore, it is fitting that the wise perceive You as identical in both—the totality and the individual.
The sense is that they investigate and seek to attain You individually, because You exist as the cause in both cases.

The sense is that this is by means of yoga—that is, specifically by the yoga of devotion (bhakti-yoga) and not by other means such as knowledge—according to Your own statement: "I am to be grasped by exclusive devotion" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.14.11).
In the case of fire, [it is produced] by means of yoga, that is, by churning; for this very reason, the explicit word "devotion" (bhakti) is not employed. ||47||
You are wind, fire, earth, space, and water; you are the subtle elements,
the vital breaths, the senses, the heart, consciousness, and grace.
O Infinite One, you alone are all things—both endowed with qualities and devoid of qualities;
there is nothing other than you that can even be described by mind or speech.
Śrīdhara says: He states that very point with the words "You are the wind" and so forth. *Hṛdaya* means the mind (*manas*). *Cit* means consciousness (*citta*).

*Anugraha* refers to the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) or the group of deities. That which possesses qualities (*saguṇa*) is gross; that which is devoid of qualities (*viguṇa*) is subtle. Furthermore, whatever else is expressed or manifested by "mind and speech" (*mano-vacas*) is nothing other than You.
It does not exist. ||48||

The sequence of the composition: "Thou" (tvam). The heart (*hṛdaya*) is the internal organ (*antar-indriya*), consisting of mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and consciousness (*citta*). Consciousness (*cit*) is the pure individual soul (*jīva*);

grace (*anugraha*) is the power of turning [the soul] toward one's own true nature. What need is there for more? [Thou art] both with qualities (*saguṇa*), which is illusory (*māyika*), and without qualities (*viguṇa*), which is non-illusory (*amāyika*).
"You alone are the fulfillment of all aims. ||48||
Viśvanātha: He explains the meaning already stated with the words "thou" (*tvam*). "Heart" (*hṛdayam*) means the mind (*manas*). "Consciousness" (*cit*) means the intellect (*citta*).
"Grace" (*anugrahaḥ*) refers to the group of deities who bestow grace. "With qualities" (*sa-guṇaḥ*) means gross; "without qualities" (*viguṇaḥ*) means subtle.
"Mind and speech" (*mano-vacas*)—that which is expressed or manifested by them is nothing other than thee.
It does not exist. ||48||
Neither are these qualities, nor are they the possessors of qualities— the principles beginning with Mahat, all those starting from the mind, together with gods and mortals.
O Wide-striding One, the wise, having thus reflected that You possess both beginning and end, cease from verbal conceptualization.
Śrīdhara: But as for the non-devotees, he says—"Not these"—to show that they do not know You, even though You are inherent within them.

These gods, who identify with the qualities (*guṇas*) and so forth, possess a beginning and an end; because their limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are insentient, they do not know You, who are without beginning or end and free from all adjuncts. For indeed, it is only those of keen intellect—the wise—who, having reflected thus, [know You].
They desist from activities such as Vedic study; the meaning is that they worship you alone through meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
And so says the Śruti: "For what purpose shall we study? For what purpose shall we perform sacrifices? and "One should not contemplate many words, for that is merely a weariness of speech."
And from the *Smṛti*:
"When your intellect has transcended the thicket of delusion, then you will attain indifference toward what is yet to be heard and what has already been heard" (Gītā 2.52), and so forth.
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: That knowledge would arise only through devotion to You, and not through the study of scriptures, intellectual skill, and so forth; thus he says, "Not... If these [means] do not [attain] You...

If they know [the truth], then, having reflected on how living beings might come to know it by means of these very faculties—the mind, intellect, and so forth—through the investigation of the scriptures via study, teaching, and other such activities, they desist from verbal expression and the operations of study and the like. And thus says the Śruti: "For what purpose are we?"

"We shall inquire: for what purpose should we sacrifice? One should not contemplate many words, for that is merely a weariness of speech. And the Smṛti says: "When your intellect has transcended the thicket of delusion..."
"Then you will attain detachment from what is yet to be heard and from what has already been heard" (Gītā 2.52),
and so forth— O Most Worthy One, to You belong salutation, praise, ritual action, and worship.

Through service to you, one attains remembrance of karma, mindfulness of the feet, and hearing of the sacred narrative; by means of this six-limbed devotion, can a person attain the bhakti that leads to the state of the Paramahaṃsas?
Śrīdhara concludes with the word "tat" (that). O most venerable one!

"Namaḥ" refers to praise, ritual action, worship, prostration, hymns of praise, and the offering of all one's deeds; "karma" refers to service, as well as mindfulness of the feet and listening to the sacred narrative. Thus, by means of this six-limbed perfect service...
Without the path of the *paramahaṃsas*, how could a person attain devotion toward You, who are the goal?

Since liberation does not occur without such devotion, and devotion does not occur without constant service, the meaning of this section is that one must first request: "Grant me the very yoga of Your service. ||50||
The sequential arrangement is as follows: *karma* refers to service; *karma-smṛti* refers to the remembrance of the Lord’s pastimes.

The phrase "of the two feet" (*caraṇayoḥ*) is connected to every [item] and serves to manifest devotion. Therefore, one should perform the sixfold service alone, which accomplishes that love and devotion—the root of all fulfillment of purpose.

"Grant [this] to all as well. The underlying sentiment is this: "Even though I have attained fulfillment through Your grace by reaching the very root of Your feet in person, or through the yoga of direct service to You, I shall consider myself truly fulfilled only by that [granting of this to all]. And thus, the favor which was first requested for Brahmā and the others—

Since this has been established by implication (*kaimutya*), once it is proven that all sentences expressing petitions form a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatva*), it follows as a matter of course (*svataḥ-siddha*) for other sentences as well that follow yours. ||50||

Viśvanātha concludes the hymn with the words "Therefore" (tad): since that knowledge cannot be attained through study and other such means, one should therefore abandon all insistence for the sake of knowing You.

He says that one should strive solely for the sake of attaining love for You, which is the essence of all human goals: "O Most Worthy One! *Namaḥ* means salutation; *stuti-karma* means the act of praising; *pūjā* means worship; *arcana* means honoring;
*karma* means service; *caraṇayoḥ smṛtiḥ* means mindfulness of Your feet; and *śravaṇam* means listening to Your stories."
Thus, without service characterized by these six limbs and devotion, how could one attain devotion or love toward You?

The meaning is that one would certainly not attain it. Since You are the goal—liberation—for the paramahaṃsas who possess knowledge, therefore, through knowledge mixed with devotion, one may somehow indeed attain liberation in You.

This is the intention. Therefore, since it is the root of all fulfillment of purpose, grant to everyone the very service consisting of six limbs that accomplishes loving devotion; for if that is difficult to attain, then by granting liberation itself, protect everyone from the suffering of saṃsāra for the time being. As for me, however—
The meaning is that he has the thought: "I exist as one who has already achieved his life's purpose solely through service to Your devotees; thus, there is no concern whatsoever.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having thus described his qualities with devotion, the Guṇa-less Lord,
pleased and with his anger subsided, spoke to the prostrate Prahlāda, who was himself devoted.
Śrīdhara: He whose qualities have been described to this extent; *yata-manyuḥ* means one whose anger has been withdrawn.
Krama-sandarbha: Qualities (*guṇāḥ*) such as compassion and so forth, as well as the forms of the powers for various acts such as giving.
Viśvanātha: Qualities (*guṇāḥ*) such as compassion and so forth; *nirguṇaḥ* means devoid of material qualities (*prākṛta-guṇa*).

The meaning is that the wrath which had become difficult to restrain—because he intended to harm even Prahlāda, who was devoted to me—that very wrath was pacified by the sight of Prahlāda’s bliss. ||51||
—o)0(o— The Blessed Lord said: O Prahlāda, blessed one, may it be well with you; I am pleased with you, O best of asuras.
Choose a boon according to your desire; I am the fulfiller of the wishes of men.
Śrīdhara: It means "one who fulfills desires"; thus, the sense is: "I am the stream of the goals of human life. ||52||

The Structural Connection (*krama-sandarbha*): Thus, approving of the compassion of the venerable Prahlāda which extends to all living beings, and desiring to offer another request while intending to perform the benediction beginning with "He who shall proclaim this" [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.10.14] and ending with that verse, he proceeds as follows.
He encourages [her] to choose another desired boon. ||52||

Viśvanātha: [The meaning is: "Choose what you desire. Since I am devoted to my servants like a father to his child and am the crest-jewel of supreme generosity, why should there be any hesitation? Even for those men on whose behalf you pray to me, I am the fulfiller of their desires;
I exist as a very stream of the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*). How much more so, then, for one [woman]?

The underlying sense is that he grants liberation alone. By this, it should be understood that although the souls present at that time were made objects of Prahlāda’s perception, they were indeed delivered; because souls are infinite, the cosmic egg was subsequently filled by other souls. ||52||
—o)0(o— "O long-lived one, you have pleased me; for my sight is difficult to obtain.
Having seen me, a living being ought not to distress himself again."
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha [explain]: *aprīṇataḥ* means "not pleasing" or "not causing satisfaction. *Taptum* means "to grieve," due to the state of having unfulfilled desires. ||53||
The sequence of composition has not been explained. —
For the wise and virtuous satisfy me with their whole being.
O highly fortunate one, those desiring the highest good [should worship] the Lord of all blessings.
Śrīdhara: They please and satisfy. ||54||
The sequence of composition: Now, for this very reason, it is solely by virtue of the desire for the chosen boon. ||54||
Viśvanātha: They please or cause [me] to be pleased; or, they are satisfied with me. "With their whole being" means through service, friendship, and so forth. (54)
Śrī Nārada said:
Although he was thus being enticed with boons that allure the world, he remained steadfast.
Because of his single-minded devotion to the Blessed One, that best of asuras did not wish for them.
Śrīdhara: Because of being exclusively devoted, that is, because of being a devotee free from all limiting conditions (nirupādhi). ||55||

The sequence of composition: thus, in the manner previously described. By Viśvanātha himself, as indicated by his own choice, because of his state of being a *ekāntin* (exclusive devotee); for the definition of such a person is given in the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* (8.3.20): "Those who are *ekāntins* do not desire any object whatsoever. ||55||
Thus ends the ninth chapter, which is well-composed for the virtuous, in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted.
Thus ends the Seventh Canto in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā, the Pāramahaṃsya, within the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, which is a commentary on the Brahma-sūtras.
The ninth chapter in the Narrative of Prahlāda.
Now begins the tenth chapter:
The Life of Prahlāda and the Conquest of the City.
Śrī Nārada said:
Considering all of that to be an obstacle to devotional yoga,
the boy, smiling, spoke to Hṛṣīkeśa.
Śrīdhara: In the tenth [chapter], however, after Hari has vanished while favoring this devotee,
the grace bestowed by Hari upon Rudra is described as a secondary topic.
All that is a collection of boons. ||1||
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha:
When Hari had granted a boon to Prahlāda and vanished at the end of the tenth [manvantara],...
By his very grace, the Lord burnt down the three cities before him.
"All that is a collection of boons. "Smiling" means: "This Lord, tempting me as a child and an ignorant one, is testing my intellect"—this thought arose and remained [in his mind]. (1)
Śrī Prahlāda said:
Do not entice me with those boons, for I am attached to desires through their arising.
Fearing attachment to that [world], despondent, and seeking liberation, I have taken refuge in you.
Śrīdhara: [I am] unattached by birth, that is, by my very nature; [yet] I am afraid of attachment to those desires. ||2||
The sequence of composition: the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu) desires to renounce those sensual pleasures (kāmān). ||2||

Viśvanātha: By their very nature of birth, O best of men, [the Lord] is afraid of attachment to those desires through the granting of boons; for this very reason, the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu) desires to abandon them. ||2||
Desiring to know the characteristics of a true servant, he urged his devotee toward his desires, saying:
"O Lord, you [should act] regarding these knots of the heart, which are the seeds of worldly existence."
Śrīdhara: [Objection: "But why should I entice a devotee? [Reply: No;
rather, he says that your intention is something else entirely when you say, "Choose a boon"—referring to the "characteristics of a servant" regarding those who are bound like knots of the heart. (3)
The sequence of composition (*krama-sandarbha*): "Of the servant" (*bhṛtyasya*)—this consists of one and a half verses.
The meaning is that [Viśvanātha], desiring to know the specific and common characteristics of a servant, wishes to make them known in the worlds.
Viśvanātha says: "Now, am I trying to entice a devotee? No, indeed not!"
He says "bhṛtya" (servant) to proclaim that his own devotee possesses the most excellent steadfastness in the world. The sense is this:

when it was asked, "Why do you not accept the boons being offered by me?", your intention was understood as follows: "My servant himself will describe the characteristics of my servant. [The word] "prabhuḥ" (the Lord).
The sense is that, since inquiry is not appropriate for you who are omniscient, the purpose [of this work] is solely to inform all others;
and the sense is that for you, the teacher of all and instructor of what is beneficial to all, [this task is unnecessary], unlike the case of Brahmā, Rudra, and the others. ||3||
Otherwise, O Teacher of All, it would not befit you whose nature is compassion.
He who seeks blessings from you is neither a servant nor a true devotee; he is merely a merchant.

Śrīdhara: The meaning is that otherwise, engaging in that which accomplishes misfortune would not be possible. To the question, "How can there be such knowledge of the characteristics of a servant? he says: "He who... [from] you. ||4||
The sequence of composition: "But he who... constitutes half a verse. ||4||

Viśvanātha: If it is asked, "Tell me that definition of a servant," he says, "I shall state the definition of both master and servant alike"—beginning with the word *yaḥ* ("who"). *Te* means "from you. *Vaṇig* means "a merchant"; [the sense is] having given you something such as a son, flowers, or an offering (*naivedya*), [he receives] wealth consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and so forth.
The sense is that he desires to seize the station of Brahmā, Indra, and the other gods. ||4||
A servant indeed does not hope for blessings for himself from his master,
nor does a master, desiring his own lordship, bestow blessings upon his servant.

Śrīdhara: [Objection: But surely, even through desire, the relationship of master and servant between the one served and the server is well known. [Reply: True; however, that is conditional and not ultimate. Thus he says: "A servant who expects blessings for himself from his master is not truly a servant; rather, he is one who desires his own mastery by means of being a servant."
He gives to the servant, yet he is not the master at all.
[Krama-sandarbha]: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: He reinforces the very point already stated with the words "āśāsāna" (expecting). [The desire] for oneself caused by the servant...
He who, desiring mastery or sovereignty, gives it to a servant is not truly a master at all. //5//
"But I, though free from desire, am your devotee, and you are my master, having no other refuge;
for in this matter, our interests are not otherwise than those of a king and his servant."

Śrīdhara says: "But for us two, this [offering] is real," as he states with the words "I, however. It is "without support" (anapāśraya), meaning free from any ulterior motive; otherwise, there would be no purpose or objective through motives such as desire and the like. ||6||
The sequence of composition: an example by way of contrast is "of the king and the servant. ||6||
Viśvanātha: He states that the relationship between us two as master and servant is real: "But I...
The meaning is that being "without support" (anapāśrayaḥ), You do not rely upon a subordinate sovereignty that is dependent on a servant.
Otherwise, in the world, the relationship of master and servant would be based on a mutual agreement through the intention of one's own desire.
It is indicated that even what is well-known is indeed subject to dispute because it possesses an adventitious condition (upādhi). ||6||
If you will grant me my desires, O bull among the givers of boons,
then I choose as my boon from you the non-arising of desires within my heart."

Śrīdhara: Now, if it be said, "Nevertheless, for the sake of my supreme satisfaction, choose something," he says in reply: "If... [meaning] the non-sprouting, that is, the non-arising, of the shoots of desire from you. //7//
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Now, if one should say, "Nevertheless, choose some boon for the sake of my supreme generosity and happiness," he says in response: "May no desires arise in my heart"—this is the meaning. (7)
The senses, mind, vital breath, self, righteousness, fortitude, intellect,
modesty, prosperity, splendor, memory, and truth— all these perish with his very birth.
Śrīdhara: Now, what is the fault when desire arises? To this he says: "He whose senses and so forth perish at birth. "Ātman" means the body. [The] sequence of the composition has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: For that desire, the very failure of the senses and so forth to perceive its sweetness is itself the state of wandering on a wrong path; that indeed is its destruction. ||8||
When a person releases the desires residing in the mind, at that very moment,
O lotus-eyed one, he becomes fit for the state of the Blessed One.

Śrīdhara: He states the benefit that arises from the absence of desire: "He is liberated," and so forth. "To the Blessed One" means to one whose sovereignty is equal to yours. And thus says the Śruti:
"When all the desires that dwell in his heart are liberated..."
"Then the mortal becomes immortal; here he attains Brahman. (KaU 2.3.14) ||9||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Now, if you do not desire desire, then tell me how you can desire my servitude while saying, "Tell me the yoga of your servitude"? To this he says: "She releases," [meaning] in the mind.

When one specifically abandons even those extraordinary desires— such as service to You, friendship, and so forth— which exist as stable states, for the sake of becoming a Lord through *sāyujya* (union), that *sāyujya* is not my desired goal.

What is the use of those qualities such as virtue (*dharma*) and the rest, which are established here through the intermingling of attributes? For us who delight in the essence, what is the point of desiring that which is devoid of quality, while we sing the praises of the feet of Him who enjoys the essential? [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.6.25]
Thus, because of my very words, I choose for myself the desire for that non-material form of service to you;
"for the sake of becoming a Lord, that is, for sovereignty equal to that of the Blessed One," so says the venerable Svāmīcaraṇa. 9.
Oṃ, salutations to you, the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, the Great Soul,
Hari, the wondrous Lion, the Brahman, the Supreme Self.
Śrīdhara: Wishing to reject him who desires to grant faultless objects of desire, he pays homage with the word "namaḥ" (v. 10).
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: [The opponent thinks: "Surely union with me (*mat-sāyujya*) is worthy of respect even by sages who delight in the Self; how much more so, then, for one who has become a mere child of the demons? Thus, he considers himself defeated by the words of the Lord.
He prostrates: "Oṃ namaḥ. ||10||
The Blessed Lord said:
Never have those who are single-mindedly devoted to Me desired any blessings from Me in this world.
Even those like you hope for such things in the hereafter;
nevertheless, enjoy the pleasures here during this Manvantara belonging to the lords of the Daityas.

Śrīdhara: It is true that you are my single-minded devotee; nevertheless, he says "no," because my command must be carried out. My single-minded devotees never desire blessings from me, either in this world or the next;
nevertheless, enjoy these pleasures for the duration of this Manvantara. ||11||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: He says "not" (*na*) to indicate that this nature belongs not only to you, but indeed to all my devotees: "I grant this for only the duration of a *manvantara*, and no more."
"Do not be angry"—this is the intended meaning. ||11||
O beloved, taking pleasure in my story, you should immerse yourself in me, who am the one abiding within the self.
Worship the Lord as the sacrifice inherent in all beings, impelling your action through yoga.
Śrīdhara: [Objection: "In that case, there would still be bondage. To this he says with two verses beginning with "kathā":

"Having established Me—the one Lord, the presiding deity of sacrifice—who dwells within all beings, in your own self, perform the sacrifice. [Objection: "In that case, would there not still be bondage through this very action? [Reply: No; he says: "By means of yoga in Me..."
Impelling action by means of dedication, perform sacrifice while relinquishing it. ||12||

Regarding the sequence of composition: "As for those whom you now remember as having been seen or heard by you, what news is there of them?"—this was intended for the sake of praising even those who have merely entered the range of his hearing. ||12||
Viśvanātha: [The Lord] says "Indeed" (nanu) because [the devotee] asks, "For what offense do you cast me into this blind well of sense-objects?

To this he replies with the word "kathā" (by discourse). Worship—that is, adore—me, the Adhiyajña, the sovereign lord of all sacrifices, solely through your own yoga, that is, through the yoga of devotion (*bhakti-yoga*). Even sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha, though not performed, are considered performed.

This is what will come to pass, as indicated by the term *adhiyajña* (the presiding deity of sacrifice). This is because Vedic and worldly ritual action (*karman*) impels one toward eligibility for devotion to Me, since the performance of such rituals is otherwise inappropriate for those who have already attained that eligibility. ||12||
Having abandoned the body through the experience of merit and virtue, or through the wickedness of evil, by the swift force of time.
Having spread a pure fame sung throughout the world of the gods,
you shall come to me, released from all bonds.
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, by means of *bhoga*—the experience of pleasure—you shall abandon the *prārabdha* merit;
being thus released from bondage, you will spread your fame for the sake of favoring the world and attain Me.
The phrase "having abandoned sin through *kuśala* (skillful conduct or merit)" is merely a deterrent (*bibhīṣā-mātra*). Otherwise, for him...

Because there is no engagement in [further] action within the kingdom [of Brahman], yet past sin does not exist. This is because of the principle stated in the *Vedāntasūtra* (4.1.13): "Upon the attainment of that [Self], there is the non-clinging and destruction of subsequent and prior sins, as indicated by scriptural designation," and also because of the Vedic revelation (*Śruti*) in the *Kaṭha Upaniṣad* (4): "He shakes off both good and evil deeds."

Nor does this refer to the intention to begin sinful acts, because such acts are exhausted solely through experience, and thus the statement "having abandoned [them] by means of the wholesome" would be untenable. Nor should it be said that he is ignorant, because the Blessed One himself will immediately state that his purpose has been accomplished. For this very reason, [the text says], "abandoning action by means of yoga..."
Thus, even this is entirely irreproachable, as it serves merely to prevent revulsion in one who has engaged in activity for the sake of gathering the world. ||13||

The sequence of the argument: By experience, one exhausts *prārabdha* merit; by skillful devotion to Me, one exhausts *prārabdha* sin as its counteragent, according to the maxim: "Even a dog-eater is fit for immediate sacrifice" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.33.6). Furthermore, devotion centered on Me purifies even dog-cookers.
And this is because of the principle stated in the Bhagavata Purana (11.14.20): "Because of the possibility [of its occurrence]. ||13||
Viśvanātha: You should not have any doubt regarding the bondage of karma caused by worldly enjoyment;

for in your previous birth, all karma was already destroyed. He says this: by "enjoyment" (bhogena), meaning the experience of pleasure; by "merit" (puṇya), meaning virtuous conduct; and by "evil" (pāpa), [he means the destruction of] the physical body and the former frame.

"Having abandoned [the world], you now attain Me. As for the phrase "you are one whose face is bound," the meaning is that in this birth you exist as one who is already liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). Thus, it should be understood that Prahlāda’s state of being perfected through spiritual practice and his state of eternal perfection are like those of Nārada and others. ||13||
Any man who shall proclaim this which has been sung by you to me,
remembering both you and me at the time of death, is liberated from the bondage of karma.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, regarding the word "yaḥ" (who): he who, remembering both you and me as well as this account of my life, recites this hymn, even he is liberated from the bondage of karma; how then can there be any fear of bondage for you? This is the meaning. ||14||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He says, "Listen to the *kaimutya* (a fortiori argument) regarding the absence of the bondage of karma for you"—beginning with the words "He who... [referring to verse 14]. "To me" means in order to propitiate me. ||14||
Śrī Prahlāda said:
O Maheśvara, choose a boon; this is from the regions of boons granted to you.
That my father, being ignorant, censured you for your divine splendor and power.

Śrīdhara: Having obtained the authority for action by the command of the Lord, he prays for the atonement of his father with three verses. "I choose this boon; I choose another besides this—from you. (15)

The sequence of the composition: "Choose a boon" constitutes one half-verse (ardhaka). By this, it is understood that Śrī Prahlāda did not possess knowledge of his own parents' names, Jaya and Vijaya, and so forth;
this is conveyed by the following two-and-a-half verses (sārdha-yugmaka). ||15||

Viśvanātha: Furthermore, previously, for the sake of the liberation of transmigrating souls, a prayer was offered at Your glorious feet; now, if You have granted such good fortune to me, then I pray for the deliverance of even a single great offender. Thus he says with three verses, beginning with "varaṃ" (I choose). I choose.
I choose. ||15||
With his heart pierced by indignation, he directly reviled the Lord, the teacher of all the worlds,
holding the false view that you were the murderer of his brother and bearing malice toward me, your devotee.
Śrīdhara: One whose disposition is pierced by impatience and anger. ||16||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: He who is pierced by indignation (amarṣa). ||16||
Therefore, may my father be purified from his wretched and insurmountable sin;
for he was then beheld by the side-glance of you, who are compassionate toward the miserable."
Śrīdhara: "He has been glanced at by you with a sidelong look; therefore, he is indeed purified. Nevertheless, O lover of the wretched, pray [for this] out of compassion"—this is the meaning. ||17||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Although he has already been purified by being glanced at with a sidelong look, the sense is that [the speaker] nevertheless begs out of wretchedness to hear words of grace from the venerable mouth. ||17||
The Blessed Lord said:
O sinless one, your father has been purified by twenty-one ancestors along with you.
O virtuous one, since you were born in this family, you are indeed the purifier of the lineage.
Madhva [attained liberation] through his seventy-three fathers from previous births. ||18||

Śrīdhara: Although Kaśyapa, Marīci, and Brahmā were the only three elder brothers of his father, it was stated that they were "together with twenty-one" (triḥ-saptabhiḥ saha) with reference to the fathers belonging to previous kalpas. This is because [of the following]... ||18||

The sequence of the composition: "By the thrice-seven" (triḥsaptabhiḥ). The meaning is that if three times seven—that is, twenty-one—ancestors of yours exist, then you shall be purified by them as well.
Otherwise, the causal statement "because [he was] in a previous kalpa" would not be consistent. This refers to Śrī Prahlāda here.

Because all of them lack any connection [to their actions] from birth onwards, and because they possess connections [to their actions] inherently, and because Hiraṇyakaśipu had no previous birth. ||18||

Viśvanātha: Regarding the phrase "by twenty-one [times]," the meaning is this: if it is said that in this present birth your father has been purified, what need is there to mention that those who were your fathers throughout twenty-one births—numbering twenty-one—are also purified? And how much more so is the statement "you purify even your father," since you are the sanctifier of the lineage!
Your family, including your father, mother, and others, is also purified. ||18||
Wherever my devotees are found— those who are tranquil, who see with equanimity, who are virtuous, and whose conduct is exemplary— even those lands are purified, even if they be the Kīkaṭas.
Śrīdhara: Those whose conduct is perfectly excellent—even the Kīkaṭa regions and lineages equal to them—are purified; that is, they become pure. ||19||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He says "where" (in verse 19) to show that my devotee purifies even the place where he dwells with his companions, let alone his parents and others—the meaning being that they are purified (*pūyanti*), that is, they become pure (*pūtā bhavanti*). ||19||
O Lord of Daityas, those who have lost all longing for my state do not harm anything whatsoever among the multitudes of living beings in their every way, whether they be high or low.

Śrīdhara: [Objection: "It is not surprising that this greatness belongs to Your devotees, but I am not such a person. To this, He says in two verses beginning with "sarvātmanā": "Those whose longing has vanished through my disposition—that is, through devotion to me... (20)
The sequence of composition: "By the Self of All" constitutes a pair of verses. ||20||
Viśvanātha: Now, if it is argued that "it is not surprising that this greatness belongs to your devotees, but I am not like that," he says in response: "All... (verse 20).
There are men in the world who are my devotees and follow you; indeed,
you bear the likeness of all my devotees.

Śrīdhara: Those men who have followed you are also characterized by these very same qualities and thus become my devotees; therefore, you are the "bearer of the likeness" (*pratirūpa-dhṛk*) for all my devotees—that is, you are their standard of comparison. The meaning is that you are indeed the most excellent. ||21||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Those persons who become devoted to you, they too become my devotees.
Of what nature are they? By my very disposition—that is, by love alone—they have lost all desire for sense objects; they are non-violent in every respect.

And since they exist, the sense is: by whom can Your greatness be described? For You, O Lord, assume a form that serves as a standard of comparison for Your devotees, because You are the most excellent among them—this is the underlying thought.
Perform all the funeral rites for your purified father;
O dear one, by the touch of my body, he who has excellent offspring shall go to the higher worlds.
Madhu and Kaiṭabha died far from the Blessed One due to a lack of devotion;
they attained only darkness (tamas), whereas he who went to Hari through devotion gradually attained [the highest state]. ||22||

Śrīdhara said: "Since your father has been purified in every way by the touch of my body, there is no longer even a suspicion of sin in him. You need only perform the duties toward a son, namely the funeral rites."

The sequence of the composition: "Do it. The meaning is that by your prayer to the Blessed One, he will grant you excellent progeny, the expiation of your offense, and the attainment of the highest world. ||22||

Viśvanātha: Since your father has been purified in every way by the mere touch of my body, there is not even the slightest suspicion of sin in him; nevertheless, perform the funeral rites for the deceased as if he were still dead, solely for the sake of maintaining worldly convention—this is the meaning. ||22||
Occupy the station of the ancestors as it has been declared by those who discourse on Brahman;
fixing your mind on me, my dear son, perform your actions with me as your supreme goal.
Śrīdhara: Without transgressing what has been taught by those who discourse on Brahman—that is, those who discourse on the Vedas—perform your actions while being intent upon Me. 23.
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Although you, being My devotee, have no further authority for ritual action (*karma*), nevertheless, by My command alone, perform actions for the sake of maintaining worldly convention—thinking "I am intent upon Him" (*mat-para*)—in all actions.
The meaning is: "Do not grieve," because for one who is devoid of faith, even the performance of actions results in non-performance. ||23||
Śrī Nārada said:
Prahlāda likewise performed for his father those rites pertaining to the hereafter.
As the Blessed One said: "O King, [he is] consecrated by the twice-born."
Seeing Narahari Hari with a countenance bright with grace, Brahmā,
surrounded by the gods and others, praised him with pure words and spoke.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
Śrī Brahmā said:
O God of gods, sovereign of all, creator of beings, first-born one!
By good fortune, that sinful asura who tormented the world has been slain by you.
Śrīdhara: [This is] the *Krama-sandarbha*; it has not been commented upon.
Viśvanātha: "The progenitors of beings" (*bhūta-bhāvanāḥ*) refers to Brahmā, Marīci, and others, from whom the ancestors were first born. (26)
He who obtained a boon from me and must not be slain by my created beings,
having become arrogant through the power of his asceticism and yoga, has destroyed all the Vedas."
Śrīdhara: "By my creations" means by the elements created by me. "I slew" means I destroyed all the Vedas, that is, all the dharmas. "He has been slain by you"—this is a matter of good fortune;
this is the sequence of the composition. Viśvanātha: [This] has not been explained.
By good fortune, that virtuous son of yours, a great devotee even as a child,
has been liberated from death by you; by good fortune, he has now been reunited with you.
Śrīdhara: *Samitaḥ* means "properly attained. ||28||
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— O Blessed One, this is Your form as You meditate upon the Supreme Self.
It is a protector from all sides against terrors, even from death that seeks to strike.
Śrīdhara: [He is so called] because of total terror; because of fear for his lineage; and because he is a protector, a guardian. ||29||
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: A protector even from death. (29)
The Blessed Lord said: "O Lord, O Lotus-born One, you must not grant this to the asuras."
He is the supreme boon for those of cruel nature, just as nectar is for serpents.
Śrīdhara: [This] *krama-sandarbha* has not been commented upon.
Viśvanātha: Thus, "the boon, the boon" means the most exceedingly great boon. ||30||
Śrī Nārada said:
O King, having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Hari then vanished from that place.
Invisible to all beings, he was honored by the Supreme Lord.
Then, having worshipped him, Prahlāda bowed his head in reverence to the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin),
to Bhava, to the Prajāpatis, and to the gods, who are all portions of the Blessed One.
Then, together with the sages headed by Kāvya, the Lotus-Seated One (Brahmā) appointed Prahlāda as the lord of the Daityas and Dānavas.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
Then the gods, having offered their congratulations and bestowed supreme blessings, [departed].
O King, having been duly honored, Brahmā and the others departed for their own abodes.
Śrīdhara: Thus, you must not grant this boon. "Kruro-nisargāḥ" means those whose nature or innate disposition is cruel.
"Amṛtam" means milk. ||34||
The *Krama-sandarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon. —
And thus, the two attendants of Viṣṇu were made sons of Diti.
Those two were slain by Hari, who resided within their hearts, through his state of enmity.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
Furthermore, due to the curse of the Brahmin, those two became Rākṣasas.
Kumbhakarṇa and the Ten-necked one were both slain by the heroic exploits of Rāma.

Śrīdhara: Regarding the question asked—how did the two enemies, Śiśupāla and Dantavakra, attain *sāyujya* with Śrī Kṛṣṇa?—that very point is now concluded by means of seven verses beginning with "evam," through the narration of their previous births and so forth. [The Lord] caused them to attain the state of being His sons.
"By the curse of the brahmin"—this is to be supplied as a continuation for what follows. ||36||
The sequence of composition by Viśvanātha has not been explained.
Lying on the battlefield with their hearts pierced by Rāma’s arrows, [the two brothers...]
With their minds fixed on that, they abandoned their bodies just as they had done in their previous birth.
Śrīdhara: "tac-cittau" refers to those two whose minds were fixed on Śrī Rāma. ||37||
The *Krama-sandarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— Now, moreover, these two who were born here as Śiśupāla and Karūṣaja...
While you were looking on, the two met with a continuous succession of hostilities.
Whatever sin they had previously committed, those kings who were enemies of Kṛṣṇa abandoned it at the end, becoming one with Him, just as a worm becomes a wasp.
The construction is as follows: "May my devotees, whose very selves are honey-sweet, preside over that [place] with a connection characterized by universal subordination. (38-39)
Śrīdhara: Not commented upon.

Viśvanātha: "Enas" means offense, such as the disparagement of Kṛṣṇa; they abandoned even that sin previously committed by contemplating Him, having become one with His self (tad-ātman). Regarding that state of being one with His self:
The illustration: just as a *peśaskṛt* insect, through meditation upon a particular kind of insect, becomes that very self. ||38-39||
Just as King Śiśupāla and others attained identity with Hari through supreme devotion to the Blessed One and by constant meditation upon Him, so too did they reach that state of union.
"Madhu, Pauṇḍraka, Naraka, Śālva, Kaṃsa, and Rukmin—though they were devotees of Hari, they were possessed by Him; yet through devotion to Him, they attained Hari.
But the demons themselves were cast into the great darkness. Thus it is said. (40)
Śrīdhara: Not explained.
Krama-sandarbha: "Just as" (yathā)—just as others attained a form similar [to that] of the Lord through supreme devotion, so too did kings such as Caidya through supreme contemplation of Him.
Through absorption in that meditation, they attained identity by means of a state devoid of separation—that is, uninterrupted;

this also qualifies both devotion and contemplation. And in that regard, it is understood that for the King of Cedi and the King of Karūṣa, their very manifestation in a form identical [to Kṛṣṇa] constitutes their attainment of Him. ||40||

Viśvanātha: Just as the knowers and the devotees attained identity—that is, non-difference—with Hari through devotion, so too did Caidya and others attain that same state by thinking of Him. Through what kind of devotion? Through one that is supreme even compared to His knowledge, dispassion, and so forth; and it is the same in what follows.
Regarding the phrase "with their minds and breaths stilled" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.87.21), it will be stated later that even her enemies attained [liberation] through remembrance of her. ||40||
All this that you have asked me has been told to you:
even how the sons of Damaghoṣa and the others, though they were enemies, attained intimacy with Hari.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
This [is the teaching] of the god Brahmā and of the high-souled Kṛṣṇa.
The meritorious narrative of the descent [of the Lord], in which the slaying of the two primordial Daityas occurs.
Śrīdhara concludes the account of Prahlāda’s life with these four verses: "This...
[and so on]. The incarnation was in the form of Śrī Nṛsiṃha; the word "narrated" (ākhyātā) is to be understood as the remainder of the sentence. ||42||
The *Krama-sandarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon. —
[Here ends] the account of Prahlāda, the great devotee of the Lord.
Devotion, knowledge, detachment, and indeed the true nature of this Hari—these are his.
Śrīdhara: [The phrase] "the life-story of Prahlāda" and so forth is to be construed with the third [chapter], as it has been traditionally handed down (*samāmnātam*).

By the word "of this" (*asya*), the meaning is the true nature (*yāthātmyam*) and reality (*tattvam*) of Hari, the Lord of creation, maintenance, and dissolution; and by "by this," the meaning is the detailed description of Hari's qualities and deeds that has been performed. ||43||

The sequence of the composition: "Of Prahlāda" refers to this triad concerning the true nature (*yāthātmya*) of that Lord known as Śrī Kṛṣṇa, as well as His majesty (*māhātmya*) exactly as it is, because He is the source of all incarnations. Having raised the reading "of Him" (*asya*) in the commentary, he explains it; by this, it is understood that [the words] beginning with "spoken by this Prahlāda" are implied. ||43||
Viśvanātha: The connection is either with the preceding clause, "the life-story has been narrated," or with the following, "it has been handed down by tradition.
Regarding *yāthātmyam*: it is the true nature (*svarūpa*) of Hari; the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied in its own sense without deviating from the base word.
A description of the qualities and activities of the Lord of creation, preservation, and dissolution;
and the great transformation of high and low states by the power of time.

Regarding the word *madhvaḥ*: by the phrase "the Blessed One who is reached," it is concluded that the Blessed One is reached solely through the *bhāgavata* dharma and not through hatred or other such means; and the repetition [of the teaching] is for that very purpose. Furthermore, the true nature (*yathātmya*) and so forth are mentioned as qualifications of knowledge.

"Devotion, knowledge, and detachment—these, as well as hell and the like, and the Bhāgavata dharma, are said to be ninefold among His devotees. Thus says Śrīdhara in the *Tantra-sāra*. Furthermore, there is a reversal of the abodes belonging to the higher and lower beings, such as gods and demons.
Error. ||44||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: By the word "creation" (*sarga*), the [other cosmic functions] such as maintenance and dissolution are also implied. The "reversal" (*vyatyaya*) of the abodes of the higher and lower—namely, the gods, demons, and so forth—is their destruction. (44)
In this narrative,
the dharma of the devotees of the Blessed One and the Blessed One by whom that dharma is attained are fully set forth,
including all matters pertaining to the supreme self.
Śrīdhara: The internal [discipline] consists of the discrimination between the self and the non-self, and so forth. ||45||
The *Krama-sandarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been explained.
Whoever [recites] this meritorious narrative, which is augmented by the heroic power (*vīrya*) of Viṣṇu...
Having heard this with faith, one who recites it is liberated from the bonds of karma.
Śrīdhara: With two verses beginning with "He who," he states the fruit of hearing this and so forth: "Having heard this, he who shall proclaim it... (46).
The *Krama-sandarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— He who [perceives] this play of Mṛgendra of the Primeval Person...
One who recites with devotion this account of the slaying of the leader of the Daitya hosts,
and having heard the holy majesty of that foremost of virtuous men, the son of a Daitya, attains a world free from fear from any quarter.

Śrīdhara: This is the play of the Lord of Beasts; he describes that very thing—the slaughter of the lord of the Daityas and the leaders of the herds. Whoever, being pure, should recite this, [attains] merit, spiritual power, majesty, or the certainty of wisdom, and reaches the world of Vaikuṇṭha. ||47||
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: This refers to "etām" (this). [The compound] "mṛgendrasya" (of the lord of beasts) means of the lion; in the alternative sense, it refers to the sport of Nṛsiṃha.
The compound is archaic (ārṣa), similar to the expression "rāja-mātaṅgāḥ" (elephants belonging to the king). He describes the sport: [it was performed] by the lord of the Daityas himself.
The elephant was his leader; [I shall describe] the slaughter of Hiraṇyakaśipu, the leader of the lords of the Daityas— O,
you are indeed highly fortunate in the world of men!
The sages, purifying the world,
approach those whose houses the Supreme Brahman— invisible yet manifest, hidden within human form— dwells in.

Śrīdhara: "Oh, how great is Prahlāda’s fortune that he has beheld the Lord! We, however, are ill-fated. To the king who was thus despondent, [the sage] replied with three verses beginning with "You": "Into whose houses the sages come from all sides—that is, they arrive there—for what reason? Into those [houses]..."

"In the houses, that Supreme Brahman known as Śrī-Kṛṣṇa dwells in person, hidden in human form"—thus says the *Krama-sandarbha*. With the words "O, the fortune of Prahlāda! the Lord spoke with wonder to the king in three verses beginning with "You all," [describing Him] as having a human form (*manuṣya-liṅga*).

It has been indicated that even the manifestation of that [divine form] does not possess such [material] nature. [Kṛṣṇa-sandarbha 59] Viśvanātha: "Oh, how great is Prahlāda’s fortune—that he has seen the Lord! But we are unfortunate"—to the king who was thus despondent, [the Lord said], "You [are superior] to Prahlāda, and to the teacher of Prahlāda..."

Nārada says "you" to indicate that you possess abundant good fortune even more than I, and even more than other devotees such as your ancestors beginning with Yadu and Purūravas, or even the sages beginning with Vasiṣṭha, Marīci, and Kaśyapa, or even Brahmā and Rudra.

You are most fortunate among living beings in this world, for even the sages— who wander everywhere in order to fulfill their own purpose by making the world their own through their very sight and so forth— come to your houses. This is because [you possess] that which is hidden and secret from all others.

The Supreme Brahman, possessing human characteristics and a human form, dwells visibly in the homes of those for whom He resides with attachment—even if uninvited—in the proper manner. Indeed, the Supreme Brahman in human form does not dwell visibly in the homes of Prahlāda and others; nor [does He so dwell] elsewhere.
The meaning is that sages go to behold him in order to become fulfilled in their purpose. ||43||
Indeed, this is the experience of the bliss of Nirvana, the absolute liberation sought by the great Brahman.
He is indeed your dear friend, your maternal cousin, worthy of honoring as himself, the ordainer of rites, and your preceptor.
"Sweetness" refers to the bliss of nirvāṇa, the bliss of the bodiless state; for it is said in the Śruti: "Having taken hold of this arrow. (49)
Śrīdhara: Now, one might object: "Kṛṣṇa is our maternal cousin; how can he be called Brahman?

To this, he says: "He indeed... He is this very Brahman. Of what nature is he? He is of the nature of the experience of that supreme bliss which is unconditional (*nirupādhi*), the bliss of liberation (*kaivalya-nirvāṇa*) sought by the great ones. He is you.

"He is indeed your dear friend," and so forth—such is his nature. Regarding the "arrangement of the sequence" (*krama-sandarbha*) as being "one who performs the ritual" (*vidhi-kṛt*) and "one who follows commands" (*ājñānuvartī*), no commentary has been provided.
Viśvanātha states: Nor should it be said that the Supreme Brahman alone became Kṛṣṇa in human form; rather...

He states that Kṛṣṇa alone is the Supreme Brahman: "This well-known one in human form is indeed Kṛṣṇa, who is Brahman. Of what nature is he? He is the experience—the very essence of realization—of that unconditioned supreme bliss which is the absolute liberation (*kaivalya-nirvāṇa*) sought by the great ones. This is the meaning. [He is] Kṛṣṇa.

However, the phrase "the Blessed One himself" should be explained here as a restatement rather than an injunction; for the *Gītā-upaniṣad* itself, in the words "I am indeed the foundation of Brahman," is the authority that determines this very meaning—this is the sense of the word "vai. Not only does he merely dwell in your house, but being beloved, he dwells there.

Thus, by him [the Lord], you are to be gladdened as a "friend"; you are to be incited toward your welfare as a "well-wisher"; you are to be followed out of affection due to a special relationship as a "maternal cousin"; you are to be regarded as one's own body as an "own self"; and you are to be protected with compassion as those who are "worthy of honor."
The sense is that [the Lord] is to be worshipped as a servant created by ritual injunction through roles such as charioteer, and He is to be instructed as a teacher;
furthermore, the intention is that He remains in the homes of Prahlāda and others in the capacity of a teacher, a servant, and so forth.
He whose form has not been directly described by those such as Bhava and Padmaja as a real entity through the intellect,
but who is worshipped through silence, devotion, and tranquility—
May this Lord of the Sātvatas be gracious to you.
Śrīdhara: Now, if he is the Supreme Brahman, how can there be pleasure with sixteen thousand women?

Or how could there be the practice of unrighteousness and so forth for him? To this, he says: "No. The true nature (*tattva*) of whose form cannot be directly grasped even by those such as Bhava and others through their own intellects (*dhiyā*), thinking "this is such-and-such" in its actual reality (*vastutayā*).
"He was not described by us; he has become gracious of his own accord. But for us, that grace must indeed be prayed for through means such as silence," thus he says: "By silence.
May this Lord of the Sātvatas be gracious to us; for the Supreme Brahman does not dwell in the houses of Prahlāda alone.

Sages do not go to his house for the sake of seeing him, nor does his Brahman reside in the form of a maternal cousin or similar relations, nor is he himself easily propitiated; therefore, the sense is that you alone are more fortunate than even he, and thus more fortunate than we as well. ||50||
The Sequence of Composition: Now, might someone consider even this form of His to be unreal?

To that he says: "Not of whom... That whose very form is directly perceived even by the supreme wise ones was not described as unreal or non-ultimate by Bhava, Padmaja, and the others; rather, [it was described as real].

The meaning is that it has been determined as the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). This is shown by such passages as "You are the supreme Brahman directly" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 11.16.1), "That which is a friend is supreme bliss" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.14.32) and so forth,
"He is the thunderbolt to the wrestlers and the best of men to human beings" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.43.17) and so forth, and "He is the cosmic Virāṭ for the ignorant."

And by the statement, "He is the supreme reality for yogīs" (Kṛṣṇa-sandarbha 59), Viśvanātha asks: "Now, if this is so, what is the reason for those like us—vulgar folk—to perform service (*kaiṅkarya*) and so forth toward Him, who is the direct Supreme Brahman and the very foundation of all? [The answer is: True; for Him...

Thinking, "Who am I, a wretched being, to know the true nature of His great sovereignty and subjection to love, since even those beginning with Brahmā do not know it? he says: "Of whom... [The meaning is: His form—that is, His reality—is not directly described as a thing in its actual state, such that "it is thus"; rather, it is [described] by the intellect (*dhiyā*), that is, by the mind.

The sense is: "precisely because there is no entry [into the heart]. Regarding the word *maunena* (by silence): we and others like us pray for grace through means such as silence; yet Kṛṣṇa prays for your grace through service (*kaiṅkarya*) and so forth. Thus, the point is that this alone is the difference between those like you and those like us. ||50||
O King, it was this very Blessed One who, in the past, caused the destruction of the glory of the god Rudra by Maya, the master of infinite illusions.
Madhva destroyed Rudra’s doubt as to whether everything was dependent on him or not,
by providing a remedy for Rudra through a mere trifle of māyā.
"In what action did Maya act perversely?
Not in that which is dependent, for where the required [element] is established, it does not lead to a fault. Thus, in the *Śabdanirṇaya*, verse 51.

Śrīdhara: Now, one might ask: "How is it that even Śrī Rudra—who performed such deeds as the destruction of Tripura, which are difficult for others to accomplish—is not aware of His true nature? In response to this expectation, the author introduces a narrative to state that even his power is due solely to this [Lord's] assistance, and does not belong to him alone. He says: "He..."
"This is it. ||51||
Kramasandarbha: This has not been explained.

Viśvanātha: Now, [one might object]: "Let the Lotus-born (Brahmā) not know; let it be that only Īśvara [knows]. To state that this is indeed true, yet his sovereignty has been granted [to Brahmā] in this very matter, he begins the narrative with the words: "He, this one... (sa eṣa).
The King said:
"In what deed did Maya offend the Lord, the Ruler of the Universe?"
And let it be told how fame was accumulated by this Kṛṣṇa.
Śrīdhara: King Yudhiṣṭhira said: "In what deed did Maya destroy the glory of the Lord, the Master of the Universe? (52)
The *Krama-sandarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon. —
o)0(o— Śrī Nārada said:
The Asuras, defeated by the gods in battle who were bolstered by him,
sought refuge with Maya, the supreme teacher of illusionists.
Śrīdhara: By this [phrase], "upabṛṃhitaiḥ" means nourished or increased by Śrī-Kṛṣṇa. ||53||
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: By this Kṛṣṇa. ||53||

Having fashioned three cities before him— one of gold, one of silver, and one of iron— the omnipresent Lord made them such that their destruction and conjunction were difficult to perceive, and their constituent parts were inconceivable.

Śrīdhara: Having constructed three cities made of gold, silver, and iron, he gave them to them—this is the ellipsis. Their going and coming involve departure and arrival that are difficult to perceive; their furnishings are difficult to conceive. (54)
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Those [women] whose ill fortune consists of misfortune and calamity, as well as coming and going;
the ellipsis is "he gave them to the Asuras after creating them. (54)
O King, by means of those [women], the commanders of the Asura armies, remaining unobserved, destroyed the three worlds along with their lords, remembering their former enmity.
Śrīdhara: O generals, commanders of armies, remembering former enmity! ||55||
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon. —o)0(o— Then those worlds, together with their lords, having approached the Lord, bowed down.
Save us, O God, your devotees who have been destroyed by the inhabitants of Tripura!
Śrīdhara: [This is] the *Krama-sandarbha*; it has not been commented upon. Viśvanātha: [He refers to] Rudra as Īśvara. ||56||
Then,
having shown favor to the gods by saying, "Do not fear," the omnipresent Lord fixed an arrow to his bow and discharged the weapon at the cities.
Śrīdhara discharged a consecrated weapon-arrow at the cities. ||57||
The *Krama-sandarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— Then, arrows with the color of fire shot forth from the solar disc.
Just as the multitude of rays could no longer be seen from that point forward.
Śrīdhara: Then, from the arrow—like masses of rays, that is, collections of light-beams, from the solar orb—from which [rays], from those [beams]. ||58||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: The word "yathā" (as) is to be joined before "from the solar disc" (*sūrya-maṇḍalāt*). "Yataḥ" means from which arrows, that is, by reason of which [arrows]. ||58||
Touched by them, all the inhabitants of the city fell down lifeless;
the great yogi Maya brought them back and cast them into the liquid of the well.
Śrīdhara: [This refers to] the nectar of the well, the immortal nectar of the well fashioned by himself. ||59||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: In the *Kūparasa* [and] in his own composed *Kūparasāmṛta*. (59)
Touched by the essence of the perfected nectar, those of great power, possessing the core of a diamond,
rose up like flashes of lightning splitting through the clouds.

Śrīdhara: "Vajrasāra" means having limbs as firm as a diamond; "mahaujasas" means possessing great strength; "meghadalanāḥ" means those who split the clouds; and "vidyadrūpāḥ" means like fires in the form of lightning. ||60||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not commented upon.
*Viśvanātha*: "Megha-dalana" means those that split the clouds; like fires in the form of lightning, they are situated within the clouds, meaning they eclipse the splendor of the clouds. ||60||
Seeing the bull-bannered god dejected and his resolve shattered,
the Blessed Viṣṇu then devised a means there.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
At that time, Vatsa was Brahmā himself, for this Viṣṇu is indeed the Bull (Gau).
Having entered Tripura at the proper time, he drank the nectar from the well of aesthetic flavor.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha: at the time of midday. ||62||
The sequence of composition has not been explained. —
Those Asuras, though seeing [this], did not prevent it, being utterly deluded.
Having understood that, the great yogi, free from sorrow yet remembering the course of destiny, smiled and spoke thus to the guardians of the elixir who were afflicted by grief:
It has not been explained by anyone at all:
"There is no god, asura, human, or any other being here who is a Lord."
Whether it be one's own or that of another, what is ordained by destiny cannot be averted by either of the two.
Neither a god, nor an asura, nor anyone else is capable of warding off Madhva, who has been commanded by Viṣṇu. ||64||
Śrīdhara: [Not commented upon].
Viśvanātha: No one at all here is capable of warding off or removing destiny—that which has been ordained by fate for oneself, for another, or for both. (64)
Then, by means of his own powers (śaktis), he [Śiva] brought about the primordial nature (prādhānika) of Śambhu through dharma,
knowledge, dispassion, supernatural power, austerity, wisdom, action, and so forth.
The chariot, the charioteer, the banner, the horses, the bow, the armor, the arrows, and so forth—
having equipped himself and mounted the chariot, he took up his arrow and his bow.
Śrīdhara: No one at all here is capable of warding off or avoiding what has been ordained and prepared by destiny, whether for oneself, for another, or for both; that [destiny] is Śrī-Kṛṣṇa.
*Pradhana* means battle; its instrument is [the bow]. (65)
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: This Kṛṣṇa sequentially fashioned the chariot and other implements worthy of that great battle (*pradhana*), which were infused with his own powers (*śakti*); this is because his own powers are imperishable.
And because of their victory, even the chariot and other components possessed by them share that same nature.

This should be understood as the penetration of one's own dharma—bhakti-yoga—into the chariot, and of knowledge and other qualities dependent on bhakti-yoga into the sons and others who depend upon the chariot. (66)
At the auspicious moment of Abhijit, the Lord fixed an arrow upon his bow.
O King, by means of that [missile], Hara, the bearer of Śrī and lord of the universe, then burnt the three cities which were otherwise impenetrable, at midday during the Abhijit constellation.
The sequence of composition has not been explained. —
In the heavens, hundreds of celestial chariots crowded together, and the drums resounded.
The celestial sages, ancestors, perfected beings, and lords cried out "Victory! and scattered heaps of flowers;
the throngs of Apsarases sang with joy and danced.
Śrīdhara: Those gods and others whose [abodes] are crowded and congested with hundreds of celestial chariots. ||68||
The *Krama-sandarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been explained. —
Thus, O King, having burnt the three cities, the Blessed One, the destroyer of cities, [departed].
Being praised by Brahmā and the other gods, he returned to his own abode.
It has not been explained by anyone whatsoever.
Such are the manifestations of this Hari through his own māyā.
What else can I say regarding the heroic deeds of the Teacher of the World, which purify the world and are sung by the sages as he appeared in this human realm in a semblance of play?
Śrīdhara: Not commented upon.

Viśvanātha: The meaning is that because He is mimicking [the world] through His own *māyā*, and consequently under the influence of delusion (*moha*), people of the human world do not worship Him. ||70||

Thus ends the tenth chapter of the seventh [section] in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted to the Lord; it is well-composed and dear to the virtuous.
Thus ends the Seventh Canto in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā, the Pāramahaṃsyam, which is the commentary on the Brahma-sūtras within the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa.
The Tenth Chapter: The Life of Prahlāda and the Conquest of the City.
Now begins the Eleventh Chapter.
The Determination of Right Conduct.
Śrī Śuka said: Having heard this well-spoken discourse, honored by the assembly, [the King]...
Yudhiṣṭhira, the foremost of the great, filled with joy, again questioned the son of the Self-born, who is the soul of the wide-striding one, regarding the lord of the Daityas.
Śrīdhara:
Thus, the yoga of knowledge and devotion have been described by means of ten chapters;
now, the yoga of action is expounded through five chapters.
In the eleventh [chapter], the duties of men have been described in general,
as well as those specific to the social classes and the primary and secondary duties of women.

Having heard of the deeds—the conduct—that were honored and well-received in the assemblies of the virtuous by Prahlāda, the lord of the Daityas, he questioned Nārada again. Of what nature were his deeds?
He was the foremost and chief among the great souls (mahattama). The reason for this is that his mind (ātman) was fixed upon the Lord of Wide Strides (Urukrama).

The sequence of composition: being filled with joy because his doubts had been destroyed, he spoke of the dharma that is both spontaneous and favorable to sovereignty; thus he says: "He asked," etc. (1).
Viśvanātha:
Pure latent disposition (*vāsanā*) is described as arising from association with the devotees of the Lord.
Its purpose is stated through fifteen [verses] as being produced by virtuous action (*sat-karma*).
In the eleventh [chapter], the Sage spoke of the duties common to men, specifically those of the Brahmins and others, as well as those of women and those born of mixed castes.

Thus, having described the cause of the latent impression of unqualified devotion (*nirguṇa-bhakti-vāsanā*) through ten chapters as being the great mercy [of the Lord], He now begins to explain the cause of the latent impression of qualified devotion (*saguṇa-bhakti-vāsanā*)— namely, selfless action-yoga (*niṣkāma-karma-yoga*)— through five chapters,
beginning with the verse starting "Having heard" (*śrutvā*). [This devotion] is honored— that is, well-received— in the assemblies of the saintly (*sādhus*).
The foremost among the most exalted, [he spoke] to the chief Prahlāda. ||1||
Śrī Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Blessed One, I wish to hear about the eternal dharma of human beings.
That which a person endowed with the conduct of the castes and stages of life attains is supreme.
Śrīdhara: The reason for the desire to hear is stated: "Because from that dharma, when practiced, one attains supreme knowledge and devotion. (2)

The sequence of the composition: He states that she too was made to speak by Śrī Nārada for the very benefit of the world, relying solely upon the ultimate truth—beginning with the words "yat pumān. (2)
Viśvanātha: "Sanātana" means the eternal yoga of devotion (bhakti-yoga), which remains steadfast even upon the attainment of the fruit.
"Endowed with the conduct of the castes and stages of life" (varṇāśramācāra-yuta) means that I desire to hear also the dharma of the conduct pertaining to the castes and stages of life. ||2||
"O Brahmin, you are the direct son of Parameṣṭhin Prajāpati; among his sons, you are esteemed for your asceticism, yoga, and meditative absorption."
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
The Brahmins devoted to Nārāyaṇa know the supreme, secret Dharma.
Virtuous people like you are compassionate and peaceful, unlike others.

Śrīdhara: [Objection: But surely the authors of the Smṛtis have already declared the Dharma; to this he replies: "Devoted to Nārāyaṇa"—this is the sequence of the composition. [Objection: But Manu and the others were indeed devoted to Nārāyaṇa; to this he replies: "Secret.
The meaning is that because it is secret, even they did not reveal it. ||4||
Viśvanātha: [Objection: "Well then, let other sages who follow the Smṛtis be questioned. To this he says—"Nārāyaṇa...
Śrī Nārada said:
Having bowed to the Blessed One, the Unborn, the bridge of dharma for the worlds,
I shall proclaim the eternal dharma as heard from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa.
Śrīdhara: To the unborn Śrī Nārāyaṇa; [this was] heard directly from his very mouth. ||5||
The sequence of the composition: "The embankments of dharma. Here, "dharma" should be understood as a specific form of dharma that generates knowledge and devotion. (5)
Viśvanātha: To the unborn, the most excellent one. ||5||
He who, having descended by means of a portion of himself into the daughter of Dakṣa according to the law,
dwells at the Badarikā hermitage performing austerities for the welfare of the worlds.
Śrīdhara: Anticipating that he himself heard this from his mouth, he specifies [the speaker] with the word "ya" (who). ||6||

The sequence of the composition: "He moves with an unmanifest gait out of compassion for those who possess the Self"—this is from the fifth book [of the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*], referring to Nara by means of the Self. (6)
Viśvanātha: Not explained.
—o)0(o— For the Blessed Lord Hari, who consists of all the Vedas, is indeed the root of Dharma.
And that which is remembered by those who know it, O King, is that by which the self becomes serene.

Śrīdhara: First, he states the authority for dharma: "Dharma... etc. The root authority for dharma is tradition (smṛti), which is remembered by those who know it—that is, by those who know the Vedas. Furthermore, that by which the self—the mind—becomes serene and satisfied. And so says Yājñavalkya:
"Revelation (Śruti), tradition (Smṛti), the conduct of the virtuous, and what is pleasing to one's own self—the desire born of right resolve: this is remembered as the root of Dharma. And Manu says:

"The entire Veda is the root of Dharma, as are the Smṛtis and the conduct of those who know it, as well as the practice of the virtuous and self-satisfaction. [Manu 2.6] Thus ends the seventh [verse].

The sequence of the composition: by these two [verses], it has been stated that external religious duties are purposeless and that the duties pertaining to the Lord alone are essential. For this very reason, even from such statements of the *Manusmṛti* as "The entire Veda is the root of dharma" (2.6), [this conclusion follows].

It has been taught as being distinguished; and that is appropriate, because it has been stated in such passages as: "Here, for the virtuous who are free from envy, dharma is supreme and devoid of deceit" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.1.2). By the phrase "by which very dharma the mind becomes serene," it is meant just as in the verse: "by which the self becomes well-pleased" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.2.8).

Because it has not been stated [elsewhere] as being distinguished by the word *su* (well), it is understood that the direct devotion characterized by hearing that [name] alone is what is praiseworthy; and by this, Viśvanātha explains that even self-satisfaction—expressed by the word *ātman*—is a valid authority (*pramāṇa*). Indeed, the Blessed Lord alone is the root, the cause, and the established authority of dharma.

"Since all Vedas..."—the sense is that without devotion to Him, religious duties (dharmas) do not at all attain fulfillment. "Smṛtam" means the Smṛti; [it refers to] those who know that, namely those who know the Lord who consists of all the Vedas. By this, it is implied that [those texts] which enjoin śrāddhas and so forth devoid of the primary worship of Viṣṇu, as well as the seventh lunar day joined with the eighth, the Rohiṇī vow, and other such rites, [are not authoritative].
"Memories are withdrawn, and by which the self and the mind become serene—

that indeed is the supreme dharma for men, from which comes unswerving and unimpeded devotion to the Transcendent Lord (Adhokṣaja), by which the self becomes perfectly serene. [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.2.6]

By the non-use of the word "su" (well), it is indicated that the mind does not become serene through mere devotion (*bhakti*) alone, nor through devotion mixed with religious duty (*dharma*) and so forth, nor through action mixed with devotion; for religious duty devoid of devotion is simply unacceptable. By this...

"Revelation (Śruti), tradition (Smṛti), the conduct of the virtuous, and what is pleasing to one's own self—the desire born of right resolve: this is remembered as the root of Dharma," according to the statement of Yājñavalkya. And Manu says:

"Veda is the root of all dharma, as are the Smṛtis and the conduct of those who know it, as well as the practice of the virtuous and self-satisfaction"— even from such a statement by Manu, the declaration of Nārada that "the Blessed Lord alone is indeed the root of dharma" is superior. As it has been said:
In the Nārasiṃha Purāṇa it is said:

"Sanaka and the others were appointed to the dharma known as nivṛtti (withdrawal), while Marīci and the others were appointed to the dharma known as pravṛtti (engagement); [the Lord appointed] the sage Nārada alone to liberation."
Thus, it is implied that Nārada alone possesses superiority over both of those groups and a mastery of the essence of all dharmas. ||7||
Truthfulness, compassion, austerity, purity, forbearance, discernment, tranquility, self-control,
non-violence, celibacy, renunciation, study of the sacred texts, and uprightness.

Śrīdhara: In that regard, he first states the qualities common to all human beings with five verses, beginning with "Truth" (*satyam*). Austerity (*tapas*) consists of fasting on the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*) and so forth. Discernment (*īkṣā*) is the discrimination between what is appropriate and what is inappropriate. Tranquility (*śama*) is the restraint of the mind. Self-control (*dama*) is the restraint of the external senses. Renunciation (*tyāga*) is giving. Vedic study (*svādhyāya*)...
The recitation as prescribed. ||8||
The sequence of composition: the five and a half verses beginning with "It is true" (satyam). ||8||

Viśvanātha: In this regard, he first describes the eternal path of devotion (*bhakti-yoga*), a duty common to all human beings, through five verses beginning with "Truth" (*satyam*). Among these, it should be understood that the twenty-one qualities beginning with truth are the instruments of devotion, whereas the nine beginning with the scriptures are devotion itself.

Austerity consists of fasting on the eleventh day of the lunar fortnight and so forth; tranquility is the restraint of the mind; self-control is the restraint of the external senses; and sacred study is the recitation of mantras as is appropriate. ||8||
Contentment, service with equanimity, gradual withdrawal from worldly pleasures,
discernment regarding their opposites, silence, and self-investigation [are the means].
