Śrīdhara: Contentment is the state of being satisfied with what is obtained by fate. Service to great beings who possess equal vision. Cessation from worldly pursuits is withdrawal from active worldly duties. Contemplation on the contrary nature is the observation of fruitless activities. Silence is the cessation of idle chatter. Self-investigation is...
The contemplation of the Self as distinct from the body and other such [elements]. ||9||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Service to great beings who view all with equanimity; reflection upon those [actions] which are fruitless endeavors due to error;
silence, which is the cessation of idle speech; and self-investigation of the self.
The contemplation on being distinct from the body. ||9||
O Pāṇḍava, one should share food and other necessities with all beings according to their merit, and maintain the perception of them as the Self and as deities, especially toward human beings.
Śrīdhara: The notion that "this is the self" and "this is the deity. ||10||

*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: Food and so forth—meaning the eating of food, the primary [delicacies] such as sweetmeats (*modaka*), and the like; clothing, garlands, sandalwood paste, and so on—one should take these after dividing them appropriately, both for oneself and for the deity.
And cognition is mental cultivation. ||10||

Hearing of Him, chanting His names, remembering His path as taken by the great souls, serving Him, worshiping Him, bowing down to Him, becoming His servant, befriending Him, and surrendering one's very self.
O Madhva: throughout beginningless and endless times, both in liberation and in saṃsāra, the one Viṣṇu alone always impels me as I abide within him.

"Thus one should know that the knowledge of mutual delight is the offering of oneself, as well as the actions prescribed for the stages of life by those whose births and deeds are pure. Thus it is stated in the *Tantramālā*. 11.
Śrīdhara: For this Śrī Kṛṣṇa, there are nine [limbs], beginning with hearing (śravaṇa). Worship (ijyā) is veneration (arcana). 11.
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— This supreme duty has been proclaimed for all human beings.
O King, he who possesses the thirty marks is the Self of all, by whom one is satisfied.
Śrīdhara: Thus, he possesses thirty characteristics. ||12||
The sequence of composition by Viśvanātha has not been explained. He, in whom the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) are uninterrupted, that twice-born one spoke of him as unborn (*aja*).
Sacrificing, studying, and giving are prescribed for the twice-born;
as are the duties enjoined for the stages of life (āśramas) for those purified by birth and their actions.
Śrīdhara: Now, in order to explain the duties of the social classes (varṇadharma), he states the definition of the twice-born (dvija):

"He in whom the sacraments (saṃskāra) such as conception (garbhādhāna) and the rest, accompanied by mantras, have been performed without interruption, is a twice-born. If that were so, then even a Śūdra would possess the status of a twice-born provided there is no interruption in his sacraments; to this he replies: "Aja" refers to Brahmā.

The twice-born man spoke [to him] as one endowed with such purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*); however, he did not speak to the Śūdra as one endowed with the *mantra*-based rites, nor as one who had undergone the initiation (*upanayana*). Therefore, he was not a twice-born (*dvija*). And so says the Smṛti:
"Let even a Śūdra always receive the sacrament of marriage alone;
Prajāpati did not create him with any [Vedic] metre.
And the Śruti says: "He created the Brāhmaṇa from the Gāyatrī, the Rājanya from the Triṣṭubh, and the Vaiśya from the Jagatī."

"A Vaiśya [is initiated], but a Śūdra by no one. Therefore, since sacraments other than marriage are not mandatory for him, and since initiation (upanayana) is strictly prohibited for him, the meaning is that he does not possess the status of the twice-born (dvijatva). In an alternative reading, the term is "vaidikādayaḥ" (those beginning with the Vedic [initiation]).
The meaning is "beginning with the rite of conception" (*garbhādhāna*). He states the duties necessarily incumbent upon those of the three *varṇas* with the word "sacrifice" (*ijyā*).

These are for those who are pure and bright through birth, lineage, conduct, and ritual action; the meaning is that these are not prescribed for those of low birth or evil conduct. They are ordained for the stages of life (*āśrama*) beginning with studentship (*brahmacarya*).
And [the duties of] action. For the Śūdra, however, there are only the duties of his caste (*varṇadharma*), because there is no distinction based on the different stages of life (*āśramabheda*).

This is the sequence of the composition: "sacraments" (*saṃskārāḥ*) constitutes half a verse. Now, one might object: if those sacraments were performed for a Śūdra as well, would he not attain the status of the twice-born (*dvijatva*)? To this he says: "Having created him, the Unborn One declared him to be a twice-born."

He designated him as a twice-born (dvija) by virtue of his birth; the meaning is that one becomes a twice-born only when the sacramental rites (saṃskāra) belonging to that caste have been obtained. ||13||
Viśvanātha: Now, in order to explain the duties pertaining to the social classes (varṇadharma), he states the definition of the twice-born (dvija):

"He in whom the sacraments (saṃskāra)—beginning with conception (garbhādhāna) and accompanied by mantras—are present is a dvija; one whose sacraments have been interrupted is a 'kinsman of the twice-born' (dvijabandhu). This is because [the lineage] begins from the creation of Brahmā, who is called Aja.
The meaning is that when the twice-born class has thus proceeded, birth from pure parents is the primary defining characteristic. ||13||
—for the Brahmin, [the livelihood consists of] study and so forth; for another, it is non-acceptance of gifts;
and for the king who protects his subjects, it is [livelihood] through taxes and the like from those other than Brahmins.

Śrīdhara: He states the duties in the form of livelihoods for all four classes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, in seven and a half verses starting with "Of the Brāhmaṇa. The phrase "six duties are prescribed for the Brāhmaṇa" is to be supplied. Among those, however, teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and receiving gifts are his means of livelihood. As Manu says:
"Of his six duties, however, three are his means of livelihood:
officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and the acceptance of pure gifts" (Manu 10.76).
For other Kṣatriyas, there is no acceptance of gifts; thus, officiating at sacrifices and teaching are [permitted] apart from the acceptance of gifts.

And he permits it in an emergency; furthermore, he will state immediately thereafter that this is "except for a member of the royal caste" (*rājanya*). It is also heard that certain Kṣatriyas, such as Aśvapati and Kekaya, acted as teachers and so forth.
Regarding the alternative livelihood for a Kṣatriya who is authorized to protect the subjects, he says: "Of the king."
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), punishments, taxes, and so forth are included. ||14||
The sequence of the composition: By the word "or" (*vā*) in the phrase "or from a non-Brahmin," the meaning is that in some cases it may even be from a Brahmin;
this refers to [prohibitions] such as shaving and the taking of wealth. ||14||

Viśvanātha: He states the duties in the form of livelihoods for the four classes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa in seven and a half verses starting with "Of the Brahmin" (*viprasya*). The phrase "six are prescribed" (*ṣaṭ vihitāni*) is to be supplied [to each]. Among those, however, teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and receiving gifts are the means of livelihood. And so says Manu:
"Of his six duties, however, three are his means of livelihood:
officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and the acceptance of pure gifts" (Manu 10.76).
For another Kṣatriya, the non-acceptance of gifts implies that officiating at sacrifices and teaching are his modes of subsistence in times of distress.

Even in times of distress, accepting gifts from him is forbidden. The meaning is that for the protector of subjects, his livelihood consists solely of the respectful offerings given by the subjects he protects. Or [he may take] from the world distinct from the Brahmins, by means of taxes, fines, and so forth. ||14||
The Vaiśya, however, should have agriculture and trade as his livelihood and should always follow the Brahmin community;
the Śūdra’s livelihood should be service to the twice-born and to his master.

Śrīdhara: One whose livelihood (*vṛtti*) consists of occupations characterized by agriculture, trade, and so forth, is a Śūdra. Service to the twice-born (*dvija*) is prescribed for the Śūdra; however, service to one's own master, the twice-born, shall be both his duty and his livelihood. (15)
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: He whose livelihood (*vṛtti*) consists of news, agriculture, trade, and so forth; his duty (*dharma*) is service to the twice-born (*dvija*). Service to the master—the twice-born—means the occupation of attending to him. (15)
Trade,
agriculture, tending cattle, and gleaning ears of grain: this fourfold livelihood for Brahmins is increasingly superior in its merit.
Śrīdhara: He states the other means of livelihood for a Brahmin according to the distinction between the primary and secondary options, beginning with "vārtā.

*Vārtā* refers to various occupations such as agriculture and the like. *Śālīna* is that which is obtained without boldness, i.e., unasked. *Yāyāvara* is the daily begging for grain. *Śila* [is obtaining food] from rice-fields and the like.
Gleaning (*uñchana*) is the taking up of ears of grain abandoned by the owner; picking (*śila*) is the taking up of grains fallen from marketplaces and the like.
These two, gleaning and picking, are combined and stated to be fourfold. "Superior" (*śreyasī*) means most excellent. ||16||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: He states other means of livelihood for a Brāhmaṇa—*vārtā* is various and manifold;
therein, *śālīna* is [obtaining food] without begging; *yāyāvara* is begging only for grain every day; *śila*...
*Uñchana* is the gathering of unhusked grains abandoned by the owner in rice fields and the like; *uñcha* is the gathering of grains fallen from marketplaces and the like. ||16||

A man should not, except in times of distress, adopt an inferior mode of livelihood that is not the highest; however, in times of distress, all [modes] may be adopted by everyone in every way, with the exception of the Kṣatriya.

Śrīdhara: Demonstrating the established order within the various modes of livelihood, he describes the modes of livelihood for times of distress: "The lowest" means base. "The highest" refers to that consisting of teaching and so forth. "Except for the Rājanya": a Kṣatriya, however, may resort to [the mode of livelihood] other than receiving gifts. ||17||
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: He states the modes of subsistence in times of distress: "The low-born (jaghanya), meaning a person of inferior status, [may resort to] the highest [means], such as teaching and the like;
however, a Kṣatriya, with the exception of a king, may resort to [the means] other than receiving gifts. (17)
One may live by means of truth and untruth, or by what is dead and what is half-dead, or even by truth and falsehood; but one should never live by the "dog's mode of life."
Gleaning ears of grain is declared to be *ṛta*; that which is obtained unasked is *amṛta*.
Constant begging is *mṛta*, while agriculture is remembered as *pramṛta*.
A Brahmin and a Kshatriya should always avoid trade involving truth and falsehood, the livelihood of a dog, and service to the low-born— conduct that is held in contempt.
For the Brahmin embodies all the Vedas, and the King embodies all the gods.

Śrīdhara: Demonstrating that the fourfold livelihood previously described for Brahmins applies to others as well, he says: "By the true and the untrue" (18). He explains the verse: "The true" (19). He states the reason for avoiding those two: "Consisting of all the Vedas" (20).
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He permits certain occupations of Brāhmaṇas and Vaiśyas for all [castes] in times of distress; he explains this verse beginning with "By means of truth and untruth" (2.28) in the following half-verse.

He states the reason for excluding those two [the Vaiśya and Śūdra] with the words "all" (sarva). The implication is that, because of this, even by serving low-born persons in times of distress, there is not such a great fault for the Vaiśya and the Śūdra. ||18-20||
— peace, self-control, austerity, purity, contentment, forbearance, and uprightness.
Knowledge, compassion, being the self of Acyuta, and truth are the characteristics of Brahman.
Śrīdhara says: He describes the qualities that manifest the [divine] form through four verses beginning with "śama.
Being the self of Acyuta means having Śrī Viṣṇu as one's supreme goal. (21)
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: He states the characteristics that manifest the phonemes with four verses beginning with "śama":
"the state of having Acyuta as one's self" means having Viṣṇu as the object of one's mind. (21)
Bravery, heroism, fortitude, splendor, renunciation, self-mastery, forgiveness,
devotion to Brahmanas, serenity, and truthfulness are the characteristics of a Kshatriya.
Śrīdhara: *Śaurya* is enthusiasm for battle; *vīrya* is power; *tejas* is boldness; *tyāga* is generosity; and the conquest of one's own mind. ||22||
The *Krama-sandarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon. —
Devotion to the God, the Guru, and Acyuta [Viṣṇu], and the cultivation of the three aims of life (*trivarga*).
Faith, constant exertion, and skillfulness are the characteristics of a Vaiśya.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
The humility, purity, and service toward the master without guile belong to the Śūdra.
For indeed, non-violence, truthfulness, and the protection of cows and Brahmins constitute a sacrifice without mantras.

Śrīdhara: A sacrifice without mantras is the performance of the five sacrifices by means of salutation alone. And so says Yājñavalkya: "One should not omit the five sacrifices by means of the mantra of salutation. (24)
The sequence of composition by Viśvanātha has not been explained.
And for women whose deity is their husband, there is the suitability of service toward him.
Constant devotion toward their kinsmen and the perpetual observance of their vows.
Śrīdhara: He describes the duties of women in five verses beginning with "Of women... Those for whom the husband alone is the deity;

service to that very husband through such acts as massaging his feet; compliance with him, which is the practice of what is beneficial; and the observance—that is, the performance—of whatever vow or rule he has undertaken. This...
The fourfold characteristic and the duty of women devoted to their husbands. ||25||
Kramasandarbha: This has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: He states the characteristics and duties of virtuous women with five verses beginning with "Of women" (strīṇām).
Those for whom the husband alone is the god to be worshipped [are virtuous women]. (25)
By sweeping and smearing [the floor], by decorating the house with various ornaments,
and by always adorning herself, she keeps all her belongings polished.

A virtuous woman should attend upon her husband at the appropriate times with various kinds of sensual pleasures, with humility and self-restraint, with truthful and pleasing words, and with affection.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, the connection of the passage beginning with "by sweeping and smearing" is with the subsequent phrase "she should serve her husband. She is one by whom the household furnishings—the implements for the home—have been polished, that is, rendered spotless by means of rubbing with unguents and so forth. (26)
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
May [those who are] contented, free from greed, skillful, knowers of dharma, and speakers of pleasant truth [be blessed].
Vigilant, pure, and affectionate, she should serve her husband as long as he has not fallen from his status.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, she is content with whatever she obtains; she is not greedy even for such limited enjoyments; she is skillful and diligent; her speech is pleasant and truthful; she is vigilant and attentive in all matters; and she is "unfallen," meaning free from the great sins (*mahāpātaka*). As Yājñavalkya says: "She must be awaited until purification."
For he is defiled by a great sin. ||28||
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
She who would worship her husband with the sentiment of [the Lord] Hari, being devoted to him like Śrī;
With her husband, who is Hari himself, she rejoices in the world of Hari like Śrī.
"The thought among women is that Hari resides in their husband;
likewise, it is always [the thought] of disciples toward their guru, of Śūdras toward Brāhmaṇas and others, and of servants toward their master—thus is the state of being Hari described. (29)

Śrīdhara: Being devoted to that [Lord], she should worship Him, just as Śrī [worships] Hari. The sequential arrangement [of the commentary] together with the husband whose soul is Hari has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: Together with the husband whose soul is Hari. ||29||
The livelihood of those born of mixed castes shall be determined by their respective families;
this applies to those who are not thieves, who are free from sin, and who dwell among the lowest castes.
Śrīdhara: He states the livelihood for those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*) and the direct order (*anuloma*) with the words "the livelihood" (*vṛttiḥ*).

He prohibits theft, violence, and so forth—even if they have been practiced by that particular family and obtained through family tradition—with the phrase "of those who are not thieves and are sinless. This is for the purpose of demonstrating that [tradition].
He mentions certain specific types of those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*): "The *antyaja*s," and so forth.
It is said: "The washerman, the leather-worker, the actor, the *buruḍa*, the fisherman, the *meda*, and the *bhillā*—these seven are remembered as the *antyaja*s."

The dependents, however, are the Cāṇḍālas, Pulkasas, Mātaṅgas, and so forth; the meaning is that their livelihood, consisting of the washing of clothes and other such tasks, has been handed down through tradition. ||30||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He describes the livelihood (*vṛtti*) of those born in the direct order (*anuloma*) and the inverse order (*pratiloma*) with the words "the livelihood. That which is performed by the family is that obtained through family lineage, such as that of barbers, washermen, and so forth.

[The phrase] "shaving, washing clothes, and so forth" [is used]. By the words "of those who are sinless," the absence of sin is stated for those who possess sins such as the drinking of liquor—which has been handed down through family tradition—and the marriage of widows; however, since even for them theft is prohibited, he says "of those who are not thieves."
The sense is that it is only when there is no lack of restraint (*acauratva*) that the conduct prescribed by the family is established and the absence of sin is declared.
To demonstrate this, he mentions certain specific types of *pratiloma* (inverse-caste) births, beginning with "the outcaste" (*antyaja*):
the washerman, the leather-worker, the actor, and the *buruḍa*.
"Fishermen, Medas, and Bhils—these seven are recorded as the Antyajas.
As for the *antevāsins*, they are the Caṇḍālas and others. ||30||
"O King, the dharma ordained by nature for men in each successive age has been remembered by those who perceive the Vedas; it brings about well-being both in this world and after death."

Śrīdhara: He says that even a lowly person’s own duty (svadharma) is better than the duty of another, however excellent that other may be—beginning with the word "prāyaḥ. A duty ordained by one's own nature—that is, by one's innate constitution consisting of *sattva* and so forth—is traditionally held to be the cause of happiness (*śarma*). By whom? By those for whom the Veda alone is the vision, the eye; [and] by the Blessed Lord.
It has been said: "Better is one’s own duty, though devoid of merit, than the duty of another well-performed" (Gītā 3.35). This is the sequence of the context; it has not yet been explained.
Viśvanātha says: Even if inferior, one’s own duty alone is better than even the most excellent duty of another.
He said: "Generally. By those who have seen the Veda—that is, by the knowers of the Veda—it is remembered that [one's own duty] is the cause of happiness (*śarmakṛt*).

And it was stated by the Blessed One: "Better is one's own duty, though devoid of merit, than the duty of another well-performed" (Gītā 3.35). Because of the inclusion of the word "generally," for those of low birth, however, the abandonment of bad conduct does not fail to produce happiness. ||31||
Acting through his own innate disposition while performing his own duties,
he should gradually attain the state beyond the qualities by abandoning actions born of that very disposition.

Śrīdhara: [Objection: Since natural action (*svābhāvika-karman*) is a cause of bondage, how can it be a cause of happiness? To this he says: "By means of its function" (*vṛttyā*). [Commentary on] the sequence of the composition: this has not been explained.

Viśvanātha: [This occurs] gradually, only after many lifetimes. As it has been said: "A man established in his own duty attains the state of Viriñca (Brahmā) after a hundred births," and so forth. ||32||
A field that is repeatedly plowed will itself lose its fertility;
it is no longer fit for sowing, and the seed that is sown perishes.
In this way, O King, a mind whose disposition is toward sensual desires may become dispassionate through excessive indulgence in those very desires, just as fire is extinguished by drops of water.

Śrīdhara: But how can one who performs actions for the sake of desired fruits and is intent on experiencing those results attain freedom from the modes (*nairguṇya*)? This was stated by Prahlāda: "How could one whose delusion is endless, who highly prizes the pleasures of the genitals and the tongue, become dispassionate? (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.6.13), and so forth.

Regarding this, he states the established rule according to the distinction of the qualified aspirant (adhikārin) by means of two verses beginning with "upyamānam" (being sown), along with an illustration.

"Punaḥ sūtyai" means for the sake of further production, that is, for the growth of the crop. That in which desires lie dormant in the form of latent impressions (vāsanā) is [the field]. The intended meaning is as follows: for one who is possessed of intense latent impressions...
Since the sudden renunciation of desire is impossible, one who repeatedly enjoys desires according to the injunctions declared in the Vedas—

possessing a purified mind through the performance of obligatory and occasional rites (*nitya-naimittika*)— gradually develops detachment by perceiving the defects therein, just as in the cases of Yayāti, Saubhari, and others; this occurs with vigor.
A field gradually loses its potency; just as a blazing fire is not extinguished by drops of ghee, but is indeed extinguished by a great flood of ghee, so it is here.
In the hymn composed by Prahlāda, the teaching on renunciation is intended for those whose latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are weak, even while they are still in their youth.

This is by way of qualification. As it has been stated in that very same place: "The ignorant, whose intellects are not corrupted, [are not moved] by activities impelled by the desire for pairs of opposites.
Therefore, everything is beyond reproach. ||33-34||
Kramasandarbha: This has not been explained.

Viśvanātha: However, for those characterized by extremely intense latent impressions (*vāsanā*), since it is impossible to renounce desire through the observances prescribed in the Vedas, [the text refers to] many desires other than those that are prohibited.

He speaks with an illustration in two verses beginning with "upyamānam" (being sown), stating that detachment may arise even for those who enjoy life with straightforward minds, such as Yayāti, Saubhari, and others. He describes their very lack of vigor: "In some places it is not fit for the production of grain for harvest; in some places the seed, once sown, perishes and burns."

That in which desires lie down perfectly in the form of latent impressions (vāsanā) is [the state]; "not like fire" means that just as a blazing fire is not extinguished by drops of ghee, but is indeed extinguished by a great flood of ghee, so it is here. ||33-34||
Whatever characteristic has been declared for a man as indicative of his caste,
even if it should be seen elsewhere, one should designate that person by that very characteristic.

Śrīdhara: He states [in the verse beginning] "of whom... that the primary designation as a Brāhmaṇa and so forth is based solely on tranquility (*śama*) and other such qualities, and not from mere birth (*jāti*). If a certain characteristic were observed even in another caste (*varṇa*), one should designate that other caste by that very characteristic which serves as the defining cause; it should not be designated by the cause of birth.
The meaning. ||35||

*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: Furthermore, for that person whose caste-indicating mark (*varṇa*)—characterized as "malla" (*wrestler*)—manifests his caste (*varṇa*), such as Brāhmaṇa and so forth, that [mark] is indeed prescribed in a general sense.

If tranquility, self-restraint, and so forth—rather than specific prescribed duties such as the recitation of the *sandhyā*—are observed even in another caste, then that other caste should also be designated by the very same terms "Brāhmaṇa" and so on;
this indicates that they are to be accorded the same respect as Brāhmaṇas and others. Furthermore, [this does not mean] the duty of another [caste].

It should be stated that [the verse beginning with] "bhayāvahaḥ" (Gītā 3.35) applies here; the intention is that tranquility, self-restraint, and so forth do not constitute duties pertaining to others. ||35||
Thus ends the eleventh [chapter] of the seventh [skandha], which is well-connected for the virtuous, in the *Harṣiṇī* commentary that reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted.
Thus ends the Seventh Canto in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā, the Pāramahaṃsyam, which is a commentary on the Brahma-sūtras within the glorious Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa.
The eleventh chapter, titled "The Determination of Right Conduct.
Now begins the twelfth chapter.
Regarding the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-dharma),
Śrī Nārada said:
A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī), dwelling in the teacher’s household, should be self-controlled and act for the benefit of his guru.
Behaving like a servant toward his guru, he was firmly established in deep affection for him.
Śrīdhara:
In the twelfth [chapter], the dharma of the student and the forest-dweller is described,
as well as certain [duties] common to all four stages of life (āśramas).
The duties (*dharma*) of the social classes (*varṇa*) and so forth have been stated; now the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama*) are being declared.

In this twelfth chapter, the specific duties of the student (*brahmacārin*) and the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), as well as those common to all four, are set forth. In the thirteenth, the duties of the ascetic (*yati*) are treated; in the fourteenth, those of the householder (*gṛhastha*); and in the fifteenth—

This is a compendium of the essence of all dharmas. The connection with what follows is that one who practices celibacy while living in the teacher’s household should attend upon the teacher and others. ||1||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha:
In the twelfth [chapter], the dharma of the student (brahmacārin) and also that of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) is described.
And likewise, the rule for relinquishing the body is common to all the stages of life.
The connection with what follows is: "A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) should serve his teacher and others. "Brahman" refers to the Gāyatrī. ||1||
Twice a day, at dawn and at dusk, one should worship the Guru, the Fire, the Sun, and the Supreme Deity;
during both twilights, with speech restrained and mind concentrated, one should mutter the sacred syllable *brahman*.

Śrīdhara says: He tells them—"In the evening," etc. One should worship the three junctions (sandhyās) while muttering the Gāyatrī, which is Brahman. Regarding "both junctions," the meaning is that one should observe silence during the evening and morning times for the purpose of the sandhyā rites, remaining restrained in speech. ||2||
The *Krama-sandarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been explained. —
One should study the meters from the teacher, being well-restrained when called upon.
At both the beginning and the end, one should bow with the head to the feet.
Śrīdhara: At the beginning, in the middle, and at the end, one should bow to the feet of the Guru. (3)
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— [He should wear] a girdle, a deer skin, garments, matted hair, a staff, and a water-pot.
And he should wear the sacred thread with darbha grass in his hand, as prescribed.

Śrīdhara: "As stated" means without transgressing the prescribed rules, such as "the staff of a Brāhmaṇa is made of *pālāśa* wood," and so forth. As for the wearing of matted hair (*jaṭā*), it consists merely in the absence of grooming the hair.
Viśvanātha: The sequence of the composition has not been explained.
Twice a day— one in the evening and one in the morning— he should go for alms and present it to his teacher;
he should eat only if permitted, otherwise he should fast at times.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha have not commented [on this].
Kramasandarbha: "If not" means, for instance, when the disciple goes elsewhere from the guru. ||5||
One who is virtuous, moderate in eating, skillful, full of faith, and has conquered his senses,
may engage with women and those conquered by women only for the sake of necessity.
Śrīdhara: [It means] only as much as is required, according to necessity. ||6||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: For as long as necessary for the purpose of serving the guru, one should remain in the guru’s house; and for the purpose of begging alms, one should go to the houses of householders only as required. ||6||
One who has not taken up household life and observes the great vows should avoid verses concerning women;
for the turbulent senses carry away the mind even of an ascetic.

Śrīdhara: One who observes the great vow, being a celibate student (brahmacārī) distinct from a householder, should avoid songs concerning women. The reason for this is that the senses are powerful and captivate the mind even of one who is self-restrained. (7)
Kramasandarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: One who is not a householder—that is, distinct from a householder—is every celibate student (*brahmacārī*) under the great vow.
A young man should have his hair dressed, massaged, bathed, anointed, and so forth performed for him by the young wives of his teacher.
Śrīdhara: Not commented upon.

Viśvanātha: Regarding the word "kārayet" (should cause to do): for the wives of the Guru look upon even their disciple with affection as if he were their own son; thus, if they perform tasks such as arranging his hair according to their own will, then—
The meaning is that one should not even cause [it] to be done. ||8||
Indeed, fire is what is called a woman, and a man is like a jar of clarified butter;
even toward his own daughter, he would abandon her in secret at any time when it serves his purpose.

Śrīdhara: The reason why one should not cause [her] to do so is stated with the words "Now then" (*nanv*). "In private" (*raha*) means in a secluded place. "At other times" (*anyadā*) means on occasions other than those for adorning the hair and so forth, or at times when there is no such seclusion. She should perform that which has been prescribed to the full extent of its purpose. ||9||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: The reason for this is—"Now, [the word] *agni*... *Rahaḥ* means in secret, in a secluded place. *Anyadā* means at other times; even elsewhere, when not in seclusion, it serves its purpose (*yāvad-artha-kṛt*) to the extent that its presence serves a specific aim.
The meaning is that one should maintain stability for exactly as long as it takes for [the state] to be accomplished. ||9||
As long as the Lord, having himself imagined this appearance,
does not cease from duality, so long indeed does his state of perversion persist.
Through the multiplicity of objects alone, the knowledge of things as they truly are is expressed;
this is called "knowledge of non-duality," whereas the knowledge of duality is otherwise.
"As the cognition is, so is the object; as the object is, so is the cognition.
There is no difference whatsoever between cognition and its object; therefore, there is the experience of their unity. Thus [it is said]. (10)

Śrīdhara: Now, since women and the like are false and extremely base, they are almost abandoned of their own accord; so what is this excessive insistence on renouncing them? To this he says: "Having conceptualized" (kalpayitvā). Having conceptualized—that is, having ascertained through the direct realization of one's own nature (ātman)—that this [world] is merely an appearance consisting of the body, senses, and so forth.

As long as this living soul (jīva) is not the independent Lord (īśvara), so long will duality—the distinction such as "this is a man" and "this is a woman"—not cease. What follows from that? To this he says: "From that duality, indeed, arises the opposite: the notion of being an object of enjoyment through the superimposition of the qualities (guṇa-adhyāsa). Therefore, the meaning is that one must certainly abandon it. ||10||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Now, one might ask: "Can young women possibly cause harm to a man of knowledge who has abandoned pride and conquered his senses? To this he replies: "Having imagined... Even though the Lord is capable of knowledge...

This [notion] of identification with the body, bodily functions, and sense objects—though appearing as a mere semblance according to the principle of "subsistence after sublation" (bādhitānuvṛtti-nyāya)—is rendered powerless by the knowledge of reality (tattva-jñāna) and remains as a mere name; yet, as long as it persists along with the mind (manas), duality remains: "I am a man," "this is a woman," and so forth.
The notion of duality, "This is dear to me," would not cease; and from that, as before, there would be perversion and the recurrence of saṃsāra.
Or rather, for one who has conquered the senses and abandoned the circle of kinsmen such as sons and sisters, what [need is there for this]?

"Is there fear from this? To that he says: "Having imagined... That by which worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is validated—that is, the appearance of relations such as "this is my sister," "this is my mother," "this is my son," and so forth—is imagined;
and one is ruled (*īśita*) by the Lord through the pleasure arising from the affection produced by those [relations].
Duality, which has that as its authority, would not cease; that is, difference would not cease.

[Objection: "But surely, because this [duality] is slight and because it is imagined, there is no cause for concern? To this he says: "For from that... (tato hi), according to the Gauḍīya Bhāṣya: "As long as this individual soul (*jīva*) has not, by means of the Self—that is, through the direct realization of its own true nature—"

As long as the Lord, though independent, determines the body, senses, and so forth—which are mere appearances—to be real appearances, duality persists; the distinction such as "I am a man" or "this is a woman" does not cease.
For from that perception of duality, this person undergoes perversion: through the superimposition of the qualities (guṇas), he develops the notion of being an object of enjoyment.
Therefore, the meaning is that one should indeed abandon it. ||10||
all this has been prescribed for the householder and also for the ascetic; however, the conduct toward the teacher is optional for the householder who approaches his wife during her season.
And it is said that, in accordance with the command of the Guru, a Madhva may become a householder even while remaining at a distance. ||11||
Śrīdhara: All of this has been stated [in the verse] beginning with "suśīla. He states the specific rule for the householder: "The conduct toward the guru" (verse 11).
The sequence of composition: "the conduct of a guru" means following after the guru. ||11||

Viśvanātha: All this has been stated [in the verse beginning] with "one of good character" (*suśīla*). The meaning is that [the practice] may be performed or not performed according to one's choice (*vikalpena*). ||11||

Gauḍīya-bhāṣya: All this, beginning with good character (*suśīlatva*) and so forth, is traditionally taught for both the householder and the ascetic (*yati*), and is described as being to be practiced. For the householder who approaches his wife only during her fertile period (*ṛtu*), in accordance with scriptural injunctions such as "one should approach one's wife during her season," he [attains these qualities].

The conduct toward the guru (*guru-vṛtti*) means that the conduct toward the guru is "heavy" (*gurvī*), which signifies celibacy (*brahmacarya*). The following of the guru is to be understood as optional; the meaning is that it need not exist with one's wife during her fertile period (*ṛtu-kāla*), but may exist at other times. ||11||
Those who observe the great vow (bṛhad-vrata) should renounce collyrium, ointments, massage, women, the pretext of writing, honey, garlands, perfumes, unguents, and ornaments.
Śrīdhara: [The compound] from *añjana* (collyrium) up to *āmiṣa* (meat) is a dvandva-samāsa treated as a singular. *Añjana* refers to [the application of] collyrium to the body;

*abhyañjana* refers to [the application of] oil to the head. *Strīm* and *avalekhām*: painting (*citra-karma*), which is either the drawing of women on walls and so forth, or the gazing upon such [drawings]. Here, the actual practice of anointing and so forth is prohibited by its very nature.
However, the distinction is that previously, even if it were somehow obtained in times of distress, anointing performed by a woman was prohibited; this is the sequence of the arrangement.

This should be considered in the commentary on the word "añjana," because of the specific qualification "by means of an ointment" (*abhyañjanena*), which implies that [anointing] performed by a woman is prohibited. ||12||
Viśvanātha: "Anjanam" refers to the anointing of the body, the head, and women; "avalekhām" refers to the art of painting.

Here, the application of ointments and so forth is prohibited by their very nature; however, the distinction is that previously, even if such acts occurred somehow during an emergency, those performed by women were prohibited. ||12||

Having thus resided in the teacher's family, the twice-born man, having studied and understood the triple Veda along with its auxiliary sciences and Upanishads, according to his capacity and for the sake of their true meaning;

Śrīdhara: Having studied the three Vedas together with their auxiliary sciences such as phonetics and the Upaniṣads, and having understood them and reflected upon their meaning—as far as necessary according to one's own qualification—[he should act]. (13)
The sequence of composition: "Having dwelt," etc., is a pair of verses (yugmaka). ||13||
Viśvanātha: Not explained. —o)0(o— If the Lord, having granted the boon, was permitted by the Guru to fulfill his desire;
One may enter either a house or a forest, or one may renounce the world and dwell therein.

Śrīdhara: If the Lord is capable, then, having granted the desired boon to the Guru, he should either enter the stage of life (āśrama) such as that of a householder according to his qualification, or renounce the world, or remain right there as a lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika); this is the meaning. ||14||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: If the Lord is capable [of bestowing grace], then, having granted the desired boon requested by the Guru, he may enter the household; the meaning is that he may become a householder. Or, he may dwell in that very place.
One should be a perpetual follower of the Buddha-moon. ||14||
In the fire, in the guru, in oneself, and in all beings,
one should perceive Adhokṣaja as being both unentered and yet entered by means of the elements and their respective abodes.
"Madhva is both unentered, being all-pervading, and entered, being possessed of a corresponding form;
thus the Lord Hari, the sole Janārdana, is of two forms. (15)

Śrīdhara: Together with the living beings (jīvas) who are his own abodes (sva-dhāmabhiḥ), that is, those who have him as their support; [this is] by way of being their controller. Viśvanātha: Together with the living beings who are his own abodes, that is, those who have him as their support; [this is] by way of being their controller. ||15||
A celibate student, a forest-dweller, an ascetic, or a householder who practices in this manner and possesses realized knowledge attains the supreme Brahman.

Śrīdhara: "Practicing thus" means acting in this manner. "That by which [the sequence] is known"—that is, the arrangement of the stages (*krama-sandarbha*) through which that which is to be known is understood.
Viśvanātha: This has not been explained.
I shall now describe the rules for the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) as approved by the sages,
by adhering to which a sage may go swiftly to the world of the ṛṣis.
Śrīdhara: [He goes to] the world of the Ṛṣis and the world of the Mahars. ||17||
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon. —o)0(o— One should not eat what ripens in unplowed land, nor that which is unplowed, nor [food] out of season.
One may bring forth food cooked by fire, or raw, or even ripened by the sun.

Śrīdhara: "Akṛṣṭa" means that which grows without being ploughed. "From the wrong time" (akālataḥ) means produced even before the proper time for ripening. "Ripened by the sun" refers to fruits and the like. "Should take" (āharet) means he should eat. ||18||
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: "Akālataḥ" means that which is already ripe even before the time for ripening [pāka-kālāt]. ||18||
One should offer sacrificial oblations of cooked rice and cakes made from wild grains as prompted by the season;
whenever fresh food is obtained, one should discard the old.
Śrīdhara: With wild grains such as *nīvāra* and the like, he should prepare the *caru* and *puroḍāśa* offerings; these are the obligatory rites prompted by the [proper] time.
"Ancient" means previously stored. ||19||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: One should offer—that is, give—with wild grains such as *nīvāra* and the like; those prescribed for the [proper] time. 0)0(0)
For the sake of fire alone, he should take refuge in a shelter, a leaf-hut, or a mountain cave;
himself enduring cold, wind, fire, rain, the sun’s heat, and hunger.
Śrīdhara: [He is] so called because he endures snow and other such things. ||20||
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: He is so called because he endures snow and other such things. ||20||
Wearing matted hair and bearing the impurities of his hair, body hair, nails, and beard,
he possessed the equipment of a water-pot, a deerskin, a staff, bark garments, and fire.
Śrīdhara: Wearing hair and so forth, as well as dirt, without washing them; and carrying a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) and other such items. ||21||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: Impurities arising from not cleaning the teeth and so forth. ||21||
The sage should dwell in the forest for twelve years, eight, four,
two, or even one year, so that his intellect does not fail him through hardship.
Śrīdhara: One should follow the sequence of the text in such a way that the intellect does not perish due to the hardship and suffering of *kṛcchra* penance; Viśvanātha: this has not been explained.
When one’s lifespan is exhausted by diseases or old age during the performance of one’s own duties,
or in the pursuit of the science of inquiry (ānvīkṣikī), one may undertake fasting and other such practices.

Śrīdhara: Even after the twelve years and so forth have passed, if one is capable of performing one's own duties, then one should dwell in the forest alone; but if one is fit for the practice of knowledge, then one should renounce—this he will state in the subsequent chapter. However, as for that which is the duty of one who is devoid of both [these conditions], that...
He said: "When one is unskilled and incapable in the science of logic (*ānvīkṣikī*) and in the practice of knowledge. (23)

Krama-sandarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: When, even in the midst of [the period of] twelve years and so forth, he is *akalpa*, meaning incapable, regarding *ānvīkṣikī*, that is, in the practice of knowledge. ||23||
Having internalized the fires within the self and renounced the sense of "I" and "mine," one should properly dissolve the aggregate into its constituent causes as is appropriate.
And Madhva says: "Dissolution is merely the knowledge that the effect has merged into its cause. (24)

Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha: He states the preliminary duties for one who is about to perform fasting and other such practices, beginning with "ātmani" and continuing until the end of the verse. "Yathārthataḥ" means according to what is appropriate. "In their own causes," namely in ether and the other elements; he should "place" the aggregate, that is, the body, meaning he should dissolve it [into them]. ||24||
The sequence of composition has not been explained.—
The self-possessed one [should place] the apertures in the ether, the breaths in the wind, and the subtle heat of fire in the self.
Blood, phlegm, and pus go into the waters; the remainder goes into the earth, according to its origin.

Śrīdhara: He shows that very point by dividing it: "In the sky" means in the ether; "its own" refers to the apertures situated in the body. "Possessing self" means possessing intelligence. "The rest" refers to the hard parts such as bone, flesh, and so forth. (25)
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "The apertures" (*khāni*) refers to the cavities of the body. The connection of all these [terms] is with the word "one should cause to enter" (*abhiniveśayet*), which follows immediately after. "The remainder" (*śeṣam*) refers to the hard portions such as bone, flesh, and so forth. (25)
One should offer speech that is to be spoken into Agni, craftsmanship into Indra,
the feet into Gati, the generative organ into Vaya, and the womb into Prajāpati.
One should assign the anus and the organ of excretion to death according to their respective locations;
the ears along with sound to the directions, and the skin to touch within the self.
O King, one should dissolve forms into the eye within light; the tongue into the waters by means of consciousness; and the sense of smell into the earth by means of odors.

Śrīdhara: Having thus described the dissolution of the gross body, he now describes the dissolution of the triad beginning with the "internal" (adhyātma), which consists of the subtle body (liṅga-śarīra), by means of the passage beginning with "Speech. In that regard, although it would be more logical for dissolution to occur according to the order of origination, [he nevertheless places them] in their respective causes among the internal and so forth.

Although dissolution (laya) should be spoken of in relation to the rājasa ego-sense and so forth, nevertheless, here this contemplation of their dissolution is intended for the realization of the non-dual Self; thus, since the deities are primary as the activators [of the senses], the dissolution of the senses and their objects is described as occurring within those deities, regardless of how that dissolution might otherwise be contemplated.
One should place speech, together with that which is to be spoken, into the fire; thus it is everywhere. The words are the feet.
In the age [of Kali], Viṣṇu. ||26||
Together with the sound of resonance (*sanāda*). Within the internal wind (*vāyu*). If the reading is *adhyātmavid*, it should be understood as "within the wind. ||27||

Regarding light, it is the sun. However, because taste and smell are intended to be emphasized as the attractors of the senses and so forth, he describes the dissolution of the sense organs together with their presiding deities into their objects:
the tongue, which is the organ of taste, dissolves into the waters that consist of taste, along with Pracetas; and by the word "nose," the two Aśvins are also included.

This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). The meaning is: on the earth, which is characterized by the sense of smell together with the two Aśvins and by the odors to be smelled (*ghreya*). ||28||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Having described the dissolution of the gross body (*sthūla-śarīra*), he speaks of the dissolution of the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*) with the words "Speech" (*vācam*).
In that context, since the senses and their objects are impelled by them, [the senses] are here [dissolved] into the deities themselves.
Laya has been explained; [it occurs] in Viṣṇu during the age. ||26||
One should point out each respective place by touching it without overstepping its proper location.

First, one should employ the speech: "I dissolve this [speech] into the fire. Then, one should cause it to enter; such is the sequence. That wise one, together with the *nāda*—this is the meaning—is within the internal wind and the light, which is the sun.

The mind (*cetas*) is excellent (*pra-kṛṣṭa*) where it resides; that is *precetā*, namely the sweet and other tastes. Together with that, the tongue dissolves into the waters, in Varuṇa, the presiding deity of water. Together with various fragrances to be smelled (*ghreya*), the sense of smell dissolves into the earth—so called because things dissolve (*kṣīyate*) and merge (*līyate*) therein—the presiding deity of which is the two Aśvins.
This is the meaning. ||27-28||

The mind [is dissolved] in the moon by means of mental desires; the intellect in the supreme poet (Brahmā) by means of the objects of awakening; actions in Rudra by means of the inner self—that which consists of the activities of "I" and "mine."
By means of *sattva*, the mind [is established] in the Knower of the Field; by means of the qualities (*guṇas*), it is modified in the Supreme.
"Madhva is the supreme seer, Bṛhaspati.

And: "Having dissolved the mind into Hiraṇyagarbha, who is the Supreme Self, the wise man should dissolve even the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) into that, and thereafter remember nothing else. (29)

Śrīdhara [comments]: "In the supreme poet, Brahman. "By means of the inner self" (*adhyātmanā*) means by means of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*). In the reading *adhyātmatām*, the meaning is "the actions and the ego-sense. In what kind of Rudra? In him from whom action arises preceded by the notions of "I" and "mine. By means of goodness (*sattva*), that is, by consciousness (*cetanā*), and by the qualities (*guṇaiḥ*).

Together with the gods who remained from before by virtue of their qualities and functions; or else, by means of the qualities such as *sattva* which serve as causes, [he merges] the *kṣetrajña*—which possesses modifications such as the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*)—into the supreme, changeless Brahman. ||29||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: By "objects of desire" (*manorathaiḥ*) are meant objects of thought; by "objects of cognition" (*bodhyaiḥ*) are meant objects of the intellect. "In the Supreme Poet" means in Brahman. "With the inner self" (*adhyātmanā*) means together with the ego (*ahaṅkāra*). "Actions" refers to those [actions] which have that [Brahman] as their object.

In Rudra, because action is preceded by the notions of "I" and "mine"; in that Rudra; in Vāsudeva, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) and the presiding deity of the mind, along with goodness (sattva) and consciousness (cetanā);
because of the absence of being an effect of the [material] qualities (guṇas), meaning by those other than them; the individual soul (jīva), which is transformative (vaikārika), in the Supreme.
In Brahman. ||29||
—o)0(o— In the waters is the earth; the waters are in light; that [light] is in the wind; the wind is in the sky;
that [sky] is in the immutable peak (Kūṭastha); that is in the Great One (Mahat); and that is in the Unmanifest (Avyakta) and the Imperishable (Akṣara).
Śrīdhara: But how can there be a dissolution of that which possesses modification into the Supreme, which is changeless?

He says "in the waters," etc., [meaning] by way of the dissolution of all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), which are the causes of modification. This light is the ether (*nabhas*); and that [ether] dissolves into the immutable principle of "I" (*ahaṃ-tattva*). And that immutable [principle] dissolves into the Great (*mahat*), the principle of the Great (*mahat-tattva*).
That [is merged] in the unmanifest Pradhāna; and that unmanifest [is merged] in the Imperishable Supreme Self. ||30||

Kramasandarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: Now, one might ask: how can that [state] be the knowledge of non-dual Brahman, given that the collective principles (samaṣṭi-tattva), such as earth and the rest, continue to exist? If this is asked, [the answer is that] even of those...

He says "in the waters" etc., meaning that this occurs only for one who knows the origin and dissolution [of things] as they arise: "This light," "this wind," and "that ether" dissolve into the immutable ego (ahaṅkāra); that immutable [ego] dissolves into the Great (mahat), the principle of Mahat; that dissolves into the Unmanifest (avyakta), the Pradhāna; and that dissolves into the Imperishable (akṣara), the Supreme Self. ||30||
" Having thus known the Self as pure consciousness alone, remaining as the imperishable syllable, one who has become non-dual should then desist, like a fire whose fuel has been consumed.

Madhva [says]: "The Self is the Supreme Self, non-dual; therefore, anything other than that is devoid of memory. 'Like fire whose fuel is burnt'—this refers merely to the absence of duty (kṛtya). And: 'For one who remembers Hari, there is no duty remaining, like a fire whose wood has been consumed. ||31||

Śrīdhara: Thus, because of the dissolution of all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), having known the Self—the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*)—as the pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) that remains without residue and as the Imperishable (*akṣara*), one should cease [from worldly activity] while being non-dual, like a fire whose wood has been consumed. ||31||
The sequence of composition by Viśvanātha has not been explained.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter of the *Sārārthadarśinī*, the *Harṣiṇī*, which is well-suited for the hearts of devotees and perfectly appropriate for the virtuous.
Thus ends the Seventh Canto in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā, the Pāramahaṃsyam, within the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, which is a commentary on the Brahma-sūtras.
The twelfth chapter, titled "The Duties of the Stages of Life" (Āśrama-dharma).
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.
Regarding the duty of the ascetic, Śrī Nārada said:
Thus, having renounced the world, one remains with only the body as a remnant.
He should wander the earth without attachment, according to the rule of staying only one night in a village.
Śrīdhara:
In the thirteenth [chapter], the great dharma of the practitioner who is a renunciant is declared;
and by means of the history of Avadhūta, the state of perfection is described.

Having meditated thus, one who is free from ritual action (*akalpa*) should practice fasting and so forth. The connection is that one who possesses ritual action (*kalpa*) in the science of inquiry (*ānvīkṣikī*) should likewise renounce the world after such meditation. What is to be abandoned here? He says: "only the body," meaning everything other than the body. He states its attributes in nine verses beginning with "staying one night in a village" (*grāma-ekarātra*). ||1||
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha:
In the thirteenth [chapter], the duty of the ascetic (yati) and his supreme state of "serpentine" (ājagarī) conduct.
This is described precisely through the dialogue between Daśa and Avadhūta Prahlāda.

Having meditated thus, if one is without ritual rules (*akalpa*), one may practice fasting and so forth. However, if one possesses the rules (*kalpa*) regarding *ānvīkṣikī*, the connection is that, having meditated thus and having renounced the world, one should practice;
he states its duties in nine verses beginning with "one night in a village" (*grāmaikarātra*).
If he should wear clothing at all, it should be nothing more than a loincloth;
except in times of distress, he must not discard the insignia of his order, such as the staff and so forth, nor possess anything else.

Śrīdhara: A loincloth (*kaupīna*) is merely that much [of cloth] by which the private parts are covered; or it may mean simply something else. It has been discarded even before the utterance of the *praṇava*. ||2||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: He should not maintain contact with worldly people that has been abandoned;

nor should he maintain anything other than the sectarian marks (*liṅga*), the staff (*daṇḍa*), and so forth—even other objects. "Except in times of distress" means that in times of distress, however, [he may keep them] for the sake of protecting the body.
One should maintain even that which has been renounced. ||2||
A monk should wander alone, delighting in the self, without dependence on others,
a friend to all beings, peaceful, and devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
One should perceive this entire universe within the Self— the supreme, immutable reality that transcends both being and non-being.
And the Self as the Supreme Brahman, present everywhere within the nature of both being and non-being.
Of the honey: in the Self, that is, in the Supreme Self. ||4||
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha: [He is] beyond both the existent and the non-existent, distinct from both effect and cause. ||4||
The sequence of composition has not been explained. —
The seer of the Self [perceives] the movement of the Self during the transition between sleep and awakening.
Seeing both bondage and liberation as mere illusion and not as real entities.

Śrīdhara: But how can there be a grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) such as "the self is the supreme Brahman," given that identity between the bound and the liberated is not possible? To this he says: "In deep sleep...
For in deep sleep, the reality of the self is veiled by darkness, whereas in waking and dreaming it appears as distracted. [This occurs] at the junction.

But there is neither darkness nor distraction. Therefore, at that time, being established by taking the vision of the Self as his object, he perceives the course—the reality—of the Self. For this very reason, perceiving both bondage and liberation as mere illusion (*māyāmātra*), he should perceive the Self as the Supreme Brahman everywhere; such is the syntactical connection. Thus it has been said:
In the Yoga-śāstra: "That state which arises at the beginning of sleep and at the end of waking—one who constantly contemplates that state is liberated, and no other ascetic. (5)
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: For in deep sleep (*supte*), the reality of the Self (*ātma-tattva*) is shrouded by darkness; in the waking and dreaming states, however, it appears as distracted (*vikṣipta*). But in the transition (*sandhi*), there is neither darkness nor distraction. Therefore, at that time—
The construction of the sentence is as follows: one who perceives the Self—that is, remaining with the Self as the focal point—perceives the course of the Self, which is its true reality;

and for that very reason, perceiving both bondage and liberation to be mere illusion (māyā-mātra), one should perceive the Self as the Supreme Brahman everywhere. This has been stated in a Yoga treatise:
"The state that arises at the beginning of sleep and at the end of waking—by constantly meditating upon that state, one is liberated; no other ascetic is. (5)
One should not rejoice in certain death nor in one's uncertain life;
one should await the supreme time, which is the source and the dissolution of all beings.
Śrīdhara: [He refers to] that Time from which there is the origin and the dissolution of this body. ||6||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Of this body. ||6||
One should not become attached to false scriptures, nor should one make one's livelihood dependent upon them;
one should abandon contentious debates and logical speculations, and should not rely upon any partisan position whatsoever.
One should not resort to the position of being purposeless;
one should not be one who holds a purposeless position, nor should one pointlessly bind disciples.
One should not remain indifferent toward the scriptures, nor should one study those that are contradictory.
"One should not live off the exposition [of scriptures], nor should one perform prohibited acts;
being thus, the ascetic who has Hari as his sole refuge goes to Him. Thus ends the section on Conduct (Samācāra). 7–8.

Śrīdhara: He does not resort with persistence to false scriptures that do not have the Self as their goal, nor to a livelihood such as the science of astrology and the like, nor to mere wrangling consisting of cavil and vituperation, nor to any partisan position whatsoever. (7)
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: Furthermore, one should not resort to any partisan position whatsoever. ||7||
One should not bind oneself to disciples, nor should one study many books;
one should not employ elaborate explanations, nor should one ever undertake new undertakings.

Śrīdhara: Do not bind the disciples through such means as enticement, nor force them by compulsion; [abandon] undertakings, which are activities such as the management of monasteries and the like. ||8||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "One should not persist" means one should not force [the disciple] through enticement and the like;
"undertakings" refers to activities such as the construction of monasteries (*maṭha*) and so forth. (8)
For a high-souled ascetic who is tranquil and even-minded, the stage of life is generally not the cause of his righteousness; he may either maintain it or abandon it.

Śrīdhara says: He states the specific distinction of the *paramahaṃsa*: "The stage of life (*āśrama*) of the ascetic (*yati*) is not for the sake of religious duty (*dharma*). Of what kind of ascetic? Of the "great-souled one" (*mahātman*). His characteristic is described by the words "of the peaceful one," and so forth. The meaning of the word "mostly" (*prāyaḥ*) is this: until the arising of knowledge, one may rely upon the emblems (*liṅga*) such as those of the *bahūdaka* and others.
One should strive for the arising of knowledge while practicing the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) for the sake of purifying the mind.

But once knowledge has arisen, there is no further need for observances; the restraints will follow spontaneously. Therefore, at that time, since there is no purpose for external signs and the like, one may either maintain them or abandon them for the sake of winning over the world.
Or so it is said. ||9||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: He states the distinction of the *paramahaṃsa* among renunciants (*sannyāsins*) with the words "of the ascetic" (*yateḥ*).
For the ascetic, the stage of life (*āśrama*) is not for the purpose of religious duty (*dharma*); its characteristic is "of one who is peaceful," and so forth. Generally...

By this [statement], it is meant that someone whose knowledge is in some way still unripened may practice the duties of *yama* and *niyama* for the sake of purifying the being; however, once knowledge has reached maturity, there is no further need for these observances (*niyama*), as the *yamas* will arise spontaneously. Therefore, at that time, there is no purpose in [using] external marks (*liṅga*) and so forth.
One should either maintain [the practice] or abandon it for the sake of gathering the world. ||9||
With unmanifested signs yet manifest purpose, wise like one who is mad or a child,
and like a mute, that sage should show himself to men through his very vision.
Śrīdhara: In order to prevent the loss of yoga due to the absence of firmness in that very knowledge, he says:

He whose external mark (*liṅga*) is not manifest, whose manifest purpose is the self-investigation (*ātmanusandhāna*), though he is wise, acts like one insane or a child; and though he is a poet, he keeps himself hidden from men like a mute.
One should show [the practice] through one's own vision. One should behave in such a way that they might perceive it as being like the form of a madman or the like.
In the reading *svadṛṣṭyā*, the meaning is "by means of the absence of external reference. ||10||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: And he says that such a person should be one who has avoided the fall from yoga—meaning one for whom there is no outwardly manifest sign (*liṅga*), and whose purpose (*artha*) is manifest.
He is one who possesses the continuous contemplation of the Self. ||10||
In this regard, they also cite this ancient history,
the conversation between Prahrāda and the sage who followed the way of the python.

Śrīdhara: He clarifies the very dharma of the paramahaṃsa through a historical narrative—from "atrāpi" up to the end of the chapter. [This concerns] the sage who observes the vow of the python (ajagara-vrata). ||11||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Of one who is like a python, whose conduct is that of a non-waker. ||11||
Him, lying upon the lap of the earth on the ridges of the Sahya mountain by the Kāverī,
his stainless splendor concealed by the dust-covered parts of his body.
Desiring to know the true nature of the worlds,
Prahlāda, the beloved of the Blessed One, wandered through the worlds surrounded by a few ministers and beheld them.

Śrīdhara: On the lap of the Earth—that is, on the surface of the earth; on the slope of the Sahya mountain. He is one whose stainless splendor is concealed by the dusty regions of his body—that is, by the parts of his frame. ||12||
The sequence of composition: the pair of verses beginning with "taṃ śayānam"; however, in the place of "tanū," the reading "aṅga" occurs in many places. 12.
Viśvanātha: On the ridge of the mountain named Sahya; by means of the body-regions—that is, the minor limbs—or by actions, forms, speech, marks, and [social status such as] caste and stage of life.
People do not know him as "this is he," nor do they know him as "it is not."
Having bowed to him and worshipped him according to the prescribed rites, the great devotee of the Lord, that asura, touched his feet with his head and, desiring to know this, questioned him.
Śrīdhara: The connection with the subsequent verse is as follows: having bowed his head to the feet of Him whom people do not know through actions and the like, he questioned Him. ||14||
The sequence of composition: the pair beginning with "by action" (karmaṇā). ||14||
Viśvanātha: "The people" refers even to those residing in his birthplace; "desirous of knowing" means wishing to understand him.

The phrase "a great devotee" (mahā-bhāgavata) implies that by the very sign of his ability to captivate his own mind—precisely because he was a great devotee—they recognized him as a person of exalted nature (mahānubhāva); this is the intended meaning. ||14-15||
"You bear a fat body like one who is industrious and wealthy;
for in this world, wealth belongs to those who exert effort, and enjoyment belongs to those who possess wealth."
Indeed, the body of those who enjoy pleasures becomes stout, and not otherwise.

Śrīdhara: [The connection with the third verse is as follows: "You bear a body that is stout and corpulent, as if possessed of exertion and as if possessed of enjoyment. To this he says, "Tell the reason for that"—and if it is argued, "I have enjoyment even without exertion," he replies, "And wealth... (verse 16).
The sequence of composition: "bibharṣi" constitutes half a verse. ||16||

Viśvanātha: "Fat" means thick or corpulent. Nor should it be said that my body is fat by its very nature; thus he says: "The wealth of those who exert effort, the enjoyment of those who possess wealth, and the corpulent body of those who possess enjoyment"—the meaning is that effort alone is the primary cause of corpulence, and not nature.
"O Brahmin, what purpose is there for you who lie down and make no effort, since enjoyment arises from that very [effort]?"
O Brahmin, this body of yours is fat despite being without enjoyment; tell us the reason for that, if it is not too much trouble.

Śrīdhara: *nu* signifies certainty; *ha* signifies what is well-known. The meaning is that it is indeed well known that there is no purpose for you. *Yato'rthāt* means "for this very reason"; *yataḥ* means "because of which [reason]"; *pīvā* means "fat"; *kṣamam* means "suitable" or "fitting.

*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: Now, one might object: "Just as in the case of the statement 'Fat Devadatta does not eat during the day,' my efforts and so forth should be conciliated. To this, he says: "No" (*na*). "Indeed" (*nu*) signifies certainty. "Ha" is for clarity. "O Brahmin" (*he vipra*)... [text continues].
For the status of being a Brahmin is understood through the very splendor of Brahman. ||18||
A poet, capable, keen-sighted, fond of varied and pleasant stories, and equanimous;
he either remains while the world performs its work, or he watches it.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, he says: "Even this person, though incapable of acquiring wealth and the like, exerts himself for that purpose; yet you, though capable, why do you not do so? He is a poet (*kavi*), learned (*vidvān*).

He is capable (*kalpa*) and dexterous (*dakṣa*). He is one of subtle vision (*nipuṇa-dṛk*) and clever (*catura*). His stories (*kathāḥ*) are dear to the heart (*cittāḥ*), beloved (*priyāḥ*), and pleasing to the world (*loka-rañjanāḥ*).

Nevertheless, while the world is engaged in performing its actions, you remain at rest; even though you behold all that—that is, even though you see it all—in another reading, the meaning is that you neither loathe that action, nor do you desire it, nor do you praise it. ||19||

Regarding the sequence of the composition: in the phrase "tad-vīkṣitāpi," the reading is "na dvekṣe na uṣi" (I do not hate nor do I burn), while the Gauḍa reading is "na dveṣī" (I am not one who hates). ||19||

Viśvanātha: If you ask, "What is the use of such deliberation for you? [the author] replies with the word "poet" (*kavi*), saying that by observing the auspicious marks on your body according to the *Sāmudrika* treatise, he infers your poetic genius and other qualities; thus, desiring someone who is like the nectar of the lips (*ālopāmṛta*) so that you may fulfill your purpose, he says: "A poet," while performing his work.
Disregarding the world that is intent on the exertion of action, do you lie upon your remaining bed either without seeing it at all, or out of curiosity, looking at it as you gaze upon it? (19)
Śrī Nārada said:
Thus questioned by the lord of the Daityas, the great sage—
Smiling and constrained by the nectar of his words, he spoke to him.
Śrīdhara: His speech alone was nectar; being constrained and brought under control by that, he spoke. ||20||
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon. —o)0(o— The venerable Brāhmaṇa said:
O best of Asuras, you are indeed esteemed by the noble;
therefore, behold with the eye of inner self these stages of activity and cessation.

Śrīdhara: You surely know this by means of the inner vision of the self (adhyātma-cakṣus). Indeed, you are esteemed by the noble ones, the wise. He states that very thing which was referred to as "this": namely, the "steps"—meaning the stages or fruits—of these two, desire and its cessation, or engagement and withdrawal. ||21||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: You already know this through the internal vision of the spiritual eye (*adhyātma-cakṣus*). What is the meaning? It refers to the stages, positions, or fruits of activity (*īhā*) and cessation (*uparama*), which correspond to being with desire (*sakāmatva*) and being free from desire (*niṣkāmatva*).
The sense is: "If I had not known the suffering of those people who nourish their bodies through exertions for the sake of enjoyment, then I too would have undertaken such exertion. (21)
He in whose heart the blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa is ever present,
by means of exclusive devotion, shakes off ignorance just as the sun dispels darkness.
Śrīdhara: The reason for [the statement] "one knows" is given by the words "of whom. Having entered the heart, he shakes off ignorance, just as the sun dispels darkness from the outside. ||22||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: The reason for [the statement] "he knows" (*veda*) is given by the words "of whom" (*yasya*). [He knows] by means of that which is "pure" (*kevalayā*), meaning unmixed with knowledge, action, and so forth.

〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇〇
Nevertheless, O King, we shall answer your questions according to what we have heard;
for you are worthy of being addressed by one who desires purity of soul.
Śrīdhara: "As I have heard" was said in order to avoid arrogance. ||23||
Kramasandarbha: This has not been explained.

Viśvanātha: Therefore, since you are indeed worthy of my respect, he says "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*), meaning that although you are silent everywhere, disregarding your silence, I shall speak to you. Even though you already know this...
"Moreover, [it is] 'as it was heard' (yathā-śruta), but not fabricated from one's own imagination (svakapola-kalpita). ||23||
Driven by craving that carries one through existence and remains unfulfilled despite appropriate desires,
I was made to perform actions and was joined to various wombs.

Śrīdhara: Regarding what was said—"The world engages in actions, but you, being withdrawn from them, why do you lie still?"—he replies with these four verses beginning with "By thirst" (tṛṣṇayā). Previously, I was impelled toward actions by that thirst which causes the flow of worldly existence and which cannot be satisfied even by objects appropriate to one's station.
He has been cast into various wombs. ||24||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "Listen to the reason why I am devoid of effort," he says with three verses beginning with "By thirst" (*tṛṣṇayā*). Just as at the end of a river connected to worldly existence (*bhava*), [the goal] is difficult to attain.

And also because of craving. Furthermore, a river is filled by waters poured by Indra, but this [mind] is not filled even by desires poured by Brahmā; thus he says, "by suitable ones. And just as the object carried by a river is joined with grass, wood, stones, thorns, and so forth, so too am I.
Just as a river is terrifying due to crocodiles, turtles, whirlpools, and the like, and various means are employed for protection from them, even so do I perform actions. ||24||
Having wandered through this world by the power of karma, one arrives here by chance;
for this [human birth] is the gateway to heaven, liberation, and even to the animal realm.

Śrīdhara: By that very thirst, one has obtained this world, the human body, by chance. Of what nature is this world? Through dharma, it is the door—the means—to heaven; through adharma, it is the door to the wombs of animals, such as dogs and pigs; and through both mixed together, it is [the door] to this [human state] once again.
It is the gateway to humanity; the meaning is that it is the gateway to liberation from all [bondage]—this is the sequence of the composition, which has not been explained [elsewhere].
Viśvanātha says: And just as by means of a river, one might [reach] even a sandy place at a crossroads at some time...
In the same way, I too have now attained this world and this human body. Of what kind?

It is the door—that is, the means—to heaven by means of merit; to liberation (*apavarga*) by means of knowledge and devotion; and to the wombs of animals, such as pigs and so forth, by means of sin. Furthermore, by both merit and sin—indicated by the word "and" (*ca*)—there is rebirth again at the conclusion of that experience.
Even for this birth as a human being, there is an entrance. ||25||
Even there, having observed the perversity of husbands and wives performing rituals for the sake of happiness and the removal of other afflictions, I have turned away.
Śrīdhara: Even here, despite being in the human state, having perceived the contrary—that is, the cessation of suffering for the sake of removing other [afflictions]—I have desisted. ||26||
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: Here too, "even in the state of being human" [is implied]. The meaning is: "In order to dispel the other [misery], that is, for the cessation of suffering, having perceived even worldly experience as nothing but suffering, I have desisted from all ritual actions. (26)
—o)0(o— This bliss is the true form of the self; it is the body consisting of the cessation of all worldly involvement.
Having seen that enjoyments arise from contact with the mind, I shall sleep while lying down.
Śrīdhara: [Objection: "Granted that happiness might sometimes arise through active engagement (*pravṛtti*), but what would happen through renunciation (*nivṛtti*)?

To this he says: "Happiness is the very nature (*svarūpa*) of this individual soul (*jīva*). [Objection: "If so, why does it not manifest? To this he says: "All... [The word] *tanu* means that which extends (*tanoti*). Upon the cessation of all activities, [it manifests] by its own nature.

The meaning is that [it] shines forth. Having seen that enjoyments born of mental contact—that is, those arising merely from the mind's desires—are impermanent, [he says] "I shall sleep"; the meaning is that he is free from exertion. If so, how does he eat at times? To this he replies: "while reclining" (saṃviśan); the meaning is that he experiences the enjoyments of his *prārabdha* karma. ||27||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
