*Viśvanātha*: If it is asked, "While happiness might sometimes arise from action, what would happen through the cessation of all action?
he says in response: "Happiness is the very nature (*svarūpa*) of this individual soul (*jīva*), which is myself. If that is so, then what?

Does it not shine forth? To this he replies: "All," etc. All endeavors (*īhā*) mean actions (*karma*) and the thirst that is their cause. Their cessation alone is the "body" (*tanu*); the meaning is that just as happiness is not obtained without a body, so too it is not obtained without that [cessation]. As for enjoyments, however, they are material (*prākṛta*), born from contact with the mind, or born merely from mental desire.

"Having seen that [the world] is momentary and decaying, I shall enter into a state of aversion toward it; enjoying the bliss of my own nature which is by its very essence imperishable, I shall sleep—or indeed, I am sleeping—upon a bed of celestial flowers such as those of the *vaitṛṣṇya* [tree].
Thus, the very cause for his corpulence is stated to be the enjoyment of bliss: 'The satisfaction of the sense organs.'"
This is according to the medical tradition.
Or rather: although at present there is no perception of the true bliss of the Self because even the appearance of thirst has not ceased, nevertheless, in five days that [thirst] too will cease.

"Entering correctly" means "I shall lie down. According to the statement in the *Medinīkośa*, "saṃveśaḥ [means] sleep, sexual intercourse with a woman, and binding," the word *saṃveśa* should be understood here as generally signifying enjoyment (*upabhoga*).
Thus, having indeed forgotten this which is his own true interest,
a person undergoes the terrible and manifold cycle of worldly existence within that which is unreal and devoid of duality.

Śrīdhara: If this were so, no one would ever enter into saṃsāra; to this he says: "Thus, having forgotten this form of the Self which consists of bliss—the goal of man (puruṣārtha) that exists within itself for its own sake—even though duality does not exist. (28)
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: If this is so, why are all beings not likewise happy?
To this he replies: "Thus, this... [referring to the verse]. Having forgotten their own purpose—their own goal consisting of happiness—in the state of duality...
Even though suffering does not exist in the body and so forth, and the self is in fact non-existent therein; or alternatively, even though [suffering] is not constant. ||28||
Just as an ignorant man, seeing water covered by its products, abandons it and runs toward a mirage out of a desire for water,
so too does one who perceives objects elsewhere [mistake them] for reality.

Śrīdhara: He clarifies this very point by means of an illustration—“water,” and so forth. By those things arising from it, such as grass and moss, [he is deluded] through the desire for water, that is, the longing for water. Seeing the goal of human life elsewhere than in his own nature, which is the Self (*ātman*). (29)

Kramasandarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: He clarifies this very point by means of an illustration—"water. It is "cut" by those things produced from it—that is, produced in the water itself—and not by things such as grass or moss that have merely emerged from the water.

Having abandoned his own happiness therein, which is severed by the illusory cravings and other afflictions that have arisen, he perceives the true human goal (puruṣārtha) as being elsewhere than within himself. ||29||
For the self that seeks its own happiness and the transcendence of suffering through the body and other means dependent on fate,
all actions performed are in vain, for it lacks mastery over itself.

Śrīdhara: Having thus stated the reason for his own lack of effort, he explains what was said regarding "seeing the contrary" through five verses beginning with "by means of the body and so forth. *Īhate* means "desires. For one who is *anīśa*, that is, devoid of destiny (*nirdaiva*), actions undertaken again and again become merely futile and fruitless.
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: He explains what was stated [in the previous verse] regarding "having seen the reverse"—namely, by means of the five verses beginning with "dehādibhiḥ": for one who strives (*īhamānasya*) for happiness and the cessation of suffering, their effort (*kriyā*) is futile and fruitless.
What can be achieved by means of wealth and sensual pleasures acquired through hardship for a mortal who is never liberated from internal and other forms of suffering?

Śrīdhara: Even though actions may be fruitful, he states that the fruit itself is useless with the words "by means of [sufferings] such as those pertaining to the self" (ādhyātmikādibhiḥ). "Of a mortal" means of one who is destined to die. "Attained through hardship" means acquired through suffering. ||31||
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: Even if they should occasionally be fruitful, he states that there is an incapacity for enjoying those fruits by saying "by means of the internal [afflictions] and so forth. Even the enjoyment of pleasure accompanied by suffering does not exist.
He said: "Of a mortal for whom death has suddenly become possible. (31)
— I see the suffering of the wealthy, who are greedy and have no self-control,
who find no sleep due to fear and are suspicious of everything.
Śrīdhara: Even when an object is obtained without difficulty, the suffering remains the same; thus he says: "I see," etc. (32).
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Thus, since objects do not bring about the cessation of suffering but rather result in an increase of suffering, he says: "I see... (verse 32).
From kings,
from thieves, from enemies, from one's own kin, from beasts and birds, from supplicants, from time, and even from oneself, there is constant fear for one's life and wealth.

Śrīdhara elaborates on this fear: "It shines forth," and so on. There is constant fear for those who possess life and wealth, thinking, "Destruction might somehow come about from me alone, through renunciation, enjoyment, forgetfulness, or the like. (33)
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: "From oneself" means that there might somehow be destruction by one's own self through giving away, enjoyment, forgetfulness, and so forth; thus there is fear for those attached to the vital breaths and objects. Here, "vital breath" (prāṇa) refers to bodily strength.

It should be understood that this serves as the motive for communal enjoyment and other such activities; however, the mere maintenance of life is indeed enjoined, as seen in passages such as, "The living being's desire to know the reality [of the Self]" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.2.10). ||33||
Grief, delusion, fear, anger, passion, impotence, fatigue, and so forth—
whatever roots these have for human beings— a wise person should abandon the craving for life and wealth.
Śrīdhara: Therefore, because they are causes of misfortune, one should not desire life or wealth; thus he says, "grief... [and so forth].
This is the sequence of the composition; it has not been explained [further].
Viśvanātha: One should abandon desire for life and wealth in order to increase the strength of the body.
And one should not strive for an abundance of wealth; the sense is that even with very little strength and very little wealth, the accomplishment of ultimate tasks is possible. ||34||
In this world, the honey-bee and the great serpent are our two supreme gurus,
for it was through their instruction that we attained dispassion and contentment.

Śrīdhara: But surely, even while experiencing such misfortunes, some do not become dispassionate, nor are they satisfied with whatever they happen to obtain; how then have you attained detachment and so forth?
To this he replies: "Like the honey-bee and the python. [These are] the honey-bee and the python. By their instruction...
By means of a thorough investigation of conduct. ||35||
The *Kramasandarbha*: not explained. Viśvanātha: Now, from which guru did you learn this? To that he replies: "Madhukārī"—o)0(o)—.
I have learned from the honey-bee the dispassion toward all desires:
wealth, acquired with such difficulty like honey, may be taken away by another even after killing its owner.
Śrīdhara says, explaining what was learned from the honey-bee: "Dispassion" (virāga). [The lesson is: having killed the master of wealth, another should take the wealth; thus [it is]. (36)
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: He speaks of what was learned from the honey-bee: "Even after killing the lord of wealth, another may take the wealth; thus I have a detachment toward wealth. (36)
Free from desire and with a contented soul, I shall lie for many days like a courageous great serpent, subsisting on whatever comes to me by chance.
Śrīdhara says: He states what was learned from the python: "without effort" (anīha). "Possessed of strength" means possessed of fortitude. ||37||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: He speaks of what was learned from the python: "without effort" (*anīha*). "I lie"—that is, I sleep—as one who possesses *sattva* and fortitude. (37)
In some places I eat little, in others much; the food may be tasty or tasteless.
In some places it is abundant and endowed with excellent qualities, while in others it is devoid of such qualities.
Sometimes, when offered with faith and free from pride, I eat;
and having eaten at some place, I may then eat again by chance, whether by day or by night.
Śrīdhara: Stating the cause for his corpulence, he elaborates upon his contentment with what is obtained by chance through six verses, beginning with "In some places, a little. (38)

The sequence of composition: "In some places" (kvacid) refers to one and a half verses. Regarding the phrase "whether sweet or not sweet" (svādv asvādu vā), there is a variant reading in some places of "whether good or not good" (sādhv asādhu vā). [Verse 38]. "I eat" (bhuñje) refers to half a verse. [Verse 39].
Viśvanātha: Not explained.
—o)0(o— Whether it be linen (*kṣauma*), fine silk (*dukūla*), deerskin (*ajina*), rags (*cīra*), or bark-garment (*valkala*).
I have obtained another boon as well; my mind is satisfied, having enjoyed what was ordained by fate.
Śrīdhara: *Cīra* means a fragment of worn-out cloth; *vase* means he wore it. *Diṣṭabhuk* means one who experiences the fruits of the karma already commenced. ||40||
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: "I place [it] upon my garment. (40)
Sometimes he rests on the ground, on grass, leaves, stones, or ashes;
sometimes on a palace couch or a bed, according to the will of others.
Śrīdhara: On a couch in the middle of the palace; there too, on a mattress upon a down-filled bed. ||41||

Kramasandarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: "In the lap of the Earth" means on the bosom of the Earth. According to the Medinī lexicon: "Upastha refers to the penis, as well as the bosom, and the abode of Madana. (41)
O Lord,
at times he moves about in chariots, elephants, and horses, bathed, his limbs anointed, well-dressed, wearing garlands and ornaments; at other times, like a planet, he wanders naked.
Śrīdhara: I wander about; in some places, naked as the sky, I roam like a planet. ||42||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: [The Lord says] "Better is the yoga of devotion," anticipating the objection that it is difficult to attain from the Blessed One; he replies with the word "uta" (but rather). *Aikātmyam* means liberation (*mokṣa*) within the Great Self, the Supreme Self. ||42||
I neither revile nor praise people whose natures are so diverse; I wish for their well-being, or rather, their identity with the Great Self.

"Madhvaḥ" refers to the one who presides over the mental fluctuations within the mind (*citta*). "In the confusion of objects" means while wandering among objects; one should reflect that this entire world is dependent upon the fire called *citta*.
One should also contemplate the fire as being under the control of the Indra named *manas*, and so forth. (43)

Śrīdhara: And he says "I am not... to show that there is no partiality on my part toward those who treat me with honor or dishonor: "I do not censure, nor do I praise; [this applies] to the Great Soul, Viṣṇu. (43)
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Thus, by means of two verses beginning with "vikalpa," he states the means for the yogi's abiding in such a state: "vikalpa" is that which is variously conceptualized; it refers to the mental modification (*mano-vṛtti*) within the mind (*citta*) that constitutes worldly transaction.

Because it proceeds from that very source: [the mind] is that in which there is the various wandering, the coming and going, of objects; [it resides] in the *vaikārika* ego (*ahaṅkāra*), that [ego] in the Great One (*mahat*), and that Great One in Māyā—here, the two words "that" and "Great One" (*tam* and *mahāntam*) are to be supplied. ||43||
One should offer conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) into the mind (*citti*), and that [mind] into the intellect (*manas*) when there is the delusion regarding objects;
having offered the mind into the ego (*vaikārika*), one subsequently offers that into *māyā*.

Śrīdhara: He states the means for remaining in such a state with the two verses beginning with "vikalpam. In the *citta*, that is, in the mental modification (*manovṛtti*) which perceives duality; in that mind wherein there is the delusion consisting of objective forms—that mind [is dissolved] into the *vaikārika-ahaṅkāra*. That *ahaṅkāra* [is dissolved] immediately after the *manas*.
The meaning is: "by means of the principle of Mahat. ||44||
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha: not commented upon.
—o)0(o— In the experience of the Self, the sage who perceives the truth should offer that *māyā* as an oblation.
Then, free from effort and established in the self of one's own direct experience, one should desist from activity.
"Because it is not based on scripture, the wise know this [Madhva's view] to be contrary to the scriptures from its very outset;
because it is accessible through the definitive conclusions of the scriptures, it is called 'scriptural' (śāstrīya). Thus [it is said]. (45)
Śrīdhara: [He is] "Tathā" because he perceives only the truth. ||45||
Kramasandarbha: This has not been explained.

Viśvanātha: [The phrase] "devoid of" (vyapeta) means "lacking" (rahita) in the view of the dull-witted, but not in the view of reality. Furthermore, the word "hi" (for/indeed) is used because you are a dear devotee of the Blessed One and a great bhāgavata.
The sense is that you have no need for this. ||45||
Thus have I described my own life-story to you, though it was kept strictly secret;
for you are devoted to the Blessed One, being free from the constraints of worldly custom and scripture.
"Because it is not based on scripture, the wise know this [Madhva's view] to be contrary to the scriptures from its very outset;
because it is to be understood through the definitive conclusions of the scriptures, that which is scriptural is so designated. Thus [it is said]. (46)
Śrīdhara: [This is] devoid of worldly perspective and scriptural learning, but not devoid of the vision of reality;
for you are devoted to the Blessed One. (46)
The sequence of composition: in some places, the reading is "bhagavat-para" (devoted to the Blessed One). ||46||

Viśvanātha: [The phrase] "devoid of both worldly custom and scripture" means it is lacking from the perspective of those with dull vision, but not from the perspective of one who perceives reality. Furthermore, the word "hi" (for) implies that since you are dear to the Blessed One and a great devotee (mahā-bhāgavata), you have no need for this; such is the sense. ||46||
Śrī Nārada said:
O sage, having heard the dharma of the paramahaṃsas from the lord of the asuras, [the king]...
Having worshipped him, he then departed for his home, pleased and taking his leave.
It has not been explained by anyone else.
Thus, in the *Harṣiṇī*, which reveals the essential meaning for those whose hearts are devoted,
the thirteenth [chapter] of the seventh [section], which is well-connected, is completed for the virtuous.
Thus ends the Seventh Canto in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā, the Pāramahaṃsya, within the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam Mahāpurāṇa, which is a commentary on the Brahma-sūtras.
The thirteenth chapter, titled "The Dharma of the Ascetic.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
In the *Sadācāranirṇaya*,
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"By what rule may a householder easily attain this state?"
O divine sage, tell me: how could one like me, whose intellect is deluded by the household life, go forth?
Śrīdhara:
In the fourteenth [chapter], the supreme duty of the householder is described;
furthermore, it is shown how differences in place, time, and so forth produce specific distinctions in spiritual welfare.

Since the duties of forest-dwellers and ascetics were first described as being more directly conducive to liberation than those of the householder, one whose mind is apprehensive that a householder might therefore lack the possibility of liberation asks: "The householder... (verse 1).
The sequence of composition: "The householder" constitutes a pair of verses.
Viśvanātha:
Having described the stage of renunciation (*nivṛtti*) among the four stages of life, he now describes the stage of active engagement (*pravṛtti*) in the householder's order (*gṛhāśrama*).
In the fourteenth [chapter], Dharma is explained according to the distinctions of place, time, and so forth.
Thus, having described the dharma of cessation (*nivṛtti-dharma*) for the three qualified persons— the student observing vows (*brahmacārin*), the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*),

and the ascetic (*yati*)— the Sage now proceeds to describe the dharma of worldly engagement (*pravṛtti-dharma*) for the single qualified person, the householder alone; it need not be said that this *pravṛtti-dharma* conforms to the stream of birth and death.

And if liberation, which is the fruit of the dharma of cessation, could be accomplished even by one following the dharma of worldly engagement, then [the author], with the intention of saying "tell me that," states: "The householder" (verse 1).

Śrī Nārada said: O King, while remaining in his home and performing his duties as was appropriate, he— (o)0(o— Śrī Nārada said: O King, while remaining in his home and performing his duties as was appropriate, he— [text continues].
One should directly worship the great sages as an offering unto Vāsudeva.
Constantly hearing the nectar-like stories of the Blessed One’s incarnations,
he was full of faith, lived according to the proper time, and was surrounded by peaceful people.
Śrīdhara: He speaks of the duties pertaining to liberation for that person, beginning with "In the houses... and so forth, until the end of the chapter.
One should practice while acting in such a way that there is direct dedication to Vāsudeva. (2)
The sequence of composition: "Directly" means solely for the sake of pleasing Him, and not for the sake of attaining a fruit; such is the meaning. ||2||
Viśvanātha: One should worship the great sages while performing actions in such a way that they are offered unto Vāsudeva.

At the proper times—such as the afternoon and so forth—one should remain surrounded by peaceful people and constantly listen to the *Ṣaṣṭha-purāṇa* (the Bhāgavata), and not listen to other news at the time of the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa’s narrations.
The meaning. ||2||

Through association with the virtuous, one should gradually abandon attachment to one's own wife, children, and so forth, as they are being relinquished, just as one who has awakened from a dream abandons the dream-objects themselves.

Śrīdhara: While [the objects] are themselves being released—that is, being disjoined—just as a person who has awakened from a dream abandons attachment to sons and others seen in that dream, so it is here. ||4||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: While they are being liberated—that is, being separated—just as a man who has awakened and risen from sleep abandons attachment to those seen in a dream, so it is here. (4)

As long as he remains present for the sake of his purpose, the wise man, detached though appearing attached, should establish his humanity here in the world of men, whether in his body or in his home.

Śrīdhara: Now, one might ask: for such a person who is being oppressed by the wicked, how can there be the activities appropriate for a householder? To this he says: "yāvad artham" (only as much as necessary). Internally detached, yet externally appearing as if attached in the world of men, he should exercise his human agency (*puruṣakāra*) among people, maintaining his status as a man.
The meaning is that one should confess. ||5||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "Sitting [near] objects such as those to be enjoyed" is the ellipsis. "A wise man in the body and in the home" means one who conducts himself with indifference toward various sense-objects; he is like one who is inwardly detached (*raktavat*).

Though detached externally, he acts as if attached internally; therein, situated in the center of the house, he should establish his human state—that is, his manhood—and manifest the form of a man. This is the reason. ||5||
Relatives, parents, sons, brothers, friends, and others—
whatever they say and whatever they desire, one who is free from the sense of "mine" should approve of it.
Śrīdhara says: "One should not, however, show obstinacy in any matter," and thus he says: "Relatives," etc. (6).
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: One who is free from the sense of "mine" and is indeed unattached should rejoice. ||6||
Whether it be celestial, terrestrial, or atmospheric wealth created by Acyuta—
the wise man, while utilizing all of that, should perform this [offering] himself.

Śrīdhara: [Objection: But if everything is thus approved, there would be the consequence of the depletion of wealth; from where, then, would livelihood come, or from where the performance of ritual action? To this he says: *divyam* refers to grain and so forth produced by rain and other such means;
*bhaumam* refers to treasures and the like; *āntarikṣam* refers to what is obtained quite spontaneously. Thus, [it comes] of its own accord.
Thus, that which was previously mentioned—action and so forth—is obtained through destiny fashioned by the Infallible One. //7//
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Divine [wealth] is that which arises from rain and so forth, such as grain; terrestrial is that which originates from mines and the like; atmospheric is that which is obtained unexpectedly. All these are [wealth] by virtue of their respective forms.
The meaning is that since this was created by Acyuta himself, one should not worry at all for the sake of wealth.
This refers to the previously mentioned obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites and so forth. "By him" means by his own self; the meaning is: by means of his own wealth. ||7||
"One's ownership extends only so far as the belly can be filled; for that is the extent of possession for embodied beings.
He who considers himself the owner of more than that is a thief and deserves punishment."
Śrīdhara: Even when abundant gain occurs by chance, one should not harbor pride therein; thus he says, "as long as... It means "it should be filled. (8)
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: Even when abundant gain occurs by chance, one should neither harbor pride regarding it nor indulge in enjoyment as one pleases; thus he says: "yāvat" means to such an extent that one should be filled or satisfied. ||8||
Deer, camels, donkeys, monkeys, mice, reptiles, birds, and flies—
one should regard them as one's own children; what difference, then, can there be between these and those?

Śrīdhara: For this very reason, he says "deer," etc., [implying] that one should not turn away anyone who has entered one's own house or field while eating. A *marka* is a monkey; a *sarīsṛpa* is a snake; and there are flies as well.
What difference is there between these deer and others on one hand, and their offspring—the monkeys, snakes, and flies—on the other? (9)

Kramasandarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: "Like unto sons" means that just as one would distribute food to one's sons, so too should one distribute it to these [disciples] according to what is appropriate. ||9||
Even a householder may pursue the three goals of life without excessive hardship,
according to place, according to time, and to the extent provided by destiny.
Śrīdhara: One should not practice with excessive hardship, but rather practice only as much as is provided by destiny. ||10||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: "Having properly prepared with great difficulty, one should not worship [only] as much as has been obtained by chance with very little effort; rather, the meaning is that one should not wait for a vast abundance."
The sense is that, because of the word "api" (even), what need is there to mention [the necessity of] practicing celibacy and so forth among the duties toward the guru? ||10||
At the conclusion of a marriage feast, one should distribute desired objects among the guests;
for even regarding a single wife of one's own, men maintain a sense of ownership.

Śrīdhara: Including dogs, outcasts (aghāḥ), those who have fallen from their caste (patitāḥ), and low-caste dwellers such as Cāṇḍālas—one should distribute desired objects to them according to their merit, giving them by sharing from what one has for one's own food. Even though one’s wife is the only wife belonging to oneself, when she is occupied with the service of guests, [one should give] for oneself...

Service would otherwise decline. One should share even that single [portion] with those men who have no sense of ownership—that is, no insistence that "this is mine"—and should employ them in the service of guests; this is the meaning, and it should not be understood otherwise, since it has been stated that one should distribute according to what is appropriate. ||11||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Dogs (*śvāna*), the sinful (*agha*), outcasts (*patita*), and those living nearby (*antevāsī*), such as *caṇḍālas* and others—even including them—he gives their respective desires, which are his own objects of enjoyment. The word "wife" (*dārām*) is used in the singular feminine form according to Vedic usage.

Even though she is the only wife of the husband, and if she is occupied with attending to guests, his own service [to her] would be neglected—even then, he should divide her duties as well; he must indeed appoint her to the service of guests and so forth. It should not be thought otherwise, because it has been stated that "he should distribute [duties] according to what is appropriate."
Thus say the venerable Svāmicaraṇas; others, however, explain it otherwise: "yat" means "in which. ||11||
One should abandon that woman for whose sake one would sacrifice one's own life, or kill a father or a teacher;
one should relinquish ownership of such a woman, for by her, even the unconquered is conquered.

Śrīdhara: If this were so, then the Lord would have been brought under his control; thus he says, "He would abandon," etc. For whose sake—that is, for what purpose—the Lord, though unconquered by others, would indeed be conquered by him. The connection of the sequence: if this were so, then the Lord would have been brought under his control; thus he says, "He would abandon," etc.
For whatever purpose and for whatever reason, even though the Lord is unconquered by others, he is indeed conquered by that [purpose]. ||12||
Viśvanātha: He says that the abandonment of pride regarding one's own wife is extremely difficult—“One should abandon...
(o)0(o)—[asking] where is this contemptible body, which ends in worms, excrement, and ashes?
Where is his wife, whose delight was in him, and where is this self that covers the sky?
Madhvaḥ: Nabhaśchadiḥ refers to the Supreme Self (paramātman) who exists pervading the sky. ||13||
Śrīdhara: Now, one might ask, how can such an identification with ownership toward her be abandoned?
He says it is through the investigation of reality (tattva-vicāra): "That whose finality or conclusion lies in worms, excrement, and ashes"—meaning that which ends in those states;
"whose delight is directed toward her body"; and "which, by its own greatness, even covers the sky"—such is she.
The sequence of composition: the Self is the Supreme Self. ||13||

Viśvanātha: He shows the discrimination for abandoning attachment to that [body]: Where is that delight which finds its finality and conclusion in worms, excrement, and ashes? And where is the Self, the Supreme Lord, who by His own majesty covers even the sky? If [one considers] it in this way, [then one should abandon it].
The sense is: "If it is attained only by the abandonment of pride, then how insignificant is this [attainment]! ||13||
The perfected ones (siddhas), using only the remnants of sacrificial offerings, should provide for their own livelihood;
by relinquishing ownership over what remains, the wise man shall attain the path of the great.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, [he is supported] by the Siddhas—those who have attained their status through destiny—with the remnants of sacrifices, that is, with food and other items left over from the five great sacrifices (pañca-yajña); [and he is supported] by the Great Ones, those who have retired from worldly life. ||14||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Regarding what was stated previously—that one should maintain pride only toward as much wealth as is necessary for filling the belly—he states the established rule even in that regard: "By the perfected ones (*siddhaiḥ*)..."

With divine, terrestrial, and celestial substances remaining from sacrifices, and with food and other items left over from the five great sacrifices, he daily honors the gods, the sages, human beings, spirits, the ancestors, and his own self.
One should worship the Supreme Person individually with wealth acquired through one's own lawful means.
Śrīdhara, explaining this, says: [One should worship] the five deities of the sacrifices, beginning with the gods, as well as oneself;
thus, one should worship the Person within, who is indeed the Inner Controller (antaryāmin), separately. ||15||
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
When all the requirements for sacrifice, such as one’s own qualification and so forth, are present;
One should perform sacrifice according to the ritual procedure involving the sacred fires, such as the Agnihotra and others.
It has not been explained by anyone at all. For this Blessed One, the consumer of all sacrifices, does not indeed have fire as his mouth.
O King, one should worship with oblations as if they were offered into the mouth of a Brahmin.
Śrīdhara: Furthermore, he says "for not" (*na hi*) to show that one should not exert excessive persistence in performing sacrifices.
For one is not worshipped (*ijyeta*) with oblations poured into the mouth of the fire in the same way as one is worshipped with food and other offerings poured into the mouth of a Brahmin. ||17||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Furthermore, he says "not indeed" (*na hi*) to show that there is no insistence [on the view] that [the sacrifice] is for the sake of the ritual alone;
for just as one might worship with food and other offerings poured into the mouth of a Brahmin, one does not worship in the same way by pouring them into the mouth of the fire.
The meaning. ||17||
Therefore, O Brahmin, worship this Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) through various desires among the gods, mortals, and others, as is appropriate, following the guidance of the Brahmins.

Śrīdhara: [Worship] the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), the Inner Controller (antaryāmin), among Brahmins, gods, the deities of the five sacrifices (pañcayajña), and other mortals as well as men, animals, and so forth. After sacrificing to the Brahmins—that is, after the sacrifice to the Brahmins—sacrifice to the others during the sacrifice to mortals and so forth. In another reading: [the same].
[He is] the one whose face is [surrounded by] Brahmins. ||18||

*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: The Brahmins themselves are the gods; worship the Supreme Lord, the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), by means of offerings of food to them. "After the Brahmins" means after the worship of the Brahmins, and [also] among mortals and others.
The reading "brāhmaṇānanam" is clear. ||18||
In the month of Prauṣṭhapada, during the dark fortnight, a twice-born man who possesses wealth should perform the Śrāddha for his parents and their relatives according to his means.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha: [the month] Bhādrapada, also called Prauṣṭhapada. ||19||
The sequence of composition has not been explained. —
One should perform [the rite] during the solstices, the equinoxes, at the conjunction of the sun and moon (vyatīpāta), or on the day of the waning of the lunar day.
During an eclipse of the moon or sun, on the twelfth lunar day, and under the Śravaṇa constellation.
On the third day of the bright fortnight, then on the ninth of Kārttika,
and likewise on all four Aṣṭakās of both the Hemanta and Śiśira seasons.
And on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, when it coincides with the Maghā constellation;
likewise, when the full moon (rākā) or the new moon (anumati) is joined with the lunar mansions of the month.
If the twelfth lunar day falls on Anurādhā, or Śravaṇa, or the three Uttarās,
or if the eleventh lunar day falls on one of those three asterisms, it is joined with the conjunction of the birth asterism and Śroṇā.

"Madhava, the triad beginning with the seventh [lunar day], as well as the thirteenth of Caitra—these four are declared to be the Aṣṭakās, specifically distinguished from all other fortnights. Thus it is stated in the Vyāsa-smṛti;
and also: "In Hemanta and Śiśira, this is the obligatory scripture [the Goṭāurasa-śāstra]. (21)

Śrīdhara: [This occurs] in the bright fortnight; the meaning is "on the Akṣayya-tṛtīyā. During the Hemanta and Śiśira seasons—that is, in the four months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa—there are four Aṣṭakās.
The full moon is Rākā; that same moon when its digits are diminished is Anumati. Likewise...

The lunar mansions (nakṣatras) associated with each respective month are the grounds for the application of those specific month-names when they are conjoined [with the full moon]. As it is stated in the *Tri-kāṇḍī*:
"When the full moon is conjoined with Puṣya, that month in which it occurs is Pauṣa."
"Pauṣa by name [occurs] after Māgha; in this way, there are eleven others ending with Āśvina. This means:

when Anurādhā, Śravaṇa, Uttarā-phālgunī, Uttarā-ṣāḍhā, or Uttarā-bhādrapadā occurs on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī); and when one of these *uttarā* constellations occurs on the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī), then likewise.

When a day is joined with the conjunction of one's birth asterism (janmarkṣa) or Śravaṇa, that is the time; the mention of "conjunction" (yoga) is for the purpose of indicating a multiplicity of such connections. ||21-24||

The sequence of arrangement: "In the solstice" refers to a group of four. Among the three [Ekādaśīs], the Ekādaśī in Capricorn (Dhanus) is to be observed as a fast by Vaiṣṇavas, because of the prohibition of performing *śrāddha* on that day. For instance, in the *Brahmayāmala*: "And *śrāddha* on the day of Ekādaśī"—this is a prohibition against making the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) for initiation (*dīkṣā*).
In the Brahmavaivarta [Purāṇa]:
"O protector of the earth, those who perform a śrāddha on the Ekādaśī day—these three go to hell: the giver, the eater, and the instigator. Thus it is said.
In the *Pādmottara-khaṇḍa*:
"When the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) coincides with the anniversary of the death of one's mother or father,
one should set that day aside and perform the Śrāddha on the twelfth lunar day (Dvādaśī)."
In the Puṣkara-khaṇḍa:
"O Rāma, whenever an occasional (naimittika) Śrāddha falls on the eleventh day, one should set that day aside and perform the Śrāddha on the twelfth day. (20–23)

Viśvanātha: "One should perform the *śrāddha* during the solstices (*ayana*) and the equinoxes (*viṣuva*)," this is the connection with what precedes. Likewise, in the subsequent cases as well, the meaning is "on the Akṣaya-tṛtīyā in the bright fortnight. And those four *aṣṭakās* which occur in the late autumn (*hemanta*) and the early winter (*śiśira*).
These times are for those seeking the highest good; they increase one's welfare.
One should devote oneself entirely to these [practices], for in them the welfare of one’s life becomes unfailing.

Śrīdhara: These times are not only for the *śrāddha* rite, but for all religious duty (*dharma*) as well; thus he says with two verses beginning "These [are]... (1.24). "That alone" means that very life is not in vain—that is, it is fruitful. ||24||
Kramasandarbha: This has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: The meaning is that it is for the sake of spiritual merit (*dharma*) alone, and not merely for the sake of ancestral rites (*śrāddha*);
at that very time, there is the fruitfulness, that is, the non-futility, of one's life. ||24||
In these [tirthas], bathing, recitation, burnt offerings, observances, and the worship of gods and twice-born ones,
as well as whatever is given to the ancestors, gods, humans, and spirits, becomes imperishable.
It has not been explained by anyone at all:
the time of the formation of the wife, the offspring, and likewise the self.
O King, the rites for the deceased, the anniversary of death, and rites for prosperity are all included within "karma."

Śrīdhara: "At the time of consecration" refers to the *puṃsavana* and other rites for the wife; the *jātakarma* and other rites for the child; the initiation (*dīkṣā*) for sacrifices and so forth for oneself; and the funeral rites (*saṃsthā*), such as cremation, for the deceased. It also applies to the annual anniversary of death, and to any other rite performed for the sake of prosperity (*abhyudaya*), which brings about spiritual merit (*śreyas*).
The word "should do" is to be supplied [to complete the sentence]. ||26||
The sequence of topics (*krama-sandarbha*) has not been explained.

Viśvanātha [comments]: "At the time of purificatory rites (*saṃskāra-kāle*)" refers to the *puṃsavana* and other rites for the wife; the *jātakarman* and other rites for the offspring; the sacrificial initiations (*yajña-dīkṣā*) and other rites for oneself; and the funeral rites (*preta-saṃsthā*), such as the cremation of the deceased.

The anniversary of the death of a father or other relative is the annual *śrāddha*. The syntactical connection (*anuṣaṅga*) is that one should perform acts conducive to spiritual welfare (*śreyas*) on these occasions, as well as on other festive events (*abhyudaya*). ||26||
Now I shall describe the regions that bring about the highest good, beginning with Dharma;
for that indeed is the most meritorious region where a worthy recipient (sat-pātra) is found.
There is the image of the Blessed One, wherein all this world of moving and unmoving things resides;
there, O Brahmin, is the family of the Brahmans, endowed with austerity, knowledge, and compassion.

Śrīdhara: That place where this world of moving and non-moving beings exists—that is the form (bimba) of the Blessed One; and wherever that true vessel [of his teaching] is found, that indeed is the most meritorious land. ||27||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: A "sat-pātra" (worthy recipient) is one who is both virtuous (*sat*) and a worthy vessel (*pātra*), namely a Vaiṣṇava. And what is such a person like? One for whom this entire world of moving and non-moving beings is the reflection (*bimba*)—that is, equal to a reflection—of that Blessed Lord.
This is the meaning. ||27-28||
Wherever there is an image of Hari, that place is the abode of all blessings;
so too are those places where rivers such as the Gaṅgā, renowned in the Purāṇas, flow.
Śrīdhara: Not commented upon.

Viśvanātha: For a "pratimā" is of the nature of a reflection; from that [reflection], the devotee attains excellence. Therefore, it is said: "Worship of My devotee is superior" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.19.21).
Thus,
he who strives with faith for worship of Hari only in the ritual image, and not toward His other devotees, is considered a materialistic devotee. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.2.47)

And this will be stated [later]: *arcā* refers to an image in the form of a *śālagrāma* stone and so forth; *arcā* refers to a fixed image such as Śrī Jagannātha, and those who take refuge in it, such as the people of Utkala and others. ||29||
Are the sacred fields such as Puṣkara and others dependent upon Arhats?
Kurukṣetra, Gayaśiras, Prayāga, and Pulahāśrama;
Naimiṣa, Phālguna, Setu, Prabhāsa, and Kuśasthalī;
Vārāṇasī, Madhupurī, Pampā, and likewise Bindusaras.
Nārāyaṇāśrama, Nandā, Sītā-rāmāśrama, and others—
all these, O King, as well as the principal mountain ranges such as Mahendra and Malaya.
Śrīdhara: [The hermitages] are resorted to by the most excellent Arhats. (30) Those of which the hermitage of Sītā and Rāma is the first;
the separate mention of the two is with the intention of referring to the time of their separation. (32)
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
These are the most meritorious regions, as well as those which are devoted to the worship of Hari.
One who desires the highest good should indeed constantly resort to these regions;
for in them, dharma practiced by men yields a fruit a thousand times greater.

Śrīdhara: "Dependent on images" (arcāśritāḥ) means those dependent on fixed icons. Since the place for worshiping the Śālagrāma stone and so forth was mentioned previously, there is no redundancy. Here, "performed" (ihitaḥ) means done in these places; it is "such" (tathā) because it results in the arising of a fruit that is a thousandfold greater. ||33||
Kramasandarbha: Not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: That from which there arises a fruit a thousand times greater than that [obtained] from another place. 0)0(0)

But here, O Lord of the Earth, the wise who are most skilled in understanding the term have explained that "pātra" (the worthy recipient) is indeed Hari alone, for the entire world of moving and non-moving beings consists of him.
Śrīdhara: Now he speaks of the recipient: "Hari alone is the recipient" is the etymological definition and the final determination. ||34||
The *Krama-sandarbha* has not been explained.

In the *Bhakti-sandarbha* (286), now, regarding the seventh [chapter], in the discourse of Śrī Nārada beginning with the words "pātram" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 7.14.34), within the investigation of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), there is that which surpasses even the person who is merely a mere man (*puruṣa-mātra*) compared to the venerable arcā-form.

Even there, he is a man of knowledge (*jñānin*), and he is one who desires liberation (*kaivalya*) while taking refuge in devotion (*bhakti*). This is because in that section, at the conclusion with the words "these should be given to one established in knowledge" (*bhā.pu.* 7.25.1), the highest excellence is declared for the man of knowledge alone as the recipient of gifts. Elsewhere, however, it is said: "To me, a devotee is dear, even if he knows not the four Vedas."

In passages such as "This Blessed One is not easily pleased" (Bhāgavatapurāṇa 6.14.4) and "Even for the liberated and the perfected ones... (Bhāgavatapurāṇa 6.14.4), the devotee alone is shown to be superior even to them; how much more so, then, the venerable arcā-form which is their object of worship?
For this very reason, it was said with reference to her: "He who, out of delusion, does not follow [the Lord]... (Bhāgavatapurāṇa).

[6.14.4] And so forth. Nevertheless, the meaning of "the worthy recipient" (*pātra*) and the following terms is also shown in sequence by means of two verses beginning with "But the worthy recipient" (*pātram tu*). Among those, [the first two apply] to the *rājasūya* sacrifice. [34–35]

Viśvanātha: Here, if one asks to whom it should be given for the sake of *dharma* and *artha*, [the author] first defines the recipient of a gift (*dāna-pātra*) in order to state that it should be given directly to those who uphold *dharma*, to Vaiṣṇavas, to Brāhmaṇas, and to all living beings—beginning with the verse: "The recipient... (34).
O King, while the celestial sages, the Arhats, and the sons of Brahmā were present there,
Acyuta was considered by all to be the most worthy recipient for the first offering.

Śrīdhara says: He states that very point: "Even though there were gods, sages, Arhats, those perfected through austerity and yoga, and even the sons of Brahmā such as Sanaka and others present there at your Rājasūya sacrifice, Acyuta alone was esteemed as the worthy recipient. (35)
The sequence of composition: "O divine sage," etc.; therein, in the Rājasūya sacrifice. ||35||

Viśvanātha: He states that your indisputable status as a worthy recipient for Hari is established by the Rājasūya sacrifice itself— "Among the gods, the sages, the venerable ones, those perfected through austerity, sacrifice, and so forth, such as Brahmā and his progeny, Sanaka and the others— in the matter of foremost worship, Acyuta alone is considered the worthy recipient."
The great tree of the cosmic egg is filled with multitudes of living beings;
because it has its root in Him, worshiping Acyuta is the gratification of the self of all living beings.

Śrīdhara states the reason for this consensus: "The very shell of the universe, pervaded by the multitudes of living beings, is the water at His feet, which provides satisfaction to all living beings and to Himself. (36)
The *Krama-sandarbha* has not been explained.
The *Bhakti-sandarbha* (287) states: the meaning is that she alone constitutes the act of satisfying all living beings as well as one's own self. ||36||

Viśvanātha states the reason for its being accepted: "The individual soul," etc. Because it is the root of that egg-shell—(o)0(o)—by this [Prakṛti], the cities [of bodies] were created: humans, animals, sages, and deities.
For that Puruṣa indeed lies within the bodies in the form of the individual soul (jīva).
Of the honey: together with the form of the living soul. ||37||

Śrīdhara: He confirms this very point by means of the etymological derivation of the name "Puruṣa," [saying] "purāṇi. Since he lies within the "puras"—the bodies in the forms of humans, animals, and so forth—as the inner controller (antaryāmin) and as the individual part (pratyag-aṃśa), he is therefore well-known as Puruṣa. ||37||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Bhakti-sandarbha* 288: "Having animated by means of the individual soul (jīva)" means by way of being the inner controller (antaryāmin) of the individual soul.
Viśvanātha: Therefore, at the time of his descent (avatāra), [he acts] directly from that very source; but at other times, however...
This is because of what was stated previously: "To his devotee, wherever a worthy recipient is found" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.14.27), and "the image of the Lord" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.14.28).
Immediately after that, however, he says "to all living beings whatsoever"—namely, "by whom the ancient [Purāṇas] are [revealed]" (37).
O King, the Blessed One abides among them according to their relative degrees of excellence;
therefore, a person is indeed a worthy recipient (pātra) insofar as they are themselves and as far as they strive.
"Among Madhu, Brahmā, and all others down to the stationary beings, there is no distinction whatsoever in Hari;
yet they speak of a gradation based solely on the degree of manifestation. (38)

Śrīdhara: Because [the quality] exists with greater intensity in the *puruṣa* than in animals and so forth according to a gradation (*tāratamya*), therefore the *puruṣa* is a worthy recipient (*pātra*). Furthermore, in that regard, to the extent that the self—the portion consisting of knowledge—is perceived through the practice of austerity and so forth, and in whatever manner it is realized, to that same extent he is a worthy recipient; such is the meaning. In that case...
And there is scriptural authority: "In the state of being a person, the Self is more fully manifest," and so forth. ||38||
The *Krama-sandarbha* has not been explained.

*Bhakti-sandarbha* 289: Therefore, because of the existence of degrees of excellence (*tāratamya*), the person—generally meaning a human being—is the recipient. In that regard, knowledge and so forth are distinguished by the preeminence of the Lord's manifestation therein.

In that regard, the meaning is that the self (*ātman*) is a worthy recipient (*pātra*) to the extent and in the manner that its measure of knowledge and other qualities exists; thus says Viśvanātha. Furthermore, because [the quality] exists with greater intensity in a human being than in animals and so forth due to its gradation, therefore the human being is the worthy recipient. Nevertheless, to the same extent as [one possesses] knowledge, dispassion, and so forth...

To whatever extent the self (ātman) may be supreme as a living being (jīva), that is the worthy recipient (pātra). And thus says the Śruti: "In the state of manhood, the Self is most fully manifested," and so forth. ||38||
O King, having observed that those men were characterized by mutual contempt,
the wise established the worship of Hari for the sake of ritual practice during the Tretā and subsequent ages.

Śrīdhara: Then, why do they perform worship of Hari in images and the like? To this he replies with two verses beginning with "Having seen": having seen the state of mind of those whose intellect (*ātman*) and understanding (*buddhi*) are fixed upon that [image] while harboring mutual contempt—which is unreal (*asan*)—[they act] for the sake of ritual action, such as worship. (39)

The *Krama-sandarbha* has not been explained. The *Bhakti-sandarbha* (290) states: Even though this is so, when, in the course of time, defects arise in the worshiper, another distinct substratum is revealed through the perception of difference; thus he says: "Having seen," etc.

The meaning is this: having seen the state of mind of those for whom there is mutual contempt and a lack of respect, and whose intellect is fixed upon that [contempt], the worship was performed for the sake of honoring them so as to demonstrate the path of their service;
thus it was revealed. By this, it is shown that even among those possessed of such defects, the goal may still be accomplished.

The superiority of the worship of the glorious arcā-form is thus clearly indicated. Furthermore, regarding the statement "the image is for those of small intellect," the meaning is "even for those of small intellect," since the worship of that [arcā] is heard of even in the case of Brahmā, Ambarīṣa, and others in the Nṛsiṃha Purāṇa and other texts. ||39||

Viśvanātha: But for those who are incapable of honoring all living beings and who possess contempt, rivalry, and the like, the image of the Lord alone is the worthy recipient; thus he says, "Having seen," etc. [Verse 39]: "The state" (*bhāvam*) refers to that condition of those whose very self or intellect (*ātma-buddhi*) consists of mutual contempt toward one another.
Then some, having placed their faith in Hari within the image through ritual worship, venerated Him;
yet even such worship does not grant the goal to those who hate the Supreme Person.
Śrīdhara: [The devotees] worship Hari. Even an image that has been worshipped does not bestow the goals of human life (puruṣārtha) upon those who harbor hatred toward persons.

The meaning is that when one worships it after abandoning hatred toward persons, even that [image], being real, certainly becomes a bestower of the goals of human life for those of dull faculties. ||40||
The *Krama-sandarbha*: not explained.

The *Bhakti-sandarbha* (291): "From that very [source]" means by virtue of such power; "some" refers to those who, due to the excellence of their spiritual basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*), are even more intent upon the supreme means than before.

One might object: "Would not success be achieved through hatred just as through contempt? Anticipating this doubt and desiring to avoid such an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), while also wishing to preserve the reverence for the person who is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the present subject, he refutes that [objection] with the words: "Even if worshipped...
(verse 40).

Viśvanātha: That even one who has been worshipped—that is, served—by those who hate persons does not come for the sake of [the devotee's] purpose, indicates that hatred arising from contempt and the like constitutes a greater offense than other faults. ||40||
O Indra among kings, they know that even among men, the Brāhmaṇa is the supreme vessel;
through austerity, learning, and contentment, he bears the Veda, which is the body of Hari.
And it is said: "The virtuous, beginning with the Brahmins, are remembered as the images of Hari, like honey-stones. (41)

Śrīdhara: Among men alone, he states another distinction based on birth, austerity, and so forth—with the words "even among men. He who wears it, they know him to be a worthy recipient (supātra). ||41||
The *Krama-sandarbha*: not explained.

The *Bhakti-sandarbha* (292): Now, he explains the previously mentioned distinction among men by means of birth and so forth, beginning with the words "Even among men. He who maintains [this] is known as a worthy recipient (*supātra*). ||41||

Viśvanātha: He states that among men, superiority arises from birth, austerity, and so forth—with the words "even among men. He who upholds this Veda, which is denoted by the word *brahman*, through knowledge is a Brāhmaṇa;
by the rule "one who studies that is a knower of that," the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the term "Brāhmaṇa" is shown. ||41||
"O King, are these Brahmins not indeed the great deity of this Kṛṣṇa, the Soul of the Universe, purifying the three worlds with the dust of their feet?"
Śrīdhara: He confirms this very point by means of the *kaimutya* logic (the "how much more so" principle) with the words: "Now, of this... (42).
The *Krama-sandarbha* has not been explained.

The *Bhakti-sandarbha* (293) praises the very vessel in the form of a brāhmaṇa mentioned previously, beginning with the words "nanv asya" and so forth. [He does so] because the Self of the universe, by means of establishing the dharma of maintaining the world within the world...
The meaning is "of its controller. It is shown as the deity by virtue of being worthy of worship. ||42||

Viśvanātha: It must be stated that the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is indeed this: because Kṛṣṇa is the Great Deity (*mahat daivata*), even he honors [the Brāhmaṇas] due to their devotion to Brahman (*brahmaṇyatvāt*);

yet it is not because they are his deities that they are Brāhmaṇas. Therefore, they are to be worshipped as venerable even from his presence by virtue of their very nature. This is so even when many Brāhmaṇas are present at the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Because of the primary worship of Kṛṣṇa alone. ||42||
Thus ends the fourteenth [chapter], which is well-connected with the seventh, in the *Harṣiṇī*, the *Sārārthadarśinī*, for those whose hearts are devoted to the Blessed One. *||*
Thus ends the Seventh Canto in the Vaiyāsikī Saṃhitā, the Pāramahaṃsyam, which is a commentary on the Brahma-sūtras within the glorious Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, the Great Purāṇa.
The fourteenth chapter on the Determination of Right Conduct.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter:
The Dialogue between Yudhiṣṭhira and Nārada.
Śrī Nārada said:
Some twice-born ones are devoted to ritual action (karma), others, the kings, are devoted to austerity (tapas);
some are intent on Vedic study (svādhyāya) and others on exposition (pravacana), while some are devoted to knowledge (jñāna) and yoga.
Śrīdhara:
Thereafter, in the fifteenth [chapter], the characteristics of liberation are described in brief according to their essence, as the binding of all castes and stages of life.

This chapter is commenced for the purpose of summarizing the essence of all the dharmas pertaining to liberation. In that regard, he states the specific details concerning *śrāddha* rites: "those devoted to ritual action" (*karmaniṣṭhāḥ*). The ellipsis to be supplied is "those who are fully established in the study of the Vedas (*svādhyāya*) and so forth. (1)
The Sequence of Arrangement: Now, with two verses beginning with "those established in action" (*karma-niṣṭhā*), he declares among them the most excellent.

These are to be understood respectively as the householder, the forest-dweller, the student, and the renunciant. By this, it is shown that here, for those seeking liberation and others, worship of the Knower (*jñānin*) alone is primary; whereas the worship of other persons is...

In the very absence of that [form], even the worship of a loving devotee should be understood as such for those who desire loving devotion (*prema-bhakti*). Furthermore, because it manifests the supreme substratum (*paramāśraya*) of the hearts of those loving devotees, the excellence of the *arcā* (the installed form) is even greater. Thus, regarding that which is the nature of the substratum—

Precisely because of His unique nature as luminosity (*vilakṣaṇa-prakāśatva*), although the illustrious Viṣṇu is all-pervasive, He is specifically determined within the *śālagrāma* stones and other such objects. And this [determination] is not dependent on the perspective of an internal controller (*antaryāmin*) like that of the Supreme Person (*puruṣa*), but is rather to be designated by His own inherent nature (*svabhāva*). This is established through the fact that it brings about the status of great pilgrimage sites (*mahātīrtha*) for the lands where He dwells and so forth.
Because it is stated that even those from Kīkaṭa and other such regions achieve their purpose [there]. Likewise, in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Wherever there is a Śālagrāma stone, that holy place extends for three yojanas;
there, a śrāddha, recitation, or a fire-oblation—all becomes ten-million-fold in merit."
"Within the distance of a *krośa* all around the vicinity of Śālagrāma, even a man from Kīkaṭa who dies goes to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha.
Thus, the superiority of the *arcā* (the image) is established. [Bhakti-sandarbha 294]
Viśvanātha: In this fifteenth chapter, titled "The Compendium of the Essence," the determination of all duties, which are internal to the duties of the householder alone, has been demonstrated.

In the preceding section, the Brahmins were established as the foremost; now he describes the gradations even among those Brahmins: "The householders are devoted to ritual action (*karma-niṣṭhā*); the forest-dwellers are devoted to austerity (*tapo-niṣṭhā*); others, namely the lifelong celibates (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārin*), are devoted to Vedic study and exposition (*svādhyāya-pravacana*);
and some, the renunciants (*saṃnyāsinaḥ*), are devoted to knowledge and yoga (*jñāna-yoga*)."

Even though the word "niṣṭhā" occurring within the compound is not explicitly repeated here, they should be explained as "those possessing the culmination" (niṣṭhāvantaḥ) through figurative indication (lakṣaṇā). Consequently, their superiority is shown to increase progressively. ||1||
Those desiring infinite results should offer the *kavya* offerings to one established in wisdom;
and for offerings to the gods (*daiva*), they should likewise be given to others as appropriate in his absence.

Śrīdhara: Oblations (kavya) should be offered to him on behalf of the ancestors; sacrificial offerings (havya) should also be given to him for the sake of the gods. The phrase "according to what is fitting" applies everywhere, meaning according to the gradations of knowledge and other qualities. ||2||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: "Kavyas" are substances intended for the ancestors; "havyas" are also substances intended for the gods, and these should be given to one established in knowledge. [This leads to] infinity, which is liberation, for the ancestors.

Regarding the phrase "or his own": for the sake of liberation, a householder should especially feed only renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*), because that work consists of five chapters and deals with the section on liberation (*mokṣa-prakaraṇa*). For this very reason, since pure devotees (*śuddha-bhaktas*) have no eligibility for ritual action (*karma*), even they are not mentioned here in this section on action and knowledge.

However, it was stated in the fifth [chapter] that when these well-established individuals— such as Bharata, Ambarīṣa, and others— perform their duties through their own representatives for the sake of protecting worldly affairs, it is done solely so that there may be no obstruction to the bliss of the path of devotion and so forth.

And this will be established in the eleventh [chapter]. Therefore, for the sake of liberation, just as the worship of the Knower alone is primary while the worship of other persons exists only in its absence, so too it is made known here that for those seeking loving devotion (prema-bhakti),
the worship of the exclusive devotee alone is primary— "That indeed is the most meritorious place."
In the commentary on this verse (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 7.14.27), [it is stated]:

"O great sage, among even millions of liberated and perfected beings, one who is solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa and whose self is perfectly tranquil is extremely rare" (*Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 6.14.5), and so forth.
Regarding His excellence even over those possessed of knowledge, from His lotus feet:
"Neither a knower of the four Vedas nor My devotee is dear to Me; My devotee, even if he be an outcaste, is dear.
To him gifts should be given and from him they should be accepted, for he is to be honored just as I am. (Gītā 9.30–32)

And because even for one who is not a Brahmin, he possesses the status of a recipient (*sampradāna*) from the lotus-feet [of the Lord]. Furthermore, regarding the worship of the wise, the statement "Indeed, there is worship when seeing them among men" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 7.14.39) explains this in terms of those with inferior qualifications; it should not be explained in the same way for devotees, for their [case is different]. Their...
For even for the primary qualified practitioners, worship and other such acts in the ritual image (*arcā*) are indeed essential limbs of devotion.
As it is said in the Eleventh [Canto]:
"Beholding, touching, and worshipping my *liṅga* and my devotees..."
"Service consists of praise and the proclamation of the qualities and deeds of one who is humble" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.11.34);
"Faith in the installation of my image and effort through collective cooperation" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.11.38).
[This is done] with garments, sacred threads, ornaments, leaf-designs, garlands, perfumes, and ointments.
"My devotee, filled with love, should worship me in a manner that is appropriate. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.27.32).

As for statements such as "the image is for those of small intellect," this should be explained either as referring to those who are supreme among the wise or as being for those of small intellect. In the Nṛsiṃha Purāṇa, even Brahmā, Ambarīṣa, and others [are described] as performing that worship at his lotus feet.
Her greatness is supreme. And in the Viṣṇu-dharma, regarding her, there is the speech of Śrī Viṣṇu to Ambarīṣa:
"Having fixed your mind upon her, abandon all other supports."
She alone has been worshipped by you with devotion, and she, being meditated upon, is indeed your benefactor.
"Whether walking, standing, sleeping, or eating, one should contemplate that very [form] first, then behind, above, below, and likewise on both sides, as well as within oneself," and so forth.
And in the *Skānda*: "Wherever there is a *śālagrāma* stone, that place is a sacred site (*tīrtha*) for three *yojanas*. [Ha.bha.vi.]
Thus it is said in the *Padma Purāṇa*:
"Within a distance of one *krośa* all around the vicinity of Śālagrāma,
even a man who dies in Kīkaṭa goes to the realm of Vaikuṇṭha" (*Hari Bhakti Vilāsa* 5.381).
One should feed two at a rite for the gods and three at a rite for the ancestors, or one for each of the two; even if very wealthy, one should not make the *śrāddha* overly elaborate.
Śrīdhara: [This] has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: "Vistaram" means the multiplicity of enjoyers. ||3||
Furthermore, offerings of faith appropriate to the place and time, as well as gifts of material wealth to worthy recipients,
do not truly become perfect when bestowed extensively upon one's own kinsmen.

Śrīdhara: [Objection: From where did this elaboration arise that it is now being prohibited? To this he says: "Because of the inclusion of one's own kinsmen. The meaning is: from such an elaboration as might arise when, for instance, if the son-in-law is invited, how could his father and others be excluded? ||3||

Kramasandarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: [The phrase] "by offering to one's own kin" means that if the son-in-law is invited because of the giving of food to one's own kin, then how could his father and others be neglected? It is from such an extensive consideration that [this is stated].
When the proper place and time have arrived, food fit for sages, dedicated to Lord Hari,
when offered with faith according to the rules into a worthy recipient, becomes an inexhaustible cow of plenty.
Śrīdhara: "Muni-food" refers to wild grains such as rice and the like; "dedicated to Hari" means that which has been offered to Hari. ||5||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: "Muni-anna" refers to forest-grown grains such as *vrīhi* and the like, or that which is acquired through righteous means.
"Having Hari as its deity" means first offered to Hari, and thereafter given to the ancestors from that very same [food].
Then it was placed in a vessel. ||5||
Distributing food among the celestial rishis, the ancestors, all living beings, himself, and his own kin, he should perceive all that as being of the nature of the Supreme Person.
Śrīdhara: [It is] the nature of the Lord, whose essence is the Puruṣa. ||6||
The *Kramasandarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon.
One who knows the true nature of Dharma should neither offer meat at a *śrāddha* nor eat it.
Supreme joy arises from the food of sages, as it does not through the slaughter of animals.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
There is no other dharma like this for men who desire the true dharma.
Renunciation is the laying down of the staff—that which arises from mind, speech, and body—toward all living beings.

Śrīdhara: "The laying down of the staff" means the abandonment of violence; there is no other dharma such as this. [The *Kramasandarbha*] has not been commented upon. Viśvanātha: "The laying down of the staff" means the abandonment of striking or harming. (8)
Some who possess knowledge and are the best among those who know sacrifice offer sacrifices consisting of ritual action into the fire of self-restraint, kindled by knowledge, being free from desire.
Śrīdhara: For this very reason, he says "one" [in verse 27] to show that those of the highest qualification renounce external actions.
"Desireless" means free from ritual action (*niṣkarma*). They offer [the senses] into the self-restraint which is illumined by knowledge—that is, which possesses the manifestation of the Self.
The meaning is that, having restrained the mind, they abandon it as an obstacle to that [self-restraint]. Thus it has been said:
By the well-spoken words of the Omniscient One:
"The manifestation of the Self and the manifestation of the unreal cause the obstruction of steadfastness in the body;
one should abandon action by observing the Real, for otherwise, one is struck down by obstacles. (9)
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: For this very reason, he says "one" [in the verse] to show that those of the highest qualification abandon external rituals—"anīhāḥ" means free from desire; "ātmanaḥ" refers to the restraint or control of the mind by means of knowledge.

In that context, sacrifices consisting of ritual action are illuminated; the meaning is that they abandon ritual actions because such actions constitute an obstacle to the restraint of the mind. ||9||
Seeing one who intends to perform sacrifices with material offerings, living beings are struck with fear, thinking:
"This pitiless man, ignorant of the Truth and greedy for life-force, will surely kill us."

Śrīdhara: "May he surely not kill me. Why? Because he is merciless. Why is that? Because he is one who delights in life, i.e., one who gratifies his own vital breaths. What of it? Because he is ignorant of that, i.e., unacquainted with the reality of the Self. And so says the Śruti:
"You do not perceive him who generated these [beings], for something else has come between you.
Enveloped by mist and idle talk, those who recite hymns wander about, seeking only their own sustenance. (Rig Veda 10.82.17) ||10||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: "May this merciless one not kill me"—that is, he will kill me. He is "unaware of that," meaning ignorant of the reality of the Self (*ātma-tattva*). And thus says the Śruti:
"You do not perceive him who generated these [beings], for something else has come between you.
Enveloped by mist and idle chatter, those who recite hymns wander about, seeking only their own sustenance. [Ṛgveda 10.82.17] ||10||
Therefore, one who knows the Dharma, being content even with the food of sages obtained by chance,
should perform the daily and occasional rites day after day.
Śrīdhara: He continues the subject at hand with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt). ||11||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained. Viśvanātha: "Content in all things" means not harming living beings. ||11||

—o)0(o— Perversion of duty, the duty of another, semblance, analogy, and deception: these are the five branches of non-dharma; one who knows dharma should abandon them as if they were non-dharma itself.
Śrīdhara: "Like unrighteousness" means like that which is directly prohibited. ||12||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Like unrighteousness, as if it were forbidden. ||12||

The obstruction of Dharma is *vidharma*; the duty of another is *paradharma* when enjoined by someone else. *Upadharma*, however, is heresy (*pākhaṇḍa*), hypocrisy, or a deceptive perversion of words.

Śrīdhara, disregarding the sequential order, explains all five [terms] together: "Dharma-bādha" (obstruction of dharma) refers to that which, when being performed even with the intention of dharma, results in the obstruction of one's own dharma; "para-dharma" (another's dharma) refers to what is enjoined for one person but constitutes the dharma of another. He explains "upamā" (comparison) by saying: "But upadharma... regarding the word.

"Bheda" refers to a different interpretation [of a word] within a given context; for example, when it is said, "one should feed ten or fewer," it is interpreted as "fewer than ten. Regarding the reading "śabda-bhṛt," it means that which merely bears the word "dharma";
for example, when it is said, "one should give a cow," it refers to the giving of a cow that is about to die. ||13||
The sequence of composition: the phrase "obstruction of dharma" consists of one and a half [verses]. A *pākhaṇḍa* is one outside the Veda;
*dambha* is hypocrisy accompanied by deceit. ||13||

Viśvanātha, disregarding the sequence, explains all five [terms] as follows: *vidharma* is that wherein, even when performed with the intention of duty (*dharma*), there is a subversion of one's own duty (*svadharma-bādha*). That which is enjoined for one person is *paradharma* (the duty of another) for someone else. That which is heretical (*pāṣaṇḍa*)...

Hypocrisy (*dambha*) consists of wearing matted hair, ashes, and so forth, or of manifesting one's own righteousness; that is "counterfeit dharma" (*upadharma*). It is a semblance (*upamā*) of dharma, but not dharma itself—this is the meaning. An etymological analysis (*bhittibheda*) is an explanation by means of another method, as in the case of the statement: "one should feed at least ten Brahmins."
Having abandoned the *bahuvrīhi* compound, [the opponent argues] that "fewer than ten" means nine or eight, and not eleven;

this is a *chala* (quibble) because it is an interpretation based on a *tatpuruṣa* compound. In the reading *śabda-bhṛt*, it means "that which merely bears the word 'dharma'. For example, when it is said, "One should give a cow," [if the opponent insists it refers to a dead cow] regarding one about to die...
The gift of a cow. ||13||

But for whom is that dharma ordained by one's own nature— not merely a semblance created by men according to their desires and distinct from the [four] stages of life— not desired for the sake of tranquility?

Śrīdhara: Even after the performance of one's own duty (*svadharma*), another's duty (*paradharma*) should not be performed for the sake of increasing merit, because it is useless; thus he says: "That which is ordained by one's own nature" (14).
The sequence of composition: "intrinsic nature" is one half-verse. ||14||
Viśvanātha: That which is fashioned by will—consisting of the worship of imagined deities and so forth—is "appearance" (ābhāsa).
Therefore, the status of being a Brāhmaṇa or other caste is ordained by one's own essential nature (svabhāva), and not merely by birth alone. 14.
Even for the sake of Dharma, or for the sake of sustenance, a wealthy man should not strive for wealth;
for non-striving provides the livelihood for one who does not strive, just as it does for the great serpent.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, "the poor man" (adhana) should not seek wealth for the sake of dharma, nor should he look toward it, or rather, he should not exert himself for the sake of wealth; for it has already been stated that the fulfillment of one's own duty (svadharma) occurs through what is obtained by fate alone. He elaborates on this point—that one should not seek even for the sake of subsistence—in six and a half verses beginning with "he does not desire" (anīha).
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: One who is "without wealth" (*adhana*) means one who is destitute; he should not "seek" (*neheta*) wealth for the sake of "subsistence" (*yātrārtha*), that is, for the sake of maintaining the body, nor should he desire it, or rather, he should not strive toward it. For one who is "without seeking" (*anīhamānasya*), meaning one who does not desire, there is "non-seeking" (*anīhā*).
It is the state of being free from desire or the state of being without activity, [characteristic] of the great serpent who does not wake. ||15||
The happiness that belongs to one who is contented, free from worldly striving, and delights in his own self—
from where could that come for one who runs in all directions, driven by desire and greed and seeking wealth?
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
May all directions be filled with auspiciousness for those whose minds are ever-contented.
Just as one whose feet are protected by shoes remains safe from gravel, thorns, and the like.
Śrīdhara and Viśvanātha: "Upānat-pāt" refers to one whose feet possess sandals; his "krama-sandarbhaḥ" (the arrangement of the sequence) has not been explained.
O King, with what would a contented man not subsist, even if it were only water? Yet, due to the wretchedness of his sexual and gustatory desires, such a person acts like a domesticated beast.
Śrīdhara: He acts like a house-guarding dog. ||18||
The sequence of the composition: "He is content. By what would he not subsist? Rather, the meaning is that he may even subsist on water alone. ||18||

Viśvanātha: By what might he not subsist? The meaning is that he may even subsist on water. Regarding the function of the generative organ (*aupasthya*), out of wretchedness for it, he is like a dog guarding a house. ||18||
The splendor, learning, austerity, and fame of a dissatisfied Brahmin flow away through the restlessness of his senses,
and even his knowledge is scattered.
Śrīdhara: [Not commented upon].
Viśvanātha: It is scattered; it becomes cast down. ||19||

For one reaches the end of desire through hunger and thirst, and that of anger through the ripening of its fruit; yet people do not reach the end of greed, even after conquering and enjoying all the quarters of the earth.

Śrīdhara: Through hunger and thirst, a person reaches the end of desire (*kāma*), because there is no other desire beyond food and water. Or, one reaches the end of anger (*krodha*), because of the non-arising—that is, the non-attainment—of its fruit, which is violence (*hiṃsā*). Even after conquering the directions and the earth...
The meaning is that even after consuming it, one does not reach the end of greed. ||20||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: For dissatisfaction is rooted in greed, and because greed is difficult to conquer, he says—in two verses beginning with "of desire"—that dissatisfaction is hard to ward off; [he adds] "by hunger and thirst."
The meaning is that when food is unavailable and hunger and thirst become excessively intense, the burning of the bodily constituents (*dhātu-dāha*) occurs.

This is because of the arising—that is, the manifestation—of the fruit of this anger, which is violence (*hiṃsā*). Even after conquering the directions and enjoying the earth, one does not reach the end of greed, which consists of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
However, because greed regarding food is pacified simply by filling the stomach, it lacks the quality of being difficult to subdue; therefore, it has not been mentioned separately. ||20||
"O King, many are the wise ones who possess great knowledge and dispel doubt;
yet even some who are masters of assemblies fall downward due to lack of contentment."
Śrīdhara: Not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: He states that when greed is predominant, virtues become useless: "The learned... (21).
One should conquer desire through the absence of volitional construction, anger by abandoning desire,
greed by discerning the true nature of gain and loss, and fear by reflecting upon reality.

Śrīdhara: Now he states the means for conquering desire and the rest with four verses beginning with "By non-visualization" (asaṅkalpāt). The word "conquer" (jayed) is to be construed as appropriate in each case. [One conquers desire] by seeing the harmfulness in objects; [one conquers delusion] by the discernment of reality through the contemplation of non-duality. ||22||

The structural arrangement: the pair beginning with "asaṅkalpāt" [is explained]; by means of the discernment of reality (*tattvāvamarśa*)—that is, by the investigation into dependence upon the Supreme Lord—and by grace (*kṛpayā*), it is accompanied by devotion (*sādardhaka*). ||22||

Viśvanātha: Then, in response to the inquiry as to how one might conquer these [desires], he says: even when desire arises through the recollection of women and the like, one should conquer that desire by means of a resolve (*niścaya*) similar to a mental resolve (*saṅkalpa*), such as "a woman must not be enjoyed while she is immersed [in water]. The negative particle (*nañ*) here denotes similarity. For example, today... [is not].

When there is the resolve that "it must be eaten," one overcomes hunger and thirst through fasting and similar practices.
