By abandoning desire—desire being any object of longing—one should conquer anger by abandoning the wish to harm, thinking, "No object whatsoever is to be injured. One should conquer greed by practicing the perception of future harm in regard to wealth, that is, toward objects of covetousness.

Through the contemplation of reality, because that which has begun to bear fruit must necessarily be experienced, one realizes through the investigation of truth such questions as "who is the cause of whose suffering? and so forth. ||22||

One should overcome grief and delusion through the science of inquiry (ānvīkṣikī), hypocrisy through the worship of the Great One (Mahat), obstacles to yoga through silence, and violence through freedom from desire and other such impulses.

Śrīdhara: [The means are] through the discrimination between the self and the non-self by means of *ānvīkṣikī* (philosophical inquiry), and by service to great, virtuous beings; [one should avoid] obstacles to yoga, such as worldly talk and the like. ||23||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: By means of *ānvīkṣikī*, that is, through the investigation of the self and the non-self. ||23||
—o)0(o— By means of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), one should abandon suffering born of the elements and that which is caused by fate;
by the power of yoga, one should abandon that born of the self; and by cultivating purity (*sattva*), one should abandon sleep.
Śrīdhara: [One should counteract] by showing compassion toward those very beings from whom fear arises, through acting for their benefit.

"Fate" (*daiva*) refers to mental anguish and the like caused by divine afflictions; as Yājñavalkya has said: "Dejected and with unsuccessful undertakings, one sinks down without apparent cause. This is that which is born of the self (*ātma-ja*).

Born of the body; by the power of yoga, such as the strength of breath control (prāṇāyāma) and so forth; and by the practice of sattva, such as through a diet conducive to the quality of goodness (sattva). ||24||
The sequence of composition: "By grace," etc., consisting of one and a half verses.

Viśvanātha: The meaning is that one should act for the benefit of those very beings from whom suffering arises, out of compassion. "Divine" (daiva) refers to mental anguish and the like caused by the afflictions of fate.
As it was said by Yājñavalkya: "Dejected and with fruitless undertakings, he desponds without apparent cause."

By means of *samādhi*, that is, one-pointedness of mind upon the Blessed One; by the vigor of yoga, that is, through the power of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and so forth; by the practice of *sattva*, that is, by means of *sāttvika* food and the like; or by service toward all living beings—[one should overcome] the suffering born of the self, which arises from the body. ||24||
Passion and darkness are overcome by goodness, and goodness by tranquility;
indeed, a person may conquer all of this directly through devotion to the Guru.
Śrīdhara: This has not been explained.
Krama-sandarbha: By means of *sattva*, which consists of cessation through tranquility (*upaśama*). "This" refers to half a verse.
And the Śruti says:
"For that high-souled one who has supreme devotion for the Lord, and for the guru as for the Lord, these truths thus explained become manifest" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.23).
Therefore, in the Brahmavaivarta [Purāṇa]:
"He is met through devotion to the Guru; He is served by the wise through remembrance.
Even when met, He cannot be attained by living beings who are intent on egoism.
Thus [it is said]. In the *Pādma Purāṇa*, in the hymn of Devadyuti:
"If I possess that same supreme devotion toward my guru as I have for Hari, by that truth, may Hari reveal himself to me. (25)

Viśvanātha: Through *sattva*—that is, by the predominance of *sattva* over *rajas* and *tamas*—and through *sattva* itself, which is characterized by tranquility and its effect, namely equanimity, one shall conquer everything directly, swiftly, and without exertion. The meaning is that this alone is like a single great medicine for the pacification of all diseases. In that regard:
The conquest of desire and the rest is the direct fruit for the wise who possess devotion to the Guru, whereas for pure devotees it is a secondary result; this distinction should be observed. ||25||
For one who harbors a false notion regarding the Guru— who is the Blessed One in person and the bestower of the lamp of knowledge—
all that he has heard is like the bathing of an elephant.

Śrīdhara: [Objection: But how can there be victory over everything through devotion to the guru, since he too, being human, remains in that same [mortal] condition? To this, he says: "Of whom... One who has the false notion regarding mortals—that they are merely men—is of wicked intellect. For such a person, listening to the scriptures is as futile as an elephant's bath. (26)

The Sequence of Composition: Now, one might ask, "How can there be victory over everything through devotion to the guru, since he too possesses a human body and is subject to that same condition? To this, he says: *yasya* (of whom). One who has the false notion regarding mortals—that they are mere humans—is of poor intellect. For such a person, listening to the scriptures is as futile as an elephant bathing. (26)
The sequence of the composition: "The notion of unreality regarding mortals," and so forth. For this very reason it was said by the ancients:
"The notion of a stone regarding the worshipful Viṣṇu; the notion of an ordinary man regarding the gurus; the notion of caste-identity regarding a Vaiṣṇava;
the notion of mere water regarding the sacred water at the feet of Viṣṇu or of the Vaiṣṇavas—which crushes the impurities of the Kali age."
"He who possesses a cognition of commonality regarding the word for that mantra— which is pure and the destroyer of all impurities—
directed toward Viṣṇu, the Lord of all lords, or who holds a view of Him as equal to others, is a denizen of hell.
[Pañcarātra 114] Thus, verse 26.

Viśvanātha: Furthermore, even when devotion is abundant, if one regards the guru as a mere human being, everything becomes utterly futile; thus he says, "Of whom... The sense is that one should not even form the notion of the guru being a partial incarnation (*aṃśa*) of the Lord, let alone thinking of him as the Lord himself. Or rather, [this refers to] the object of worship...
The meaning is that while the Blessed One himself is directly present, the notion of his being a mortal— that is, the evil-mindedness of thinking "he is a mortal"—
renders his hearing of the Blessed One’s mantras and so forth, as well as his listening and reflection upon them, all in vain.
He is indeed the Blessed One, the Lord of Pradhāna and Puruṣa in person,
whose feet are sought after by the masters of yoga, yet whom the world considers a mere man.

Śrīdhara: [Objection: But surely even the teacher’s sons and others regard him as merely a human being? To this he says: "This teacher would indeed be the Lord himself. The meaning is that the world's notion that "this is a man" is an error. Or rather, it is not the case that he is perceived by his sons and others as a mere human being, even though they perceive him as such.
The venerable guru would not be [such]; the meaning is that he is like this Śrī Kṛṣṇa. ||27||
The sequence of the composition: Nor is this a wonder in the worlds—that such contemplation occurs toward the Lord directly—as he says: "This... (27).
Viśvanātha: But surely the guru’s father, son, and others, as well as his neighbors, regard him as merely a human being? How can this single disciple alone regard him as the Supreme Lord?
To this, he says: "This one... Whether he be the Blessed Lord, the delighter of the Yadus, or the delighter of the Raghus, he is certainly (*vai*) indeed [the Lord].

The Lord is the master of both Pradhāna and Puruṣa. Is that person—who is regarded as a man by the world at the time of his incarnation—actually a man? On the contrary, he is indeed the Supreme Lord; such is the sense in which the Guru also [is]. ||27||
All injunctions regarding the observances have as their sole purpose the restraint of the six groups [of afflictions];
if they do not lead to yoga, they are merely exhausting.

Śrīdhara: Having thus conquered the impulse of desire and the like through all means, and having become one whose senses are restrained, one should be devoted to meditation. Otherwise, for such a person, all the scriptures would be rendered futile; thus he says: "The group of six," etc. All injunctions regarding observances (*niyama*), as well as the rules for *iṣṭāpūrta* and so forth, [are intended for this purpose].

The meaning is that those whose end is in that very single restraint of the group of six sense organs are "intent on that alone. Yet, even with that much, their purpose is not yet fully accomplished; thus he says: "Even if they have that as their goal, if they do not bring about—that is, do not accomplish—the yogas, namely *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi*, then [they are] merely..."
The meaning is that they are indeed merely causes of fatigue. ||28||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: Furthermore, he states with the words "the sixfold group" (*ṣaḍ-varga*) that the very conquest of desire and the rest, which is accomplished through devotion to the Guru, is indeed the actual fruit of all the various means taught in every scripture.

The meaning is that all injunctions regarding observances (*niyama*)—which concern such acts as sacrifices and charitable works (*iṣṭāpūrta*)—have their ultimate end in that single thing: the restraint of the group of six senses; thus, they are solely devoted to that.
Now, one might object: "But surely, through devotion to the Guru, desires and the like are conquered, and even the Blessed One is attained."

"I am the self of all beings; I am pleased by service to the guru" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.80.34), and "Those who cross the ocean of worldly existence by means of my word or that of the guru" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.80.33)—from such statements of the Blessed One. Likewise, through the injunctions for observances (niyamas), the restraint of the sixfold group (ṣaḍ-varga) is accomplished.

"Is the Blessed Lord attainable or not? To this he says: "Those who end with that [the individual self] would not bring about, nor accomplish, yogas such as meditation on the Blessed Lord because they are solely intent upon that alone; how then could they cause one to reach the Blessed Lord? This is the meaning. And if they do not bring it about, then they are merely a source of weariness in this matter—of what doubt is there?"
The state of being. ||28||
Just as worldly pursuits such as agriculture and the like do not support the goal of yoga and may instead lead to misfortune,
so too for one who is not established in truth, ritual offerings and sacrifices become useless.

Śrīdhara: He states this very point by means of an illustration: "Just as worldly pursuits such as agriculture and their fruits do not accomplish the goal of yoga, which is liberation, but rather lead to misfortune and to saṃsāra itself;
so too it is with the rites of iṣṭāpūrta and the like for one who is untruthful and outward-looking. (29)

*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: He states this very point by way of an illustration: "Just as agriculture and the like, though they accomplish objects that are to be enjoyed, do not accomplish the goal of yoga, which is liberation (*mokṣa*); and if..."
If they do not accomplish liberation, then those [rites] would lead only to misfortune and a lack of purpose;
likewise, for one who is non-existent—that is, one who is not a devotee of the Lord—sacrificial offerings, charitable works, and so forth, result only in fruitlessness. ||29||
He who is intent on the conquest of the mind, free from attachment and without possessions,
solitary, taking refuge in seclusion, and a mendicant whose food is limited to alms; ||| o)0(o— ||| he is a true monk.

Śrīdhara: Even for one who thus practices yoga, if the mind should become distracted through attachment to family and the like, he states what must be done for such a person: "He who is striving, exerting himself for the conquest of the mind, should become a mendicant; he should renounce. And so says the Smṛti:

"Having clearly perceived that the life of a householder is struck by pairs of opposites (dvandva) and is a cause for the disruption of meditation and other such hindrances, a householder should renounce without hesitation. Thus it is said. He is one whose food is limited and obtained through begging. (30)
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: Thus, the conquest of desire and the like, as well as the method for liberation, have been described even for the householder.
However, he who—due to the fault of attachment to family and the like—is unable to conquer desire and the like despite his efforts, he [should proceed as follows].
He says that a monk (*bhikṣu*) indeed should be free from attachment—referring to the word "he" (*yaḥ*). He who is *yataḥ*, meaning diligent, he should be a monk.
And thus says the *Smṛti*:
"For one struck by the pairs of opposites (*dvandva*), the state of a householder is a cause for the interruption of meditation and so forth."
"Having clearly perceived [the truth], a householder should renounce without hesitation. Thus it is said. He is one whose food is limited and obtained through begging. (30)
O King, having established his seat in a clean and level place, he should sit upon it—
firm, comfortable, and even— with his limbs straight and uttering "Om."
Śrīdhara: He whose limbs are straight and even; he should sit in such a way that there is comfort. The words "uttering 'Om'" are to be understood as the ellipsis. ||31||
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: He whose limbs are straight and even; the words "uttering 'Oṃ'" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. —o)0(o—
One should restrain the prāṇa and apāna breaths through inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka),
while gazing at the tip of one's own nose, until the mind abandons all desires.
Whithersoever the mind, struck by desire and wandering, goes forth,
from there the wise man should draw it back and gradually restrain it within the heart.
It has not been explained by anyone at all.
Thus, for the ascetic who practices in this way, the mind is mastered in a very short time.
His nirvana proceeds incessantly, like a fire without fuel.
Śrīdhara: Thus, for that ascetic who practices incessantly, the mind attains extinction and peace. (34)
Kramasandarbha: Not commented upon.
Viśvanātha: He attains *nirvāṇa*, which is peace. ||34||
The mind that is unpierced by desire and other passions, whose all functions have been stilled,
and which has touched the bliss of Brahman, shall never again arise at any time.

Śrīdhara: Furthermore, he says that it should not be distracted again: "That mind which is undisturbed by desire and the like shall not rise up. Why? Because all its mental fluctuations (vṛttis) have become completely stilled. How so? Because it has been touched by the bliss of Brahman. ||35||
The *Krama-sandarbha* by Viśvanātha has not been commented upon. —
He who, having previously gone forth from his home— which is the field for sowing the three aims of life— once again...
If a monk should serve them, he is indeed one who eats what has been vomited and is devoid of shame.

Śrīdhara: He censures one who, even after having taken up the life of renunciation (*pravrajyā*), might still desire enjoyment; such a person is referred to by the word "yaḥ" (who). From that house in which the triad of dharma and the other [ends of human pursuit] is sown (*upyate*) on all sides (*ā*), he departs those very things—dharma and so forth. He is a consumer of vomit (*vāntāśī*), eating what has been spat out, and is utterly shameless. ||36||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: Having previously renounced from that house in which the three aims of life (*trivarga*) were sown, he later again pursues those very same duties of a householder; he is one who eats what has been vomited (*vāntāśī*), a consumer of what has been spat out, and is devoid of shame.
Those who consider their own body— which is non-self, mortal, and like excrement, worms, or ashes— to be the self,
and who, having identified with it, boast of it, are indeed the most wretched of men.

Śrīdhara: Nor is this impossible, for it is observed in experience; thus he says: "Those by whom their own body was previously remembered and contemplated as being non-self and so forth, they indeed, having again considered it as the self, praise and extol it. (37)
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: It has been contemplated that the non-self, the body, is not the self; [it is thought] that at the end, like excrement, worms, or ashes, it will take the form of excrement, worms, or ashes—oh, even now!
The meaning is that [the body] is equal to excrement, worms, and ashes. For this very reason, "having made this body one's own" means having regarded it as the self itself. ||37||
The abandonment of ritual duties by a householder, the abandonment of vows by a student,
the service of a village by an ascetic, and the restlessness of the senses in a mendicant.
For these are indeed outcasts from the stages of life, mere mockeries of the stages;
one should look upon them with compassion, for they are deluded by divine illusion.
Śrīdhara: Taking the ascetic as a representative example, he censures others who abandon their own duty as well, by means of two verses beginning with "gṛhasthasya.
The sequence of the composition has not been explained.

Viśvanātha: *Lolatā* means fickleness. One should overlook [the disciple] out of compassion; that is, having approached him out of compassion, one should provide instruction in reality (*tattva*) and so forth. The sense is that [otherwise], such efforts would be rendered futile for him regarding those [teachings]. ||38-39||
If one who has shaken off all mental impurities through supreme knowledge should realize the Self,
desiring what or for what reason would that sensualist nourish a body?
Śrīdhara: Now, one might ask: what fault is there even if a mendicant who knows the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) still possesses longing for the senses?

To this he says: "If he should know the Self as the Supreme Brahman. The meaning is that for such a knower whose latent tendencies (*āśaya*, *vāsanā*) have been shaken off—that is, eliminated—by knowledge, such longing is simply impossible. And so it is said:
The Śruti says:
"If a person were to know the Self as 'This am I,' desiring what, or for the sake of what desire, would he suffer along with the body? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.12).

*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: Among those [categories], he specifically censures the mendicant (*bhikṣu*) with the words "the self" (*ātmānam*). Here, the optative suffix (*liṅ*) in "one should know" (*vijānīyāt*) is injunctive; by it, this meaning is obtained through implication (*ākṣepa*).

"Being one whose latent tendencies have been purified by knowledge, he should know himself"—if this were the object of an injunction, then [the question would be] "desiring what," and so forth. By the phrase "he nourishes the body," the greed of the tongue-faculty is indicated; by the word "lascivious," the greed of the organ of generation is implied. "But distinct from the body" means separate from the physical frame. (40)
They say that the body is the chariot, the senses are the horses, and the mind is the reins of the lord of the senses.
The eyelids, the measure, the intellect, the charioteer, the essence, the broad seat, and that which is created by the Lord;

Śrīdhara: However, because the ignorant person falls into hell due to restlessness, one must always strive for the knowledge of reality with vigilance; this is the meaning [of the verse]: "Know the self as the rider in the chariot, and the body as the chariot itself" (KaU 1.3.3).

He speaks by means of the allegory of the chariot as described in such scriptural passages, using six verses beginning with "They say": they say that the mind is the lord of the senses and the reins are the rays; they say that the objects of the senses, such as sound and so forth, are the paths—the destinations to be traveled—and that the mind (*sattva*) is the broad seat that pervades the body, for without the mind there is no binding.
The body becomes as if unbound; the meaning is that it is created by the Lord (īśa), for the Lord alone is the agent of bondage. ||41||
The sequence of the composition: the phrase "they say" constitutes a *yugmaka* (couplet). Here, "unrighteousness" (*adharma*) refers to renunciation (*sannyāsa*) in the form of abandoning one's duty.
Thus, even though there is the entirety of the chariot and the *Sāman* chants, it is indeed useless without the bow and so forth; therefore he says: "For the bow... (41).

Viśvanātha: That very body, senses, and so forth which are a cause of misfortune for one who is heedless, become the means for achieving the desired goal for the heedful yogin; this is the meaning [of the passage]: "Know the self as the rider in the chariot, and the body as the chariot itself" (KaU 1.3.3).

He speaks by means of the metaphor of the chariot as described in such scriptural passages, using six verses beginning with "They say": they call the mind the lord of the senses and the reins the cords; they call the objects of the senses, such as sound and so forth, the paths—the destinations to be traveled;
and they call the mind (*sattva*), which is vast and pervades the body, the seat and the fastening. Without the mind...
The meaning is that the body becomes unbound. The implication is that the Lord is the creator of the bondage;
thus, "created by the Lord" (īśa-sṛṣṭam) is an adjective qualifying all things, such as the chariot and so forth. ||41||
The senses are the ten vital breaths; unrighteousness and righteousness are the two wheels; and the individual soul (jīva) is the charioteer who possesses self-conceit.
For they declare that his bow is the syllable Om (praṇava),
the arrow is the individual soul (jīva), and the supreme goal alone is the target.

Śrīdhara says: The tenfold vital breath (*prāṇa*) consists of the five beginning with *prāṇa*, as well as *nāga*, *kūrma*, *kṛkala*, *devadatta*, and *dhanañjaya* [Gorakṣa-śataka 24]. He identifies the ego-consciousness (*abhimāna*), which is accompanied by the sense of "I," as the individual soul (*jīva*) acting as the charioteer; the pure *jīva* as the arrow; and the Supreme Brahman as the target.
Just as an arrow is brought down upon the target by means of a bow, so too the individual soul (jīva) is brought down into Brahman by means of the syllable *praṇava*; this is the meaning. ||42||
Kramasandarbha: This has not been explained.

Viśvanātha: They describe the tenfold vital breath (*prāṇa*) as the chariot, and the individual soul (*jīva*), consisting of egoity (*abhimāna*), as the charioteer. They describe the *praṇava* (the syllable Om), obtained through the great value of the Guru’s grace, as the bow.

The pure individual soul (*jīva*) is the arrow; the Supreme Brahman is the target. Just as an arrow is made to fall upon a target by means of a bow, so too the individual soul is made to fall into Brahman by means of the *praṇava*—this is the meaning.
Now, one might object: since the Supreme Brahman is also treated as a target due to its association with the metaphors of the chariot and so forth, [is it not merely an object?]
The state of being an enemy has arrived. For it is the enemy himself who, having mounted the chariot, is both pierced and joined by the arrow;
is his enmity toward the individual soul (jīva) due to his binding the soul through his own power of māyā? True;
for that which [is established] in the heart of one who is firmly yoked in yoga through the restrained breath, mind, and senses—

The verse, "Even enemies resort to that [the Lord] through remembrance, as do the sages" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 10.87.23), reveals a commonality between the sages and enemies by their association with one another; for both alike have surrendered themselves at the feet of the Supreme Lord. As for the Supreme Lord:

Some maintain that He grants liberation from both of these [the Lord and the devotees] upon perceiving His own assistance through the bliss of the heroic sentiment (*vīra-rasa*) and the subtle portion of His own devotion existing within their consciousness. Others, however, hold that although the Supreme Self is the object of perception, He acts like a fish for Rādhā— the sovereign queen present at the *svayaṃvara* of Draupadī and others.

It is exactly so and not otherwise. Just as Arjuna and others attained Draupadī and the rest by piercing him with arrows through the very strength of their own arms, in the same way, the wise declare that even those possessed of knowledge attain liberation solely through the power of devotion. ||41||
Passion, hatred, greed, sorrow, delusion, fear, and pride;
arrogance, contempt, envy, deceit, violence, and jealousy.
Passion, negligence, hunger, sleep, and so forth are the enemies;
they are of the nature of *rajas* and *tamas*, though occasionally they may be of the nature of *sattva*.

Śrīdhara: Passion and the like are the enemies to be conquered. (43) Among these, *rajas* is dogmatic attachment (*abhiniveśa*). Furthermore, for one who has ascended to samādhi, even activities such as helping others—which arise from the nature of *sattva*—are enemies. (44)
Kramasandarbha: Not explained.

Viśvanātha: Just as wicked kings who obstruct the attainment of a maiden at her *svayaṃvara* are slain by one who is more powerful, even so, by the power of devotion to the Lord, the ascetic takes up the sword of knowledge (*jñānāsi*) and—
Attachment, aversion, and so forth have the nature of *rajas* and *tamas*; in some cases, such as altruism and the like, they have the nature of *sattva*. ||43-44||
As long as he maintains this human body-chariot, made serviceable through his own mastery, sharpened by the worship of the most venerable feet;
Wielding the sword of knowledge with the power of the Infallible, having destroyed all enemies, satisfied in his own bliss and being utterly tranquil, he would abandon this world.

Śrīdhara: As long as one maintains this chariot in the form of a human body, under one's own control and equipped with the retinue of the senses and so forth, for that very duration, one should— taking refuge in Acyuta and wielding the sharp sword of knowledge sharpened by service at the feet of the most venerable gurus— [proceed].
The meaning is that, having become one whose enemies are cast out, who is tranquil, and satisfied with his own bliss, he should remain indifferent toward this chariot and so forth. ||45||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: As long as one maintains that chariot which has the form of a human body and is equipped with a retinue of senses and so forth under one's own control, for that long [one remains] among the most venerable gurus.

The meaning is that by serving the feet [of the Guru], one wields the sharpened sword of knowledge; being endowed with the strength of devotion to Acyuta, one becomes one who has cast out all enemies.
Then, becoming satisfied through the attainment of one's own kingdom—namely, one's own bliss—one should abandon this chariot and so forth precisely because they are no longer of use.

In this regard, just as a person is not separated from his chariot, bow, arrows, and so forth— which are superior to [mere] strength— when he achieves his goal of conquering an enemy or regaining his own kingdom, so too the man of knowledge is not separated from the body, which is a constituent of *prakṛti*, nor from knowledge, which is the means for attaining liberation.

Separated from knowledge, one attains union (*sāyujya*) with the Supreme Self through exclusive devotion (*bhakti*) alone, which is inherent within knowledge; one is never separated from that [Self]. This is because devotion functions as a mode of the Supreme Self’s own essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*), and thus is identical with the Supreme Self, whereas both knowledge and ignorance function as modes of the power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*); therefore, those two are disregarded.

This is indeed appropriate. For this very reason, they recite that his bow is the *praṇava* (the sacred syllable Om) and the arrow is the *jīva* (the individual soul), while the supreme goal alone is the target. Just as in the case of chariots and the like, even when separated from the bow, the arrow—by means of human effort that has attained the nature of velocity—reaches the target through the power of that [effort] alone.

In the same way, the pure soul (*śuddha-jīva*), having abandoned the body, senses, and so forth— which constitute the impure soul— as well as *avidyā* whose nature is ignorance, and being accompanied solely by the power of devotion (*bhakti-śakti*) residing within the impure soul,
comes to know the Supreme Self through that very power and attains union (*sāyujya*) with Him.
He attains it. As it was said by the Blessed One:
"One who has become Brahman, whose self is serene, neither grieves nor desires;
equal toward all beings, he attains supreme devotion to Me."
"By devotion he comes to know Me in truth—both who I am and what I am;
then, having known Me in truth, he enters into Me immediately thereafter. (Gītā 18.54–55) This is the meaning of these two verses.
The meaning is as follows: through the ripening of knowledge mixed with devotion (*bhakti*), upon the removal of what is to be abandoned, one becomes Brahman;

that is to say, by virtue of unobscured consciousness, one is of the nature of Brahman. Furthermore, because the turbidity of the *guṇas* has departed, this self is serene; thus, it is "that" [the Self]. Consequently, it is not as if [consciousness] were lost, as it was in the previous state.

He grieves, yet he does not long for what is unattained, because of the absence of ego-identification with the body and so forth; this is the sense. He is equal toward all beings, whether auspicious or inauspicious, because of the absence of external mental preoccupation; this is the sense. And therefore, even when knowledge has become tranquil like a fire whose fuel is exhausted, his devotion to Me—which is imperishable and inherent within that knowledge—[remains].

He attains it; for since that [state] consists of the function of my own essential nature (*svarūpa-śakti*), it is distinct from the power of *māyā*, and thus it does not cease even when ignorance (*avidyā*) and knowledge (*vidyā*) have both disappeared. For this very reason, as previously stated, he attains the "supreme" (*parām*) which is "absolute" (*kevalām*) because it remains after desireless action, knowledge, and so forth.

The sense is that although she existed by means of a portion (*kalā*) for the sake of accomplishing liberation through knowledge, dispassion, and so forth, there was no clear perception of her among all beings, as if she were their inner controller (*antaryāmin*).
For this very reason, instead of using the verb "performs" (*kurute*), the form "attains" (*labhate*) is employed. [She was] mixed among the black gram, green gram, and other grains.

Just as one might obtain a golden jewel-casket—unspoiled even when those [other objects] have perished—separately and exclusively from among them; however, for one possessing complete *prema-bhakti*, there is no possibility of obtaining that at such a time, nor is its fruit *sāyujya*. Therefore, [the text speaks of] the supreme...
The phrase "the characteristic of love" (*prema-lakṣaṇam*) need not be explained further.
Now, one might ask: "What would happen to Him by means of that devotion once it is attained?
To this, he says "by devotion" (*bhaktyā*), introducing another point: "Me, who I am and how great I am. Me.

Only a person of realized knowledge (*jñānī*) or a devotee of various kinds knows that reality (*tat-padārtha*) through devotion alone in its true essence, according to my statement: "I am to be grasped by exclusive devotion" (*bhāgavata-purāṇa* 11.14.11).
Since this is so, therefore, immediately after that [realization], through that very devotion, upon the cessation of [theoretical] knowledge (*vidyoparamāt*), [one attains the goal].

Only at a later time, having known Me, he enters Me and experiences the bliss of union with Me (*matsāyujya*). The sense is that because I am beyond *māyā* and ignorance (*avidyā*) is itself *māyā*, I am unattainable even by knowledge (*vidyā*).
As for that which...
"Sāṅkhya and Yoga, dispassion, austerity, and devotion to Keśava—this is the five-fold knowledge by which a wise man enters Hari" (Nārada Pañcarātra).
Thus, devotion is heard of as being the very mode of that knowledge; for that indeed follows upon the bliss of union with Me.

A certain portion of devotion itself, which functions as the *hlādinī* potency, has entered into knowledge for the sake of making that knowledge fruitful, just as it enters into the yoga of action (*karma-yoga*) for the sake of making that action fruitful. For it is stated that without it, the yogas of action, knowledge, and so forth are mere labor. Therefore, devotion is *nirguṇa*.
In reality, there is no functioning of knowledge (*vidyā*) that consists of the quality of *sattva*.

Furthermore, according to the traditional teaching (smṛti), "From *sattva* arises knowledge" (Gītā 14.17), just as *sattva* is knowledge and indeed *vidyā*, so too the knowledge arising from devotion is itself devotion; thus, knowledge is also [devotion].
It should be understood as being twofold. ||45||
Otherwise, if it is heedless, the unwholesome horses of the senses, driven by their charioteer, lead it onto a wrong path and cast it among the robbers that are the sense-objects.
Those robbers cast him, along with his charioteer, into the blind darkness of this worldly pit, which is filled with the great fear of death.

Śrīdhara: He states the refutation [of the opposite view] regarding the absence of taking refuge in Acyuta with the words "If not. Those who are non-existent and outward-turned, who are the horses of the senses and the charioteer, lead one onto the wrong path—the path of worldly activity (*pravṛtti-mārga*)—and cast one among the bandits known as sense-objects. This refers to that which exists together with the horses and the charioteer; [it is cast] into the blinding darkness (*tamas*).
In that which is pervaded by great fear of death. ||46||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.

*Viśvanātha*: [He says] "If not," meaning that if there were an absence of the power of Acyuta, the goal would not be accomplished; on the contrary, there would even be a downward fall. If the charioteer (the Lord) had no power, or in the alternative case, if the individual soul (jīva) [had no power]...

The meaning is that devotion would not arise. Just as climbing [a tree] is itself negligence for the purpose of hitting a target when one is intoxicated and lacks strength, so too are those bandits—namely, attachment, aversion, and the rest.
Vedic action is of two kinds: that which leads to worldly involvement and that which leads to withdrawal.
Through the former one revolves in saṃsāra; through the latter one attains immortality.

Śrīdhara: Now, raising the objection, "How could such a calamity befall a person who performs the sacrifices and works of public utility (*iṣṭāpūrta*) prescribed by the Vedas?", he states the difference in results while showing the twofold nature of Vedic actions with the ten verses beginning with "pravṛttam ca" (47).
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: Now, one might object: "The enjoyment of sense objects is also enjoined by the scripture, not merely prohibited.
True; however, the systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*) therein should be understood according to the difference in qualified practitioners (*adhikārī*) and the difference in results (*phala*).
He said: "And the active [life]... with ten [verses]. The householder revolves; the ascetic partakes of the immortal.
(o)0(o)—The Agnihotra and other rites consist of material substances, involve violence, are performed for specific desires, and do not grant peace.
The New Moon sacrifice, the Full Moon sacrifice, the Four-Monthly sacrifices, the Animal sacrifice, and the Soma extraction;

Śrīdhara: *Hiṃsra* refers to acts such as those involving hawks and the like. *Aśāntida* means characterized by excessive attachment. The explanation of the meaning of the word "etc. (*ādi*) is shown by the phrase "and the Darśa sacrifice. *Paśu* refers to the animal sacrifice; *suta* refers to the Soma sacrifice.
This is the sequence of the composition: the pair beginning with *hiṃsra*, and *pūrta*, which is characterized by the construction of temples and similar works.
The meaning is "that which is called the active [state]."

Viśvanātha: "Violent" refers to acts such as those involving hawks and other birds; it bestows no peace and grants excessive attachment. He explains the meaning of the word "etcetera": "Darśa" refers to the animal sacrifice (paśu-yāga); "Suta" refers to the Soma sacrifice.

This is what is intended by the term "pravṛtta": namely, *huta* and *prahuta*, as well as *pūrta*, which is characterized by the construction of temples, pleasure groves, wells, and other such works of public utility.

Śrīdhara: *Huta* refers to the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice; *prahuta* refers to the offering of the *bali*. All of this is called *iṣṭa*. The meaning is that if this very same [activity] is performed for selfish desire (*kāmya*) and does not bring peace, then it is also termed *pravṛtta*.
*Ājīvya* means a water-station (*prapā*). 49.
Kramasandarbha: This has not been explained.
Viśvanātha: *Huta* is the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice; *prahuta* is the offering of the *bali*. All of this is called *iṣṭa*. *Ājīvya* refers to a water-shed (*prapā*). (49)
Subtle matter, fruition, smoke, night, waning,
the southern solstice, the moon, the new moon, and herbs and creepers.
"Food is semen," O Lord of the Earth; this is the path of the ancestors, leading to rebirth.
Having become each [element] in successive order, one is born here again and again.

Śrīdhara: By means of active karma, he describes the manner of return through ascent and descent—the subtle transformation (*vipāka*) of substances such as the *caru* and *puroḍāśa* offerings, which is the modification (*pariṇāma*) that initiates another body; enveloped by this, one departs, which is precisely what is referred to in the Śruti by the word "waters" (*ap*). Thus...
"At the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.3.3).

In an alternative reading, by the word *dravya* (substance), the sense organs—which were referred to by the term "elements of fire" (*tejo-mātrā*)—are meant; and by the words "heat" (*uṣma*) and "digestion" (*vipāka*), the illumination at the tip of the heart is indicated. And so says the Śruti: "He [the self], these..."
"Taking up the subtle elements of fire (*tejo-mātrāḥ*), he enters into the heart" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.1).

Likewise: "The tip of his heart flashes forth; by that, this self (*ātman*) departs" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2). The words "smoke" and so forth refer to the deities presiding over those respective elements.
In this context, *apakṣaya* refers to the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa-pakṣa*). *Soma* refers to the world of Soma.
Regarding the manner of descent for one who has experienced his enjoyments there, he says "at the new moon" (*darśa*), and so forth.
By means of a figurative indication (*viparīta-lakṣaṇā*), "disappearance" is expressed as the dissolution of the body through the fire of grief caused by the exhaustion of distinguished enjoyments.

This is what is meant: one who is joined with the subtle elements (bhūta-sūkṣma) and led by the presiding deities of the *ātivāhika* body to the world of Soma through meditation and so forth, at the conclusion of those enjoyments, his body dissolves and he is born again through the medium of rain, following the sequence of attaining the state of herbs, creepers, and the like. ||50||

Thus, the cause of rebirth is the path of active karma known as the "father's vehicle" (pitṛ-yāna). O Lord of the Earth! He speaks further of rebirth: having come into being one by one, individually and in succession, and having attained various proximate states, one is born here upon this earth. (51)
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: He describes the manner of return through ascent and descent by means of active karma—starting with the word "dravya. First, he shows the steps for the ascent up to Soma. Initially...

The subtle transformation (*vipāka*) of the substance—the *caru*, *puroḍāśa*, and so forth—is the modification (*pariṇāma*) that initiates another body; enveloped by this, the soul departs, and it is precisely this which is designated by the word "water" (*ap*) in the Śruti. It attains that first [element], for thus it is said: "But here, at the fifth oblation, the waters come to possess human speech."

Thus [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.3.3]. In the reading "substance (dravya) and digestion by heat (uṣma-vipāka)," the word "substance" refers to the sense organs mentioned by the term "fiery elements" (tejo-mātrā), while the phrase "digestion by heat" refers to the radiance at the tip of the heart.
In that case, one first attains the sense organs which accomplish good deeds, and thereafter the smoke.

Such is the sequence. And so says the Śruti: "Taking these particles of light (tejo-mātrā) with him, he descends into the heart" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.1). And likewise: "The tip of his heart flashes forth; by that, this self departs" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2). By means of the words "smoke" and so forth...

The deities presiding over each of those [stages] are so called. From there, one reaches the deity presiding over smoke, and from there the deity presiding over night, and so forth. "Apakṣaya" refers to the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇa-pakṣa).
"Soma" is the world of the moon. Having reached the world of Soma by means of the deities who serve as superintendents of the path beginning with smoke, one experiences enjoyments.
The meaning is "he enjoys.
Regarding that, he describes the manner of descent for one who has finished enjoying [the fruits of his actions] with the words "at the new moon" (*darśe*).
By the new moon, which is characterized by the waning of the moon, the waning of the body of enjoyment is indicated. From that...

Through the medium of rain and so forth, [the soul becomes] herbs, creepers, and the like; from that, it is that very semen which was consumed. O Lord of the Earth! He explains the aforementioned manner of descent with the words "one by one":
the meaning is that it becomes herbs and so forth in due order. (50–51)
The twice-born, consecrated by the purificatory rites beginning with conception and ending at the cremation ground,
offer the sacrifices of action into the senses, which are lamps of knowledge.
[She] remembers the gods presiding over the sacrifice as being under the control of those who preside over the senses;
they are subject to the mind, remaining under the sway of the Lord of the Gods (Indra),
and remain under the sway of Rudra, [who is] Pārvatī, whose essence is the Vedas.
One should place Rudra, who consists of the three *varṇas*, in the remainder which is of the nature of the *praṇava*;
one should place him, in the form of the *bindu*, in Sarasvatī, and her again in him. From the root-place, one should place her in the Formless One, and him in Vāyu, and that in Janārdana.
"Or rather, one should place the vital breath (prāṇa) in Prakṛti or in that very Puruṣottama," thus it is stated in the Brahma-tarka. 52.

Śrīdhara: Regarding this, he states the qualified person: "From conception... and so forth. The meaning is that another person, even if they perform rites such as sacrifices (*iṣṭādi*), does not obtain birth in this way. Teaching the specific practice of meditation and so on for one who is established in renounced action (*nivṛtta-karma-niṣṭha*), he describes the attainment of the world of Brahman by way of the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi-mārga*) starting from the verse beginning with "In the senses... and so forth.

Alternatively, since violence is difficult to avoid in sacrifices involving material substances (*dravya-yajña*), he speaks as follows to demonstrate that the most primary [form of sacrifice] is indeed the action of renunciation (*nivṛtta-karman*): "In those [sacrifices], they shine by means of knowledge. The meaning is that they cultivate the state of the mere instruments of the senses within the activities of the senses, such as *iṣṭāpūrta* (sacrificial rites and public works). Thus...
Also in what follows. ||52||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained. *Viśvanātha*: Therein, he states the primary qualified person for ritual action (*karmādhikārin*) with the words "from conception" (*niṣekāt*) etc.

Having described one who is devoted to active ritual action (*pravṛtta-karma*), [he now describes] one who is devoted to renounced ritual action (*nivṛtta-karma*) by way of the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi-mārga*).
He speaks of the attainment of the world of Brahman: they offer the sacrifices of action into the senses, which shine by means of knowledge.
The meaning is that, because they consist of the activity of the senses, they cultivate the state of being merely the senses. The same applies to the subsequent cases as well. ||52||
One should dissolve the sense organs into the mind, the mind— which is subject to transformation— into speech,
speech into the collection of phonemes, and that collection into the syllable *oṃ*, which is the primordial tone.
One should place the syllable Oṃ in the Bindu, that [Bindu] in the Nāda, and that [Nāda] in the Prāṇa, and that [Prāṇa] in the Mahat.

Śrīdhara: In the *ūrmi*—that is, in the mind whose nature consists of the volitions (*saṅkalpa*) of seeing and so forth; "modified" (*vaikārika*) means possessed of modification. The mind undergoes modifications such as agency through speech, which is characterized by injunctions and the like. [This occurs] in the collection (*samāmnāya*), that is, the aggregate of phonemes (*varṇa*), because it is a particular instance thereof.

[One dissolves] speech into the vowels; the vowels, consisting of the triad beginning with *a*, into the syllable *o*; that into the *bindu*; that into the *nāda*; that into the vital breath (*prāṇa*) whose nature is the *sūtra*; and that into the Great Brahman. ||53||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not explained.
*Viśvanātha*: [The mind] is in the *ūrmi* (wave) which consists of the volitions of seeing and so forth;
the *vaikārika* (transformative) mind, characterized by modification, resides in speech; for it is by means of speech, characterized by injunctions and the like, that the mind [is directed].

It undergoes modifications such as agency and so forth. [This occurs] in the collection of phonemes within the traditional recitation (samāmnāya). Because speech has that as its object, [it dissolves] into the vowel, which consists of the three vowels beginning with *a*; into the syllable *o* within the *bindu*; and that into the resonance (*nāda*).
[Finally, it dissolves] into the vital breath (*prāṇa*) whose nature is the thread (*sūtra*), and into the Great Brahman. ||53||
Agni, Sūrya, Divā, Prāhṇa, Śukla, Rākā, Uttara, and Svarāṭ; Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña— the fourth is the Self (Ātman) through their synthesis.
Madhva, Svarāṭ, Indra,
Viśvādya, and Aniruddhādya— these are proclaimed as the two groups;
those others who possess the form of Viṣṇu, the liberator goes to all of them.
Other sons of Dyu as well, all those who dwell near Dyu, cause him to reach Dyu; he [reaches] Vāyu and Hari separately.
"Viśvādirūpa, Turya, and Vāsudeva are none other [than the Self]," it is said; and also:
"Having become superior by means of happiness and the like, the devotee who knows the path shall certainly not attain a low state. ||54||

Śrīdhara: "Agni"—these are the deities presiding over those respective [periods]. He attains them, as before. *Divāha* means day; *prāhṇa* is its end. *Rākā* is the end of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pakṣa*).
Alternatively, according to the Purāṇic view, *prāhṇa* and *rākā* refer to the same thing. The subsequent [term] is the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*). *Svarāṭ* is Brahmā.
Thus, regarding one who has gone to the world of Brahmā (brahma-loka), he describes the manner of liberation at the conclusion of enjoyment: "The universe," and so forth.
The universe is the gross adjunct; having dissolved that gross [state] into the subtle, it becomes Taijasa, which has the subtle as its adjunct.
Having dissolved the subtle into the causal, it becomes Prājña, which has the causal as its adjunct. And the cause...

By being associated with the state of being the witness of all, [the Self] dissolves into the nature of the witness and becomes the Fourth (turya). Upon the dissolution of those changing objects of witnessing, the Self becomes pure; this means it is liberated.
This sequence of the composition has not been explained.

Viśvanātha: "Agni" refers to those deities who preside over the respective [elements]. He "attains" them, as explained previously. "Day" (*divāha*) means the forenoon; its end is the same. "Bright" (*śukla*) means the end of the bright fortnight; its end is the same as *rākā*. "Northern" (*uttara*) means the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*). "Svarāṭ" is Brahmā. Thus, [he attains] the world of Brahmā (*brahma-loka*).

He describes the manner of liberation for one who has departed at the conclusion of his enjoyment: the Viśva, whose gross adjunct is the body, dissolves that gross state into the subtle and becomes the Prājña, whose adjunct is the causal state. And the causal state, by virtue of its persistence as the witness of all, dissolves into the nature of the Witness itself and becomes the Turya Self. Of these...
And through the dissolution of the wavering witnesses, the self becomes pure; the meaning is that it is liberated.
They call this the path of the gods, which proceeds by becoming [the various stages] one after another in due order.
For one who sacrifices to the Self, whose self is tranquil and who is established in the Self, does not return.
Śrīdhara: The meaning is that he does not return in the same manner as others do;
this is the sequence of the textual connection (*krama-sandarbha*), though it has not been explicitly explained.
Viśvanātha: Having become situated on the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi-mārga*), [he proceeds] "in succession" (*anupūrvaśaḥ*), that is, by way of sequential order (*ānupūrvya-krameṇa*).
He who knows these two paths of the ancestors and the gods, fashioned by the Veda,
does not become deluded even while living among people, for he sees with the eye of the scripture.

Śrīdhara: By such passages as "Those who follow the Veda proceed toward smoke" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.16) and "They proceed toward light" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.1), the matter is determined and made known through discernment; thus, even while remaining among people and situated in a body, one does not become deluded.

Krama-sandarbha: This has not been explained. Viśvanātha: By means of the passage beginning with "By the fire produced by the Veda, they attain the smoke" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.16), and by the passage beginning with "They attain the flame" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 5.10.1).
And: "Even though staying among people, even though staying in the body. ||56||
At the beginning and at the end of people, existing both externally and internally, as the higher and the lower;
He Himself is knowledge and the object of knowledge, speech and that which is to be spoken, darkness and light.
Because honey causes exhaustion, it is darkness. ||57||

Śrīdhara: He states the reason for this with the words "in the beginning. That which exists as the cause at the beginning of the bodies of living beings and as the limit at the end—that which is external as the object of enjoyment and internal as the enjoyer;
that which is supreme and inferior, high and low; darkness (tamas) as non-illumination and light (jyotis) as illumination—all that is this Knower.

The meaning of the sequence of the composition is this: there is no object whatsoever that exists as distinct from Him by which one might be deluded. He explains the cause for the absence of delusion—the fact that everything is non-different from the Supreme Self—with the words "In the beginning" (*ādau*). That reality which is characterized as the Supreme Self is *sat*, that is, existing.

That very [consciousness] itself shines forth externally as the object of enjoyment, as light and radiance, and nothing else. The sense is that anything other than that cannot be established by its own inherent manifestation without it. ||57||

Paramātma-sandarbha 62: He explains the reasoning for the non-difference of the world from Him through five verses, beginning with "In the beginning and at the end. That which exists as the reality characterized by the Supreme Self—the cause of all—is present as the causal principle in the beginning of beings, such as their bodies, and as the ultimate limit at the end.

Thus, it is He alone who manifests externally as the object of enjoyment and internally as the enjoyer; as the superior and the inferior, as darkness and non-luminosity, and as light and luminosity. There is nothing else, because the meaning is that anything other than Him cannot be established as manifesting by itself independently of Him. ||57||

Viśvanātha: Here, he states that the cause is solely the realization that "all is Brahman" and the absence of delusion—beginning with the words "In the beginning. That which exists as the cause at the beginning of beings—their bodies and so forth—and as the ultimate limit at the end, that very Self, Brahman, is itself both the external object of enjoyment (the illusory thing) and the internal enjoyer.
The multitude of living beings consists of the higher and the lower, the exalted and the base. Knowledge is the sense organ;
the object of knowledge is sound and so forth, or words such as "pot" and "cloth. Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the darkness of the soul regarding caste and so on, while knowledge (*vidyā*) is light.
There is no other entity whatsoever apart from that by which one might be deluded; this is the intended meaning. ||57||
For just as an appearance, though afflicted by a disorder, is remembered as a real object despite its difficulty of occurrence, so too is sensory perception conceptualized as an external object.
Because it is difficult to establish [otherwise], the word *madhvaḥ* has been conceived as having this meaning by the Supreme Lord himself. ||58||
Śrīdhara: [Objection: But then, how is its separate object perceived?

To this he says: Just as a reflection or the like—which, though sublated on all sides by contradiction with reasoning (*tarka*) and thus appearing as a fallacy (*ābhāsa*), is nevertheless remembered as a real entity (*vastu*)—so too everything perceived through the senses is conceptualized as an object (*artha*), yet it is not [ultimately so].
But from the perspective of ultimate reality, it is impossible because of its inherent contradiction. ||58||

The Sequence of Composition: Now, one might ask, "How then is a multitude of objects perceived as if they were entirely separate from that [consciousness]? To this he replies: "Obstructed" (*ābādhita*). This means obstructed on all sides by the contradiction of logical reasoning (*tarka-virodha*); even though it is cast out from the perspective of independent existence, it remains as a mere appearance (*ābhāsa*).

Just as the individual rays of the sun and other luminaries, appearing separately to children and others, are imagined and conceived as real entities and independent objects due to perception; likewise, everything perceived through the senses is variously imagined as independent objects by the deluded. However, that is not so from the perspective of ultimate reality.
The meaning is that the definition of independence is difficult to establish. [End of] the *Paramātma-sandarbha*.

Viśvanātha: Now, is the objectivity of entities such as the enjoyer and the enjoyed not perceived by all people as being distinct? To this he says: "In every respect, [it is] uncontradicted, [even] by contradiction with reasoning... [58] The *Viśvanātha-sandarbha*.

Just as an appearance such as a reflection, though sublated, is remembered as a real entity, so too everything perceived by the senses is conceptualized as an object, but not in an ultimate sense, because it is logically untenable. ||58||
Indeed, among the objects here such as earth and the rest, there is no shadow whatsoever;
it is neither a composite nor a transformation, neither separate nor inherent, and is thus false.

In the *Śabdanirṇaya*, it is stated: "The shadow-form (*chāyā-rīti*), the mode (*prakāra*), and the state (*bhāva*) are designated as *madhvaḥ*. None of these modes apply to categories such as earth and the rest, because they are fashioned by the Supreme Lord; therefore, it is appropriate to call them simply "effects" (*kārya*). Indeed, they are not merely names.

Earth is not merely its transformation, for earth does not exist merely through transformations such as turbidity; nor does it exist separately from these [qualities]; nor is it like two distinct entities. Śrīdhara says that it is merely their coexistence; he states this very point: "The shadow of the five elements, beginning with earth."

The form that serves as the objective support for the cognition of unity does not belong to any one among the various stages of the composition and transformation of the aggregate of the body and so forth. To begin with, it is not their aggregate, like a forest [is not the aggregate] of trees; for if one part were pulled, it would follow that the whole could not be pulled, which is not the case. Indeed, when one tree [is pulled...]

When one part is pulled, the entire forest is pulled; yet no modification has been initiated in the whole (avayavin). By the word "api" (also), it is implied that there is no transformation (pariṇāma) either. Why? Is it distinct from its own parts, or is it associated with them after they have undergone transformation? It cannot be entirely distinct, because it is not perceived as such. Nor is it associated [with them]. That...

Does it follow [into the body] entirely with respect to every limb, or only partially? In the first case, the cognition of a "body" would arise even for a mere finger. In the second case, if one must further admit parts for that [finger], there would be an infinite regress; therefore, the meaning is that [the self's presence in the body] is merely illusory. ||59||

Regarding the sequence of composition: "of earth and the rest. By them [the question] "whence? is raised at the end; one should consider whether that [body] is produced separately from its parts, or whether it transforms while being associated with them.
Therefore, in the phrase "it is indeed false," the meaning is that the existence of the body and so forth as independent entities is indeed false.
This is to be known. ||59||

Paramātma-sandarbha (64): He states that very point: the "shadow" (*chāyā*) of the five elements, beginning with earth—which consists of the objective basis for the notion of unity—is not any one of the various transformations involved in the origination of the aggregate of the body and so forth. It is certainly not their mere collection, as in the case of trees.

Because when one part of a forest is pulled, it is impossible for the whole forest to be pulled; for when a single tree is pulled, the entire forest is not pulled. Nor is a composite whole (avayavin) produced as a modification (vikāra)—by the word "api" (also), a transformation (pariṇāma) is also excluded.
Why? Is it produced or transformed separately from its parts?
Or [the self] is conjoined with that [body]. First, it is not entirely separate, because it is not perceived as such. Nor is it conjoined.
For does it join with each limb individually, or by way of its parts? In the first case, the cognition of a "body" would arise even in a single finger.
In the second case, if one must likewise admit parts for that [self], there would result the fallacy of infinite regress. Therefore, [there is no self] in the body and so forth.
The meaning is that existence in independence is indeed false. ||59||

Viśvanātha says this very thing: the "shadow" of the five elements, earth and so forth—the body and its like, which is the objective support for the notion of unity—is none of the following among the categories of a composite whole (*saṅghāta*), a beginning (*ārambha*), or a transformation (*pariṇāma*).
First, it is not a composite whole of the five elements, like a forest of trees; for [if it were], by pulling one part [of the body], [the whole would be pulled].
Because it is impossible for there to be a drawing-in of the whole [from the drawing-in of a part]. For when one tree is pulled, the entire forest is not pulled along.
Nor is it a modification (*vikāra*) of the five elements; the meaning is that it is not a composite whole (*avayavī*) originated by the five elements.
If one asks why, he says in response: "Neither separate nor conjoined. The whole is not [separate] from its parts.

To that extent, they are absolutely distinct, because [the whole] is not perceived as such. Nor is it inherent in them. Does that whole (avayavin) pervade every single limb, or does it pervade everywhere only partially? In the first case, when there is the cognition of the body in the hand, or in the fingers of the hand, or elsewhere, upon the destruction of that [part], the cognition "the body is destroyed" would arise.

It would lead to an infinite regress; for if even a portion of a portion were admitted in the second case, there would be no end to it. Furthermore, because of the word "api" (also), the transformation of the five elements is also not distinct from the five elements, nor is it inherent within them;
therefore, it is merely false and illusory. The meaning is that the doctrine of illusory manifestation (*vivarta-vāda*) alone is to be accepted.
And because the elements possess parts, they could not exist without their constituent parts;
for if the whole does not exist, ultimately the part cannot exist either.
Just as with honey, so it is also with the parts and the whole. ||60||

Śrīdhara: [Objection: But if there were no whole (*avayavin*), then there could be no recognition such as "this is that same Devadatta" amidst changing states like childhood and so forth. As it was said by the Bhaṭṭas:
"That which remains unchanging amidst things characterized by appearance and disappearance is the substratum (*dharmin*). To this, he says: *syād*...

Thus [it is said]. In reality, since there is no conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*) or distinction (*bheda*) in the Supreme Self; or rather, since there is conceptual differentiation in the real entity due to ignorance (*avidyā*), there may arise the delusion that "this is that very same thing" because of its similarity to successive superimpositions (*pūrva-pūrvāropa*). And that [delusion] persists only so long as ignorance has not ceased. Now, if everything were false, what of the scripture?
To explain how there can be the function of injunction and prohibition therein, he says: "Just as the distinction between waking and sleeping exists even in the midst of a dream. (60)

The Structure of the Sequence: Having thus stated the falsity of the body and so forth, he now states the falsity of the earth and other elements which are its causes: "They sustain" refers to the *dhātus*, the great elements (*mahābhūtas*). These could not exist without their subtle constituent parts, the *tanmātras*. This is because they too possess the nature of being wholes (*avayavin*). [Objection: In that case, the constituent part must be real.
To this he replies: if the whole (*avayavin*) does not exist in the manner described, then even the part (*avayava*) would, in the final analysis, be as if non-existent.
The meaning is that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of the part apart from the otherwise inexplicable nature of the cognition of the whole.
This has been stated in the *Pañcaskandhaka*: "Thus the application of the word 'earth' (*kṣiti*) has been etymologically explained."
And so forth, as in Bhāgavata Purāṇa 5.12.9. ||60||

Paramātma-sandarbha 65: Having thus stated that the body and so forth cannot be established as independent, he says "the elements" (dhātavaḥ) to show that their causes—the earth and other gross elements—likewise cannot be established in that way. "The elements" means the great elements; they do not exist without their subtle components, the *tanmātras*.
[They] would [exist], because they too possess the nature of being wholes. If it is argued that, in that case, the part alone is independent, he says in response:

since a whole cannot be established in the manner previously described, the part also would ultimately be as if non-existent to be established, without the fact that the cognition of the whole would otherwise be inexplicable.

The meaning is that there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of parts characterized as atoms (*paramāṇu*). This has been stated in the *Pañcama-skandha*: "Thus is explained the application of the word 'earth' (*kṣiti-śabda-vṛtta*)" [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 5.12.9], and so forth.
Therefore, that which is perceived everywhere as having the form of an object of the notion of unity (*aikya-buddhyālambana-rūpa*)...

It has been rightly stated at the beginning and at the end, with the words "for people it is 'existent' (sat)," etc., that the Supreme Self alone is the reality that is the cause of all. In the same way, it is also stated in the third [skandha], from "iti tāsām" [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.6.1] up to "prabodhayan" [3.6.3]. For this very reason, [it is said]: "He whose body is the earth" [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad...].

In such scriptural passages as [3.7.3], everything is established as being the body of the Supreme Self, while the Supreme Self is established as the possessor of that body. Thus, it is proven that the modification of primordial matter (*pradhāna*) exists everywhere in the form of constituent parts (*avayava*), whereas the whole (*avayavin*) is indeed the reality that is the Supreme Self. Consequently, it follows that this [Supreme Self] is certainly not illusory (*amithyātva*).
The world would come into being. ||60||

Viśvanātha: Having thus stated the falsity of the body and so forth, he declares the falsity of the earth and other elements that constitute its causes, beginning with the words "the constituents" (dhātavaḥ). They are called "constituents" (dhātavaḥ) because they support; these great elements would not exist without their subtle parts, the *tanmātras*. Since they possess parts, they too must have constituent parts.
If it is argued that [the whole] exists, he says in response: in the manner already stated, if the composite (avayavin) does not exist, the part (avayava) would also ultimately be non-existent;

for there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for the existence of the part apart from the fact that its existence would otherwise be impossible without the cognition of the composite. This is what was stated in the fifth chapter: "Thus it has been defined."
"The function of the word *kṣiti*," [Bhāgavata Purāṇa 5.12.9], and so forth. ||60||
There may indeed be an illusion of similarity regarding a real object when conceptualization occurs;
just as waking and sleeping appear within a dream, so too do injunctions and prohibitions [appear].

Nor is there mere similarity, for that is only appropriate when there is a difference between real entities. Therefore, just as the waking state and the dream state are seen to be distinct from one another, so too this specific distinction of earth, water, and so forth—which would otherwise be difficult to account for—is seen to exist through the conceptualization of the Lord. ||61||

Śrīdhara: [Objection: But if there were no whole (*avayavin*), then there could be no recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) such as "This is that Devadatta" amidst states like childhood and so forth, which appear and disappear. This has been stated by the Bhaṭṭas: "That which persists through those things characterized by appearance and disappearance is the substratum (*dharmin*). To this he replies: It would be so...

Thus [it is said]. In reality, since there is no conceptual differentiation or division within the Supreme Self; or rather, when conceptual differentiation exists due to ignorance regarding the real, the delusion that "this is that very same thing" may arise because of its similarity to previous superimpositions. And that [delusion] persists only so long as ignorance has not been removed. Now, if everything were false, what would become of the scripture?
He explains how there can be the function of injunction and prohibition therein: "Just as the distinction between waking and sleeping exists even in the midst of a dream. (61)

The Sequence of Arrangement; The Section on the Supreme Self (66): Now, if the body were everywhere merely the substance of the Supreme Self, then, since the designations such as "brahmin" and so forth would apply to that very [Self], injunctions and prohibitions—which have merit and demerit as their cause—would also apply to it. Yet these two are not possible. Therefore...
Fearing that "only another [entity], namely the whole (avayavin), would be joined [to the parts]," he says: "It might be so.

The meaning is: as long as there is no determination of the reality—the Supreme Self—in its true nature, while it remains in a state of conceptualization or doubt; for that long, therefore, from that which is the cause of the cognition of the identity of all...

The cognition of the body as a single unit would be an error based on similarity. This is because, when there is a synthesis of preceding and succeeding parts, they appear as one due to their mutual connection, their coexistence in a single location, and the commonality of being constituent parts; thus, each part is perceived as a unity, leading to the error: "This is that very body."
The meaning is that it becomes exactly thus, just as one says, "This forest is [present] in every tree. As was stated by the Blessed One himself:
"This very lamp is like that of flames; this very water is like that of streams."
"This person is indeed he"—such is the false cognition of those whose lives are in vain, like the [false] perception of a cow by those whose life-span is exhausted (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.22.45).

Consequently, since the conceit of being a Brahmin and so forth exists therein, injunctions and prohibitions regarding that [conceit] would be like the waking and dreaming states concerning the objects of a dream; thus he says "jāgrat" (waking).
In that manner, by that method, it means that there is the affirmation of an injunction and the negation of a prohibition.
Thus—
one should neither praise nor censure the action of another's nature.

"Seeing the universe as having a single essence through both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.28.1)—the twenty-eighth chapter of the eleventh book should be understood from such passages. And therein, questions such as "What is auspicious?
What is inauspicious? How much is there of this unreal duality? would constitute, for the time being, a delusion of similarity.
It should be explained in accordance with these and other [passages]. The meaning is: "of that duality which is non-substantial.
Therefore, the sense of the section is that because nothing can be defined independently, everything is indeed non-different from the Supreme Self. ||61||
Viśvanātha: Now, one might ask, "Even so, why does the perception of earth and the other elements as real lead [to error]?

To this he says: "It may be"—that is, even when earth and the rest are non-existent, being illusory (*mithyā-bhūta*), there arises a delusion (*bhrama*) due to the similarity between those things and the reality (*satya-bhūta*) of the Lord’s eternal abode, earth, and so forth.
The meaning is: "as in the case of water in a mirage. Just as when there is a superimposition (āropa) based on delusion of truly existent water upon truly existent light, the mirage becomes water;
in the same way, when there is a superimposition of truly existent earth and so forth—residing in the abode of the Lord—upon truly existent Brahman.

The meaning is that this would occur when there is a superimposition rooted in ignorance (*ajñāna*). Nor should it be said that even in the abode of the Blessed Lord (*bhagavad-dhāman*) a false appearance (*vivarta*) proceeds, such that it too would be unreal;
for within the circle of the earth (*bhū-gola-cakra*), there are seven cities, and in their midst is Brahman directly (*sākṣāt*).

Regarding the statement "Gopāla-purī" (Goṭā.u. 2.25), since the *śruti* establishes that Gopāla-purī is of the very nature of Brahman, the use of the genitive case in "tāsām" (of them) for the purpose of specification (*nirdhāraṇa*), as well as the words "sākṣāt" (directly) and "brahma" (Brahman), would otherwise be redundant; for [otherwise], it would imply that other objects [are superimposed] upon Brahman, as if Brahman were something distinct from them.

Because it is impossible to explain [the Lord] as being superimposed upon Gopālapura; furthermore, modern Advaitins do not accept any internal powers such as Āhlādinī and others, nor their manifestations, nor the earth and so forth belonging to the eternal abode of the Lord, as being distinct from the power of Māyā.
Not recognizing this, they revile those who explain the delusion of similarity regarding that which is purely illusory as revolving solely through a blind succession of one another.
But if the world is thus illusory, how can even the omniscient Veda prescribe injunctions and prohibitions?
It is said: "Are the qualities and defects of the water in a mirage not taught by the wise?

To this he replies: "Waking and dreaming. The meaning is that just as the distinction between waking and dreaming exists within a dream, so too, since the world is illusory, both of those states are likewise illusory.
"Because it is intended for those who are ignorant"—as in: "The Vedas have the three qualities as their domain; be free from the three qualities, O Arjuna" (Gītā 2.45). ||61||
By practicing here through his own experience the non-duality of existence, the non-duality of action, and likewise the non-duality of substance regarding the Self,
the sage shakes off the three dreams.

Śrīdhara: Now, he confirms the non-duality (advaita) already stated by means of the instruction on the three contemplations (*bhāvanā*) through four verses beginning with "bhāvādvaitam. "Vartayan" means perceiving. "By his own experience" means by the realization of the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*). "The three" refers to the waking state and so forth. "The three abodes" refers to the three dream-states.

Thus it is from the Śruti (Ai.U. 1.12). Alternatively, the first dream is the cognition of the distinction between objects; the second is the cognition of the distinction between various actions according to their respective specific capacities; the third is the thought, "This fruit accomplished by my action is to be enjoyed by me alone. He shakes off these.
He causes [them] to turn back. ||62||
*Krama-sandarbha*: Not commented upon.

*Viśvanātha*: Now he strengthens the non-duality (advaita) already mentioned by means of the instruction on the three contemplations (*bhāvanā*) through four verses beginning with "bhāvādvaitam," while reflecting upon it through his own experience.

Through the realization of the true nature of the Self, the notion of the diversity of objects is the first dream. From that, the notion of the diversity of actions according to the distinctions of various offices is the second.
The thought, "This fruit accomplished by my action is for my enjoyment alone," is the third. He shakes off—that is, he turns away from—these. 62.
The perception of identity between cause and effect, such as that of a cloth and its threads,
is called the non-duality of existence (*bhāvādvaita*) because conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) lacks substantial reality.
Śrīdhara: The investigation and reflection upon the identity of substance between cause and effect is [the view that] "it is the thread itself, not the cloth. ||63||
Kramasandarbha: This has not been explained.

Viśvanātha: *Ālocana* is the perception of the identity of substance between cause and effect—such as "it is the thread itself, not the cloth"—[applied here] to the identity between the world and its primordial nature (*prakṛti*), which stand in the relation of effect and cause. (63)
O Pārtha, that which consists of the direct dedication of all actions to the Supreme Brahman through mind, speech, and body— that is called the non-duality of action (kriyādvaita).

Śrīdhara: It is the dedication of actions performed by means of mind, speech, and body; or, it is dedication by means of those [three]. For indeed, a difference in the intended object or the fruit is the cause for a difference in action; and since that [difference] is absent when there is dedication to the Lord, there is non-duality of actions. (64)
The sequence of composition: although [the practice] is not established as knowledge, one should nevertheless perform one's own duty; thus he says: "That which... (verse 64).
Viśvanātha: "Offering" (arpaṇa) means the dedication of actions performed with mind, speech, and body to Brahman.

For indeed, a difference in action is caused by a difference in the intended object and the fruit; however, since these are absent when [action] is offered to the Lord, there is non-duality of actions. 64.
The unity of one's own self, wife, children, and others— that is, all embodied beings— with respect to one's own interests and desires, is called the non-duality of substance (*dravyādvaita*).
Śrīdhara: "One's own" refers to oneself; "of one's wife and so forth" refers to others. "Artha" is wealth and "kāma" is desire.

The meaning is that there is a perception of the unity of these two—wealth and desire—through the contemplation of non-difference: because the body and so forth consist of the five elements, and the enjoyer is the Supreme Self.
Krama-sandarbha: Not explained.
Viśvanātha: One's own [ātman], one's wife and others, and others who are not related to oneself—the accomplishment of their respective purposes and desire, and that which is to be attained by them.

The sense is this: because there is identity between the two—the object of enjoyment and its means—there is the cultivation of identity; for whatever wealth and desire belong to oneself, those same ones belong to all, since all bodies and so forth are identical in being composed of the five elements, and all individual souls are identical as enjoyers, such that no distinction exists. ||65||
O King, whatever is not forbidden for anyone, by whomsoever, wherever, and from whatever source,
